tx_tree.title: Input Embedding
tx_tree.summary: "cat" yazıyorsun ama bilgisayar harfleri anlamıyor. Bu katman her kelimeyi 512 sayılık bir vektöre dönüştürüyor — modelin sıfırdan öğrendiği bir "kelime koordinat sistemi". Eğitim boyunca bu koordinatlar ayarlanıyor ve sonunda benzer kelimeler uzayda birbirine yakın oturuyor: king ile queen yakın, king ile pizza uzak.
points: Vocab × 512 boyutlu bir tablo var, her kelimenin bir satırı. "cat" gelince o satırı alıyorsun, bu kadar — lookup tablosu gibi.
Tablo eğitim sırasında backprop ile öğreniliyor. Başta rastgele, ama sonunda "king − man + woman ≈ queen" ilişkileri kendiliğinden ortaya çıkıyor.
d_model = 512 (küçük), 768 (BERT), 1024 (büyük) — bu sayı ağ boyunca hiç değişmiyor, her şey bu boyutta.
Son katmandaki output embedding tablosuyla genellikle aynı ağırlıklar paylaşılıyor — "anlarken kullandığım kelime temsili, üretirken de aynı olmalı" diye düşünüyorsun, ve çalışıyor.

tx_tree.title: + Positional Encoding
tx_tree.summary: Self-attention'ın kör bir noktası var: "cat bites dog" ile "dog bites cat" aynı kelimelerden oluşuyor, ama anlam tamamen farklı. Attention bunları ayırt edemiyor çünkü kelimelere sıra değil sadece kimlik bakıyor. Bu katman her tokena "sen 3. sıradasın" bilgisini sinüs/kosinüs dalgalarıyla vektörüne ekliyor.
points: Neden sinüs/kosinüs? Her pozisyon için benzersiz imza üretiyorlar. Ayrıca PE(pos+k), PE(pos)'un lineer fonksiyonu — yani model "şu token 5 adım geride" gibi göreceli mesafeleri hesaplayabiliyor.
Embedding'e ekliyoruz (concat etmiyoruz), boyut değişmiyor. Kelime anlamı + sıra bilgisi aynı vektörde birleşiyor.
Parametre yok, öğrenilmiyor — bu yüzden eğitimde 128 kelimelik cümleler gördüysen, çıkarımda 200 kelimelik cümleye de genelleşebiliyor.
Düşük frekanslı boyutlar (i küçük) global konum bilgisi taşıyor, yüksek frekanslı boyutlar (i büyük) yerel. Birlikte zengin bir konum temsili oluyor.

tx_tree.title: Multi-Head Self-Attention
tx_tree.summary: Tek bir attention head tek bir bakış açısı öğrenebiliyor. Ama bir cümlede aynı anda birden fazla ilişki türü var — subject-verb uyumu, zamir referansı, yerel komşuluk. Tek head bunların hepsini aynı W_Q, W_K, W_V ile öğrenmeye çalışırken biri kazanır öbürü kaybeder. Çözüm: D boyutunu H parçaya böl, her head kendi subspace'inde farklı bir pattern öğrensin. Parametre sayısı değişmiyor: H × (D × D/H) = D².
points: Denklem: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k) × V. Multi-head: head_i = Attention(X×W_Qi, X×W_Ki, X×W_Vi), sonuç Concat(head_1...head_H) × W_O.
Giriş X (N×D). Her head i için: Q_i = X×W_Q_i, K_i = X×W_K_i, V_i = X×W_V_i — W matrisleri D×(D/H) boyutunda, her head'e özel.

Scaled Dot-Product içi: MatMul(Q_i, K_i^T) → N×N skor matrisi. ÷√d_k ile scale — büyük dot product softmax'ı one-hot yapar, gradient ölür. (Mask decoder'da: gelecek pozisyonlara −∞.) Softmax row-wise. MatMul(attn_weights, V_i) → N×d_v output.

Neden scale? d_k=64 ise dot product ~8, d_k=512 ise ~22 büyüklüğünde. Büyük değer → softmax tek yere yığılır → diğer pozisyonların gradientleri sıfır → model o bağlantıları öğrenemiyor. √d_k ile variance ≈1'e çekiliyor.
Concat([head_1, ..., head_H]) → N×D. × W_O → N×D. W_O head'lerin bağımsız öğrendiklerini koordine edip tutarlı bir temsile çeviriyor.
Cross-attention'da (decoder): Q_i = X_decoder × W_Q_i, K_i ve V_i = X_encoder × W_K_i / W_V_i. İki farklı kaynak, ama W'lar yine içeride.

tx_tree.title: Add & Norm
tx_tree.summary: İki şey var burada: residual bağlantı ve layer normalization. Residual olmadan 6 katmanlı ağı eğitmek pratikte neredeyse imkansız — gradient geri giderken her katmanda küçülüyor ve ilk katmanlara hiçbir şey ulaşmıyor. Residual bunu çözüyor.
points: x + Sublayer(x): attention'ın çıktısını üzerine yazmıyoruz, ekliyoruz. En kötü ihtimalle attention sıfır üretse bile eski bilgi kaybolmuyor.
Gradient highway: loss'tan gelen gradient direkt ilk katmana akabiliyor, 6 katmanı çarparak geçmeden. Vanishing gradient sorunu büyük ölçüde çözülüyor.
Neden Layer Norm, Batch Norm değil? Farklı uzunluktaki cümlelerde batch istatistikleri tutarsız oluyor. Layer Norm her token'ı kendi boyutları üzerinden normalize ediyor, bu daha güvenli.
Pre-norm (GPT-2 ve sonrası): LayerNorm önce uygulanıyor, sonra sublayer. Büyük modellerde eğitimi daha stabil hale getiriyor.

tx_tree.title: Feed-Forward
tx_tree.summary: Attention'ın yaptığı şey tokenlar arası bilgi alışverişi — "kimden ne alayım?" Ama bir de "aldığım bilgiyle ne yapacağım?" sorusu var. Bunu FFN yapıyor. Her tokena aynı ağı bağımsız olarak uyguluyorsun, ama her tokenin girdisi farklı.
points: FFN(x) = max(0, xW₁+b₁)W₂+b₂ — önce 4× genişlet (512→2048), ReLU ile sıkıştır, tekrar dar (2048→512).
Neden 4×? Daha zengin nonlinear dönüşüm için. Deneysel olarak bu oran iyi çalışıyor — daha az genişletince model kapasitesi düşüyor, daha fazla da parametre boşa gidiyor.
Attention = "hangi tokenlardan bilgi toplayacağım?" | FFN = "topladığım bilgiyle ne yapacağım?" Birbirini tamamlayan iki farklı işlem.
Araştırmalar FFN'nin faktüel bilgi depoladığını gösteriyor: "Paris" gördüğünde "France"ı tetikleyen, "Einstein" gördüğünde "physicist" bağlantısını kuran nöronlar FFN'de bulunmuş.

tx_tree.title: Add & Norm
tx_tree.summary: Encoder'ın bir bloğu burada tamamlandı: Self-Attn → Add&Norm → FFN → Add&Norm. Bu blok N kez tekrarlanıyor (genellikle 6). Her tekrarda tokenlar birbirinden daha fazla bilgi toplayıp daha soyut temsillere dönüşüyor.
points: İlk katmanlar syntactic ilişkileri öğreniyor: "the" ile "cat" birbirine bağlı. Son katmanlar semantik ve global anlam: "bu cümle bir olumsuzlama mı?"
Son encoder bloğunun çıktısı özel: decoder'daki TÜM cross-attention katmanlarına Key ve Value olarak gidiyor. Encoder bir kez çalışıyor, çıktı kalıcı.
Residual + LayerNorm burada da aynı görevi yapıyor: gradient akışı ve aktivasyon stabilizasyonu.

tx_tree.title: Output Embedding
tx_tree.summary: Decoder'ın girişi hedef dildeki tokenlar. Ama eğitimde akıllıca bir trick var: teacher forcing. "The cat sat" üretmesini istiyorsan [START, The, cat] veriyorsun, model [The, cat, sat] üretmeli. Doğru cevabı girdi olarak verince eğitim hem hızlanıyor hem stabilleşiyor.
points: Teacher forcing: modelin önceki tahminlerine güvenmek zorunda kalmıyor. Kendi yanlış tahminini görse zincirleme hata birikir. Eğitimde bunu atlıyoruz.
Çıkarımda ise: bir önceki adımda ne ürettiysen onu girdi olarak veriyorsun. Hata birikme riski var ama başka seçenek yok.
[START] tokeni ilk adımı tetikliyor. Model [END] üretince duruyor — ne zaman biteceğini kendisi öğreniyor.
Encoder embedding tablosuyla paylaşılabilir: GPT gibi sadece decoder olan modellerde kaynak-hedef aynı dil olduğu için çok mantıklı.

tx_tree.title: + Positional Encoding
tx_tree.summary: Decoder için de aynı positional encoding. Decoder "şu an kaçıncı kelimeyi üretiyorum?" bilgisine ihtiyaç duyuyor — bu bilgi olmadan her adımda aynı kararı verirdi. Pozisyon bilgisi sonunda cross-attention'ın Q'suna da giriyor.
points: Encoder PE ile özdeş formül — aynı sinüs/kosinüs tabanlı imza.
Bu pozisyon bilgisi cross-attention'da Q'ya giriyor: "3. kelimeyi üretirken encoder'da neye bakmalıyım?"
Çıkarımda her adımda bir token üretiliyor, her seferinde yeni pozisyon encodingı ekleniyor.

tx_tree.title: Masked Self-Attention
tx_tree.summary: Bir problem: eğitimde teacher forcing ile tüm hedef tokenleri aynı anda veriyoruz. Ama "cat" üretirken modelin "sat"ı görmemesi lazım — yoksa cevaba bakarak soru çözüyor. Maskeleme bunun için: gelecekteki tokenlerin attention skorlarına −∞ atıyoruz, softmax'tan sonra sıfır oluyor.
points: Uygulaması: softmax(QKᵀ/√dk + M)·V, burada M matrisinin üst üçgeni −∞, geri kalanı sıfır.
−∞ → exp(−∞) = 0 → softmax'tan sonra o tokenın ağırlığı sıfır. "Bu tokena hiç bakma" anlamına geliyor.
Çıkarımda maskelemeye gerek yok zaten: sadece üretilmiş tokenlar mevcut, gelecek yok ki maskelensin.
Eğitimdeki büyük avantaj: maskelenmiş halde bile tüm pozisyonlar aynı anda paralel işleniyor. RNN'de sırayla adım atmak zorundaydık, bu çok daha hızlı.

tx_tree.title: Add & Norm
tx_tree.summary: Masked self-attention + Add&Norm. Decoder artık "şu ana kadar ne ürettim?" sorusunu yanıtladı ve bunu bir vektöre sıkıştırdı. Bu vektör bir sonraki adımda cross-attention'ın Query'si oluyor: "şimdiye kadar ürettiklerime bakarak encoder'dan ne öğrenmem gerekiyor?"
points: Decoder kendi geçmişini öğrendi: hangi kelimeler, hangi sırada, nasıl bir bağlamda.
Bu çıktı Q olarak cross-attention'a gidiyor — artık "kaynaktan ne soracağımı biliyorum" aşamasına geçiyor.
Residual + LayerNorm: her sublayer gibi aynı işlev.

tx_tree.title: Cross-Attention
tx_tree.summary: Q decoder'dan geliyor (ne üretmek istiyorum?), K ve V encoder'dan geliyor (kaynak cümle ne diyor?). "Je suis fatigué" → "I am tired" çevirisinde "tired" üretirken, Q_tired encoder'daki "fatigué" K'sıyla yüksek dot product veriyor ve V_fatigué alınıyor. Tam bilgi transfer bu şekilde oluyor.
points: Q = decoder çıktısı (masked self-attn sonrası) — "şu an ne üretmeye çalışıyorum?"
K = V = encoder son katman çıktısı — kaynak cümledeki tüm tokenların temsilcisi.
Cross-attention olmadan decoder kaynak cümleyi hiç göremezdi. Sadece kendi ürettiklerini bilirdi, bu çeviri için feci olurdu.
Encoder bir kez çalışıyor, çıktı sabit kalıyor. Decoder'ın her N katmanı bu aynı encoder çıktısına bakıyor — tekrar hesaplanmıyor.
Güzel tarafı: her adımda kaynak cümlenin farklı bölgelerine odaklanabiliyor. "am" üretirken "suis"e, "tired" üretirken "fatigué"ye yüksek attention.

tx_tree.title: Add & Norm
tx_tree.summary: Cross-attention + Add&Norm. Artık decoder vektörü iki ayrı bilgiyi birleştirmiş: kendi ürettiklerinden öğrendikleri (masked self-attn) + kaynaktan aldıkları (cross-attn). FFN bu zenginleştirilmiş temsili her token için ayrı ayrı işleyecek.
points: İki bilgi kaynağı birleşti: "şimdiye kadar ne ürettim" + "kaynak cümle ne diyordu".
Residual ile cross-attention çıktısı üzerine yazılmıyor, ekleniyor. Önceki bilgi korunuyor.
Sonraki FFN için temiz, normalize edilmiş bir temsil hazır.

tx_tree.title: Feed-Forward
tx_tree.summary: Encoder FFN ile aynı yapı ama farklı ağırlıklar. Encoder "anlama" yapıyor, decoder "üretim" yapıyor — iki farklı görev, iki farklı öğrenilmiş ağırlık seti. Attention'ın topladığı bilgiyi her token için bağımsız, derin bir şekilde işliyor.
points: FFN(x) = max(0, xW₁+b₁)W₂+b₂ — encoder ile aynı formül, ama ağırlıklar tamamen farklı.
4× genişleme yine var: 512→2048→512. Nonlinear kapasite için aynı mantık.
Decoder katmanı burada tamamlandı: Masked-Attn → A&N → Cross-Attn → A&N → FFN → A&N.

tx_tree.title: Add & Norm
tx_tree.summary: FFN + Add&Norm. Bir decoder bloğu bitti — 3 sublayer tamamlandı. Bu blok N kez tekrarlanıyor. Sonunda her decoder pozisyonu için d_model boyutlu bir vektör elde ediyoruz. Bu vektör "buraya kadar ne gördüm, ne ürettim, şimdi ne gelecek?" bilgisini taşıyor. Linear + Softmax bunu kelimeye çevirecek.
points: Decoder 3 sublayer: Masked Self-Attn → Cross-Attn → FFN, her biri Add&Norm ile paketlendi.
N = 6 (base), 12 (large), 24 (xl) kez tekrar. Her tekrarda daha soyut, hedefe daha yakın bir temsil.
Son decoder bloğunun çıktısı Linear'a gidiyor — artık kelime üretme vakti.

tx_tree.title: Linear Projection
tx_tree.summary: d_model boyutlu vektörü vocab_size'a açıyorsun. "Şu ana kadar gördüklerime göre, sözlükteki her kelime için ham bir puan (logit) veriyorum." 50.000 kelimeli bir vocab'ta bu 512×50.000 = 25M parametreli tek bir matris — ve modelin en büyük katmanlarından biri bu.
points: Yüksek logit = "model bu kelimenin gelmesini güçlü bir şekilde bekliyor."
Genellikle input embedding tablosuyla aynı ağırlıklar paylaşılıyor (weight tying). Mantığı şu: bir kelimeyi anlamak için kullandığın temsil, onu üretmek için de kullanılmalı.
Çıktı henüz olasılık değil — ham sayılar. Softmax bunu düzeltecek.

tx_tree.title: Softmax → Output
tx_tree.summary: Logitleri 0-1 arasına sıkıştırıp olasılığa çeviriyorsun. Eğitimde "doğru token buydu, sen ne öngördün?" diye cross-entropy loss hesaplıyorsun. Çıkarımda ise bir seçim yapman lazım: en yüksek olasılıklı kelimeyi mi al (greedy), yoksa dağılımdan mı örnekle (sampling)?
points: softmax(z_i) = exp(z_i) / Σexp(z_j) — tüm vocab üzerinde toplamı 1 olacak şekilde normalize ediyor.
Eğitim: cross-entropy loss = −log p(hedef token). Doğru tokenın log olasılığını maksimize et, yanlışları minimize et.
Greedy decoding: her adımda argmax al. Deterministik, hızlı, ama tekrarlayan ve yaratıcısız çıktı verebiliyor.
Temperature: logitleri t'ye bölüyorsun. t=0.7 → daha keskin, deterministik (GPT sohbette). t=1.2 → daha dağınık, yaratıcı (şiir, hikaye).
Top-p (nucleus) sampling: kümülatif olasılık 0.9 olana kadar olan kelimeler arasından örnekle. Saçma düşük olasılıklı kelimeler otomatik eleniyor.

backprop.title: Backpropagation — A Complete Walkthrough
backprop.context: Backprop · ML ch07 · Lab 3 · CS231n 3 · ML-OVERALL 12
backprop.summary: How millions of gradients come out of a single loss number: why finite differences do not work, the computational graph and the chain rule, the upstream-times-local rule, the backward pass of a linear layer with its dimensions, and why gradients vanish and explode.

sections.heading: 1. The problem
sections.text:
The network has millions of weights. For each one you want to know: if I nudged this weight slightly, how much would the loss change?

That number is the gradient of that weight. If you had all the gradients, you would shift every weight a small step in the direction that decreases the loss. That is exactly what learning is.

The question is how you obtain those numbers.

sections.heading: 2. Why the first method that comes to mind does not work
sections.text:
The most direct route: change one weight slightly, run the network from scratch, and look at how much the loss changed. Then restore it and move on to the next one.

Mathematically correct, practically impossible. In a network with a hundred million parameters, a single gradient step would require a hundred million forward passes.

Backprop instead computes all gradients in one forward plus one backward pass. The backward pass costs two to three times the forward pass, and that ratio is independent of the number of parameters.

This difference in scaling is what makes deep learning possible. The essence of the trick is reusing intermediate results.

sections.heading: 3. The computational graph
sections.text:
Do not think of the network as a stack of layers, think of it as a graph of operations. The nodes are operations — multiply, add, take a maximum, apply a sigmoid. The edges are data flow.

The forward pass walks the graph from start to end and computes the loss, storing intermediate values along the way.

The backward pass walks the same graph in reverse.

The power of this view is here: each node only needs to know its own local derivative. Nobody has to know the whole graph. This is where modularity comes from — it is why you can write your own layer in PyTorch.

sections.heading: 4. One rule: upstream times local
sections.text:
During the backward pass a gradient arrives at a node from above: "if your output had changed slightly, the loss would have changed this much."

The node knows its own local derivative: "my output changes this much when my input changes."

You multiply the two and pass the result downward. That is the entire chain rule.

The behaviour of the commonly used nodes is simple enough to memorise. An addition node distributes the incoming gradient to both of its inputs unchanged. A multiplication node swaps the gradient with the other input. A maximum node sends the whole gradient to the winning input and zero to the other. ReLU passes the gradient through in the positive region and cuts it in the negative one.

sections.heading: 5. From one number to millions of gradients
sections.text:
The loss is a single number, say 2.3. But the derivative of the loss with respect to the output vector is a vector.

Suppose in a three-class problem the network said: cat 0.72, dog 0.20, bird 0.08, and the true label is cat. The derivative of the loss with respect to the output roughly says: if you increase the cat prediction the loss decreases, and if you decrease the other two the loss decreases.

This is where the information first unfolds: a single number turned into a vector with as many components as there are classes.

Backprop then takes that vector and walks backwards layer by layer. At every layer the gradient is reshaped to the input dimension of that layer and widens. At the last layer it had three components, at the previous one hundreds, at the one before that thousands.

Every layer only looks at two things: the gradient coming from above and its own input, which it stored during the forward pass.

sections.heading: The backward pass of a linear layer
sections.text:
# forward:  x_out = x_in @ w.T + b

def backward(self, d_out):
    d_in    = d_out @ self.w                      # (batch, n_in)
    self.dw = d_out.T @ self.x_in                 # (n_out, n_in)
    self.db = d_out.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)    # (1, n_out)
    return d_in

# shapes
# d_out : (batch, n_out)   coming from above
# d_in  : (batch, n_in)    going downward
# dw    : same shape as w
# db    : same shape as b

sections.heading: 6. Why those three lines look the way they do
sections.text:
The transposes are not memorised, they fall out of the shapes. In the forward pass the input has shape (batch, n_in), the weight has shape (n_out, n_in), and the product has shape (batch, n_out). In the backward pass what you hold is (batch, n_out) and what you must produce is (batch, n_in). The only compatible product between them is the incoming gradient times the weight itself. The transpose appears naturally so that the dimensions line up.

The gradient of the weight is the product of the incoming gradient with the input stored during the forward pass, summed over the contribution of every example in the batch. The matrix product already performs that summation.

The gradient of the bias is a sum along the batch, and the reason is instructive: in the forward pass the bias was broadcast, that is, copied into every row. So it contributed to the loss through a separate path from each row. The chain rule says that when a value is used along several paths, the contributions are summed.

The rule worth memorising: if there is broadcasting in the forward pass, there is summation in the backward pass.

sections.heading: 7. The layer recursion
sections.text:
You can write the same thing in the language of layers. Define an error signal for each layer: the derivative of the loss with respect to the linear output of that layer.

At the last layer this signal comes directly from the loss. Going backwards, at each layer it is multiplied by two things: the transpose of the weight matrix of the next layer, and the derivative of its own activation function.

The weight gradients also come out of the product of this signal with the input of the layer.

This formula explains the whole of the next section — because it shows explicitly what the gradient is multiplied by at every layer.

sections.heading: 8. Why the activation function exists
sections.text:
Let us pause and put a basic point in place.

Every layer performs a linear transformation. But the composition of two linear transformations is again linear. So without activations, even ten stacked layers would be mathematically equivalent to a single layer — depth would mean nothing at all.

The activation inserts a non-linear step between layers and makes stacking meaningful.

But which activation you choose directly determines trainability, because of the recursion above.

sections.heading: 9. Vanishing and exploding gradients
sections.text:
At every layer the gradient is multiplied by the derivative of the activation.

The derivative of the sigmoid is at most 0.25. In a ten-layer network the gradient is multiplied, in the best case, by 0.25 to the tenth power — that is, down to the order of one in a million. The signal reaching the first layers is practically zero and those layers cannot learn. This is the vanishing gradient.

With ReLU the derivative is exactly one in the positive region. The gradient passes through the activation without any attenuation and reaches the first layers at its own magnitude.

The answer to "but do not half of the neurons output zero" is: yes, and this is actually desirable. Different neurons specialise in different patterns; a neuron that looks for horizontal edges does not need to fire on every input.

In the other direction, if the norm of the weights is large, the same chain of products makes the gradient explode. The countermeasures: gradient clipping, careful initialisation, normalisation layers, and residual connections — the last one is particularly effective because it opens a shortcut for the gradient that skips over layers.

sections.heading: 10. Where learning actually happens
sections.text:
The order is this: the forward pass produces a prediction and stores intermediate values. The loss gives a single number. Backprop unfolds that number into a gradient for every weight. The update step shifts the weights in the direction opposite to the gradient.

Learning only happens in the last step. Backprop does not learn anything — it only produces directional information.

A single step looks meaningless, the weights barely move. But after thousands of steps every weight has accumulated in the right direction.

There is also a cost: the intermediate values stored in the forward pass sit in memory. In deep networks most of the memory consumed during training comes not from the weights but from these intermediate values that will be needed in the backward pass.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: Measuring gradients one by one is impossible; backprop produces all of them in one forward plus one backward pass, and its cost is independent of the number of parameters. See the network as a graph of operations; each node only knows its own local derivative, and the rule is upstream times local. The loss is a single number but its derivative with respect to the output is a vector, and it widens at every layer going backwards. The transposes are not memorisation, they follow from shape compatibility. If there is broadcasting in the forward pass, there is summation in the backward pass. Because the gradient is multiplied by the weight and the activation derivative at every layer, the sigmoid vanishes with depth while ReLU does not. Learning does not happen in backprop, it happens in the update step.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: The computational graph, the delta rule and the efficiency analysis are in ch07; the account that goes from activation to gradient and from backprop to the training loop is also in ch07; the layer by layer implementation, the dimensions and the chain rule intuition are in lab03; the node-level gradient rules are in cs03. The optimisation step itself (SGD, momentum, Adam) is in ch08.

optim.title: Optimization — A Complete Walkthrough
optim.context: SGD · Momentum · Adam · AdamW · ML ch08 · CS231n 2 ve 5 · ML-OVERALL 5 ve 13
optim.summary: One continuous thread from the difference between batch, SGD and mini-batch, to the two structural problems of plain gradient descent, how momentum and the adaptive rate solve them separately, Adam's formula and its bias correction, what AdamW repairs, the learning rate schedule, and the role of normalization in all of this.

sections.heading: 1. First: how many examples is the gradient computed from
sections.text:
Say you have a thousand data points.

Full batch. You push all thousand through the network, accumulate their errors, compute a single gradient and take a single step. The gradient is the most accurate direction possible, but one step for a thousand examples — very slow.

Pure SGD. You update after every example. A thousand steps for a thousand examples. Fast, but every step rests on a single example and is therefore noisy; that example may not be representative.

Mini-batch. You push thirty-two examples through, average them, then update. Around thirty steps for a thousand examples. The average of thirty-two examples is far more reliable than a single one, yet you do not have to wait for all thousand. This is what is used in practice.

Note that the noise is not purely harmful: it can help escape a bad local minimum. So mini-batch is not a compromise, it is often a direct preference.

sections.heading: 2. The two problems of plain gradient descent
sections.text:
Keeping these two problems apart makes everything else understandable.

Problem one: zigzagging. The loss surface is not a neat bowl. It is very steep in some directions and almost flat in others. In the steep direction the gradient keeps changing sign and swings left and right, while in the flat direction it advances very slowly. You cannot travel straight towards the target.

Problem two: a single learning rate does not fit everyone. Some weights constantly receive large gradients — frequently activated neurons, common words. Others receive gradients rarely and in small amounts — rare words, seldom triggered filters. Applying the same step size to both throws one of them around while the other barely moves.

Momentum solves the first. The adaptive rate solves the second. The two are independent.

sections.heading: 3. Momentum
sections.text:
The idea is to step with an exponential moving average of the gradient instead of the instantaneous gradient. A typical coefficient is 0.9 — that is, the weight of the new gradient is one tenth and that of the past nine tenths.

Why this damps the zigzag is directly visible: in the swinging direction the gradient keeps alternating between plus and minus, so the terms cancel in the average and the step in that direction shrinks. In the consistent direction the gradient always points the same way, accumulates in the average, and you accelerate along it.

The physical counterpart is a ball rolling down a slope: it does not change direction with every local tilt, it carries its momentum.

Note: momentum does not touch the second problem. All weights are still updated with the same learning rate.

sections.heading: SGD + Momentum
sections.text: $$m \leftarrow \beta m + g, \qquad x \leftarrow x - \alpha\, m$$

sections.heading: 4. The adaptive rate and Adam
sections.text:
The solution to the second problem is to look at each weight's own history. A moving average of the square of the gradient is kept; this is a measure of how large the gradients that weight has been receiving are.

The step size is divided by the square root of that measure. The step of a weight that constantly receives large gradients shrinks, and the step of a weight that is rarely updated grows. So a single global learning rate turns into an effective per-weight learning rate.

Adam combines the two: the first moment carries momentum, the second moment carries the adaptive rate.

sections.heading: Adam
sections.text:
$$m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1) g, \qquad v \leftarrow \beta_2 v + (1-\beta_2) g^2$$
$$\hat{m} = \frac{m}{1-\beta_1^t}, \qquad \hat{v} = \frac{v}{1-\beta_2^t}$$
$$x \leftarrow x - \alpha\,\frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \varepsilon}$$

Typical values: $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, $\varepsilon = 10^{-8}$.

sections.heading: 5. Why bias correction exists
sections.text:
A small but forgotten detail, and its logic is clean.

Both moving averages start from zero. In the first steps the average comes out close to zero even if the true gradient is large, because there is no history and the zeros drag the average down. That means artificially small steps at the beginning of training.

The term placed in the denominator corrects exactly this bias. As the step count grows the correction factor approaches one and its effect disappears — so it is a patch that only operates at the start.

The small constant in the denominator merely prevents division by zero.

sections.heading: 6. So why is SGD with momentum still used
sections.text:
Adam converges faster, that is beyond dispute. But on the vision side many strong results are still obtained with SGD and momentum, and the reason is interesting.

In Adam every weight is scaled according to its own history; this also means artificially suppressing the step of some weights. A training loss that falls faster does not always mean a solution that generalises better.

In SGD with momentum there is no such scaling — every weight is updated in proportion to its own gradient. Slower, but the minimum it reaches often generalises better.

Practical summary: in Transformers and language models AdamW is nearly standard; in convolutional vision models SGD with momentum is still competitive.

sections.heading: 7. AdamW: how weight decay got broken
sections.text:
Weight decay penalises weights from growing. Its classical implementation adds the penalty to the loss, which adds a term proportional to the weight into the gradient.

The problem is that this term gets inside Adam. Since the penalty is mixed into the gradient it also enters the second moment, so the adaptive scaling scales the penalty as well. The result is distorted: the decay of weights that receive large gradients weakens, while that of rarely updated weights strengthens. What you actually want is a pull applied equally to every weight.

AdamW's fix is simple: separate the decay from the gradient entirely and apply it directly to the weight. The adaptive scaling then looks only at the task gradient, and the decay acts the same way on everyone.

This is the direct reason AdamW became standard in Transformer training.

sections.heading: The chain
sections.text:
Plain GD       fixed step, raw gradient        -> zigzag + single speed
SGD+Momentum   average of gradients (m)        -> zigzag damped
Adam           m + avg of squared grads (v)    -> zigzag damped + per-weight speed
AdamW          Adam, decay outside gradient    -> decay equal for every weight

Gradient is swinging          -> add momentum
Each weight wants own speed   -> add adaptive rate
Weight decay got broken       -> take it out of the gradient

sections.heading: 8. The learning rate: the real hyperparameter
sections.text:
What makes more difference than the choice of optimizer is the learning rate.

If it is too large the loss explodes or gets stuck oscillating somewhere. If it is too small training does not progress and stays in a bad region.

There are two standard practices. The first is warmup: raising the learning rate from zero to the target value over the first few hundred steps. The reason is that Adam's moment estimates are unreliable at the start; warmup prevents large steps during that period. In Transformer training it is nearly mandatory.

The second is decay: lowering the learning rate as training proceeds — with a cosine curve or in steps. The logic is simple: coarse search at the beginning, fine-tuning later.

Practical diagnosis: if the loss explodes the learning rate is too high; if the loss falls but very slowly it is too low; if the training loss falls while validation rises the problem is not in the optimizer but on the generalisation side.

sections.heading: 9. The role of normalization here
sections.text:
Batch normalization is usually taught as a separate topic, but it intervenes directly in the optimisation problem.

What it does is pull the input of every layer to zero mean and unit variance within the mini-batch, and then leave the model the option of restoring the distribution it wants through a learned scale and shift.

Its gains fall under three headings: a much larger learning rate becomes usable, training becomes insensitive to weight initialisation, and the noise coming from mini-batch statistics acts as a mild regularization.

It has one trap that bites often in practice: during training the mini-batch statistics are used, while at test time the moving averages accumulated during training are used. Forgetting to put the model into evaluation mode leads to computing meaningless statistics from a single image.

If the batch size is small the statistics become unreliable; there layer normalization is preferred — and that is also why Transformers use it instead of batch norm.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: Mini-batch is the practical point between the accuracy of the full batch and the speed of pure SGD, and its noise is sometimes useful. Plain gradient descent has two separate problems: zigzagging, and a single learning rate not fitting everyone. Momentum solves the first, the adaptive rate the second; Adam does both. Bias correction is a patch for the first steps only. AdamW repairs the regularization Adam broke by separating the decay from the gradient. The learning rate is still the most decisive hyperparameter; warmup and decay are standard. Normalization is an optimisation tool, and forgetting evaluation mode is the classic mistake.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: The batch/SGD/mini-batch comparison with concrete numbers, the full explanation of Adam and AdamW, batch normalization and initialisation are in ch08; regularization (L1, L2, elastic net) is in cs02; dropout, initialisation and normalization layers are in cs05. For where the gradient comes from see the backpropagation guide, and for why weight decay is a prior see the MLE guide.

cnn.title: CNN — A Complete Walkthrough
cnn.context: Convolutional Networks · ML ch09 · CS231n 4-5 · Lab 4 · ML-OVERALL 14
cnn.summary: One continuous thread from why a fully connected network collapses on images, to which three assumptions convolution embeds into the architecture, how the receptive field grows with depth, the choice between pooling and stride, the architectural line from LeNet to ViT, and the components that keep training alive in practice.

sections.heading: 1. Why a fully connected network collapses on images
sections.text:
There are two separate reasons, and the second one is deeper.

The first is counting. A 224x224x3 image means over 150 thousand inputs. A single fully connected layer of a thousand neurons attached to it carries 150 million weights — for one layer. Training that with the data you have produces nothing but memorisation.

The second, and the essential one: a fully connected layer has no notion of spatial structure. The moment you flatten the image into a plain vector, the information about which pixel sits next to which is erased. For the model, pixel 37 and pixel 38 are as unrelated as pixel 37 and pixel 900.

The consequence: a network that learns to see a cat in the top left corner cannot see the same cat in the bottom right. It has to learn it from scratch for every location.

Before deep learning the solution was to hand-code this structure: colour histograms, histograms of oriented gradients, bags of visual words. A simple classifier was placed on top of human-designed features. The hard work was not in the model but in feature engineering.

sections.heading: 2. Three properties of images
sections.text:
A CNN embeds three observable properties of natural images into the architecture.

Locality. Nearby pixels are strongly related to each other, distant pixels are almost independent. To see an edge you do not need to look at the whole image, a small neighbourhood suffices.

Translation equivariance. A cat is a cat in the top left as well as in the bottom right. A filter that finds an edge in one place finds an edge elsewhere too.

Hierarchy. Edges combine into corners, corners into parts, parts into objects. This is an observation that comes from biology — that cells in the visual cortex also work in such layers was shown in 1959.

Their counterparts in the architecture are direct: small filters for locality, using the same filter everywhere for translation equivariance, and stacking layers for hierarchy.

sections.heading: 3. What convolution actually does
sections.text:
A small filter — typically 3x3 — is slid over the image and an inner product is taken at every position. The resulting number says: how much of the pattern this filter is looking for is present here?

The result is a feature map: the spatial distribution of the filter's response. Not a single number but a map — the position information is preserved.

The critical point is weight sharing. The number of parameters of a 3x3 filter is independent of the size of the input image: nine numbers times the number of input channels. The same nine numbers are used at every position.

This has two consequences. The parameter count collapses, and translation equivariance stops being something that must be learned and becomes a guarantee of the architecture. A fully connected network was trying to learn it from data; a CNN never learns it, because by construction it is already so.

A CNN layer carries not one filter but many. Each specialises in a different pattern; the output is as many feature maps as there are channels.

sections.heading: Shape arithmetic
sections.text:
$$o[i,j] = \sum_m \sum_n f[m,n] \cdot I[i+m,\ j+n]$$

Output size (for each spatial axis):
$$H_{out} = \left\lfloor \frac{H_{in} + 2p - k}{s} \right\rfloor + 1$$

$k$ is the filter size, $s$ the stride, $p$ the padding. To preserve the size with a 3x3 filter, $p=1$, $s=1$.

sections.heading: 4. Receptive field: what depth buys
sections.text:
A single 3x3 filter only sees a 3x3 patch of the input. That is very narrow.

But when you stack two 3x3 layers, every point the second layer looks at summarises a 3x3 neighbourhood of the first layer, and each of those points had seen a 3x3 of the input. In effect the second layer sees 5x5 of the input. The third sees 7x7.

So depth is the cheap way of growing the field of view. Two 3x3 layers cover the same area as a single 5x5 layer — but with fewer parameters and with one more non-linearity in between. VGG's choice of "use only 3x3 and go deeper instead" rests exactly on this arithmetic.

Stride and pooling accelerate this growth: when you halve the spatial resolution, the same filter comes to cover twice the area of the input. The typical CNN profile of "resolution falls while the channel count rises" comes from here — spatial detail decreases while semantic information increases.

sections.heading: 5. Pooling: what it gains, what it loses
sections.text:
Pooling reduces neighbouring values to a single value — usually by taking their maximum.

What it gains is insensitivity to small translations: even if an edge shifts one pixel to the right, the maximum stays the same. It also makes the computation cheaper and grows the receptive field.

What it loses is exact position information. In classification this is not a problem, it is even desirable. But in segmentation you have to produce a label for every pixel; there, bringing back the position information thrown away by pooling is a job of its own — the whole segmentation guide revolves around that problem.

Some modern architectures drop pooling entirely and use strided convolution instead: performing the same downsampling with a learnable operation.

sections.heading: 6. The architectural line
sections.text:
1998, LeNet: the first working CNN, digit recognition. The idea was right but there was neither enough data nor enough compute.

2012, AlexNet: pushed the error of the best non-CNN method on ImageNet back by about ten points. What it brought was practical rather than architectural — ReLU, dropout, data augmentation, and training on two GPUs. The gap was so large that it ended the debate.

2014, VGG: only 3x3 filters, but sixteen to nineteen layers. It showed that depth itself works.

2014, GoogLeNet: modules running different filter sizes in parallel, with far fewer parameters.

2015, ResNet: residual connections. This is the real break — thanks to shortcuts that skip over a layer, hundreds of layers became trainable. The reason lies directly in backprop: the gradient flows backwards through that shortcut without attenuation.

2021, ViT: split the image into 16x16 patches, treat every patch as a token, feed it to a standard Transformer. It removes the locality and weight sharing assumptions from the architecture and chooses to learn them from data — which is why it demands a lot of data, and why with enough data it catches up with and overtakes the CNN.

sections.heading: 7. The components that keep training alive in practice
sections.text:
Convolution alone is not enough; getting a CNN to actually work depends on several standard pieces.

Normalization layers keep the activations within a fixed band, so a larger learning rate becomes usable and training becomes less sensitive to weight initialisation.

Dropout switches off a random subset of neurons during training and prevents the network from depending on a single path. It is used less in the convolutional part and more in the fully connected part.

Weight initialisation is chosen at a scale that lets the signal neither vanish nor explode with depth — a variance rule that depends on the layer width.

Data augmentation is an almost free gain: random cropping, horizontal flipping, colour jittering. It injects into the data the invariances the model already knows about.

Transfer learning is what is used most in practice: because the early layers of a network trained on a large dataset are generic edge and texture detectors, they can be reused; only the last part is trained for the new task. This is why training from scratch on a small dataset is almost never the right thing to do.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: A fully connected network collapses on images both because of the parameter count and because it erases spatial structure. A CNN embeds three assumptions into the architecture: locality (small filters), translation equivariance (weight sharing), and hierarchy (depth). Thanks to weight sharing the parameter count is independent of image size. The receptive field grows with depth, which is why two 3x3 layers beat one 5x5. Pooling gains translation insensitivity and loses position information — the entire concern of segmentation is to win that loss back. ResNet's residual connections made depth possible; ViT removed the assumptions and put data in their place.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: The motivation and the mechanics of convolution and pooling are in ch09; the transition from hand-crafted features to CNNs and the architectural history are in cs04; normalization, dropout, initialisation, data augmentation and transfer learning are in cs05; the PyTorch implementation and the shape flow are in lab04. What follows: the segmentation guide (winning back position information) and the attention guide (the mechanism ViT rests on).

segmentation.title: Segmentation — A Complete Walkthrough
segmentation.context: Semantic Segmentation · IDA 5 · Lab 5 · CS231n 8 · ML-OVERALL 24
segmentation.summary: One continuous thread from how producing a per-pixel label differs from classification, to the ways of winning back the position information the CNN threw away, transposed convolution and the checkerboard artefact, skip connections, the U-Net, instance segmentation, and why mIoU is used instead of pixel accuracy.

sections.heading: 1. Three different tasks
sections.text:
There are three things that get confused.

Semantic segmentation: a class label for every pixel. Two adjacent sheep come out as a single sheep region — objects are not separated, only classes.

Instance segmentation: every object separately. Two sheep become two separate masks. Meaningful only for countable objects — there is no instance of the sky.

Panoptic: the union of the two. Countable objects separately, and the remaining areas at the class level.

The frame of this text is semantic segmentation; I touch on the instance side at the end.

sections.heading: 2. Why a classification network cannot be used directly
sections.text:
A classification network takes an image and produces a single vector. In segmentation what you want is an output of the same spatial size as the input, with as many channels as there are classes.

The first solution that comes to mind — cutting out the patch around every pixel and passing it through a classifier — works but is absurdly expensive: neighbouring patches repeat almost the same computation over and over.

The right idea is to turn the fully connected layers at the end of the classification network into convolutions. A fully connected layer can be written as a convolution that sees the whole of its input. Once you do this the network starts producing a map instead of a fixed-size vector — and the input size no longer has to be fixed either.

This is the fully convolutional network idea. But it leaves one problem: the map that comes out is very coarse.

sections.heading: 3. The real problem: loss of resolution
sections.text:
A typical classification backbone reduces the spatial size by a factor of thirty-two. A 320x320 image comes down to a 10x10 map.

Every cell in that map represents a 32x32 pixel area of the input. So the information you hold is at the level of "this 32x32 region is probably sheep". Object boundaries do not exist at that resolution.

You need two things at once and they conflict: to know the class you need wide context, that is, deep and downscaled features; to know the boundary you need fine detail, that is, high-resolution early features.

All segmentation architectures are the resolution of this conflict.

sections.heading: 4. Ways of upsampling
sections.text:
The coarse map has to be brought back up to the input size.

The simplest route is interpolation: bilinear upsampling. It has no parameters to learn and is fast, but it only smooths — it does not bring back the lost detail.

The learnable route is transposed convolution. Its mechanism works like the reverse of convolution: zeros are sprinkled between the input values, padding is added at the edges, and an ordinary convolution is applied. The output ends up larger than the input and the upsampling operation itself is learned.

There is also a route that never downscales the input at all: dilated convolution. By putting gaps between the elements of the filter it grows the receptive field without losing resolution.

sections.heading: Transposed convolution output size
sections.text:
$$H_{out} = (H_{in} - 1)\cdot s - 2p + k$$

Example: from 10 to 320 with $s = 32$. Choosing $k = 64$ and $p = 16$ gives $(10-1)\cdot 32 - 32 + 64 = 320$.

sections.heading: 5. The checkerboard artefact
sections.text:
The classic failure of transposed convolution, and its cause is entirely arithmetic.

If the filter size is chosen equal to the stride, every output pixel is influenced by only a single input cell. The contributions of neighbouring cells never overlap, sharp transitions form between them, and in the upsampled image the original coarse grid appears as a checkerboard pattern.

The solution is to guarantee overlap: choose the filter size to be twice the stride. Then every output pixel sees at least two neighbouring cells and the transitions soften.

This is the standard practice: filter size twice the stride, padding half the stride. With these values the output size also comes out exactly as the input times the stride.

There is also an initialisation detail: initialising the weights of the transposed convolution with values corresponding to bilinear interpolation, instead of at random, gives sensible upsampling behaviour at the start of training — the model starts from a good point instead of learning from scratch.

sections.heading: 6. Skip connections: winning back the lost detail
sections.text:
If you upsample only the deepest map by a factor of thirty-two the boundaries come out blurry. The detail is not there, so the upsampling cannot produce it.

The solution is to use the high-resolution features coming from the early layers as well. The deep map carries the "what is this" information and the early map the "where exactly is the boundary" information; you combine the two.

In the FCN family this is done in stages: first the deepest map is upsampled by a factor of two and added to the output of the previous pooling, then this sum is upsampled again and added to an even earlier output, and finally the remaining factor is upsampled in one go. Compared with the version that uses only the deepest map, the boundaries sharpen markedly.

There are two different ways of combining and they get confused: combining by addition (the ResNet-style shortcut) and combining by adding channels (the U-Net style). FCN uses addition, U-Net channel concatenation.

sections.heading: 7. The U-Net
sections.text:
The U-Net seats the same idea in a symmetric architecture: a descending path, an ascending path, and connections between the levels of the same resolution.

On the descending path the resolution falls while the channel count rises — context is gathered. On the ascending path the reverse happens, and at every level the features coming from the descending path are added as channels.

It was designed for biomedical imaging and is still the default architecture in that field. The reason is partly the data: medical datasets are small, the U-Net can work with little data, and it generalises well with strong data augmentation.

Note: this skeleton of the U-Net is everywhere outside segmentation too. The noise prediction network of diffusion models has the same structure — the input and output have the same spatial size, and every pixel needs both local and global context. The same problem shape, the same architecture.

sections.heading: 8. The loss: per-pixel classification
sections.text:
The loss of segmentation is the same as that of classification, only computed separately for every pixel and averaged.

The difference in practice is in the shapes: in classification the prediction has shape (batch, classes) and the target (batch,); in segmentation the prediction is (batch, classes, H, W) and the target (batch, H, W). The target is a map carrying a class index for every pixel.

Two practical details: an index reserved for unlabelled or ambiguous pixels is excluded from the loss; and if the class imbalance is severe the per-pixel loss is weighted, or a Dice-based loss that directly optimises set overlap is added.

sections.heading: 9. Why pixel accuracy is not enough
sections.text:
This is the most instructive measurement lesson of segmentation.

In a typical dataset the great majority of pixels are background. A model that calls everything background can obtain over seventy per cent pixel accuracy — by doing nothing.

This is why the real metric is intersection over union: for every class, the intersection of the prediction and the ground truth mask divided by their union. It is computed per class and averaged.

The critical point is that the average is taken per class: if you never find a rare class, the ratio of that class comes out zero and directly drags the average down. This is what makes visible the failure that pixel accuracy hides.

A related measure is the Dice coefficient — twice the intersection divided by the total size. More common in medical imaging; it is more forgiving on small structures.

sections.heading: 10. The instance side
sections.text:
Semantic segmentation does not separate objects. There are two approaches for separating them.

Detect first, then mask. For every box found by an object detection network a small mask branch is run. Mask R-CNN is on this line, and it introduced a cropping layer that corrects the alignment error arising from rounding the box coordinates to integers — in mask work a shift of a few pixels shows up directly in the quality.

Direct instance separation. In fields with very many objects — such as cell imaging — the box-based approach gets stuck. Instead, domain-specific methods are used, such as predicting for every pixel a flow field pointing towards the object centre and grouping the pixels that flow to the same centre, or representing objects with star-shaped polygons.

The current direction is to unify the tasks: instead of producing the mask directly, Transformer-based architectures working with query vectors handle semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation within a single framework.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: Segmentation is the problem of winning back the position information thrown away by the CNN. The classification backbone gathers context but drops the resolution by a factor of thirty-two; knowing the class needs deep features and knowing the boundary needs early features, and the architectures resolve that conflict. Upsampling is done either by interpolation or by learnable transposed convolution; in the latter, if the filter size is not chosen to be twice the stride you get a checkerboard. Skip connections bring the detail back — FCN by addition, U-Net by concatenating channels. The loss is per-pixel cross-entropy. Pixel accuracy misleads because the background dominates; IoU averaged per class is used instead.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: The semantic-instance distinction, the U-Net, Mask R-CNN and the biology-specific methods are in ida05; the conversion into an FCN, the mechanics of transposed convolution, the checkerboard, bilinear initialisation, the FCN-8s skip connections, the per-pixel loss and IoU/mIoU are in lab05; the comparison of detection and segmentation is in cs08. For the backbone itself see the CNN walkthrough, and for the use of the U-Net in diffusion see the DDPM walkthrough.

rnn.title: RNN and LSTM — A Complete Walkthrough
rnn.context: Sequence Modelling · ML ch11 · CS231n 6 · ML-OVERALL 16
rnn.summary: One continuous thread from why sequences demand their own architecture, to the structure of the vanilla RNN, why backpropagation through time makes the gradient vanish, how the LSTM's gates solve that problem, the GRU, and why the Transformer took over.

sections.heading: 1. Why sequences demand their own architecture
sections.text:
The input size of a fully connected network is fixed. But sentences have different lengths, audio recordings have different lengths, video has different lengths.

Moreover, the order carries information: "the dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" are the same words with different meanings.

Third, the same pattern can appear anywhere in the sequence. Just as in images, here too you want shared parameters: a mechanism that learns to process one word should work the same way at the tenth word.

The RNN's answer: apply a single cell over and over along time, and carry the past in a single vector. That vector is called the hidden state, and at every step it is updated by looking both at the input and at its own previous value.

The same weights are used at every step — that is, the counterpart of the CNN's weight sharing on the time axis.

sections.heading: Vanilla RNN
sections.text: $$h_t = \tanh\bigl(W_{hh} h_{t-1} + W_{xh} x_t + b\bigr), \qquad y_t = W_{hy} h_t$$

sections.heading: 2. What exactly the hidden state carries
sections.text:
The hidden state is the summary of the sequence up to that moment. A fixed-size vector — that is, the history of a thirty-word sentence has the same size as that of a three-word one.

There is a tension here that will explode later: a fixed-size vector has to carry a history of arbitrary length. As the sequence lengthens the compression loss grows.

The usage patterns vary with the input-output correspondence: labeling that produces an output at every step, classification that produces a single output from the whole sequence, and the encoder-decoder setup that translates one sequence into another. In the last one the encoder reduces the sentence to a single vector and the decoder generates from it — and that single vector is the very bottleneck that caused attention to be born.

sections.heading: 3. Backpropagation through time
sections.text:
Training means unrolling the network along time and applying ordinary backprop. A sequence of thirty steps behaves like a network thirty layers deep — but all the layers share the same weights.

On long sequences this is truncated in practice: the network is unrolled over a certain window and the gradient is stopped there, otherwise neither the memory suffices nor does the computation stay manageable.

The real problem, though, is not the computational cost but the gradient itself.

sections.heading: 4. Why the gradient vanishes
sections.text:
The error signal coming from a distant step is multiplied at every intervening step by two things: the recurrent weight matrix, and the derivative of the activation.

This is a chain of products, and chains of products behave exponentially. If the activation is tanh its derivative is at most one and typically far smaller. If the magnitude of the weight matrix is less than one the product falls to zero quickly.

Looked at with numbers it is dire: in a dependency reaching thirty steps back, even an attenuation of the order of 0.25 per step drives the signal down by twenty orders of magnitude. Effectively zero.

The practical consequence: in a sentence that begins with "Although ..." and continues thirty words later with "but ...", the gradient the network would need in order to learn this long-range relation never reaches it. The RNN learns the recent past and cannot learn the distant past.

There is a failure in the other direction too: if the weight matrix is large the same product makes the gradient explode. That is solved more easily — if the norm of the gradient exceeds a threshold it is clipped. Vanishing is not solved by clipping; it requires an architectural change.

sections.heading: 5. The LSTM: opening a motorway for the gradient
sections.text:
What the LSTM brought is a second line alongside the hidden state: the cell state.

Along the cell state the main operation is not multiplication but addition. At every step part of the old value is preserved and new information is added on top. Which part is preserved, and how much of the new information is written, are determined by learned gates.

There are three gates. The forget gate decides what will be erased from the cell memory — close to zero means forget, close to one means keep. The input gate determines how much of the new candidate will be written. The output gate selects how much of the memory will be reflected outward, into the hidden state.

The essence of the solution is in a single place: along the cell state the gradient passes multiplied by the value of the forget gate. When the gate is open this factor is close to one — that is, the gradient flows without attenuation. In a vanilla RNN it had to pass through both the saturation of the activation and the multiplication by the weight at every step.

This is the same idea as ResNet's residual connections: opening an additive path for the gradient that skips over layers. Both are the same answer to the question "how is the gradient preserved with depth".

sections.heading: LSTM
sections.text:
$$f_t = \sigma(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t]), \quad i_t = \sigma(W_i [h_{t-1}, x_t]), \quad o_t = \sigma(W_o [h_{t-1}, x_t])$$
$$g_t = \tanh(W_g [h_{t-1}, x_t]), \qquad C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t, \qquad h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(C_t)$$

The critical line: $\partial C_t / \partial C_{t-1} = f_t$ — when the gate is open the gradient passes without vanishing.

sections.heading: 6. What the gates learn in practice
sections.text:
The gates are not tuned by hand, they are learned from data, and what they learn can be interpreted.

In a relation such as subject-verb agreement, when the network sees the subject it writes its singular-plural information into memory and preserves it throughout the sentence, using it when the verb arrives.

When the end of a sentence is reached the forget gate zeroes many dimensions — a kind of reset. The new sentence has no business with the subject of the old one.

It has been shown that with suitable gate settings an LSTM can carry information for hundreds of steps. From 2014 to 2018 it was the standard of sequence modelling.

The GRU is the simplified form of the same idea: two gates, and no separate cell state. Fewer parameters, comparable performance on most tasks.

sections.heading: 7. What the LSTM did not solve
sections.text:
The vanishing gradient was solved. But two problems stayed where they were, and they are the reason the Transformer took over.

Sequentiality. Every step has to wait for the previous one. This conflicts directly with the parallel nature of modern hardware: processing a sequence of hundreds of steps means hundreds of sequential computations. In attention all positions are processed at the same time.

The bottleneck. In the encoder-decoder setup the whole source sentence is squeezed into a single vector. As the sentence lengthens this compression loses information.

The first solution to the second problem was attention — and the striking thing is this: attention was first added on top of the RNN as a patch. While producing each word the decoder looked back at the whole source. It was then realised that if you can produce the query vector from the input as well, the RNN is not needed at all. The Transformer was born exactly with that step.

The RNN did not die entirely: it is still used in very long streams, in embedded systems and where low latency is required. Moreover modern state space models (the Mamba family) bring the same recurrent structure back in a form that can be trained in parallel.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: The RNN carries weight sharing over to the time axis and holds the past in a fixed-size vector — all the tension is in that fixed size. Because backpropagation through time is a chain of products, the gradient vanishes exponentially; explosion is solved by clipping, vanishing is not. The LSTM opens an additive path along the cell state and passes the gradient multiplied by the value of the forget gate — when the gate is open there is no attenuation. This is the same idea as ResNet's residual connection. The LSTM solved vanishing but not sequentiality nor the single-vector bottleneck; attention and the Transformer are the answer to those two.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: The RNN architecture, backpropagation through time and the vanishing gradient analysis are in ch11; the LSTM gates and the GRU again in ch11 and in cs06; the step by step flow of RNN attention and its comparison with the vanilla RNN in ch11. What follows is directly the attention walkthrough — it begins where this text ends. For the general form of the vanishing gradient see the backpropagation walkthrough.

attention.title: Attention and Transformer — A Complete Walkthrough
attention.context: Attention · ML ch12 · CS231n 7 · IDA 7 · Lab TC · ML-OVERALL 16-17
attention.summary: One continuous thread from the bottleneck of the RNN, to the first attention, why the decoder state was removed, why Q-K-V are three separate vectors, why the scaling and the positional encoding are needed, the multi-head structure, masking, the KV cache and the full Transformer block.

sections.heading: 1. The beginning: the bottleneck of the RNN
sections.text:
Think of the classical setup that translates a sentence into another language. The encoder reads the sentence word by word and summarises it in a single hidden vector. The decoder produces the translation from that vector.

There are two separate problems.

The first is the bottleneck: the whole of a forty-word sentence is compressed into a single vector. As the sentence lengthens the information at the beginning gets crushed.

The second is sequentiality: every step has to wait for the previous one. Processing a long sequence means a long chain, and as the gradient flows backwards along that chain it either vanishes or explodes.

Attention was born first as an answer to the first problem. Solving the second came later, and as a side effect.

sections.heading: 2. The first attention: look again at every step
sections.text:
The idea is this: do not settle for a single summary vector; while producing each word let the decoder look back at the whole source and decide which part matters at that moment.

The mechanism has three steps. The decoder's current state is compared with every position in the source and a compatibility score is produced. The scores are turned into weights with a softmax. The sum of the source vectors with those weights is taken — the context vector.

In image captioning it is the same: the encoder produces regional features from the image, and while producing each word the decoder decides which region to look at.

But there is a hidden dependency here: all three steps depend on the decoder's current state. Without that state the compatibility score cannot be computed, and without the score the context vector does not come out. The system is still tied to a sequential decoder.

sections.heading: 3. The turning point: produce the query from the input too
sections.text:
The critical question is this: why do we need the decoder's state? It is a vector after all. Could we not produce it directly from the input?

We can. And the moment you do, the dependency on the decoder disappears.

Every position now produces its own question itself. Every position can look at the whole sequence at the same time, independently of the others. Sequentiality disappears.

This is called self-attention, and its difference from the old attention is a single thing: the query does not come from outside, it is produced from the input itself.

The correspondence is this: what the decoder state used to do is now done by the query; the place of the compatibility function was taken by the dot product and the key; the role of the source vectors in the weighted sum was taken over by the value.

sections.heading: 4. Why three separate vectors
sections.text:
Three vectors are produced for every position — query, key, value — and all three come out of the same input through three separate learned matrices. Why three?

Query is clear: what am I looking for.

The real question is why the key and the value are separate. Had they not been separate, the same vector would have to say both "how am I to be searched for" and "what do I give once found".

The phone book analogy settles it exactly: you search by name and you get a number. If the two were the same, you would search for "Ahmet" and receive "Ahmet" — useless.

A concrete example: in the sentence "The cat sat on the mat", the word "sat" asks — who is my subject? The word "cat" has two separate vectors. Its key says: I am a noun, I am at the start of the sentence, I am most likely the subject. Its value says something entirely different: I am a cat, I am animate, I am singular, I have these semantic properties.

The search criterion and the carried content are different things. Keeping them apart lets the model optimise the two independently.

sections.heading: The flow of the computation for a single token
sections.svg: <svg width="560" height="300" viewBox="0 0 560 300" role="img" aria-label="attention for a single token"><text x="30" y="22" class="sm">query: the q vector of the token "mat"</text><text x="30" y="52" class="sm">token attended to</text><text x="190" y="52" class="sm">q·kᵢ / √d</text><text x="300" y="52" class="sm">softmax</text><text x="400" y="52" class="sm">weight</text><line class="axis" x1="30" y1="60" x2="536" y2="60" stroke-width="1"/><text x="30" y="82" class="sm">cat</text><text x="190" y="82" class="sm">3.2</text><text x="300" y="82" class="sm">0.51</text><rect class="cell-hi" x="400" y="70" width="66.5" height="14" fill-opacity="0.8"/><text x="30" y="116" class="sm">slept</text><text x="190" y="116" class="sm">2.0</text><text x="300" y="116" class="sm">0.15</text><rect class="cell-hi" x="400" y="104" width="20.0" height="14" fill-opacity="0.8"/><text x="30" y="150" class="sm">on</text><text x="190" y="150" class="sm">1.8</text><text x="300" y="150" class="sm">0.13</text><rect class="cell-hi" x="400" y="138" width="16.4" height="14" fill-opacity="0.8"/><text x="30" y="184" class="sm">mat (itself)</text><text x="190" y="184" class="sm">2.3</text><text x="300" y="184" class="sm">0.21</text><rect class="cell-hi" x="400" y="172" width="27.0" height="14" fill-opacity="0.8"/><line class="axis" x1="30" y1="204" x2="536" y2="204" stroke-width="1"/><text x="300" y="226" class="sm">sums to 1.00</text><text x="30" y="260" class="sm">output = 0.51·v(cat) + 0.15·v(slept) + 0.13·v(on) + 0.21·v(mat)</text><text x="30" y="284" class="sm">q: what am I looking for · k: what do I hold · v: what I give if chosen</text></svg>
sections.caption: The computation for the token "mat". Its own query is multiplied with every key, the scores are divided by $\sqrt{d}$, passed through a softmax and turned into weights that sum to 1. The output is the mixture of the value vectors with those weights. The scores here are example values; in a real model they come out of the product of the q and k vectors.

sections.heading: Self-attention
sections.text:
$$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V$$

For a single position: $e_{ij} = q_i \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d_k}$, then $a = \text{softmax}(e)$ and $y_i = \sum_j a_{ij} v_j$.

sections.heading: 5. Why we divide by the square root of the dimension
sections.text:
This is the most memorised and least understood piece of the formula.

If the query and key components are roughly independent and of unit scale, the dot product is a sum of $d_k$ terms, so its variance grows with $d_k$. That is, as the dimension increases the scores are thrown towards large numbers.

When very large numbers enter a softmax, the output gives almost one to a single position and zero to the rest. This breaks two things at once: attention sharpens to the point of carrying no information, and in that saturated region the gradient of the softmax approaches zero — learning stops.

Dividing by the square root pulls the variance back to one. So the scaling is not a nicety, it is necessary for training to work at all.

sections.caption: Self-attention weights in the sentence "cat slept on the mat because it"; the values were computed with a softmax and every row sums to 1. The row is the query token, the column the token being attended to. The row to watch is "it": it gives 0.65 of its weight to "cat", that is, whom the pronoun refers to is resolved in this matrix. "slept" also looks at its subject. In a real model these patterns emerge through training, they are not set by hand.

sections.heading: 6. The real gain: parallelism
sections.text:
The whole computation can be written with matrix products: the product of the queries with the keys gives the scores of all position pairs in one go.

This is the characteristic difference from the RNN itself. In an RNN a forty-word sentence means forty sequential steps. In self-attention all positions are computed at the same time.

There is another gain: the distance between two positions no longer matters. In an RNN there was a forty-step path between the first and the fortieth word and information was crushed along that path. In self-attention there is a single connection between the two.

The cost is here too: because all pairs are computed, the cost grows with the square of the sequence length. All of the long-context literature wrestles with this term.

sections.heading: 7. Why position information disappears
sections.text:
Self-attention has a side effect and it is critical: it destroys order information entirely.

If you shuffle the positions the output shuffles the same way, but the content does not change. So the mechanism looks at the input as a set, not as a sequence.

Concrete proof: in the sentences "cat bites dog" and "dog bites cat" the embedding of the word "cat" is the same, so its key is the same as well. When the word "bites" asks its question, the information "is cat before or after me" exists nowhere. The same scores come out in both sentences.

But the meaning is completely different: in one, cat is the subject, in the other the object.

The solution is to add position information to the embedding. "cat" becomes a different vector when it is in first position and when it is in third; its key changes accordingly. Now the scores separate and the syntactic role becomes learnable.

Note: the key was already resolving the ambiguity of "which word am I". Positional encoding resolves a different ambiguity — "which word am I, in which position".

sections.heading: 8. Multi-head attention
sections.text:
A single attention computation produces a single weight distribution for every position — that is, a single kind of relation.

But a word has several relations at once: the subject of its verb, the preposition it attaches to, the pronoun that refers to it, its topical context. A single distribution cannot carry these at the same time; it takes an average of all of them.

The solution is to run the same computation several times in parallel. Every head has its own query, key and value matrices; each can specialise in a different kind of relation. The outputs are concatenated and passed through a single linear layer.

The cost does not increase, because the dimension of each head is the total dimension divided by the number of heads. So you split the same compute budget into several narrow relations instead of one wide one.

sections.heading: 9. Masking: two separate jobs
sections.text:
Masking is used for two different purposes and they get confused.

The causal mask. In a model that generates text, every position must be able to look only at the ones before it; if it sees what comes after, it copies the answer during training and collapses at generation time. To ensure this, the scores of future positions are pulled to minus infinity before the softmax and their weights become zero. The whole GPT family works this way.

The padding mask. Because sentences in a batch have different lengths, the short ones are padded to make them equal. Those padding positions are not real data, so attention must not give them any weight.

Both are done with the same technique but their purposes differ: one prevents information leakage, the other meaningless input.

sections.heading: KV cache: not repeating the same computation at generation time
sections.text:
The decoder generates token by token and applies attention over the whole sequence at every new token. But there is waste here: the key and value vectors of the previous tokens do not change. The $K_1, V_1$ you computed at the third step and the ones at the fourth step are exactly the same.

The reason is masking. Because every position only sees what comes before it, tokens that arrive later do not affect the representation of the earlier ones. Therefore a key and a value computed once remain valid forever.

The KV cache stores them. At every step only the $K$ and $V$ of the new token are computed, and the rest are read from memory. The cost per step stops being proportional to the sequence length and becomes constant; in long generations the difference is many-fold.

The cost is memory. What is stored is a pair of vectors for every layer, every head and every token; in long contexts the cache can occupy more space than the model itself. Variants such as multi-query and grouped-query attention share keys and values across heads precisely to lower this cost.

Note: the cache is only meaningful at generation time. In training the whole sequence is already processed in one go and in parallel, and there is no intermediate state to store.

sections.heading: 10. Cross-attention: the query from one place, the key from another
sections.text:
Up to now all three vectors came from the same sequence. If you take the query from one source and the key and value from another, you obtain cross-attention.

In translation the decoder uses this: the queries come from the translation being produced, and the keys and values from the output of the encoder. That is, "for the word I am producing right now, where in the source sentence should I look".

The same mechanism also works across modalities. In image captioning the queries come from the text and the keys and values from the image features. In text to image diffusion models the direction reverses: the queries come from the image and the keys and values from the text — every pixel selects which word concerns it.

So this mechanism is the most general answer to the question "how do I give the condition to the model".

sections.heading: 11. The rest of the block is not decoration
sections.text:
A Transformer block does not consist of attention alone; there are three more pieces, each solving a specific failure.

The residual connection. The attention output is added to the input. This lets the gradient flow backwards along a shortcut in deep stacks; without it a deep Transformer cannot be trained.

Layer normalization. After attention and the addition the scales drift; normalization keeps the activations within a fixed band.

The feed-forward layer. Attention is really only a weighted average — it moves information between positions but performs no non-linear operation within a single position. This layer does that job: a small network applied separately to every position, expanding and then contracting.

The division of labour between the two is clear: attention mixes across positions, the feed-forward layer processes within a position.

sections.heading: 12. Encoder-only, decoder-only, and both
sections.text:
Three different architectures come out of the same block.

Encoder-decoder. The original translation architecture. The encoder reads the source without a mask, the decoder generates with a causal mask and looks at the encoder through cross-attention.

Encoder-only. No masking, every position sees every position. Not suitable for generation but ideal for understanding: classification, labeling, extracting embeddings. The BERT family is like this, and its training objective matches — hiding some words in the sentence and having them predicted.

Decoder-only. Only causally masked blocks. The objective is simple: predict the next word. The GPT family is this, and almost all of today's large language models take this form.

The same mechanism was carried over to images as well: if you split the image into patches and treat every patch as a position, you get the Vision Transformer. It gives up the local bias of convolution and chooses to learn everything from data — which is why it demands a lot of data.
