sections.caption: The encoder processes the input once and produces the keys and values; the decoder advances token by token and at every step looks both at its own past (masked self-attention) and at the encoder's output (cross-attention). Every block is stacked N times. In the cross-attention box the query comes from the decoder and the key and value from the encoder.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: Attention was born as the idea of looking again at every step instead of relying on a fixed summary. Self-attention removed the dependence on a sequential decoder by producing the query from the input as well — parallelism and distance-independent access come from there, at the cost of the square of the sequence length. The key and the value are separate because how you are found and what you carry are different things. The square root scaling protects the softmax from saturation. Without positional encoding the mechanism sees the sequence as a set. Multi-head exists in order to carry several kinds of relation instead of one. The residual connection, the normalization and the feed-forward layer are not decoration, each solves a specific failure. And cross-attention is the most general way of giving a condition to the model.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: The query-key-value distinction, the justification of positional encoding, the mathematics of the multi-head structure and the encoder-decoder shape flow are in ch12; the step by step correspondence from RNN attention to self-attention also in ch12; the CS231n side in cs07; the image side (ViT, Swin, DETR) in ida07 and ida08; for implementation, the labtc captioning session. For the diffusion form of text conditioning see the DDPM walkthrough.

pca.title: PCA — A Complete Walkthrough
pca.context: Principal Component Analysis · EE499 vs01 · ML-OVERALL 11
pca.summary: One continuous thread from why dimensionality reduction is needed, to the encode-decode setup, why minimising the reconstruction error is the same thing as maximising the variance, the derivation of the eigenvector solution, the residual logic behind the following components, the connection with SVD, and the traps in practice.

sections.heading: 1. The problem
sections.text:
You have m data points, each one n dimensional. n is large — you cannot visualise it, storing it is expensive, processing it is slow, and in high dimensions almost everything looks equally far from everything else.

What you want: bring the data down to l dimensions, with l much smaller, and lose as little information as possible.

Here "information loss" is in need of a definition, and PCA's definition is this: when you compress and then expand again, how close do you come back to the original.

sections.heading: 2. The setup: encode and decode
sections.text:
You define two operations.

Encode: reduce the n dimensional point to an l dimensional coordinate vector. You do this with a matrix — the columns of that matrix are the basis directions you chose.

Decode: climb back from the l dimensional coordinates into the n dimensional space. The weighted sum of those same directions with those coordinates.

The point you come back to will not be identical to the original, because you threw information away along the way. The difference between them is the reconstruction error, and that is what you want to minimise.

You want the directions you choose to be of unit length and orthogonal to each other. Being orthogonal matters: otherwise two directions carry the same information twice and you waste your dimension budget.

sections.heading: 3. Where the two objectives turn out to be one objective
sections.text:
Start with a single direction, that is l = 1. You are projecting every point onto a single line.

Pythagoras steps in: the square of the point's distance from the origin equals the square of its projection plus the square of the residual left orthogonal to the projection. The first term depends on the data and is independent of the choice of direction — it is constant.

Therefore shrinking the residual and growing the projection are two statements of the same thing. If the data is centred, the sum of the squares of the projections is exactly the variance along that direction.

The turning point in one sentence: the direction that loses the least information is the direction along which the data spreads the most. "Minimise the information loss" and "maximise the variance" are the same optimisation problem.

A warning follows from this as well: if you forget to centre the data, the first component most of the time simply points along the mean and PCA becomes meaningless.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text:
$$\max_{d}\ d^\top A d \quad \text{such that} \quad d^\top d = 1, \qquad A = X^\top X$$

$X$ is the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the centred data points; $A$ is symmetric and positive semi-definite (the covariance matrix once it is scaled).

sections.heading: 4. Why eigenvectors: the derivation
sections.text:
Because A is symmetric it has an orthonormal eigenvector basis and its eigenvalues are non-negative. Order that basis: the largest eigenvalue first.

Write the unit vector you are looking for in this basis — that is, as a combination of the eigenvectors. The sum of the squares of its coefficients equals one, because the vector is unit and the basis is orthonormal.

Now expand the objective expression in this basis. The cross terms vanish thanks to orthonormality and a single thing is left: the weighted average of the eigenvalues, with the squares of the coefficients as the weights.

The question has now become very simple: distribute non-negative weights summing to one so as to make the weighted average of fixed numbers as large as possible. The answer is clear — give all the weight to the largest number.

That is, the direction you are looking for is the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. The eigenvector here is not a recipe, it is the solution of a constrained optimisation problem.

And the eigenvalue itself acquires a meaning: it is precisely the variance along that direction.

sections.heading: 5. The following components: the residual logic
sections.text:
You found the first direction. For the second you do not solve the same problem from scratch; first you remove from the data the information the first one carries.

When you subtract from every point its projection along that direction, the residual that is left is orthogonal to the first direction — no variance remains along it.

When you solve the same problem on the residual data, the eigenvectors of the matrix stay the same but the eigenvalue of the first one has been zeroed. Therefore what gives the maximum is the eigenvector of the second largest eigenvalue.

It continues by induction: the best l dimensional subspace is the subspace spanned by the eigenvectors corresponding to the largest l eigenvalues.

The nice thing is this: the components are nested. Working with two components and then going up to three does not require recomputing the first two.

sections.heading: 6. Where the coordinates come from
sections.text:
In an orthonormal basis, the coordinate of a point along a direction is its inner product with that direction. For a single point this is one inner product.

For all the points at once: when you multiply the data matrix by that direction, each row gives that point's coordinate along that direction. That is, a single matrix-vector product produces all the projections.

When you place the l directions you chose side by side and multiply, what you have in hand is a matrix of size m x l: each row is the reduced representation of one point. This is the compressed data you were after.

sections.heading: 7. The connection with SVD
sections.text:
In practice PCA is usually computed not by building the covariance matrix and decomposing it, but directly through the singular value decomposition of the data matrix.

The reason is numerical: to build the covariance matrix you have to multiply the data matrix with itself, and this product squares the condition number — that is, small errors grow. SVD works directly on the data matrix.

The correspondence is one to one: the right singular vectors correspond to the eigenvectors, and the squares of the singular values to the eigenvalues. The same result, a more stable computation.

sections.heading: 8. How many components to choose
sections.text:
Because the eigenvalues are the variance along their direction, how much of the total variance the first l components preserve can be computed directly.

Common practices: choosing the smallest l that preserves a certain fraction of the variance (ninety five percent, say), or plotting the eigenvalues from largest to smallest and taking the place where the curve bends.

Neither is a hard rule. The choice depends on what you will do after PCA: two or three for visualisation, the bend point for noise reduction, and if you are preparing an input to a model, looking directly at that model's accuracy is the most honest.

sections.heading: 9. When it does not work
sections.text:
PCA has three structural limits and all three bite often.

It is sensitive to scale. If one feature is in metres and another in millimetres, the variance of the second comes out a million times larger and the first component shows only that. On data with differing units standardisation is mandatory.

It is linear only. If the data lies on a curved surface — a spiral, a ring — PCA cannot see that structure, a linear projection crushes it. For those situations there are kernel PCA and manifold methods.

Variance is not always useful information. PCA is unsupervised, it does not see the labels. The direction that separates the classes may be a low variance direction; when PCA throws it away the classification accuracy drops. If you are aiming at separation the right tool is linear discriminant analysis.

Finally interpretability: the components are mixtures of the original features, and therefore the question "what does this component measure" most of the time has no answer.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: PCA looks for the subspace that, once you compress and expand again, stays closest to the original. Thanks to Pythagoras this is the same problem as looking for the directions along which the data spreads the most — provided the data is centred. The eigenvector is not a recipe but the solution of a constrained maximisation: the objective reduces to a weighted average of the eigenvalues, and giving all the weight to the largest one is best. The eigenvalue is the variance along that direction itself. The following components come out by solving the same problem on the residual data, which is why they are nested. In practice it is computed with SVD. It is sensitive to scale, it is linear, and it does not see the labels.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: The full derivation of PCA, the eigenvector proof and the residual logic are in vs01; eigendecomposition itself, orthonormal bases, the projection theorem and SVD again in vs01; the connection between the covariance and the Gram matrix in vs03. For the unsupervised learning frame see the generative models walkthrough — the autoencoder can be regarded as the non-linear relative of PCA.

mle.title: MLE — A Complete Walkthrough
mle.context: Maximum Likelihood · ML ch03 · EE499 vs03 · Math 06 · CS231n 12 — to be read in one sitting
mle.summary: One continuous thread from the single question of maximum likelihood, to why the log is taken, the Gaussian and Bernoulli derivations, how MSE and cross-entropy come out of them, why training a neural network is MLE, the single-factor difference of MAP, and why weight decay is a prior.

sections.heading: 1. The single question
sections.text:
You have five numbers: 2.1, 3.4, 2.8, 3.9, 3.0. Lay them out one by one on a number line — they all cluster around 3.

Now imagine you hold a bell curve and can slide it left and right along that line. The question is: where do you put the curve so that these five points become the least surprising?

Put the curve at 10: the points fall far to the left of the curve, in the tail. In such a world, seeing exactly these five numbers would be astonishing. Put the curve at 3: the points fall under the peak, not surprising at all.

MLE is just this: by sliding the unknown around, finding the place that makes the data you observed the least surprising. The answer here is 3.04, that is, the mean of the five numbers.

The same move is made everywhere on this site. The only thing that changes is what the object you slide is: sometimes a single number, sometimes a signal vector, sometimes the millions of weights of a network.

sections.heading: 2. The letters
sections.text:
$x$ — what you see, the data. Here, those five numbers.

$\theta$ — what you are looking for, the unknown. Here, where the curve sits, that is, the mean.

$p(x \mid \theta)$ — the likelihood: "if $\theta$ had this value, what would my chance of seeing exactly this data be?"

That is all. The formula amounts to choosing the $\theta$ that makes this chance largest.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text:
$$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}\ p(x \mid \theta)$$

If the data are independent and come from the same distribution, the likelihood unfolds into a product:
$$p(x \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} p(x_i \mid \theta)$$

sections.heading: 3. The likelihood is not a probability distribution
sections.text:
This is the most confused point, and it has to be killed by name.

You have a single function $p(x \mid \theta)$, but you can look at it with two different eyes.

First eye: $\theta$ fixed, $x$ varying. "If the true mean is 3, what number will I measure?" The answer is a bell curve centred at 3. This is a genuine probability distribution — its integral over x is 1.

Second eye: $x$ fixed, $\theta$ varying. You have already taken the measurement, the data is in your hands. The question is reversed: which $\theta$ makes this data most probable? You are now looking at the same function as a function of $\theta$. This is called the likelihood.

And the likelihood is not a probability distribution. Its integral over $\theta$ does not have to be 1, and it is not. That is why you are not talking about anything like "the probability of $\theta$" — MLE does not tell you how probable $\theta$ is, only which $\theta$ explains the data best.

If you miss this distinction, the difference between MAP and MLE also becomes incomprehensible, because the difference is exactly here.

sections.heading: 4. Why we always take the logarithm
sections.text:
There are three separate reasons and all three are practical.

Numerical underflow. The likelihood is a product of thousands of numbers between 0 and 1. When N grows a little, the product drops to exactly zero in floating point arithmetic, and you cannot maximise zero. The log turns the product into a sum and opens the interval (0,1) into (minus infinity, 0).

It does not change the answer. The log is monotonically increasing, so the $\theta$ that maximises $\log L$ is the same as the one that maximises $L$. A free transformation.

It prepares the ground for differentiation. There is an exponential inside the Gaussian; the log eats it and what remains is a quadratic expression. Taking the derivative and setting it to zero becomes something you can do by hand.

And on the optimisation side we take the negative: minimisation instead of maximisation, because all optimisation libraries minimise. The negative log-likelihood is exactly this.

sections.heading: 5. Apply it to the Gaussian: where the mean comes from
sections.text:
Return to the bell curve example. Take the logarithm of the Gaussian density: the exponential disappears and what remains is a constant plus $-(x_i-\mu)^2 / 2\sigma^2$. Sum over all data points. While maximising over $\mu$ the constants change nothing, so drop them. What you are left with:

Maximising the likelihood = minimising the sum of squares.

If you differentiate and set it to zero the answer is the sample mean. The 3.04 from the beginning comes from here.

This is the first appearance of the most important sentence in this text: a probability question turned into a loss function, and that loss function is MSE.

sections.heading: Gaussian MLE
sections.text:
$$\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\mu}\ p(x \mid \mu) \;=\; \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mu} \sum_{i} (x_i - \mu)^2$$

$$\mu_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} x_n \qquad \sigma^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}(x_n - \mu_{\text{MLE}})^2$$

sections.heading: 6. Why the variance comes out biased
sections.text:
The estimate of the mean is unbiased. The estimate of the variance is not — it comes out systematically too small, and the reason is instructive.

In the variance formula, instead of the true mean the estimate computed from the same data is used. But the sample mean is by definition the point closest to that data: it is precisely the thing that minimises the sum of squares. Therefore the distances of the data points from it are on average smaller than their distances from the true mean.

The magnitude of the bias is exactly $\sigma^2/N$. Its intuitive counterpart: one degree of freedom was spent estimating $\mu$. When you use $1/(N-1)$ instead of $1/N$ (Bessel's correction) the estimate becomes unbiased.

The general lesson from here: MLE does not always give an unbiased estimate. The guarantee it gives is different — it converges to the truth in the large data limit, but it can be biased with finite data.

sections.heading: 7. Three worked examples
sections.text:
Bernoulli. n trials, k of them 1 (7 heads in 10 tosses). The log-likelihood is $k\log p + (n-k)\log(1-p)$; setting the derivative to zero gives $p = k/n$. The MLE is the observed frequency itself.

Exponential. The log-likelihood is $n\log\lambda - \lambda\sum_i x_i$; from the derivative $\lambda = n/\sum_i x_i$, that is, the reciprocal of the sample mean. This makes sense, because the mean of the $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ distribution is $1/\lambda$.

$\mathrm{Uniform}(0,\theta)$. Here the method changes, and this is the real lesson. The likelihood is zero if $\theta$ is smaller than the largest observed value (that observation would have been impossible), and $1/\theta^n$ if it is larger. In the second case the likelihood falls as $\theta$ grows. So the best $\theta$ is the smallest possible $\theta$: the largest observed value.

Note: taking a derivative and setting it to zero does not work here, because the maximum is not at an interior point but on the boundary. The memorised rule "MLE means taking a derivative and setting it to zero" breaks exactly here. MLE is an arg max; the derivative is merely one way of finding it.

sections.heading: 8. The turning point: MLE is a loss function
sections.text:
Now the frame of the text is built.

Think of a regression model: $y = f(x;\theta) + \epsilon$, with $\epsilon$ Gaussian. The probability of one data point is the Gaussian density centred at $f(x_i;\theta)$. Take the log, sum over all points, drop the constants that do not depend on $\theta$. What remains is exactly this: the sum of the squares of the differences between $y_i$ and $f(x_i;\theta)$.

So MSE is not an arbitrarily chosen cost function. Under the assumption of Gaussian noise it is maximum likelihood itself.

Make the same move in classification. The model produces a probability $p_i$ for every example, and the label $t_i$ is either 0 or 1. Instead of picking the correct probability by hand, the Bernoulli formula does it automatically: $p_i^{t_i}(1-p_i)^{1-t_i}$. If the label is 1 the first factor is active, if it is 0 the second one is. Multiply over all examples, take the log, take the negative — what comes out is binary cross-entropy.

In the multi-class case the same computation with softmax: the sum of log-likelihoods reduces to the sum of the log probabilities of the correct classes only, and its negative is cross-entropy.

sections.heading: The result of the two derivations
sections.text:
Gaussian noise:
$$-\log p(y \mid x,\theta) \;\propto\; \sum_i \bigl(y_i - f(x_i;\theta)\bigr)^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{MSE}$$

Bernoulli label:
$$-\log p(t \mid w) = -\sum_i \bigl[\, t_i \log p_i + (1-t_i)\log(1-p_i) \,\bigr] \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{BCE}$$

sections.heading: Noise assumption, resulting loss
rows: negative log probability of the correct class

sections.heading: 9. Choosing a loss is choosing a noise model
sections.text:
The reading direction of the table above matters. It is usually read from left to right: "if my data looks like this, I use that loss." What is truly illuminating is reading it from right to left.

The moment you write L2 in code, you are saying, without noticing, "the error is Gaussian distributed." The moment you write L1 you are saying "the error is Laplace distributed, occasionally very deviant measurements arrive."

This is also the answer to the outlier question. Under the Gaussian assumption MLE gives you the mean; under the Laplace assumption, the median. Why the median is robust to outliers follows from here: the tails of the Laplace are heavy, that is, the model already expects an extreme observation now and then, so a single extreme value cannot drag the estimate.

The turning point in one sentence: under every loss function that looks deterministic there is a hidden probability model.

sections.heading: 10. Training a neural network is already doing MLE
sections.text:
Now scale it up, keeping the move the same.

In the bell curve example the thing you slid was a single number. In an MLP the thing you slide is millions of weights. The question does not change: set the weights so that the probability of seeing the training data is largest.

The sentence that completes the connection is this: the last layer of the network does not produce a number, it produces the parameter of a distribution.

In regression the output of the network is the mean of the Gaussian that generates y. In classification the softmax output is the set of probabilities of a categorical distribution. In both cases the network builds a probability model and you maximise the log-likelihood of that model.

Therefore your training loop — forward pass, loss, backpropagation, step — amounts to solving a maximum likelihood problem by gradient descent. Because it cannot be solved in closed form (as in the Gaussian mean), it is solved numerically; that is the whole difference.

One more connection: maximising the log-likelihood over the training data is the same as minimising the KL divergence between the model distribution and the true data distribution. This is what stands behind the sentence "we are approaching the true distribution" in generative modelling.

sections.heading: The same three steps at three scales
sections.text:
the theta you seek    route to the solution
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
five numbers, mu      a single number       closed form (the mean)
y = Ax + n            a signal vector       closed form (least squares)
MLP / VAE / DDPM      millions of weights   gradient descent

In all three rows the job is the same:
  1. write a probability model       p(data | theta)
  2. take the log, flip the sign     -log p
  3. minimise over theta

sections.heading: 11. When MLE is not enough
sections.text:
You tossed a coin three times and got heads three times. MLE's answer is p = 1: "this coin never comes up tails."

The answer is mathematically correct — what truly makes that data most probable is p = 1. But it is absurd, because the information you hold is very little and MLE accepts it without question.

This is the general failure mode: MLE mistakes the noise in the data for signal and fits it. This is precisely the probabilistic description of overfitting. As data grows the problem eases by itself, but with little data it is serious.

The same failure is in the Uniform example: the estimate is the largest observed value. The true upper bound is almost certainly larger than that, but MLE cannot see it because all it holds is what it has seen.

Two ways out: more data, or taking into account what you knew before seeing the data.

sections.heading: 12. MAP: not a separate method, a single extra factor
sections.text:
MAP adds a belief about $\theta$ to MLE: what did you think about $\theta$ before seeing the data?

In Bayes' rule the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior. MAP maximises this product. Taking the log turns the product into a sum, so MAP's loss function is MLE's loss function plus a penalty term.

Return to the three-heads example: if you place a reasonable prior saying the coin is close to fair, the answer is not 1 but a reasonable number pushed towards 1. As data grows the likelihood term overwhelms the prior and MAP approaches MLE. The weight of the prior is inversely proportional to the amount of data — decisive with little data, invisible with a lot.

The one distinguishing question, and the sentence worth memorising, is this: is the prior on the thing you are estimating? A prior on something else does not move you to MAP.

sections.heading: MLE and MAP
sections.text: $$\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta} \log p(x \mid \theta) \qquad \hat{\theta}_{\text{MAP}} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta} \bigl[\log p(x \mid \theta) + \log p(\theta)\bigr]$$

sections.heading: 13. Weight decay is exactly here
sections.text:
Place a zero-mean Gaussian prior on the weights: "I expect the weights to be small."

The logarithm of a Gaussian gives the square of the norm of the weight vector with a minus sign. Translated into the language of minimisation, your loss function becomes: the data term plus $\lambda$ times the square of the weights.

This is the weight decay you write in code every day.

The turning point in one sentence: L2 regularization is placing a Gaussian prior on the weights and doing MAP. Not an arbitrary trick, but the mathematics of a sentence.

By the same logic L1 regularization is placing a Laplace prior on the weights — and because the sharp peak of the Laplace encourages the solution to sit exactly at zero, it produces sparsity.

So your model contains two hidden probabilistic assumptions: your loss function chooses the noise, and your regularization term chooses the prior on the weights.

sections.heading: 14. VAE: what you are looking for is the weights, not z
sections.text:
In a VAE there is also a z, the latent variable. Are we looking for that too? No, and the difference is the key to the topic.

In the five-number example, once you found $\mu$ the job was done, you held 3.04. In a VAE there is no moment at which you can say "I found z", because z is separate for every image. There are 200,000 images with 200,000 z's and you are not chasing them one by one. You do not say "the z of this image is 3.2"; you say "the z of this image comes from this distribution."

What you are looking for is the rule that produces that distribution — that is, the weights again. When training ends you hold an encoder and a decoder; the z's themselves are nowhere. z is not something estimated, it is something integrated over.

From here comes a frequently asked question: there is a p(z) inside the VAE, is that not a prior? A prior, yes — but on z, and z is not being estimated. What is being estimated is the weights, and there is no prior on them.

The conclusion: the VAE, despite having variational in its name and a prior inside it, is doing MLE with respect to the weights. The KL term is also not a regularization — it keeps the distributions produced by the encoder around the standard normal so that the z you draw at generation time falls into a region the decoder recognises.

sections.heading: 15. Why the ELBO comes into play
sections.text:
In a VAE you cannot maximise the log-likelihood directly, because computing p(x) requires integrating over z and that integral has no closed form.

The solution is to work with a lower bound: you derive an expression that stays below the real target but is computable, and maximise that. Its name is the ELBO.

What matters is this: the target did not change. You are still doing maximum likelihood, you are just climbing a ladder underneath it because you cannot climb directly.

The same story holds in diffusion models, where the integral runs over a path of T steps. For the full derivation and a line by line comparison of the two models see the DDPM guide — it begins where this text ends.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: By sliding the unknown around, find the place that makes what you observed least surprising. The likelihood is not a probability distribution, it is a measure of explanatory power over the data. Taking the log does not change the answer, it only turns a product into a sum and makes the computation possible. If you assume Gaussian you get MSE, if you assume Bernoulli you get cross-entropy — that is, choosing a loss function is choosing a noise distribution. Training a neural network is the large-scale version of this: the network produces the parameter of a distribution and gradient descent climbs the log-likelihood. If you put a prior on the thing you are estimating it becomes MAP, and the name of the Gaussian prior is weight decay. In the VAE and in DDPM the target is still maximum likelihood; the only change is that, since the integral cannot be taken, one works with a lower bound.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: This text gives the order, the details are in the cards: the Gaussian derivation and the bias of the variance in ch03; the Bernoulli, Exponential and Uniform worked examples in math06; the step by step derivations from MLE to MSE and BCE in vs04; the MLE-MAP-Bayesian transition, the discussion of whom the prior is on, the connection between MAP and regularization and the LMMSE side in vs03; MLE and the KL reading for generative models in cs12; the diffusion form of the ELBO in ida11.

generative.title: Generative Models — The General Frame
generative.context: Generative Models · CS231n 12-13 · IDA 10-11 · ML-OVERALL 19-21 — the introduction to the other three walkthroughs
generative.summary: From the difference between classifying and generating, to why generating is structurally harder, to the axis along which the models separate (explicit or implicit density) and where autoregressive models, the VAE, the GAN and diffusion sit on that map. The introduction to the VAE, GAN and DDPM walkthroughs.

sections.heading: 1. Three questions, three model types
sections.text:
Think of a photograph of a dog. Looking at it you can ask three different things, and the three mean three separate models.

The first: **what is in this photograph**? The model takes the image and produces a label. What it learns is the probability of the label given the image. This is called a **discriminative** model — the classifier you already know.

The second: **produce a new photograph** for me. There is no label and no input. The model has to learn the distribution of images itself. This is a **generative** model.

The third: produce a photograph of a dog for me. You supply the label and the model produces images matching that label. A conditional generative model.

All three look like they belong to the same family, but there is a chasm between their difficulties, and the reason is hidden in something very simple.

sections.heading: 2. The density competition: why generating is harder
sections.text:
Probabilities have to sum to one. The critical question is: what is competing?

In a classifier, the labels compete for a single image. Dog or cat or bird — say you have a thousand labels, and a thousand things share one unit of probability. The model only has to be able to rank those thousand things.

In a generative model all possible images compete. Giving this photograph a high probability means taking probability away from some other image. And those other images are every image that could exist — all dogs, all cats, all landscapes, and beside them the astronomical multitude of meaningless pixel piles.

The model has to be able to rank all of them consistently. It has to learn by itself to give a real photograph a higher probability than noise.

The turning point in one sentence: classifying is solving a finite competition, generating is ranking the entire space of images.

The conditional generative model sits in between: the competition is still among all images but is split separately for each class. Harder than classifying, easier than unconditional generation.

sections.heading: Three models, three normalisations
sections.text:
$$\text{discriminative: } p(y \mid x), \quad \sum_y p(y \mid x) = 1 \qquad \text{(labels compete)}$$
$$\text{generator: } p(x), \quad \int p(x)\,dx = 1 \qquad \text{(all images compete)}$$
$$\text{conditional generative: } p(x \mid y) \qquad \text{(all images compete within each class)}$$

sections.heading: 3. What drawing a sample actually means
sections.text:
Maximum likelihood hands you a density. Drawing from it is a **separate ability**, and it is not free in every distribution — this is the step that is usually skipped and it is where the whole subject turns.

Take the one dimensional case, because there everything is visible. You have a few hundred measurements clustered around 3. Fit a Gaussian by maximum likelihood and you get a mean of 3 and a standard deviation of, say, 0.32 — in fact for a Gaussian the maximum likelihood solution is exactly the sample mean and the sample standard deviation, nothing more.

Now produce a new number. The recipe is this: draw $z$ from the standard normal, which a computer can do directly, and write $x = 3 + 0.32\,z$. That is the whole of sampling. **The recipe exists.**

Notice what the model does and does not say. The value $x = 1$ is not forbidden. It is six standard deviations out, so it will appear roughly once in a billion draws. The model never says do not produce this; it says **produce this almost never**.

This changes what the question even is. Asking whether a single sample fits the model is the wrong question — fit is not a property of one point. **The right picture is a histogram**: draw ten thousand samples, plot them, and lay that next to the histogram of the real data. If the two shapes sit on top of each other, the model is good.

sections.heading: 4. Why maximising likelihood does not collapse onto the data
sections.text:
There is an objection to raise here, and raising it explains the whole constraint.

If the goal is to make the observed points as probable as possible, why does the answer not simply pile all the mass onto exactly those points — an infinitely sharp spike at every measurement? That would make their likelihood enormous.

The answer is that **a density must integrate to one**. Mass placed at one point is mass taken from everywhere else. Spiking on the training points would make everything between them impossible, and the next measurement you take — which will land between them — would then have near-zero likelihood.

So the normalisation is not bookkeeping. It is the thing that forces the model to **cover** the data instead of memorising it. The plain autoencoder's failure, which is the subject of a later section, is exactly what happens when this constraint is absent.

And then the hard part. In one dimension the recipe $\mu + \sigma z$ existed. For images there is no such recipe: even if you could write $p_\theta(x)$ down, you could not invert it, and the space has a hundred thousand dimensions with no obvious place to start. **Generative modelling is therefore the business of building a sampler, not of writing down a density.** Every family in this walkthrough is a different answer to that one problem.

sections.heading: 5. Low density does not mean a bad sample
sections.text:
A natural question follows: if samples are drawn in proportion to density, does drawing from a low density region give you a bad image, and a high density region a good one?

No, and the distinction matters.

In a correct model a low density sample is **rare but real**: an unusual pose, odd lighting, an uncommon face. In the one dimensional height example it is the person who is 1.50 m tall. They exist. A model that never produced them would not be better — it would be broken, because it has lost the tail of the distribution.

A broken face is a different object entirely. It is not a rare point of the data distribution; it is a point where the data density is **zero** and the model put mass anyway. That is not rarity, it is **error**. The height analogue is not 1.50 m, it is four metres.

So: 1.50 m is the tail of the distribution, four metres is the mistake of the model.

sections.heading: 6. Why the one dimensional picture hides the real difficulty
sections.text:
The reason the height example cannot show you a broken sample is dimension, and seeing this is worth more than the example itself.

On the height axis nearly every point is a plausible value. The axis is dense with legitimate numbers, so a model that misses slightly still produces something sensible.

In pixel space the opposite holds. The set of real images is a **vanishingly thin sheet** inside the space; pick a point at random and you get noise with overwhelming probability. The model's task is to place essentially all of its mass onto that thin sheet. A broken face means the sample **fell slightly off the sheet**.

That is the whole difference: in one dimension missing slightly still gives a plausible number, in a hundred thousand dimensions missing slightly gives garbage.

There is also a second, more practical reason low density and poor quality end up correlated in real models. A model's error is largest exactly where it saw the fewest examples, and low density regions are by definition the sparsely sampled ones. So the tails of a real model are not only rare, they are also **where it is least trustworthy** — two separate facts that happen to point the same way.

sections.heading: 7. Cutting the tails on purpose
sections.text:
Which raises the obvious thought: if the tails are the risky part, why not refuse to sample them? There is no threshold in plain sampling — the density is already the mechanism, and a rare region is rarely visited by construction. But the thought is a real technique, and it appears in three places under three names.

The truncation trick, from BigGAN: draw the latent vector, and if its norm exceeds a threshold, **throw it away and draw again**. This cuts the tails of the prior literally.

Classifier-free guidance with a scale above one: the sampled distribution becomes proportional to $p(x)\,p(y \mid x)^{s}$, sharpened towards the typical region.

Temperature and top-p in language models: the same idea written on a token distribution.

All three buy the same thing and pay the same price. **Fidelity and prompt adherence go up, diversity goes down** — and pushed far enough, every sample starts to look like every other. That is why the 1.50 m case matters: a model that refuses it looks cleaner and is worse.

sections.heading: 8. The bridge between them
sections.text:
The three are not disconnected. **Bayes**' rule lets you build a conditional generative model out of a classifier and a generative model you already hold: you weight the ratio given by the classifier with the unconditional density.

This is not only a theoretical link. In diffusion this was exactly classifier guidance — using the gradient of a separately trained classifier to push generation towards a class. Classifier-free guidance then does the same job inside a single model.

So the root of the question "how do I give the condition to the model" is here.

sections.heading: 9. What these models are good for
sections.text:
Generation is what comes to mind first, but the full list is wider, and some of the items are more useful.

Producing samples: synthesis, **data augmentation**, completing a missing modality.

Anomaly detection: examples to which the model assigns low probability are outliers. For this the model must actually be able to compute a probability — that is the practical counterpart of the distinction coming shortly.

Learning features without labels: a network that learns to model the data also learns its structure; a classifier can then be attached on top with a small labelled set.

Modelling uncertainty: cases where a single input admits several correct outputs. Text to image generation is like this — there is no single correct answer, there is a distribution. Classifier logic collapses here, because taking an average produces a meaningless output.

sections.heading: 10. The real distinction: can you write down the density
sections.text:
The fundamental axis separating generative models is not the architecture but this question: can the model assign a probability to an image placed in front of it?

Explicit density. The model can compute p(x). It can say how probable an image is, and can therefore be used in anomaly detection and model comparison.

Implicit density. The model cannot compute p(x) but can draw samples from it. It produces images for you, but cannot answer the question "how probable is this image".

The **explicit** ones split in two among themselves: those that can compute the density exactly, and those that can only approach it with a lower bound.

The entire map is built on these two questions.

sections.heading: The map
sections.text:
Generative models
├── Explicit density  (p(x) computable)
│   ├── Exact
│   │   └── Autoregressive       chain rule, full log-likelihood
│   └── Approximate
│       ├── VAE                  ELBO, lower bound
│       └── Diffusion            ELBO, lower bound
└── Implicit density  (p(x) not computable, samples drawable)
    └── GAN                      adversarial training

sections.heading: 11. Autoregressive: splitting the density into pieces
sections.text:
The most direct route. Think of the image or the text as a sequence and split the probability with the **chain rule**: the probability of the first element, times the probability of the second conditioned on the first, times the probability of the third conditioned on the first two, and so on.

Every factor is a small prediction problem modelled by a network. The whole product is the true probability — no approximation, no lower bound. That is why the training signal is the most honest in this family.

All language models are of this kind. A causally masked Transformer trains exactly this, in parallel.

The cost shows up at generation: samples have to be produced in order. Generating a 1024 by 1024 image over raw pixels means millions of sequential steps — practically impossible.

The modern solution is to abandon raw pixels: first compress the image into discrete codes, then generate that short code sequence autoregressively. A few thousand steps instead of millions.

sections.heading: 12. The autoencoder: why it is not a generative model
sections.text:
An autoencoder compresses and unfolds: the encoder reduces to a narrow code, the decoder rebuilds, and the loss is the reconstruction error. No labels are needed and the code it learns is genuinely meaningful — the classical route to learning features without labels, the ancestor of modern self-supervised methods.

But it cannot generate, and the reason is instructive: to produce a new image you have to sample a new code, and nothing tells you which codes are valid. There are **holes** in the code space, and the gaps produce garbage.

So producing a valid code is as hard as directly producing a valid image. You have gained nothing.

The only thing missing is knowing where the code comes from. The VAE adds exactly that.

sections.heading: 13. Three answers, three different trade-offs
sections.text:
VAE. It forces the code to come from a known distribution, so at generation time you know where to sample from. The cost is that the marginal likelihood is no longer computable — you work with a lower bound. Its training is stable, its latent space legible, its output **blurry**.

GAN. It abandons computing probabilities entirely. It builds a model that only samples and has the quality measured by a discriminator. Its output is sharp and generation is single-step, but training is a search for an equilibrium; there is no honest number you can track, and **mode collapse** is a structural risk.

Diffusion. It splits the hard problem into a thousand easy ones: instead of generating in one step, it walks from noise to image in small steps. Its training is as stable as the VAE's, its quality better than the GAN's, and its mode coverage the best. The cost is generation speed — dozens of forward passes instead of one.

The common denominator of the three trade-offs is this: quality, diversity, speed and training stability cannot all be had at once. Every model is defined by which of these four it sacrifices.

sections.heading: 14. The common principle underneath the three
sections.text:
The training principle of all of them except the GAN is the same: **maximum likelihood**. You look for the parameters that make the training data most probable.

Autoregressive models do this directly, because they can compute the probability exactly. The VAE and diffusion cannot do it directly — in the first there is an intractable integral over a latent variable, in the second over a T-step path — so they work with a computable **lower bound**. The target does not change, only the ladder being climbed changes.

The GAN stands outside this line, and its whole character comes from that: there is no honest likelihood it optimises, and in its place there is a learned criterion.

If you need to recall MLE itself, see the MLE guide; the sentence there, "choosing a noise is choosing a loss", applies here too — that is exactly why the reconstruction term of the VAE is a sum of squares.

sections.heading: 15. Where things stand today
sections.text:
The era in which the families competed is over; modern systems use all three at once.

A text to image model is typically built like this: a VAE compresses the image into a small latent space, what keeps that VAE's decoder sharp is a GAN discriminator, and the actual generation is done by a **diffusion** model in the latent space. The condition comes from text and is attached with cross-attention.

The language side remained autoregressive, and it has come back to image generation too: converting the image into discrete codes and generating those codes autoregressively is competitive again.

So the map is not a ranking, it is a toolbox. The right question is not "which one is best" but "what can I sacrifice in this problem".

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: In classification the labels compete for a single image, in generation all images compete universally — this is the only reason generating is structurally hard. The real axis separating the models is not architecture but whether they can compute the density. Autoregressive computes it exactly but generates slowly; the VAE and diffusion work with a lower bound; the GAN abandons computation entirely. A plain autoencoder cannot generate because there is no telling where a valid code comes from. Quality, diversity, speed and stability cannot be had at once; every model is defined by which one it sacrifices. Under all of them except the GAN lies maximum likelihood. Maximum likelihood gives you a density; **drawing from it is a separate ability** and for images no recipe exists, which is why generative modelling is the business of building a sampler. Likelihood does not collapse onto the training points only because the density must integrate to one. A low density sample is **rare but real**, not bad — a bad sample is a point where the data density is zero and the model put mass anyway. The one dimensional picture hides this because in high dimension the set of real images is a vanishingly thin sheet. Cutting the tails deliberately — truncation, guidance above one, temperature — buys fidelity and costs diversity.

sections.heading: Where to go next
sections.text: This text is the introduction; it continues in three separate walkthroughs: VAE (how it solved where the code comes from, the ELBO, reparameterization), GAN (the learned loss, mode collapse, DCGAN-StyleGAN-CycleGAN) and DDPM (the forward and reverse process, the collapse of the ELBO into MSE, CFG, latent diffusion). On the card side: the discriminative-generative distinction and the taxonomy are in cs12, the autoregressive chain rule also in cs12, GAN theory and the wide frame of the diffusion family in cs13.

vae.title: Autoencoder and VAE — A Complete Walkthrough
vae.context: CME 296 Lecture 4 Part 1, following the slides · Autoencoder · VAE · refined VAE · VQ · latent diffusion · CS231n 12 · ML-OVERALL 19
vae.summary: From pixel space to a latent space, in the order of CME 296 Lecture 4: the three limitations of pixels and the wish list, semantic against perceptual similarity; attempt 1, the autoencoder with its encoder, decoder, compression ratio and loss, and why it cannot generate; attempt 2, the VAE, with probabilistic encoder and decoder, the ELBO derived through Jensen and expanded into reconstruction and KL, the squared error and KL in closed form, reparameterization, and why the result is blurry; attempt 3, the refined VAE with weighted terms, LPIPS and an adversarial critic, each with its failure mode; VQ as a third way; and latent diffusion, training in the frozen encoder's latent with the flow matching loss and decoding at the end.

sections.heading: 1. Where this lecture starts: the representation box
sections.text:
Lecture 4 is about multimodal guided generation, and its opening slide draws the whole pipeline as three boxes: a condition (the text "A teddy bear reading a book"), a black-box architecture, and the image that comes out. Part 1 looks only at the last box, the representation: in what space should the image live while the model generates it? Part 2 is about representing the condition (text encoders, CLIP), Part 3 about using it to guide generation.

Why this question matters before anything else: to generate, you need a small control panel. You cannot draw a face by tuning a million numbers by hand, but if you had twenty dials, age, pose, hair colour, expression, every combination would give a face. That set of dials is the latent space, a single setting is $z$, and generating means choosing a $z$ and turning it into an image. The rest of Part 1 is the sequence of attempts to build that panel.

sections.heading: 2. The naive approach: pixel space
sections.text:
The simplest representation is the image itself. A colour image of height $H$ and width $W$ is three stacked grids, one per channel (R, G, B):

$$x_{\text{image}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}, \qquad n = \underbrace{H \times W}_{\text{number of pixels}} \times 3$$

Every pixel holds three numbers, so the image is one point in an $n$-dimensional space. Generation in pixel space means learning a distribution over these points directly, which is what the previous three lectures did.

sections.heading: 3. Three limitations of pixel space
sections.text:
High dimensionality. The slide's example is a $1024 \times 1024$ image: $n = 1024^2 \times 3 \approx 10^6$ numbers (exactly 3,145,728, so a few million). Every step of a diffusion or flow model runs a network on all of them, and the cost of attention grows quadratically with the number of positions. Most of the model's capacity goes into handling the size, not the content.

Redundant information. Zoom into the teddy bear's arm: a patch of fur where neighbouring pixels are almost identical. Pixels are strongly correlated, so most of the $n$ numbers are predictable from their neighbours. A model working in pixels devotes a large part of its capacity to fine texture a human barely notices.

A representation that is not meaningful. Take an image $z$ and move a little in pixel space, $z + \epsilon$: the result is not a slightly different teddy bear but gibberish, a noisy smear. The same happens with an innocent change: shift the image one pixel to the right and, to a human, it is the same picture, but in pixel space the two are far apart. Distances in pixel space do not follow what the image shows. The slide draws the good case and the bad case: in a meaningful space, images sit inside a smooth density and the point between two teddy bears is again a teddy bear (thumbs up); in pixel space the images are isolated points and the space between them is empty (thumbs down).

sections.heading: 4. The wish list of an ideal space
rows: few enough numbers that a generator can be trained and run
every number carries information, nothing is predictable from the rest
moving a little gives a different but valid image: $z + \epsilon$ turns a brown teddy bear into a white one, not into noise

sections.heading: 5. Two kinds of similarity
sections.text:
Before building the space, the lecture fixes two words, because "these two images are similar" can mean two different things.

Semantic similarity: the two images show the same thing in the same arrangement. The slide's adjectives are structural, global geometry, and "low" frequency. A teddy bear reading a book on a table and a teddy bear reading a book on a bed are semantically close: the overall shapes and their layout agree, even though the pixels do not.

Perceptual similarity: the two images look alike to the eye up close. The adjectives are local, texture, and "high" frequency. Two close-ups of fur, with the same fluffiness and the same grain, are perceptually close even if the bears are posed differently.

A third notion is what a pixel-wise distance measures: how much the pixel values overlap. It is neither of the two above. A one-pixel shift destroys it while keeping both semantic and perceptual similarity; a slight blur barely changes it while ruining perceptual similarity. Keep this triangle in mind: the whole story of the refined VAE in sections 29 to 34 is about replacing the pixel-wise distance with losses that measure the other two.

The frequency words come back at the end: the encoder of a latent diffusion model keeps the low-frequency, semantic content, and the decoder has to recreate the high-frequency, perceptual content.

sections.heading: 6. Attempt 1: learn the representation with an autoencoder
sections.text:
Goal: learn a latent representation through a proxy task, reconstruction (Masci et al., Stacked Convolutional Auto-Encoders, 2011). Nobody can write down the ideal space by hand, but we can ask a network to compress an image and then rebuild it. If the rebuilt image is right, whatever sits in the middle must contain what matters.

The slide's picture: the image in pixel space, $H \times W$ with $C$ channels, goes through an encoder into the latent space, a smaller grid $h \times w$ with $c$ channels, and a decoder brings it back to $H \times W \times C$. The narrow middle is the bottleneck. Encoder and decoder together form the autoencoder.

The bottleneck is the forcing element. Had the latent been as wide as the image, the network would learn nothing and copy the input. Because it is narrow, it has to decide what to keep and what to throw away, and what it keeps turns out to be the real structure in the dataset.

Note that the latent is still a grid, not a flat vector: it keeps the spatial layout, only coarser. How much coarser is measured by one number.

sections.heading: The spatial compression ratio
sections.text:
$$f = \frac{H}{h} = \frac{W}{w}$$

$f$ is how many pixels along each side are summarised by one latent position. With $f = 8$, a $1024 \times 1024$ image becomes a $128 \times 128$ latent grid, and each latent position stands for an $8 \times 8$ block of pixels. The total number of values drops by $f^2 \cdot C / c$: with $C = 3$ and $c = 4$ that is $64 \cdot 3 / 4 = 48$. The ratio does not depend on the resolution, only on $f$ and on the two channel counts.

sections.heading: 7. The encoder: downsampling with convolutions
sections.text:
The encoder is a network $E_\varphi$ with parameters $\varphi$ that maps an image $x$ to its latent code:

$$z = E_\varphi(x)$$

It reduces the size with downsampling operations built from convolutions. The slides recall the two building blocks. A convolution slides a small kernel over the image and writes one number per position, a weighted sum of the neighbourhood; with a stride of 2 it writes every second position and halves each side. Pooling takes a small window and keeps one summary of it, for example the maximum; it also halves each side. Three halvings give $f = 8$.

Each step trades spatial size for channels: the grid gets smaller, the description at each position gets richer, until the last layer projects down to the $c$ channels of the latent.

sections.heading: 8. The decoder: upsampling with transposed convolutions
sections.text:
The decoder is a second network $D_\theta$ with parameters $\theta$ that maps a latent code back to pixel space:

$$\hat{x} = D_\theta(z)$$

It mirrors the encoder with upsampling operations, the slide's reverse convolutions, also called transposed convolutions: each input value is spread over a small output window through a learned kernel, so each side grows, typically by 2 per layer. The hat in $\hat{x}$ marks a reconstruction, the network's estimate of $x$.

sections.heading: 9. The loss of the autoencoder
sections.text:
Goal: learn how to reconstruct the input. Loss: compare the input $x$ with the reconstructed input $\hat{x}$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{AE}} = \bigl\| x - \underbrace{D_\theta(\overbrace{E_\varphi(x)}^{z})}_{\hat{x}} \bigr\|^2$$

Read from the inside out: the encoder makes $z$, the decoder turns $z$ into $\hat{x}$, and the loss is the squared pixel-wise distance between the two, summed over all $n$ numbers. Both networks are trained together by gradient descent on this one number. No labels are needed: the supervision signal is the input itself, which is why the autoencoder is unsupervised.

sections.heading: 10. What an autoencoder is good for
sections.text:
Even before generation, the trained pair is useful.

Learning features without labels. When training ends you discard the decoder and keep the encoder; a small classifier attached on top can be trained with far fewer labels. This is the ancestor of modern self-supervised methods.

Denoising. If you deliberately add noise to the input and give the clean version as the target, the network learns to clean.

Anomaly detection. An autoencoder trained on normal data reconstructs normal examples well. When an outlier arrives the reconstruction error rises, and that error itself becomes the anomaly score.

Dimensionality reduction. A linear autoencoder does roughly what PCA does; with non-linear layers it also captures curved structures PCA cannot see.
