sections.caption: Top: the plain autoencoder. The encoder $E_\varphi$ maps the image to one latent point $z$, the decoder $D_\theta$ maps it back, and the only loss is the reconstruction error. Bottom: the variational autoencoder. The encoder now outputs a mean and a standard deviation, $z$ is drawn around the mean with the noise $\epsilon$, and a second loss term pulls these distributions towards $p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, which is what lets generation start from $p(z)$ with no encoder at all.

sections.heading: 11. Checklist for attempt 1, and why a plain autoencoder cannot generate
sections.text:
The slide's checklist: tractable dimension, yes; compact representation, yes; meaningful representation, no.

The first two come for free from the bottleneck. The third fails, and the slide shows why with the same picture as the thumbs-down case: the training images land as isolated points in the latent space, with nothing in between.

Try generating with it. Training ends and the reconstructions are good. Now pick a random $z$ and give it to the decoder: what comes out is garbage. The encoder was free to place the codes wherever it liked; it may put one image around 50 and another at minus 30. Huge gaps remain in between, regions the decoder has never seen. And you do not even know which $z$ are valid: nothing tells you where to sample from.

What is missing fits in one sentence: the latent space has no structure. The whole of the VAE is the answer to that sentence.

sections.heading: Why a plain autoencoder cannot generate
12. Attempt 2: learn a constrained latent space
sections.text:
Goal: enforce some structure on the latent space (Kingma and Welling, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, 2013). The architecture on the slide is the same picture as attempt 1; what changes is only the middle, now labelled a constrained bottleneck, and the pair is a constrained autoencoder.

The constraint is a decision about where $z$ comes from. Since the codes have no structure, model them as if they were drawn from a fixed, known distribution, the prior. The standard choice is the standard normal:

$$p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$$

Now it is clear where $z$ should be, and at generation time you know where to sample from: draw from the standard normal and hand it to the decoder. But this is still a wish. Something has to force the encoder to comply, and that force will be the KL term that comes out of the derivation below. To get there, both networks first have to become probabilistic.

sections.heading: 13. The revised encoder: a distribution, not a point
sections.text:
The encoder no longer outputs one code but a distribution over codes:

$$z \sim q_\varphi(z \mid x), \qquad q_\varphi(\cdot \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu_\varphi(x), \sigma_\varphi^2(x)\bigr)$$

You cannot ask a neural network for "a distribution"; it can only output numbers. So the network $q_\varphi$ outputs the parameters of one: a mean $\mu_\varphi(x)$ and a standard deviation $\sigma_\varphi(x)$, one pair per latent dimension (a diagonal Gaussian). Read it as: "the code of this image is around $\mu_\varphi(x)$, with this much uncertainty $\sigma_\varphi(x)$." The letter changes from $E_\varphi$ to $q_\varphi$ to mark that the output is now a distribution; the parameters $\varphi$ are the same kind of object, the encoder's weights.

sections.heading: 14. The revised decoder, and the constant-variance assumption
sections.text:
The decoder becomes a distribution over images given a code:

$$z \sim p(z), \qquad x \sim p_\theta(x \mid z), \qquad p_\theta(\cdot \mid z) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu_\theta(z), \sigma_\theta^2(z)\bigr)$$

The slide adds an assumption, for simplicity: the variance is constant, $\sigma_\theta^2(z) = \sigma^2 I$. So the decoder network outputs only a mean image $\mu_\theta(z)$, and that mean is what we call the reconstruction, $\hat{x} = \mu_\theta(z)$. This small assumption will explain later why the reconstruction term turns into a sum of squares (section 22).

The roles are asymmetric. The decoder $p_\theta$ together with the prior $p(z)$ is the generative model itself: draw $z$, decode. The encoder $q_\varphi$ is a helper that exists to make training possible, as the next sections show.

sections.heading: 15. The objective: maximum likelihood again
sections.text:
There is no new principle:

$$\max_\theta \ \log p_\theta(x)$$

We look for the decoder weights that make the training images most probable. If we knew the code of every image this would be easy. But $z$ is hidden, so the probability of an image has to be summed over every code that could have produced it, each weighted by the prior:

$$p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz$$

This is the marginal likelihood, "marginal" because $z$ has been integrated out.

sections.heading: 16. Why the integral cannot be computed
sections.text:
This integral has no closed form and cannot be taken numerically either. The decoder is a neural network: whatever $z$ you give it, it produces something. You do not know in advance which codes are candidates for producing this image; $z$ is continuous and high dimensional, so summing over all of them is out of reach, and random draws from the prior almost never land on the few codes that matter.

Try going around it with Bayes' rule, which relates $z$ and $x$: the posterior is the decoder times the prior, divided by the marginal. Solve it for the marginal and the integral seems to disappear. The equation holds for any single $z$, so pick one, evaluate the numerator, divide, done.

Except for the denominator. $p_\theta(z \mid x)$ is the true posterior, the distribution of which codes could have produced this image. Evaluating it needs its normalising constant, and that constant is exactly $p_\theta(x)$, the integral we were running away from. The numerator is computable; the denominator sends you back to the start.

sections.heading: Bayes' rule between z and x
sections.text:
$$p_\theta(z \mid x) = \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{p_\theta(x)} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad p_\theta(x) = \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{p_\theta(z \mid x)}$$

The numerator is the decoder and the prior, both computable. The denominator is the true posterior, which needs $p_\theta(x)$ again. The VAE breaks this circle by replacing $p_\theta(z \mid x)$ with a learned $q_\varphi(z \mid x)$.

sections.heading: 17. The encoder was not derived from the equation, it was added from outside
sections.text:
This distinction is easy to miss, and if you miss it the VAE never settles.

The true posterior $p_\theta(z \mid x)$ is the mathematical object that appears when you unfold the equation, and it cannot be computed.

The encoder $q_\varphi(z \mid x)$ is a decision: since the posterior cannot be derived, place a separate network next to the model to approximate it. It answers the question "which codes could have produced this image?" in a single forward pass, $x$ in, $\mu_\varphi$ and $\sigma_\varphi$ out, no integral. The slide's phrase for it is a convenient variational distribution, and "variational" in the name of the model refers to exactly this: optimising over a family of distributions $q_\varphi$.

sections.heading: 18. Step 1: a lower bound with Jensen's inequality
sections.text:
The slide's title: re-using the ELBO trick from Lecture 1. There is a peak you cannot climb directly; underneath it you build a computable ladder and climb that. The slide gives the result and the hint, "use Jensen's inequality on a convenient variational distribution". Here is the derivation in three lines.

Multiply and divide by $q_\varphi(z \mid x)$ inside the integral, which changes nothing:

$$\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x, z)\, dz = \log \int q_\varphi(z \mid x)\, \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\varphi(z \mid x)}\, dz = \log \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\varphi(z \mid x)}\Bigl[\frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\varphi(z \mid x)}\Bigr]$$

The integral against $q_\varphi$ is now an average over codes drawn from the encoder, something we can estimate by sampling. The logarithm is concave, so the log of an average is at least the average of the logs (Jensen's inequality). Swapping them gives the bound:

$$\log p_\theta(x) \geq \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\varphi(z \mid x)}\Bigl[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\varphi(z \mid x)}\Bigr] = \text{ELBO}$$

ELBO stands for Evidence Lower BOund; the evidence is $\log p_\theta(x)$. A two-number check of Jensen: for the values 1 and 100 with equal weight, the log of the average is $\log 50.5 = 3.92$, the average of the logs is $(0 + 4.61)/2 = 2.30$. The bound is below, as promised.

sections.heading: How tight the ladder is
sections.text:
The gap between the two sides is not arbitrary. Writing it out exactly:

$$\log p_\theta(x) = \text{ELBO} + D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(q_\varphi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\bigr)$$

The missing piece is how far the encoder is from the true posterior. You cannot compute it, but a KL divergence is never negative, which is exactly why the ELBO is a lower bound. The better the encoder approximates the posterior, the smaller the gap and the closer the ladder reaches the peak. Maximising the ELBO over $\varphi$ therefore trains the encoder to approximate the posterior, and maximising it over $\theta$ trains the decoder to explain the data.

sections.heading: 19. Step 2: expand the terms
sections.text:
The slide's hint: use the properties of the log function and rearrange. The joint factorises as decoder times prior, $p_\theta(x, z) = p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)$, so the log of the ratio splits into a sum:

$$\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q_\varphi(z \mid x)} = \log p_\theta(x \mid z) + \log \frac{p(z)}{q_\varphi(z \mid x)}$$

Take the average over $z \sim q_\varphi(z \mid x)$. The second part, averaged under $q_\varphi$, is minus the KL divergence from $q_\varphi$ to the prior, by the definition of KL. What remains is the slide's line:

$$\text{ELBO} = \mathbb{E}_z\bigl[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\bigr] - \mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_\varphi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\bigr)$$

The intractable posterior is gone. Both terms involve only the encoder, the decoder and the prior.

sections.heading: 20. The loss function of the variational autoencoder
sections.text:
VAE stands for Variational AutoEncoder. Goal: learn how to reconstruct the input using a structured latent space. Training minimises, so the loss is the negative ELBO:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = \underbrace{-\mathbb{E}_z\bigl[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\bigr]}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_\varphi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\bigr)}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}}$$

The slide's labels: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}$ is the reconstruction, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}$ the regularization of the latent space. And the slide's word for the relation between them: a trade-off.

sections.heading: 21. The two terms pull in opposite directions
sections.text:
The reconstruction term says: let the code of every image be distinguishable, otherwise the decoder cannot know which image to rebuild. On its own it would push the encoder to make $\sigma_\varphi$ tiny and the means far apart, which is the plain autoencoder and its isolated points again.

The KL term says: let every code distribution look like the standard normal. On its own it would make the encoder output the same $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ for every image; the code would then carry no information and the decoder would print an average blur.

The balance is between the two. The result is a latent space that is both full and discriminative: no gaps for a sampled $z$ to fall into, yet the codes of different images are not stuck together either. If you had to explain the VAE in one sentence, this would be it.

sections.heading: 22. Why the reconstruction term becomes a squared error
sections.text:
Recall the constant-variance decoder of section 14, $p_\theta(x \mid z) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta(z), \sigma^2 I)$. Take the log of this Gaussian density for an image with $n$ numbers:

$$\log p_\theta(x \mid z) = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \bigl\| x - \mu_\theta(z) \bigr\|^2 - \frac{n}{2} \log(2\pi\sigma^2)$$

The exponential is gone and what remains is the squared distance between the image and the decoder's mean, plus a constant that does not depend on any weight. So, with $\hat{x} = \mu_\theta(z)$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\, \mathbb{E}_z\, \| x - \hat{x} \|^2 + \text{const}$$

Two lessons. First, this is the general rule from the MLE walkthrough in local form: assume Gaussian noise and you get MSE; had the decoder been Bernoulli (used for black and white images), cross-entropy would have come out in the same place. Second, the assumed variance $\sigma^2$ is not innocent: it sets the weight of reconstruction against the KL term. A small $\sigma^2$ means "trust the pixels" and a large reconstruction weight. Attempt 3 will make this weight an explicit knob, $\lambda_{\text{rec}}$.

sections.heading: 23. The KL term in closed form
sections.text:
The slides keep $\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}$ as a symbol, but for a diagonal Gaussian encoder and a standard normal prior it is a short formula, summed over the latent dimensions $j$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{j} \Bigl( \mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - \log \sigma_j^2 - 1 \Bigr)$$

Read the two parts separately. $\mu_j^2$ pulls every mean towards 0, so codes cannot run away to 50 or minus 30. $\sigma_j^2 - \log \sigma_j^2 - 1$ is zero exactly at $\sigma_j = 1$ and positive elsewhere: at $\sigma_j = 0.1$ it is $0.01 + 4.61 - 1 = 3.61$, at $\sigma_j = 3$ it is $9 - 2.20 - 1 = 5.80$. So it punishes both a code that is too sure of itself (the isolated-point failure) and one that is too vague. No sampling is needed for this term; it is computed directly from the encoder's outputs.

sections.heading: 24. The reparameterization trick: why it is compulsory
sections.text:
The reconstruction term needs a $z$ drawn from $q_\varphi(z \mid x)$. But sampling is a random operation and the gradient cannot pass through it: the question "how would the loss change if the encoder's mean moved slightly" has no derivative through a dice roll.

The solution is to take the randomness out of the path. Instead of drawing $z$ directly, draw a noise from the standard normal and write $z$ as the mean plus the standard deviation times that noise:

$$z = \mu_\varphi(x) + \sigma_\varphi(x) \odot \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$$

Now the randomness is a separate input that does not depend on any parameter; $\mu_\varphi$ and $\sigma_\varphi$ reach $z$ through a multiplication and an addition, and the gradient flows through both. ($\odot$ is element-wise multiplication.) You have seen the same move in diffusion, where $x_t$ is written as a weighted sum of the clean image and a noise: in both places the point is to put the randomness in a form the gradient can flow around.

sections.heading: 25. The difference between training and generation
sections.text:
In training the chain is: an image arrives, the encoder gives the distribution of its code, a $z$ is drawn by reparameterization, the decoder rebuilds the image, and the two-term loss is computed.

At generation the encoder is not used at all. You draw $z$ directly from the standard normal and hand it to the decoder.

This is the practical proof of why the KL term exists: the $z$ you draw at generation has to fall into a region the decoder recognises, and the only thing pulling the training codes there is that term. The encoder is not thrown away, though: if you want to turn an image into a latent code (search, editing, anomaly detection, or the latent diffusion of section 37) you still need it.

sections.heading: 26. How the latent dimensions acquire meaning
sections.text:
The prior is diagonal, so its dimensions are independent. Because the KL term pushes the encoder to comply, the dimensions of $z$ also tend to become independent of each other.

The result: changing a single dimension tends to change a single thing in the image. In a digit dataset one dimension may change the digit itself, another the stroke thickness or the slant. This is a tendency, not a guarantee, but it is why a VAE produces a more legible latent space than a GAN, and it is the slide's "meaningful representation" in practice.

sections.heading: 27. Is the VAE doing MLE or MAP?
sections.text:
A frequent question: there is a $p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ inside, is that not a prior, and does the VAE therefore do MAP?

The distinguishing test is: is the prior on the thing you are estimating? In a VAE what you estimate is the weights $\theta$ and $\varphi$, and there is no prior on them. $p(z)$ really is a prior, but on $z$, and $z$ is not estimated; it is integrated over. So the VAE, despite the word variational in its name, does maximum likelihood with respect to the weights (through a lower bound), exactly the slide's $\max_\theta \log p_\theta(x)$. To do MAP you would put a prior on the weights, and the name of that is weight decay.

sections.heading: 28. Checklist for attempt 2: the reconstruction is not truthful
sections.text:
The slide's checklist: tractable dimension, compact representation and meaningful representation are all ticked. A fourth line appears and fails: truthful representation. Next to it the slide shows the teddy bear $x$ and its reconstruction $\hat{x}$: the same bear, clearly blurred.

The cause is not the architecture but the loss. Section 22 showed that the reconstruction term is a squared error, and a squared error chooses the average in the face of uncertainty. If the model is not sure exactly where an edge is, the cheapest answer is the middle of the possibilities, and the average of sharp edges is a blurry edge. The numbers in the figure below: with two equally likely edge positions, guessing either sharp edge costs an expected MSE of 0.100, printing their average costs 0.050, half as much. The loss literally rewards the blur.

A KL that is too strong adds to it: if the code carries little information, the decoder cannot know the details, and the average is again its best answer.

Other model families escape this in two different ways, and both reappear below. A GAN changes the loss: a discriminator catches average images as fake, so averaging is no longer rewarded (attempt 3 borrows exactly this). Diffusion does not have to resolve all the uncertainty in one step: it spreads it over many small denoising steps, each of which commits to a little more detail. Latent diffusion uses both at once: a VAE for compression, a discriminator for a sharp decoder, and diffusion for generation.

sections.heading: Why squared error blurs: the average of sharp edges
sections.caption: Computed on one row of 40 pixels. Left: the decoder cannot tell whether the edge is at position 0.4 (blue) or 0.6 (green). The prediction that minimises the expected squared error is their pixel-wise average (amber), a two-step edge that matches neither possibility, and its expected error is half that of committing to one sharp edge. Right: with the edge anywhere in a range, the average of the sharp possibilities becomes a smooth ramp, which is exactly what blur looks like. The fix cannot come from a better network; it has to come from a loss that stops rewarding the average.

sections.heading: 29. Attempt 3: address the limitations of the original VAE
sections.text:
Goal: avoid blurriness. The first move is to put an explicit weight on each of the two terms:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = \lambda_{\text{rec}}\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} + \lambda_{\text{KL}}\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}$$

The labels are the same as before, reconstruction and latent space regularization. The lecture then revisits each term with its typical weight and what goes wrong when the weight is too high, and adds two new terms aimed at the blur.

sections.heading: 30. Refresher on the reconstruction loss
sections.text:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} = \| x - \hat{x} \|^2$$

Idea: check the reconstruction of the input. Description: an $L_1$ or $L_2$ pixel-wise distance between output and actual image ($L_2$ is the square above, $L_1$ the sum of absolute differences, which is a little less prone to averaging because its optimum under uncertainty is the median rather than the mean). Weight: $\lambda_{\text{rec}} \approx 1$. If $\lambda_{\text{rec}}$ is too high, this can produce blurry outputs: the pixel-wise term dominates and, as the figure in section 28 showed, its optimum under uncertainty is the blur.

sections.heading: 31. Refresher on the KL regularization
sections.text:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} = \mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_\varphi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\bigr)$$

Idea: make the latent space more structured. Description: the KL divergence between the output of the encoder and the prior. Weight: $\lambda_{\text{KL}} \approx 10^{-6}$. If $\lambda_{\text{KL}}$ is too high, this can lead to posterior collapse.

Posterior collapse is the KL term winning the tug of war of section 21: the encoder outputs the prior, $q_\varphi(z \mid x) \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, for every image. The KL is then zero, but the code carries no information about $x$, and the decoder learns to ignore $z$ and print an average image.

Read the number $10^{-6}$ against $\lambda_{\text{rec}} \approx 1$: the regularization is a million times weaker than the reconstruction. Such a VAE behaves almost like a plain autoencoder. That is deliberate in latent diffusion: the aim is not to sample from $p(z)$ (the generator of section 37 will learn the latent distribution) but only to keep the latent space from drifting, a gentle leash rather than a mould. In section 22's terms, it corresponds to a decoder variance $\sigma^2$ so small that the pixels are trusted almost completely.

sections.heading: 32. Combat blurriness with perceptual loss: the feature maps
sections.text:
The squared error compares pixels, and section 5 said pixels measure neither semantic nor perceptual similarity. The fix is to compare the images through a network that sees what humans see.

The slides show it in three steps. Start with the image $x$. Pass it through a pretrained image network and look at the activations of its layer $l$, the feature maps $\phi_l(x)$. The slide's example is from Zeiler and Fergus (Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks, 2013): in early layers the feature maps respond to oriented edges, colour blobs and simple textures, in deeper layers to parts and shapes. These are the things the human eye is sensitive to.

Idea: force the model to pay attention to shapes sensitive to the human eye (edges, shapes) and have some translation invariance. The invariance comes for free: convolutions and pooling respond to a pattern wherever it is, so a one-pixel shift barely changes the features, while a lost texture changes them a lot. That is exactly the opposite of the pixel-wise distance.

sections.heading: The perceptual loss, term by term
sections.text:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{perc}} = \sum_{l} \frac{1}{H_l W_l} \bigl\| w^l \odot \bigl( \phi_l(x) - \phi_l(\hat{x}) \bigr) \bigr\|^2$$

Read it from the inside out. $\phi_l(x)$ and $\phi_l(\hat{x})$ are the feature maps of the original and the reconstruction at layer $l$, each a grid of size $H_l \times W_l$ with one vector of channels per position. Their difference says, position by position, which features disagree. $w^l$ is a vector of weights, one per channel, and $\odot$ scales each channel by its weight: some channels matter more to human judgement than others. The squared norm adds up the weighted disagreements, $\frac{1}{H_l W_l}$ turns the sum into an average over positions so that large early layers and small deep layers count comparably, and the outer sum collects all the chosen layers.

Description: Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity, LPIPS (Zhang et al., The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Deep Features as a Perceptual Metric, 2018). "Learned" refers to the weights $w^l$: the feature network is a fixed pretrained classifier, and only $w^l$ is fitted, on a dataset of human judgements of which of two distorted patches looks closer to a reference. The result is a distance that agrees with people far better than MSE or SSIM.

Weight: $\lambda_{\text{perc}} \approx 1$.

sections.heading: When the perceptual weight is too high: checkerboard artifacts
sections.text:
The slide compares two reconstructions of a ship: one with no checkerboard artifact, and one with a visible grid pattern laid over the whole image. If $\lambda_{\text{perc}}$ is too high, this can produce checkerboard artifacts.

Where the pattern comes from (Odena et al., Deconvolution and Checkerboard Artifacts, 2016): a transposed convolution whose kernel size is not divisible by its stride spreads its outputs unevenly, so some output pixels receive contributions from more input positions than their neighbours, in a regular grid. Normally the reconstruction loss pushes the decoder to cancel that unevenness. When the feature-matching term dominates, the decoder is rewarded for matching the network's features rather than the pixels, and a regular high-frequency pattern that the feature network barely penalises can survive. The fixes are a moderate $\lambda_{\text{perc}}$ and, in the architecture, resize-then-convolve upsampling instead of plain transposed convolutions.

sections.heading: 33. Make the output more realistic with an adversarial loss
sections.text:
Perceptual loss reduces the blur but is not enough on its own: outputs still come out a little too smooth, and the high-frequency detail of real photographs is missing.

The slide's picture: the decoder produces $\hat{x}$, and a discriminator $C_\omega$, a separate network with parameters $\omega$, looks at it and answers one question, real or fake? Its score $C_\omega(\hat{x})$ is high when the image looks real. The dashed arrows go back to both networks: both learn from the outcome. The next build of the slide replaces the arrows with two fencers: the decoder and the discriminator are opponents. This is the GAN game of the GAN walkthrough, used here not as a separate generator but as one more term in the decoder's loss.

sections.heading: The adversarial loss
sections.text:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}} = -\mathbb{E}_x\bigl[ C_\omega(\hat{x}) \bigr]$$

Read it from the decoder's side: minimising minus the critic's score means maximising the score, that is, producing reconstructions the discriminator rates as real. The discriminator is trained at the same time with its own objective, scoring real images high and reconstructions low; the slide calls it a critic, the name used when the output is a realness score rather than a probability.

Idea: prevent blurriness by being forced to produce a realistic image. A blurred image is easy to catch as fake, so averaging is no longer rewarded, which attacks the cause seen in section 28 directly. Description: incentivize the discriminator (critic) to be fooled. Weight: $\lambda_{\text{adv}} \approx 0.1$ to $1$. If $\lambda_{\text{adv}}$ is too high, this may lead to mode collapse and ignore the latent: the decoder learns that some realistic-looking textures always pass, produces them whatever $z$ says, and stops being faithful to the input. In practice the adversarial term is often switched on only after the autoencoder has learned to reconstruct, so that the discriminator does not dominate from the start.

sections.heading: 34. Summary of the refined VAE
sections.text:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = \lambda_{\text{rec}}\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} + \lambda_{\text{KL}}\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} + \lambda_{\text{perc}}\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{perc}} + \lambda_{\text{adv}}\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}$$

The first two terms are the VAE of attempt 2; the slide boxes the last two together under one purpose: mitigate blurriness. The VAE used by latent diffusion models is exactly this, not the classical VAE of 2013 but its refined form with perceptual and adversarial terms (Rombach et al., 2021, after Esser et al.'s VQGAN).

sections.heading: 35. Beyond the slides: a third way to regulate the latent, VQ
sections.text:
The lecture regulates the latent with a soft penalty, the KL. There is a third way, used by a large family of models, and its logic differs from both the plain autoencoder (no regulation, faithful but unstructured) and the VAE (soft penalty towards a known distribution, structured but blurry): instead of pushing the latent, seat it on a finite set of options. Its name is vector quantization, VQ for short (van den Oord et al., VQ-VAE, 2017).

Quantization means rounding a continuous value onto a permitted finite set. The classic example in images is the colour palette: you save a photograph containing millions of colours with a palette of 256, and every pixel is forced to choose the nearest colour in the palette.

In VQ the thing being rounded is not a single number but an entire vector. You hold a list of 1024 small vectors, the codebook. The vector produced by the encoder at a position is replaced by the nearest vector in the list.

Two things are worth separating, because the word index means two different things. The latent is a grid, say $64 \times 64$, and at each of those 4096 positions sits a vector of $c$ numbers. A codebook entry is also a vector of $c$ numbers: the size of one position, not of the whole latent. The rounding happens per position and swaps the vector as a whole: the $c$ numbers at that position are not rounded one by one, all of them are replaced together by the $c$ numbers of the chosen code. What changes from position to position is therefore which code was chosen, a single integer between 0 and 1023. After quantization the image is described by 4096 such integers, and nothing stops two positions from choosing the same code.

sections.heading: A small codebook does not limit expressive power
sections.text:
A common mistake: thinking that 1024 codes means 1024 different images.

Return to the palette: a palette of 256 colours does not mean only 256 different photographs. Every pixel picks a colour from the palette; what makes the photograph is the arrangement.

Here the number of possibilities is $1024^{4096}$: the base is the number of options, the exponent the number of choices. That is of the order of $10^{12000}$; the number of atoms in the observable universe is $10^{80}$.

The key sentence: the constraint is local, the expressive power is combinatorial. Every single piece is condemned to one of 1024 options but the arrangement is free. It is the same in language: a dictionary of 50 thousand words, and no limit on the sentences.

sections.heading: How the codebook is learned
sections.text:
The codebook is not fixed; it is learned during training, and there is no external source telling the truth.

The chain is: the encoder produces a vector, the vector is replaced by the nearest code, the decoder rebuilds the image from the codes, and the result is compared with the original. If the codebook is bad, the decoder receives bad input and the error grows. So the only thing grading the codebook is the reconstruction error.

The update logic is that of k-means: every vector is assigned to its nearest prototype, every prototype moves towards the mean of the vectors assigned to it, the assignments change, and it repeats. With the palette: start with 1024 random colours, move every palette colour to the mean of the pixels that chose it, and after a few rounds the palette settles on the true colours of the data.

The loss has two extra terms for this: one pulls the chosen code towards the encoder's vector (the k-means step itself), the other pulls the encoder towards the code it chose, "you made a choice, stick to it" (the commitment term). Without the second the encoder keeps drifting and the assignments never settle.

One technical wrinkle: finding and substituting the nearest neighbour is a discrete operation and the gradient cannot pass through it. The solution is crude but works, the straight-through estimator: the gradient coming from the decoder is copied to the encoder as if the quantization step were not there.

Its known failure is dead codes: some prototypes are never chosen, therefore never updated, and having never been updated are never chosen again. This is codebook collapse; the countermeasure is to move a long-unused code close to a vector that is actually in use.

sections.heading: 36. A note on letters before the last part
sections.text: Latent diffusion puts the VAE and the generator of Lectures 1 to 3 in the same picture, and several letters now mean two things. The slides use them as listed below; none of the clashes is a mistake, but each is easy to trip over.

sections.heading: Same letter, different meaning
rows: $\phi_l$: feature maps of a fixed pretrained network in $\mathcal{L}_{\text{perc}}$
curly $\varphi$ is trained, $\phi$ with a layer index is frozen
weights of the latent generator $u_t^\theta$ in sections 37 and 38
two different networks trained at different stages
$C$: channels of the image, $c$: channels of the latent
a size is a plain letter, the critic always carries $\omega$
only the encoder's has a subscript

sections.heading: 37. Latent diffusion: training
sections.text:
The lecture's second section, latent diffusion models (Rombach et al., High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models, 2021), puts everything together. Training has two stages.

First, train the VAE: the refined VAE of section 34, on images alone.

Second, train the image generation model in the VAE latent space, using the frozen VAE encoder. Frozen means its weights are no longer updated; its only job is to turn each training image into a latent. The slide draws it: $x_1 \sim p_{\text{data}}$ goes through the encoder $q_\varphi$ and comes out as $z_1 \sim q_\varphi(z_1 \mid x_1)$, a point in the latent space. From then on the generator never sees a pixel.

The slide writes the generator's loss with flow matching, and it is the Lecture 3 loss with $x$ replaced by $z$: draw a noise latent $z_0 \sim p_0$, a time $t$, form the point on the straight line, and regress the velocity:

$$z_t = t\, z_1 + (1 - t)\, z_0, \qquad \mathcal{L} = \bigl\| u_t^\theta(z_t) - (z_1 - z_0) \bigr\|^2$$

Nothing in the flow matching derivation cared what the data was; the latents are simply the new data. The same holds for DDPM or score matching: the generator is trained on $z_1$ instead of $x$.

One practical detail connects to the noise schedules of Lectures 1 and 2. The generator's noise is $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$, so the data it transports should have roughly unit scale too. Because $\lambda_{\text{KL}}$ is tiny, nothing forces the latents to have variance 1, so implementations measure the spread of the latents once and divide by it (Stable Diffusion's well-known factor 0.18215). This is also why a completely unregulated autoencoder is avoided: its latent scale could drift anywhere during training.

sections.heading: 38. Latent diffusion: inference
sections.text:
Inference also has two steps. First, start from a noisy latent and perform diffusion, score matching or flow matching in the latent space: draw $z_0 \sim p_0$ and walk to a clean latent $z_1$ with the learned model. Second, use the VAE decoder to obtain the final image in pixel space, $x_1 \sim p_\theta(x_1 \mid z_1)$; in practice the decoder's mean is taken.

The slide's last picture makes the division of labour explicit: the walk from noise to data happens entirely in the small latent space, and the decoder is called once at the very end. The encoder is used only to prepare training data; the decoder only to finish generation.

The gain comes directly from the dimension. With $f = 8$ and $c = 4$, a $1024 \times 1024 \times 3$ image of 3,145,728 numbers becomes a $128 \times 128 \times 4$ latent of 65,536 numbers, 48 times fewer, and every one of the dozens of generator steps runs on the small one.

sections.heading: 39. What the VAE does inside an image generation model
sections.text:
The lecture closes Part 1 with three observations about the VAE in large generators (it points to experiments in Black Forest Labs' FLUX.2 latent space analysis, 2025, and to Rombach et al., 2021).

The encoder acts as a low-pass filter. It keeps the global geometry and layout, the low-frequency, semantic content of section 5, and discards most of the fine, high-frequency detail.

The decoder is responsible for conveying the low-level details, through texture hallucination. It takes a highly compressed, low-dimensional latent and has to turn it into a high-dimensional image; the fur, the grain of the paper, the exact noise of the photograph are not in the latent, so the decoder must invent plausible ones. That is precisely the perceptual, high-frequency content of section 5, and it explains why the perceptual and adversarial terms of Attempt 3 are aimed at the decoder: they teach it to hallucinate textures that look right instead of averaging them away.

The decoder is 2x bigger than the encoder. The asymmetry follows from the two jobs: summarising is easier than inventing, so the decoder gets the larger share of the parameters.

sections.heading: 40. The cost of compression is a design decision
sections.text:
No detail the decoder cannot unfold can ever be generated: the decoder's output is the quality ceiling of the whole system. The more aggressively the latent is compressed, the lower that ceiling.

Two knobs set the trade-off. The spatial factor $f$: a larger $f$ makes generation cheaper and the latent coarser. The latent channels $c$: more channels let the latent carry more detail and raise the reconstruction ceiling, but give the generator a harder, higher-dimensional distribution to learn. The first latent diffusion models used $c = 4$; SD3 and FLUX moved to 16 channels with $f = 8$, a compression of $64 \cdot 3 / 16 = 12$ instead of 48, accepting a harder generation problem for a better decoder ceiling.

sections.heading: 41. Which one is right, and when
sections.text:
The single question that settles the choice: will you draw samples directly from the latent?

If you will, you need a VAE with a real KL weight. The KL term is exactly the price of that: it seats the latent on a known distribution so that a point drawn from there lands where the decoder recognises it. In return you give up some reconstruction.

If you will not, the KL is not needed, and a strong one only does harm. This is exactly the situation in latent diffusion: you never sample the latent from $p(z)$; the distribution of the latent is learned in the second stage by the diffusion or flow model. So the first stage only needs a compressor that is as faithful as possible.

But a completely free autoencoder is not used either, because the scale of the latent can drift during training while the generator's noise is tuned to a particular scale. So a light regulation is kept: either a KL with a very small weight ($\lambda_{\text{KL}} \approx 10^{-6}$; Stable Diffusion is like this, called a VAE and behaving like an AE), or VQ.

VQ has a second gain that diffusion does not need: the latent is discrete. Every position is an index, that is, a token. The image becomes a text of 4096 words written with a dictionary of 1024 words, which opens the door to generating images autoregressively, token by token, like a language model.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: Pixel space fails three ways: it is huge ($n = H \times W \times 3$, about $3 \times 10^6$ at $1024^2$), redundant (neighbouring pixels are predictable), and not meaningful ($z + \epsilon$ is gibberish). The wish list is a tractable, compact and meaningful space, where meaningful is about semantic (global, low-frequency) and perceptual (local, texture, high-frequency) similarity, neither of which a pixel-wise distance measures. Attempt 1, the autoencoder $\hat{x} = D_\theta(E_\varphi(x))$ with $\mathcal{L}_{\text{AE}} = \|x - \hat{x}\|^2$ and compression $f = H/h$, gets the first two but leaves isolated points in the latent space, so it cannot generate. Attempt 2, the VAE, makes both networks probabilistic, $q_\varphi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\varphi, \sigma_\varphi^2)$ and $p_\theta(x \mid z) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta, \sigma^2 I)$, and maximises $\log p_\theta(x)$ through the ELBO (Jensen, then splitting the log): reconstruction minus $\mathrm{KL}(q_\varphi \| p(z))$. The encoder was added from outside in place of the intractable posterior; the two terms pull in opposite directions; reparameterization lets the gradient through the sampling. Its failure is truthfulness: squared error rewards the average, and the average of sharp edges is a blur. Attempt 3 weights the terms ($\lambda_{\text{rec}} \approx 1$, $\lambda_{\text{KL}} \approx 10^{-6}$) and adds LPIPS ($\lambda \approx 1$) and an adversarial critic ($\lambda \approx 0.1$ to $1$), each with its own failure when too strong: blur, posterior collapse, checkerboard, mode collapse. Latent diffusion trains this VAE first, freezes its encoder, and learns the Lecture 1 to 3 generator on $z$, with the same loss and $x$ replaced by $z$; at inference the decoder, twice the size of the encoder, hallucinates the texture the low-pass encoder threw away.

gan.title: GAN — A Complete Walkthrough
gan.context: Generative Adversarial Networks · IDA 10 · Lab 6 · CS231n 13 · ML-OVERALL 20
gan.summary: One continuous thread from why the GAN abandons computing probabilities entirely, to the race between the two networks, why training is fragile, mode collapse, the DCGAN and StyleGAN design decisions, CycleGAN's unpaired data trick, and why diffusion took over.

sections.heading: 1. Where generative models split in two
sections.text:
You can ask two different things of a generative model.

The first: tell me how probable the image I give you is. This requires the model to be able to compute a probability. Autoregressive models do this exactly, the VAE approximately — through a lower bound.

The second: produce a new image for me. For this you do not need to compute a probability. Being able to provide a sample is enough.

The GAN uses exactly this distinction. It abandons computing probabilities entirely and builds a model that can only sample. Its name is implicit density: you cannot write down the distribution but you can draw from it.

What it gains is large — no more integrals, lower bounds, or intractable posteriors. What it loses is also large: you are left without an honest number you are optimising, and all of its problems come from here.

sections.heading: 2. The counterfeiter and the police
sections.text:
There are two networks.

The generator produces an image from a random noise vector. The counterfeiter: it tries to print fake money.

The discriminator decides whether the image handed to it came from the real dataset or from the generator. The police.

The two train each other. When the counterfeiter produces better fakes the police have to look more carefully; when the police sharpen, the counterfeiter has to become more realistic.

The real innovation here is this: the loss function is not written by hand, it is learned. In a VAE you fix the answer to the question "what does a good image mean" yourself, as a sum of squares. In a GAN the discriminator produces that answer, and it changes throughout training.

sections.heading: 3. Two losses, one competition
sections.text:
The discriminator's job is ordinary binary classification: it tries to say 1 to real ones and 0 to fakes. Its loss is familiar too, binary cross-entropy.

The generator's job is the opposite: to fool the discriminator.

In its first formulation the generator minimised the probability of the discriminator saying fake. In practice this does not work: at the start of training the generator is very bad, the discriminator catches it easily, and in that region the gradient is almost zero — so the generator receives no signal precisely when it needs to learn the most.

The solution is a simple rewriting: instead of minimising, maximise the probability of the discriminator saying real. It pushes in the same direction but its gradient is strong at the start of training. All implementations use this.

This detail is the first example of a general pattern in the GAN literature: the method is right, but a great many practical corrections are needed to make it work.

sections.title: GAN training step
lines: $\tilde{x} = G(z)$ >> fake image, detached from the graph

sections.heading: Why detach is mandatory
sections.text: While $D$ is being updated the fake image is detached from the graph. If it is not detached, the loss of $D$ flows into $G$ as well and updates $G$ in the wrong direction — the direction that proves the discriminator right.

sections.heading: 4. A small but instructive detail: why tanh
sections.text:
The last layer of the generator is a tanh, and the real data is also normalised to between minus one and one. The reason for this is not aesthetic.

Two kinds of input arrive at the discriminator: real images and generated images. If the real data were between zero and one and the generated ones between minus one and one, the discriminator would separate the two by looking only at the numeric range, without looking at the content at all. It would have nothing left to learn and no useful signal would reach the generator.

When the two inputs are in the same range, the discriminator is forced to learn the real difference — the structure and the content.

This is an example of a way of thinking you will meet again and again when working with GANs: always check whether you have left the discriminator a free clue.

sections.heading: 5. Why it produces sharp results
sections.text:
The cause of the VAE's blurriness was the squared loss: faced with uncertainty it took an average.

In a GAN averaging has a cost. If you print the middle of two possible edges, the result is an image never seen in the real data, and the discriminator is trained precisely to catch this. So blurriness is directly penalised.

The sharpness of the GAN comes from here: its loss function does not reward averaging.

sections.heading: 6. Why it is fragile
sections.text:
When training an ordinary network you drive a single number down and you understand from that number whether things are going well.

In a GAN there is no such number. Two networks pull in opposite directions and what you are seeking is not a minimum but an equilibrium. A fall in the discriminator's loss can be good news or bad: either it improved, or the generator collapsed. Nor can you estimate image quality by looking at the generator's loss.

Moreover the equilibrium is fragile. If the discriminator becomes too strong the gradient reaching the generator dries up. If the generator becomes too strong the discriminator falls to random guessing and no directional information remains.

This is why GAN training is spoken of as "an art": there is no single reliable indicator to follow, so looking at the produced images by eye is in effect a measuring instrument.

sections.heading: 7. Mode collapse
sections.text:
This is the most characteristic failure.

Real data is multi-modal: a digit dataset contains ten digits. If the generator discovers one mode and sees that it can fool the discriminator with it, it starts neglecting the remaining modes. In time it comes to produce only one or two digits.

The genuinely insidious part is this: in that state the loss values can look perfectly reasonable. The generator is doing its job — it only lost diversity, and there is no term in the loss function that measures diversity.

For diagnosis, watch throughout training the values the discriminator assigns to real and to fake images. If they stay pinned at one for real and zero for fake, there is either mode collapse or a general breakdown.

Countermeasures: giving the discriminator the ability to see the diversity within a batch, switching to the Wasserstein form for smoother gradients, restraining the discriminator's function with spectral normalization, lowering the learning rate. None of them is a definitive solution — mode collapse is a structural risk of GANs.

sections.heading: 8. DCGAN: the design rules that settled the architecture
sections.text:
The first GANs were built from fully connected layers and were hard to train. DCGAN gave the design rules that settled the convolutional structure into the GAN.

The generator unfolds low-dimensional noise into a small feature map and then enlarges it step by step. There is no pooling layer — upsampling and downsampling are done with strided convolutions. ReLU is used in the generator and leaky ReLU in the discriminator; batch normalization is present except in the input and output layers.

These rules do not have individual mathematical justifications, they were found empirically. But their effect was large: this is the first GAN family that reliably produced recognisable images.

A side finding also came out of here: arithmetic works in the latent space. Adding and subtracting vectors corresponds to meaningful changes in the image.

sections.heading: 9. StyleGAN: separating control
sections.text:
The idea StyleGAN brought was to stop feeding the noise directly to the generator.

First the noise passes through a mapping network made of a few fully connected layers and turns into a style vector. This intermediate space is less entangled than the original noise space — that is, its dimensions line up more cleanly with the axes of variation in the image.

Then the style vector is injected separately at every resolution level of generation. The form of the injection is adaptive instance normalization: the feature map is normalised, then a scale and a shift coming from the style are applied.

The result is this: the style at coarse resolutions determines pose and overall structure, and the ones at fine resolutions determine details such as colour and texture. You can change the hair colour without changing the pose of the face.

In addition, independent noise is added at every layer; completely random details such as individual hairs and pores come from there — the generator does not have to carry them in the style vector.

sections.heading: 10. CycleGAN: translation with unpaired data
sections.text:
The natural approach to image to image translation demands paired data: two versions of the same scene. In practice collecting this is often impossible — there is no zebra version of the same horse.

CycleGAN works with two separate collections: a pile of horse photographs, a pile of zebra photographs, no pairing.

Two generators are set up, one translating forwards and one backwards. Each direction has its own discriminator; this much provides the pressure that "the output should look like a zebra".

But this alone is not enough: the generator could satisfy the discriminator even by producing a zebra with no relation at all to the input. The missing constraint is preservation of content.

Cycle consistency provides it: when you translate an image and translate it back, you must return to where you started. For it to be able to return, the forward translation must carry the content.

This idea went beyond GANs — diffusion-based unpaired translation models also use the same cycle constraint.

sections.heading: 11. What the Wasserstein form fixed
sections.text:
The original GAN loss has a structural problem: if the two distributions are far enough apart, the gradient of the distance between them becomes almost zero. The generator is left without a signal at the very moment it needs directional information the most.

The Wasserstein form defines the distance between distributions with another measure — roughly, "how much mass has to be transported to turn one pile into the other". This measure is meaningful and gives a smooth gradient even when the distributions are disjoint.

The cost is that the discriminator's function must not be too steep; this is provided by additional constraints such as a gradient penalty or spectral normalization.

The practical result: training is markedly more stable, and for the first time the discriminator's loss becomes a number genuinely related to quality.

sections.heading: 12. Why diffusion took over
sections.text:
GANs were the standard of image generation between 2016 and 2021. The reason diffusion overtook them is not individual quality but character.

Diffusion's training is stable: there is no discriminator, no equilibrium, there is a single trackable loss and as it falls things get better. Its mode coverage is better: it tries to learn the whole data distribution instead of getting stuck in a corner of it. Conditioning attaches more easily.

Against this, the GAN's one great advantage still stands: it generates in a single step. One forward pass against diffusion's dozens.

The ironic ending is this: the GAN did not disappear, it settled inside modern pipelines. In latent diffusion architectures, what keeps the decoder that compresses the image sharp is a GAN discriminator. And some diffusion distillation methods again use an adversarial loss to compress a multi-step teacher into a single-step student.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: The GAN abandons computing probabilities and builds a model that can only sample; what it gains is simplicity, what it loses is a single trackable objective. The loss function is not written by hand, it is learned by the discriminator — this is the cause of the sharpness, and of the fragility as well. What you seek is not a minimum but an equilibrium, which is why the loss curves say nothing about quality. Mode collapse is a structural risk, because there is no term in the loss measuring diversity. DCGAN solved the architecture, StyleGAN control, CycleGAN unpaired data. Diffusion took over thanks to stability and mode coverage, but the GAN remained inside the pipeline as the instrument of single-step generation and of sharp decoders.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: The setup of the generator and the discriminator, the PyTorch implementation and the normalization details are in lab06; the symptoms of mode collapse and the countermeasures also in lab06; the DCGAN and StyleGAN architectural decisions and the summary of the GAN era in cs13; CycleGAN and cycle consistency in lab06; the taxonomy of generative models in cs12. For the comparison with the VAE see the VAE walkthrough, and for the comparison with diffusion see the DDPM walkthrough.

ddpm.title: DDPM — A Complete Walkthrough
ddpm.context: Diffusion · IDA 11 · Lab 7 · CS231n 13 — to be read in one sitting
ddpm.summary: One continuous thread from why diffusion models appeared to latent diffusion: which gap they closed, the forward and reverse process, why the ELBO collapses into MSE, the inside of the U-Net, classifier-free guidance and what came after. The cards give individual facts, this text gives the order.

sections.heading: 1. The problem: why sampling from a distribution is hard
sections.text:
You have 60,000 handwritten digits. What you want is to produce the 60,001st — an image that is not in the dataset but looks as if it came from it.

The reason this is hard: a 28x28 image is a point in a 784-dimensional space. Almost all of that space is noise. The points that look like digits sit on a very thin, very curved surface. You do not know the equation of that surface, all you hold are 60,000 examples on it.

Generating means being able to place a new point on that surface. If you cannot write down the distribution itself, you have to learn to sample from it some other way.

sections.heading: 2. What the previous approaches could not do
sections.text:
Before diffusion there were two main routes for this job and both had a characteristic failure.

GAN: a generator and a discriminator compete. The image quality is high and generation is single-step — but training is a search for an equilibrium, and that equilibrium breaks easily. Its best known failure is mode collapse: the generator finds a few images that fool the discriminator and starts producing them forever. There are ten digits in the dataset, the model produces three of them, and its loss looks perfectly fine. Moreover there is no single number telling you how well things are going; you cannot tell from the loss curve whether training is going well.

VAE: its training is stable and you hold an honest lower bound that you optimise. But the generated images are blurry. The cause is not the architecture but the loss function itself: squared error chooses the average in the face of uncertainty. If the model is not sure exactly where an edge is, it prints the middle of the two possibilities — and the average of two sharp edges is a blurry edge.

The gap diffusion closed is exactly here: the sharpness of the GAN, the stability of the VAE. There is no discriminator and no search for an equilibrium; what remains is plainly a regression problem.

sections.heading: 3. The one-sentence idea
sections.text:
The hard thing is producing an image from noise. The easy thing is adding noise to an image.

So do not learn the hard direction directly: build the easy direction yourself, and ask the network only to undo it by one step.

Add one part in a thousand of noise to a photograph. The result is still a photograph, only slightly dirty. Now repeat this a thousand times. At the end you hold pure noise with no trace of the photograph in it. If you could walk this path in reverse, you could start from pure noise and produce a photograph.

What a diffusion model learns is not the whole of this path but a single step of it: give me a slightly dirty image and I will tell you the dirt that was added. During generation this single step is repeated a thousand times.

The turning point is in this sentence: the model does not predict the image, it predicts the noise. Why it does so comes below, but keep it in mind from now — half of the topic is in that choice.

sections.heading: 4. The forward process: how noise is added
sections.text:
At every step we add a little Gaussian noise to the image. How much is added is dictated by a predetermined list: $T$ numbers from $\beta_1$ to $\beta_T$. This list is called the variance schedule and it is not learned, it is chosen by hand. The original choice of Ho and colleagues in 2020: $T = 1000$ steps, with $\beta$ increasing linearly from 0.0001 to 0.02.

Two things happen at every step at once: noise is added, and the current image is shrunk a little. The shrinking factor is $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}$.

Why is there shrinking? Because if you only add noise the total variance grows at every step and the process explodes. The shrinking exactly balances the variance brought by the added noise: if the variance of the input is 1 the variance of the output also stays 1. That is why this family is called variance preserving. There is an alternative (variance exploding, where the noise grows without bound), but DDPM uses this one.

sections.heading: Forward process — step by step and in closed form
sections.text:
A single step:
$$q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(x_t;\ \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\bigr)$$

Shorthands: $\alpha_t = 1-\beta_t$ and $\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s=1}^{t}\alpha_s$ (the cumulative product).

To any time $t$ in one move:
$$q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(x_t;\ \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,x_0,\ (1-\bar{\alpha}_t) I\bigr)$$

Written in sampling form:
$$x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\,\epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$$

The letters: $x_0$ the real image, $x_t$ its version with $t$ steps of noise added, $\epsilon$ the added noise, $\bar{\alpha}_t$ the measure of how much of the image remains.
