sections.heading: 5. Why the closed form matters so much
sections.text:
The third line above is the only reason diffusion is trainable.

Consider: if you had to run a loop 500 times to obtain the noisy image at $t = 500$, you would have to take 500 steps for every training example. Training would be practically impossible.

But successively added Gaussian noises give a Gaussian again, and their variances add. That is why all 500 steps collapse into a single formula: multiply once by $\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{500}}$ and add $\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{500}}$ worth of noise on top. Done.

Concretely: during training you pick a random $t$ for every image (say 500), produce $x_{500}$ in one line, and feed it to the network. Nothing is sequential. Training is fully parallel.

This is called the reparameterization trick, and you have seen the same trick in the VAE: writing randomness in a sum-and-product form the gradient can flow through.

Note: this convenience exists only in the forward direction. Generation (sampling) is still step by step, and that is the reason for the slowness.

sections.heading: 6. The schedule itself is a design choice
sections.text:
The linear schedule has a flaw: $\bar{\alpha}$ falls very fast in the early steps. That is, the image is almost entirely destroyed at the very beginning of the process, and the remaining hundreds of steps go into adding a bit more noise to something that is already noise. Part of the training budget is wasted.

Nichol and Dhariwal (2021) proposed the cosine schedule instead: $\bar{\alpha}$ falls more slowly and more smoothly, and structure is preserved for longer at middle noise levels. Sample quality rises markedly.

The general lesson here holds throughout diffusion: the forward process is not learned but it is designed, and how you design it directly affects the result.

sections.heading: 7. The reverse direction: why it has to be learned
sections.text:
In the forward direction you know exactly what you did. So why is the reverse direction not free?

Because someone who sees $x_t$ cannot know $x_{t-1}$ with certainty. There are several plausible ways of going back from a noisy image — you do not know which clean image it came from. That distribution depends on the whole data distribution, and you do not know it. Had you known it you would have known how to generate as well.

But there is a rescue: if you know the true $x_0$, the reverse step can be computed analytically. That is, $q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0)$ is a Gaussian in closed form, with its mean and variance following from the schedule.

In training you hold $x_0$. In generation you do not. The whole matter is teaching a network to imitate, without $x_0$ at generation time, this target that is known during training.

sections.heading: 8. The ELBO: exactly the same move as in the VAE
sections.text:
At this point the mathematical frame starts from the same place as the VAE and follows the same steps. The target is maximum likelihood: find the $\theta$ that makes the training data most probable.

In both cases the marginal cannot be computed directly — in the VAE an integral over z, in DDPM an integral over a T-dimensional path. In both cases the same remedy is applied: insert an auxiliary distribution, split the logarithm into three terms, drop a KL term known to be non-negative and move to the lower bound (the ELBO).

There are two real differences, and both favour DDPM.

First: in the VAE the inserted auxiliary distribution is the encoder, that is, it is learned (the $\phi$ parameters). In DDPM what is inserted is the forward process — fixed and parameterless. There is no encoder to learn.

Second: in the VAE the prior KL term is a genuine penalty that regularises the encoder and must be optimised. In DDPM the corresponding term is the KL between the distribution of $x_T$ and $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ — but if T is large enough the forward process already guarantees this and the term contains no parameters to learn. It is constant, and is therefore dropped.

What remains is T denoising terms: at every step, the KL between the known true reverse step and the reverse step the network predicts.

sections.heading: The DDPM ELBO — three pieces
sections.text:
$$\log p_\theta(x_0) \ \ge\ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x_0|x_1)]}_{L_0}\ -\ \underbrace{D_{KL}\bigl(q(x_T|x_0)\,\|\,p(x_T)\bigr)}_{L_T}\ -\ \underbrace{\sum_{t>1} D_{KL}\bigl(q(x_{t-1}|x_t,x_0)\,\|\,p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t)\bigr)}_{L_{t-1}}$$

$L_T$ is constant and is dropped. $L_0$ is the reconstruction of the last step. The entire job is in the $L_{t-1}$ sum.

sections.heading: 9. Why the KL collapses into MSE
sections.text:
This is the most overlooked step of the topic, and the place that completes the narrative.

Both distributions in the $L_{t-1}$ term are Gaussian: the true reverse step is Gaussian (derived above), and the reverse step produced by the network was also defined as Gaussian. The KL between two Gaussians has a closed form. If you choose the variances to be fixed, all that remains of that closed form is the square of the difference of the means.

So the KL does not disappear — under the Gaussian assumption it turns into squared error.

One more simplification comes on top. If you write the mean in terms of $\epsilon$ rather than $x_0$, the thing the network has to predict becomes directly the added noise. Once the time-dependent weighting coefficients coming from the ELBO are also dropped, what remains is this:

Loss = the mean squared error between the added noise and the predicted noise.

That is all. At the end of an eight-line derivation what you hold is a regression loss.

sections.heading: $L_{\text{simple}}$
sections.text: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_0,\,\epsilon}\bigl[\ \|\ \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\ \|^2\ \bigr]$$

sections.heading: 10. Why we predict the noise and not the image
sections.text:
Mathematically the three options are equivalent: the network can predict the clean image ($x_0$), the mean of the reverse step ($\mu$) or the added noise ($\epsilon$). One passes from one to another by algebra. When the full ELBO is used all three give close results.

The difference appears once you move to the simplified loss. The ablation in the DDPM paper (CIFAR-10, FID; lower is better):

  $\mu$ prediction, full ELBO: 13.22 — with the simple loss: unstable
  $\epsilon$ prediction, full ELBO: 13.51 — with the simple loss: 3.17

More than a fourfold improvement, and the reason is interesting: the discarded time coefficients were in fact performing a reweighting. Once the coefficients are dropped, small $t$ values (nearly clean images, an easy job) receive relatively less weight and the network focuses on the hard job — recovering coarse structure at high noise.

The practical intuition works in the same direction: the distribution of $\epsilon$ is always $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. The target has a fixed scale and fixed statistics. $x_0$ on the other hand varies with the dataset. Regression against a fixed target is always more stable.

Remember it this way: moving to the simple loss was not free, its price was a reweighting, and that reweighting happened to be a beneficial one.

sections.heading: 11. The network: why a U-Net
sections.text:
The network's job is this: take the noisy image and output the noise on it as an image of the same size. The input and output have the same size, and every pixel of the output depends both on the texture around it and on the overall structure of the image. This is a problem of the same shape as segmentation — which is why the same architecture is used.

The three parts of the U-Net fit this job exactly:

The encoder goes down, the resolution falls and the receptive field grows. Deep down, every position summarises a large region of the image.

The decoder goes up, and through skip connections retrieves the fine detail coming from the early layers of the encoder. Without this the output could not bring back the high frequencies lost on the way down.

Attention blocks, at the low-resolution layers. Convolution is local; for the two ends of the image to be consistent with each other a layer is needed in which every position can see every position. It is not placed at full resolution because the cost of attention grows with the square of the number of positions — feasible at 28x28, not at 256x256. That is why the first block is plain and the deep blocks carry attention.

Note: the attention here is self-attention. It has nothing to do with text. Text conditioning is added into the same slot as cross-attention, but that is a separate topic and comes below.

sections.heading: The U-Net flow, with dimensions (MNIST example)
sections.text:
x_t  (B, 1, 28, 28)

── Encoder ──────────────────────────────
conv1x1:              (B, 32, 28, 28)
ResBlock + time:      (B, 32, 28, 28)
ResBlock + time:      (B, 32, 28, 28)
Downsample:           (B, 32, 14, 14)
ResBlock + time:      (B, 64, 14, 14)
Attention:            (B, 64, 14, 14)
Downsample:           (B, 64,  7,  7)

── Bottleneck ───────────────────────────
ResBlock + time:      (B, 64,  7,  7)
Attention:            (B, 64,  7,  7)
ResBlock + time:      (B, 64,  7,  7)

── Decoder ──────────────────────────────
Upsample:             (B, 64, 14, 14)
ResBlock + skip+time: (B, 64, 14, 14)
Attention:            (B, 64, 14, 14)
Upsample:             (B, 32, 28, 28)
ResBlock + skip+time: (B, 32, 28, 28)
ResBlock + time:      (B, 32, 28, 28)
conv1x1:              (B,  1, 28, 28)

Output: eps_theta — the predicted noise, same shape as the input.

sections.heading: 12. How the timestep enters the network
sections.text:
A single network is responsible for all noise levels. At t = 10 the job is cleaning fine detail, at t = 900 recovering coarse structure. The network has to know which situation it is in.

The route is the same as positional encoding in the Transformer: t is an integer, first converted into a sinusoidal embedding (typically 256 dimensions), then passed through a small MLP. The resulting vector is reduced to the channel count of each ResBlock with a linear layer inside that block and added to the feature maps.

The addition is broadcast from shape (B, C) to (B, C, 1, 1) across all pixels. This has a meaning: the question "how much noise is there right now" gives the same answer for the whole image, it does not vary with position. So the condition is injected globally, not spatially.

Keep this detail in mind — shortly, in text conditioning, exactly this will not be enough.

sections.title: Training
lines: $x_0 \sim q(x_0)$ >> an image from the dataset
$t \sim \mathrm{Uniform}\{1, \ldots, T\}$ >> a random step for each example
$x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon$ >> in one move, no chain
take a gradient step on $\nabla_\theta \, \| \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \|^2$

sections.heading: The difference between the two loops
sections.text:
Nothing in the training loop is sequential — $t$ is chosen at random, $x_t$ is built in one move with the closed-form formula, and the whole batch is processed in parallel.

The sampling loop on the other hand is necessarily sequential: $x_t$ is needed for $x_{t-1}$, and $x_{t+1}$ for $x_t$. This loop is the only reason for diffusion's slowness, not the network itself.

sections.heading: 13. Why noise is added at the last step
sections.text:
In the generation loop, after computing the mean, noise is added on top once more ($\sigma_t z$). At first this feels backwards: we are trying to remove noise, why put it back?

Because we are sampling, not optimising. If at every step you take the mean of the reverse distribution and carry on, you walk the same path every time and produce the same image on every run. Diversity comes precisely from that added noise.

At the last step ($t = 1$) it is not added, because there what is being produced is no longer a sample but the final output.

This choice is itself a tuning point: if you remove the noise entirely and make the process deterministic you obtain DDIM — the same trained network, a different sampling rule, similar quality in 50 to 200 steps instead of 1000.

sections.heading: 14. Conditioning: how you say what you want
sections.text:
The model described so far produces random samples from the data distribution. For it to be useful you have to be able to say what you want: this class, this text, this source image.

The simplest route: give the condition to the network as an input as well. Convert the class label into an embedding and add it at the same place as the timestep embedding. This is exactly what is done in the CS231n assignment — there the condition was a CLIP embedding and was added to the context vector in a single line.

Its limit is this: the condition is pooled into a single vector and affects the whole image in the same way. Enough to say "cat". Not enough to say "a small cat at the bottom left, a table on the right".

The stronger route is to keep the condition as a sequence and attach it to the attention slots of the U-Net as cross-attention: query from the image, key and value from the text. Then every position can select which word concerns it. All text to image models use this.

sections.heading: 15. Classifier-free guidance: why it was needed
sections.text:
You gave the condition and the model complies with it — but weakly. The generated image belongs to the class, yet it does not have to be a typical, pronounced example of that class.

The first solution was classifier guidance: a separate classifier is trained and during sampling its gradient pushes generation towards the right class. It works but it is expensive — you have to train and maintain a separate classifier that can operate at every noise level.

Classifier-free guidance removes that classifier entirely, and the method is surprisingly cheap: during training, drop the condition with some probability. The same network learns to make both conditional and unconditional predictions.

During sampling you run the network twice — once with the condition, once without — and exaggerate the difference between the two. The unconditional prediction points in the direction of "an image in general", the conditional one in the direction of "an image matching this condition". The difference between them is the contribution of the condition alone. You enlarge that difference with a coefficient w and go beyond the conditional prediction.

sections.heading: CFG
sections.text:
$$\hat{\epsilon} = (1+w)\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t, y, t) \ -\ w\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t, \emptyset, t)$$

$w = 0$ is ordinary conditional generation. As $w$ grows the output becomes more faithful to the condition and sharper, but less diverse; taken to excess it produces saturated and clichéd images.

sections.heading: The price of CFG
sections.text: At every sampling step the network runs twice — the cost of generation doubles. This is the direct target of part of the diffusion distillation literature: making a student model produce CFG quality in a single pass.

sections.heading: 16. What happened afterwards
sections.text:
DDPM founded this in 2020, and the following five years were built on the same skeleton. Four main directions:

Fewer steps. DDIM made sampling deterministic and brought it down to 50 to 200 steps. Distillation methods (progressive distillation, consistency models, adversarial diffusion distillation) pushed this down to single-digit steps.

Better design. The cosine schedule, v-prediction, noise level sampling distributions — all of them are "the same frame, better tuning".

Higher resolution: latent diffusion. Diffusion on raw pixels does not work at high resolution, because most of the model's capacity goes into pixel-level detail. The solution is two-stage: first a VAE (supported by a GAN discriminator for sharpness) compresses the image into a small latent space — typically from 256x256x3 to 32x32x16, that is, about 128 times fewer dimensions. Then diffusion works on those latents; the encoder is frozen, and at the end of generation the decoder turns the latent into an image. Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 3, FLUX — all of them use this architecture.

A more general frame. The same process can be written in three different languages: a latent variable model (DDPM itself), the score function (learning the gradient of the density), and a stochastic differential equation (continuous-time noising and its reverse solution). Rectified flow meanwhile draws a straight line between noise and data and learns the velocity vector — fewer steps in practice, a simpler derivation. All three are different coordinate systems of the same family.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: Build the easy direction yourself and teach the network only to undo one step. Because the forward process collapses into a closed form, training is parallel; because generation is sequential, it is slow. The ELBO derivation is the same as the VAE's, but since the forward process is fixed all the terms melt away and a single regression loss remains. The network predicts the noise, because the distribution of the target is fixed and the reweighting brought by the simplified loss makes it focus on the hard noise levels. If the condition enters through the same door as the timestep it stays global; if it enters through cross-attention it becomes position-sensitive. CFG enlarges the effect of the condition without a separate classifier, at the price of a double pass.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text: This text gives the order, the details are in the cards: the full forward and reverse derivation and its line by line comparison with the VAE are in ida11; the inside of the U-Net, the ResBlock and the shape flow again in ida11 and lab07; the code side (corruption, training loop, DDPMScheduler, UNet2DModel) in lab07; CFG, latent diffusion and the SDE/score view in cs13. Rectified flow and flow matching have their own walkthrough: Flow Matching and Rectified Flow.

score.title: Score Matching — A Complete Walkthrough
score.context: The second language of diffusion · CME 296 Lecture 2, following the slides
score.summary: Why the gradient of the density cannot guide a sampler (the unknown Z in p = f(x)/Z, and gradients that vanish far from the data), how the logarithm fixes both through grad p / p, Langevin sampling, why score matching hits a wall, implicit and sliced score matching, denoising score matching and the noise-level trade-off, NCSN and annealed Langevin, the equivalence with DDPM, the Wiener process and the SDE with drift and diffusion, VP and VE, training and the reverse SDE, and the probability flow ODE derived from Fokker-Planck, up to DPM-Solver.

sections.heading: 1. Where we are coming from
sections.text:
The previous lecture ended with a surprisingly simple recipe. Take a clean image $x_0$, mix it with noise as $\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon$, and train a network $\epsilon_\theta$ to tell you which noise $\epsilon$ was added:

$$\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon} \bigl\| \epsilon_\theta\bigl(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon,\ t\bigr) - \epsilon \bigr\|^2$$

That recipe came out of a long derivation: a lower bound on the likelihood (the ELBO), KL divergences, Bayes' rule and Gaussian algebra.

This lecture arrives at almost the same recipe from a completely different direction, with no likelihood bound at all. It starts from a geometric question. The two roads meeting at the end is the real point of the lecture: it shows that diffusion is not one trick but something several pieces of mathematics agree on.

sections.heading: 2. The question: which way is the data?
sections.text:
Picture the distribution of images $p_{\text{data}}$ as a landscape. Where realistic images live (the teddy bears in the lecture's picture), the landscape is high; everywhere else it is flat and almost zero. Now drop a point $x$ somewhere far away, a random noisy image, and ask the only question a generator really needs answered: from here, which way should I move to get closer to realistic images?

That is exactly the question a gradient answers. For any function $f(x)$ of a vector $x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)$, the gradient collects the partial derivatives

$$\nabla f(x) = \Bigl( \tfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(x), \ldots, \tfrac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(x) \Bigr)$$

and this vector points in the direction in which $f$ increases fastest. Draw the contour lines of $f$ like a map of a hill, and $\nabla f$ at any point is the arrow pointing straight uphill.

So the natural idea is: compute $\nabla_x p_{\text{data}}(x)$, the uphill direction of the data density, and walk along it. Here $f$ is just a name for "some function"; the slides use $f(x)$ for the generic hill when they introduce the gradient.

sections.heading: 3. Why the gradient of the density itself does not work
sections.text:
Two things go wrong, and the slides list them in turn.

The first is the normalization constant. A probability density has to integrate to one:

$$Z = \int p_{\text{data}}(x)\, dx = 1$$

The slides make this concrete by writing the density as a shape divided by its total mass:

$$p_{\text{data}}(x) = \frac{f(x)}{Z}$$

Read it like this. $f(x)$ is any positive function that has the right shape: it is high where images are likely and low where they are not, but nobody has made it add up to one. It is the landscape with the right relative heights and an arbitrary overall scale. $Z$ is the number that rescales it, the total volume under $f$. A neural network can easily output an $f(x)$, a single positive number per image. What it cannot do is compute $Z$, because that means integrating $f$ over every possible image, a space of $256 \times 256 \times 3 = 196{,}608$ dimensions. This is what the red word intractable on the slide means.

Taking the gradient does not help: $\nabla_x p_{\text{data}}(x) = \nabla_x \bigl( f(x)/Z \bigr) = \nabla_x f(x) / Z$. The unknown $Z$ is still sitting there as a factor, so the length of the arrow is unknown, "still intractable".

The second problem is numerical. Far from the data the density is not just small, it is astronomically small, and so is its gradient. If $p$ is $10^{-40}$ the hill is perfectly flat as far as a computer is concerned, and the arrow that should tell a random starting point where to go has length essentially zero. The very points that need directions most get none.

Aside, because the term appears everywhere in the literature: many papers write the same shape as $f(x) = e^{-E(x)}$ and call $E$ an energy. It is only a change of name. Low energy means high $f$, that is, a likely image, the way a ball settles at the bottom of a valley. The lecture never needs it; $f(x)$ is the same object.

sections.heading: 4. The fix: take the logarithm first
sections.text:
The proposal on the slide is to use $\nabla_x \log p_{\text{data}}(x)$ instead. Both problems disappear.

The constant disappears because the logarithm turns the division into a subtraction:

$$\nabla_x \log p_{\text{data}}(x) = \nabla_x \log f(x) - \nabla_x \log Z = \nabla_x \log f(x)$$

$\log Z$ is one fixed number. It does not change when $x$ changes, so its gradient with respect to $x$ is zero. We never learn what $Z$ is, and we do not have to: the shape $f$ alone gives the answer. "Not intractable anymore!"

The direction is unchanged. By the chain rule,

$$\nabla \log p = \frac{\nabla p}{p}$$

The right-hand side is the old gradient divided by $p$, a positive number. Dividing a vector by a positive number changes its length but not its direction, so the new arrow still points uphill.

And the length is now useful. This is the $\nabla p / p$ picture on the slide, and it is the reason the logarithm is "more numerically stable". $\nabla p / p$ is a relative rate of change, the same idea as a percentage. A shop whose income rises from 1 to 2 and a company whose income rises from 1,000 to 2,000 have very different absolute changes but the same relative change: both doubled. The logarithm measures exactly that. Far from the data, $\nabla p$ is tiny but $p$ is tiny too, and their ratio is a perfectly ordinary number. The arrow no longer fades away where it is needed most.

sections.heading: The density, its gradient and its score
sections.caption: One-dimensional mixture of two bumps. Top: the density. Middle: its gradient, which is visible only on the slopes of the bumps and is flat zero elsewhere. Bottom: the score, the gradient divided by the density. Far away on the left, at $x = -5$, the density is about 1e-06 and its gradient about 1e-05, useless for steering; the score is about +8.3, a clear instruction to move right. It crosses zero at the top of each bump, where there is nothing left to climb, and once more between them, where the two pulls balance.

sections.heading: 5. The score function
sections.text:
This object gets a name:

$$s(x) = \nabla_x \log p(x)$$

it is the score function, or simply the score. At every point of image space it is an arrow pointing in the direction in which the data becomes more likely, with a length that stays informative even far from the data. The slide's picture shows it as a field of arrows around the density: long arrows far away pointing towards the data, short arrows near the peaks, where there is not much further to climb.

One point that is easy to get wrong: the derivative is with respect to the input $x$, not with respect to the network's parameters $\theta$. The derivatives in a likelihood discussion are usually with respect to $\theta$. Here we ask how the log-density changes when the image changes, at fixed parameters.

sections.heading: The score as a vector field
6. Using the score: Langevin sampling
sections.text:
Suppose we had the score. Generation then becomes following the arrows, with a little randomness added at every step. Starting from a random point, the slide's Langevin sampling repeats

$$x_t = x_{t-1} + \frac{\alpha}{2} \nabla_x \log p_{\text{data}}(x_{t-1}) + \sqrt{\alpha}\, \epsilon_t$$

Read the three terms from left to right. $x_{t-1}$ is where you are. $\frac{\alpha}{2} \nabla_x \log p_{\text{data}}$ is a small step uphill, with $\alpha$ a small step size. $\sqrt{\alpha}\, \epsilon_t$ with $\epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ is a random kick.

Why the kick? Without it you would only climb to the top of the nearest bump and stop there, producing the single most likely image again and again. The kick keeps you moving around the whole high-probability region, so that after many steps the points you visit are distributed like $p_{\text{data}}$ itself, which is what sampling means. The particular balance, step $\alpha/2$ and noise $\sqrt{\alpha}$, is what makes that last statement true.

A notation warning: this $\alpha$ is a step size. It has nothing to do with the $\bar{\alpha}_t$ of DDPM. Section 21 lists every letter in this lecture that gets reused.

sections.heading: 7. Score matching: the goal, and the wall
sections.text:
Since we do not have the true score, train a network $s_\theta(x)$ to approximate it. The obvious loss compares the two arrows at data points:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SM}} = \mathbb{E}_x \bigl\| s_\theta(x) - \nabla_x \log p_{\text{data}}(x) \bigr\|^2$$

SM stands for score matching. The problem is printed in red on the slide: the target $\nabla_x \log p_{\text{data}}(x)$ is exactly what we do not have access to. We only have samples of images, not their density.

sections.heading: 8. Two attempts to get around it
sections.text:
Implicit score matching (Hyvärinen, 2005) uses integration by parts to rewrite the loss so that the unknown target disappears:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{ISM}} = \mathbb{E}_x \Bigl[ \tfrac{1}{2} \| s_\theta(x) \|^2 + \nabla_x \cdot s_\theta(x) \Bigr]$$

Only the network appears now, which is a genuine solution in principle. The cost is the second term, the divergence $\nabla_x \cdot s_\theta$: the sum of how much each output coordinate changes with its own input coordinate. For an image of $d$ pixels that needs $d$ separate backward passes per example, about 200,000 for a $256 \times 256$ colour image. Fine for toy problems, hopeless for images.

Sliced score matching (Song et al., 2019) makes this affordable by projecting onto random directions $v$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SSM}} = \mathbb{E}_{x, v} \Bigl[ 2\, v^\top \nabla_x s_\theta(x)\, v + \bigl( v^\top s_\theta(x) \bigr)^2 \Bigr]$$

Instead of measuring the change of every coordinate, it measures the change along one random direction at a time, which costs a single extra backward pass. Cheaper, but still awkward, and the lecture moves on to the idea that actually won.

sections.heading: 9. A score we can write down: the Gaussian
sections.text:
Before the trick, one example. For a one-dimensional Gaussian $x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$,

$$p(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\Bigl( -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \Bigr), \qquad \log p(x) = -\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \text{const}$$

so the score is

$$s(x) = -\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma^2}$$

Read it. The numerator $x - \mu$ is how far you are from the centre, and the minus sign turns it around: the arrow always points back towards the mean. The farther away you are, the longer the arrow, like a spring. And the $1/\sigma^2$ says that a narrow Gaussian pulls harder than a wide one: with $\sigma = 0.5$ a point at distance 1 gets an arrow of length 4, with $\sigma = 2$ only 0.25.

The normalizing factor $1/\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}$ vanished on the way, exactly as $Z$ did in section 4.

sections.heading: 10. The new idea: add noise and use a score you know
sections.text:
Denoising score matching (Vincent, 2010) starts from the Gaussian example. Take a data point $x$ and add noise yourself:

$$\tilde{x} = x + \sigma \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$$

Given $x$, the noisy point is Gaussian around it, $q_\sigma(\tilde{x} \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(x, \sigma^2 I)$, and by section 9 its score is known exactly:

$$\nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log q_\sigma(\tilde{x} \mid x) = -\frac{\tilde{x} - x}{\sigma^2}$$

This arrow points from the noisy point back to the clean point it came from. And since $\tilde{x} - x = \sigma \epsilon$, it equals $-\epsilon / \sigma$: the target is the noise you drew yourself, scaled. Nothing unknown remains in it.

sections.heading: 11. What distribution does this target belong to?
sections.text:
Doing this for every data point defines a new distribution, the noised data:

$$q_\sigma(\tilde{x}) = \int q_\sigma(\tilde{x} \mid x)\, p_{\text{data}}(x)\, dx$$

In words: pick a real image at random, add noise of size $\sigma$, and $q_\sigma$ is the distribution of what comes out. It is $p_{\text{data}}$ blurred. The slide shows three panels: the sharp data density, then $q_\sigma$ with $\sigma \ll 1$, almost the same shape slightly softened, then $q_\sigma$ with $\sigma \gg 1$, a wide smear in which the original modes have run into each other.

sections.heading: 12. The key result: the conditional target is enough
sections.text:
We would like to match the score of the blurred distribution:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SM}}(q_\sigma) = \mathbb{E}_{\tilde{x}} \bigl\| s_\theta(\tilde{x}) - \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log q_\sigma(\tilde{x}) \bigr\|^2$$

That target is still unknown, because $q_\sigma(\tilde{x})$ involves the unknown $p_{\text{data}}$. Vincent showed that the following loss differs from it only by a constant that does not depend on $\theta$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}} = \mathbb{E}_{x, \tilde{x}} \Bigl\| s_\theta(\tilde{x}) - \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log q_\sigma(\tilde{x} \mid x) \Bigr\|^2 = \mathbb{E}_{x, \tilde{x}} \Bigl\| s_\theta(\tilde{x}) + \frac{\tilde{x} - x}{\sigma^2} \Bigr\|^2$$

So minimising one minimises the other. The derivation (expand the square, use the definition of the marginal) is in Vincent's paper; the intuition is worth more. A given noisy point $\tilde{x}$ could have come from many different clean images, and each training example gives the network a different target arrow. The network cannot satisfy all of them, so the squared loss makes it output their average. And the average of "the arrows back to every clean image that could have produced $\tilde{x}$", weighted by how likely each one is, is exactly the score of $q_\sigma$ at $\tilde{x}$. The network learns the right thing without ever seeing it. It is the same move DDPM made when it used the noise of a single example as the target.

sections.heading: 13. The catch: which $\sigma$?
sections.text:
We now have a tractable loss, but the slide adds a warning: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{SM}}(q_\sigma)$, and $q_\sigma$ is not exactly $p_{\text{data}}$. We learn the score of the blurred data, not of the data. Remember what we wanted from section 2: arrows that guide a point from far away all the way into the data. The noise level decides which half of that wish we get.

With $\sigma \ll 1$, $q_\sigma$ is close to $p_{\text{data}}$, so the arrows near the data are accurate. But the noisy training points also stay close to the data, so the network never sees the empty regions far away. There it has no training signal and its arrows are guesses: poor estimations in low-density regions.

Why exactly, made visible by writing the expectation out as an integral, as the lecture does on the board:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{SM}}(q_\sigma) = \mathbb{E}_{\tilde{x} \sim q_\sigma} \bigl\| s_\theta(\tilde{x}) - \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log q_\sigma(\tilde{x}) \bigr\|^2 = \int q_\sigma(\tilde{x})\, \bigl\| s_\theta(\tilde{x}) - \nabla_{\tilde{x}} \log q_\sigma(\tilde{x}) \bigr\|^2 d\tilde{x}$$

The squared error of the arrow at each point $\tilde{x}$ is weighted by $q_\sigma(\tilde{x})$, how likely that point is to appear. You are weighing your loss by how probable your points are. Where $q_\sigma(\tilde{x})$ is large, a wrong arrow costs a lot and the network is pushed hard to fix it. Where $q_\sigma(\tilde{x})$ is almost zero, even a completely wrong arrow adds almost nothing to the loss, so the network has no incentive to get it right. With numbers: if an arrow is off by 10 at a point where $q_\sigma = 10^{-6}$, it adds $10^{-6} \times 100 = 10^{-4}$ to the integrand, invisible next to the errors made where the data is. With small $\sigma$, $q_\sigma$ is practically zero everywhere away from the data, and that is exactly where a sampler starting from random noise begins. Raising $\sigma$ spreads $q_\sigma$ out, which gives those far-away points weight in the loss, and that is why their arrows become well trained.

With $\sigma \gg 1$, the noisy points spread everywhere, so the arrows are well trained even far away: good estimations in low-density regions. But $q_\sigma$ is far from $p_{\text{data}}$: the arrows lead into the blurred smear, not to sharp images.

No single $\sigma$ gives both.

sections.heading: How the noise level changes the score
sections.caption: A data distribution consisting of two points, at two different noise levels. The curve is the density and the arrows below it the score; the arrow length shows the magnitude. On the left the density is squeezed around the data and in the distant regions the score is almost zero, so a sampler starting there does not know which way to go. On the right the same data is spread out with wide noise; the score is defined everywhere and points towards the data. This is why annealed sampling starts at a high level and comes down.

sections.heading: 14. NCSN: learn every noise level at once
sections.text:
The resolution (Song and Ermon, 2019) is not to choose. Pick a ladder of noise levels $\sigma_1 < \ldots < \sigma_T$ and give the level to the network as an extra input, $s_\theta(x) \to s_\theta(x, \sigma_i)$. One network, a Noise Conditional Score Network, learns the score of every blurred version:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{NCSN}} = \sum_{i=1}^{L} \lambda(i)\, \mathbb{E}_x \bigl\| s_\theta(x, \sigma_i) - \nabla_x \log q_{\sigma_i}(x) \bigr\|_2^2$$

Each term is a denoising score matching loss at one level, so in practice the target is again $-(\tilde{x} - x)/\sigma_i^2$. The weights $\lambda(i)$ balance the levels; since the target scales like $1/\sigma_i$, the usual choice $\lambda(i) = \sigma_i^2$ keeps every level contributing a similar amount.

sections.heading: 15. Sampling: annealed Langevin dynamics
sections.text:
The intuition slides show the plan as a sequence of pictures. Start far away in the widest blur $q_{\sigma_T}$ with $\sigma_T \gg 1$: everything is smeared, the arrows are reliable even where you start, and following them brings you into the broad region where data lives. Then switch to $q_{\sigma_{T-1}}$, a little sharper; you are already in the right area, so its arrows are reliable for you, and they refine your position. Keep lowering the noise. By the time you reach $q_{\sigma_1}$, close to the real data, you are already next to a mode, exactly where the low-noise arrows are accurate. Each level hands the next one a starting point in the region where that level is good.

This is annealed Langevin dynamics. Annealing is a term from metallurgy: cool slowly, so that the material settles into a good state instead of freezing wherever it happens to be.

sections.title: Annealed Langevin Dynamics
lines: Input: noise levels $\sigma_T > \ldots > \sigma_1$, steps per level $K$, step sizes $\alpha_i$
$x \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_T^2 I)$ >> pure noise at the largest level
$x \leftarrow x + \frac{\alpha_i}{2}\, s_\theta(x, \sigma_i) + \sqrt{\alpha_i}\, \epsilon$ >> predicted score to move towards, plus a random kick

sections.heading: 16. The same thing as DDPM
sections.text:
Put DDPM's forward process next to this. In DDPM the noisy image at step $t$ is

$$x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon \quad \Longrightarrow \quad q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\bigl( \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0,\ (1-\bar{\alpha}_t) I \bigr)$$

Its score, by the Gaussian formula of section 9 with mean $\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0$ and variance $1-\bar{\alpha}_t$, is

$$\nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t \mid x_0) = -\frac{x_t - \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t} = -\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}$$

The slide labels the two sides: on the left the score, the direction from noisy to clean; on the right the noise to remove from the noisy sample. They are the same vector up to sign and the factor $\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}$. So a network trained to predict $\epsilon$ is, after rescaling, a network that predicts the score:

$$s_\theta(x_t, t) = -\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}$$

DDPM and NCSN were developed independently, one from a likelihood bound and one from score matching, and they train the same network.

sections.heading: 17. Why move to continuous time
sections.text:
Line the two methods up. DDPM goes $x_0 \to x_1 \to \ldots \to x_T$; NCSN goes $x_0 \to x_{\sigma_1} \to \ldots \to x_{\sigma_T}$. Both chop the corruption of an image into a fixed number of steps, and the slide points out that this number is arbitrary: nothing about images says it must be 1,000. The steps are a choice we made, not part of the problem. So consider the corruption as a continuous process in time and let any number of steps be just one way of approximating it.

What that buys, concretely:

The number of steps becomes free. With a discrete chain, the coefficients $\beta_t$ and $\bar{\alpha}_t$ are tied to $T$. In continuous time the model is trained once and sampled with 1,000, 50 or 20 steps by the same network.

Unification. DDPM and NCSN become two choices of the same equation, VP and VE (section 20).

Ready-made mathematics. Reversing a stochastic process in time, the probability flow ODE and high-order numerical solvers all exist already, and they apply as soon as the process is written in this language. DPM-Solver comes through that door.

sections.heading: 18. The continuous noise: the Wiener process
sections.text:
To add noise continuously we need the continuous version of "add a little Gaussian noise at every step". That object is the Wiener process $W_t$, also called Brownian motion: think of the jittering of a speck of dust on water. Its three properties, as listed on the slide:

$W_0 = 0$: it starts at zero.

$W_t - W_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, (t - s) I)$: the change over any time interval is Gaussian, with variance equal to the length of the interval.

Independent increments: what happens in one interval tells you nothing about what happens in the next.

The second property has a consequence that will appear repeatedly: over a short time $dt$ the increment $dW$ has variance $dt$, so its size is $\sqrt{dt}$, not $dt$. We write $dW = \sqrt{dt}\, \epsilon$ with $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. The reason is that variances of independent pieces add: 100 small independent steps have 100 times the variance of one, but only 10 times the standard deviation. This square root is what makes random motion behave so differently from smooth motion.

sections.heading: 19. From the discrete chains to equations
sections.text:
DDPM first. Its discrete step is $x_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\, x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\, \epsilon$. If you used twice as many steps, each step would have to add half as much noise, otherwise the total corruption would change. So the quantity that does not depend on the step size is the noise per unit time; call it $\beta(t)$, and set $\beta_t = \beta(t)\, \Delta t$. This is the reparametrization of $\beta$ mentioned on the slide.

For a small step, expand the square root with $(1 + u)^a \approx 1 + a u$, here $u = -\beta(t)\Delta t$ and $a = \tfrac{1}{2}$:

$$\sqrt{1 - \beta(t)\Delta t} \approx 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\Delta t$$

A number check: for $\beta(t)\Delta t = 0.01$ the true value is 0.994987 and the approximation 0.995. Substituting and writing the change $x_t - x_{t-1}$ gives

$$\Delta x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x\, \Delta t + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, \sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon$$

and with $\sqrt{\Delta t}\, \epsilon \to dW$ as $\Delta t \to 0$, this is the slide's continuous formulation:

$$dx = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x\, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\, dW$$

NCSN is simpler. Its discrete step only adds noise, $x_t = x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\sigma_t^2 - \sigma_{t-1}^2}\, \epsilon$, chosen so that the total variance after step $t$ is exactly $\sigma_t^2$. The variance added per unit time is the rate of growth of $\sigma^2(t)$, so by the definition of the Wiener process

$$dx = \sqrt{\frac{d[\sigma^2(t)]}{dt}}\, dW$$

sections.heading: 20. The general form: drift and diffusion
sections.text:
Both equations are special cases of one stochastic differential equation (SDE):

$$dx = f(x, t)\, dt + g(t)\, dW$$

The slides walk through it term by term with pictures.

The drift $f(x, t)\, dt$ is the deterministic part. If it were the only term, $x$ would follow a smooth path: at each instant it moves by $f(x, t)\, dt$, like a boat carried by a current. In DDPM the drift is $-\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\, x$, a gentle pull of the image towards zero.

The diffusion $g(t)\, dW$ is the random part. If it were the only term, $x$ would jitter around with no direction, by steps of size $g(t)\sqrt{dt}$, like the speck of dust.

Together, every small step is a push by the current plus a random jolt, and the path looks like a drifting, trembling line.

An important warning about notation. This $f(x, t)$ is not the $f(x)$ of section 3. There, $f(x)$ was the unnormalized density, the shape of the data landscape. Here $f(x, t)$ is the drift, a velocity-like function that tells the process where to push. The lecture reuses the letter for a completely different object; in the rest of this walkthrough $f$ always means the drift.

sections.heading: 21. Same letter, different meaning
rows: unnormalized density: the shape of $p_{\text{data}}$ before dividing by $Z$
drift: the deterministic push of the process
the drift when it is linear in $x$, with $f(t)$ a scalar coefficient
step size of one Langevin update
how much of the clean image remains at step $t$ (VP)
standard deviation of the noise added to the data
an iteration counter in Langevin; continuous time in the SDE

sections.heading: 22. Two settings of one equation: VP and VE
rows: the network's input always has the same magnitude
the data is never shrunk, only added to
signal and noise are scaled together
the network must handle a huge range of $\sigma$

sections.heading: Why the difference matters
sections.text:
Both make the data unrecognisable and end at a known distribution; they differ in how.

VP shrinks the image a little at every step and puts noise in its place, so the total stays the same. Like pouring out part of a glass of coloured water and topping it up with clear water: the level never changes, the colour fades. Because the input has the same scale at every $t$, the network is comfortable.

VE never touches the image and only pours more and more noise on top. Like never pouring anything out and adding buckets of clear water: the colour fades again, but the vessel overflows. The difficulty is scale: $\sigma$ may range from 0.01 to 50, and one network must work at all of them.

sections.heading: Making the table concrete: what the network sees
sections.text:
In VP the squares of the two coefficients always add to one, so the pixel values stay in the same band:

$$x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon$$

$$t \text{ small: } 0.99\, x_0 + 0.10\, \epsilon \qquad t \text{ middle: } 0.71\, x_0 + 0.71\, \epsilon \qquad t \text{ large: } 0.10\, x_0 + 0.99\, \epsilon$$

In VE the image keeps coefficient 1 and only the noise grows, $x_t = x_0 + \sigma(t)\, \epsilon$. At $\sigma = 0.01$ the input is the clean image with values between $-1$ and $1$; at $\sigma = 50$ the same image's values spread over roughly $-150$ to $150$ and its structure is gone.

Each side pays somewhere. VE pays in range: the input magnitude changes by a factor of thousands, which networks dislike, so in practice the input is divided by its scale and $\sigma$ is given as a separate input. VP pays in sensitivity: to recover the image you divide by $\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}$, which is 0.10 at large $t$, so a small error in the predicted noise becomes ten times larger in the predicted image. That is why clean-image estimates at high noise are blurry.

sections.heading: 23. The timeline: two lines that met
sections.text: The slide's timeline shows why the unification was a real event. On the score-matching line: Hyvärinen's principle of score matching (2005), Vincent's denoising score matching (2010) and Song and Ermon's NCSN (2019). On the diffusion line: Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues' original diffusion paper (2015) and Ho and colleagues' DDPM (2020). The two lines were built by different people with different mathematics, and in 2020 Song and colleagues showed with the SDE formulation that they describe the same process. Their paper, Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations, is the source of most of the rest of this walkthrough.

sections.heading: 24. Training: one recipe for both
sections.text:
The objective is now a score network for every time, $s_\theta(x_t, t)$, trained with denoising score matching:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, x_t} \Bigl[ \lambda_t \bigl\| s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t \mid x_0) \bigr\|^2 \Bigr]$$

What does $x_t$ given $x_0$ look like? In VP (DDPM-style) $x_t \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0, (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t) I)$; in VE (NCSN-style) $x_t \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(x_0, \sigma_t^2 I)$. Both fit one form,

$$x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \epsilon$$

with $\alpha_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}$, $\sigma_t = \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}$ for VP and $\alpha_t = 1$ for VE. (Yet another $\alpha$: here the signal coefficient.) The Gaussian score then gives the target directly:

$$\nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t \mid x_0) = -\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma_t}$$

The design space of these choices, which $\alpha_t$, $\sigma_t$, $\lambda_t$, is analysed carefully in Karras and colleagues' Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models (2022).

sections.title: Training recipe
lines: $x_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}$, $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, $t \sim \mathcal{U}(0, T)$ >> clean image, noise, time step
$\mathcal{L} = \lambda_t \| s_\theta(x_t, t) + \epsilon / \sigma_t \|^2$ >> use $x_t$ and $t$ to predict $-\epsilon/\sigma_t$

sections.heading: 25. Going backwards in time: the reverse SDE
sections.text:
Training gives us the score at every time. To generate, we have to run the corruption backwards: start from noise and end at data. Anderson (1982) showed that an SDE can be reversed in time, and that the reverse process is another SDE:

$$dx = \bigl[ f(x, t) - g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x) \bigr] dt + g(t)\, d\bar{W}$$

The derivation uses the Fokker-Planck equation and is beyond the scope of the lecture; the slides instead build the equation up term by term, and that reading is what matters.

$f(x, t)\, dt$, the forward drift coefficient: the same current as in the forward process.

$g(t)\, d\bar{W}$, the forward diffusion coefficient times a Wiener process. It is a Wiener process, but a different one from the forward process: fresh randomness, run backwards in time.

$-g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)$, the correction to the drift, and inside it the score. Going forward, the noise kept pushing points away from the data. Going backward, the noise term still jitters points randomly, which on its own would spread them out further. To end up concentrated on the data instead, the process must go even more towards regions of high density, and the score is exactly the arrow pointing there. Its coefficient is $g(t)^2$ because the stronger the noise that has to be compensated, the stronger the push must be.

Here $p_t$ is the distribution of the noisy data at time $t$: take the whole dataset, corrupt every image to level $t$, and $p_t$ describes the resulting cloud, with $p_0 = p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_T$ close to pure noise. We never have a formula for $p_t$, only samples, but its score is precisely what $s_\theta(x, t)$ was trained to output.

sections.title: Inference recipe (reverse SDE, Euler-Maruyama)
lines: $x_{t_{i-1}} = x_{t_i} + \bigl[ f(x_{t_i}, t_i) - g(t_i)^2 s_\theta(x_{t_i}, t_i) \bigr] \Delta t + g(t_i) \sqrt{|\Delta t|}\, \xi_i$

sections.heading: Reading the inference step
sections.text:
Euler-Maruyama is the simplest way to step through an SDE: freeze everything at the current point, take one step of size $\Delta t$ for the deterministic part, and add a Gaussian kick of size $\sqrt{|\Delta t|}$ for the random part, the square root coming from section 18.

One detail that the compact formula hides: we are moving backwards, from $t_i$ to the earlier time $t_{i-1}$, so $\Delta t = t_{i-1} - t_i$ is negative. With the minus sign in front of the score term, a negative $\Delta t$ turns $-g^2 s_\theta\, \Delta t$ into a step along the score, towards the data, which is what the intuition demanded. The random kick uses the absolute value, because a standard deviation cannot be negative.

sections.heading: 26. The weakness of the SDE: randomness costs time
sections.text:
The stochastic term $g(t)\, d\bar{W}$ has two costs.

A slower solver. Typically 1,000 to 2,000 steps are needed, partly because we do not know in advance which parts of the trajectory are easy and could take big steps, and which are hard. With fresh randomness injected at every step, large steps quickly degrade quality.

More sources of error. There is the usual discretization error from finite steps, and on top of it the injected noise itself.

Suppose, hypothetically, the same process could be written with something in place of the drift and nothing in place of the random term: no stochasticity at all. That would mean a faster solver, because the mathematics of ordinary differential equations lets you go fast where the path is smooth and slow where it bends, and a single source of error, only the finite step size. Is there such an equation, and what goes in the box labelled "something"?

sections.heading: 27. Finding the ODE: from particles to the crowd
sections.text:
The derivation on the slides has three arrows, and each has a plain meaning.

Forward SDE to Fokker-Planck. Instead of following one noisy particle, describe how the whole crowd's density $p_t(x)$ changes in time. The Fokker-Planck equation does this:

$$\frac{\partial p_t(x)}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot \bigl( f(x, t)\, p_t(x) \bigr) + \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \Delta p_t(x)$$

The first term is the current carrying density along with it; $\nabla \cdot$ (the divergence) measures how much flows out of each small region. The second term is the spreading caused by the noise; $\Delta$ is the Laplacian, which makes peaks melt and valleys fill in, the way a drop of ink spreads in water.

Fokker-Planck to the continuity equation, by algebra. Here the trick of section 4 comes back. Since $\nabla \log p = \nabla p / p$, we have $\nabla p = p\, \nabla \log p$, and therefore $\Delta p = \nabla \cdot \nabla p = \nabla \cdot \bigl( p\, \nabla \log p \bigr)$. The spreading term can be written as a flow too, and both terms combine into one:

$$\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t}(x) = -\nabla \cdot \Bigl( \bigl[ f(x, t) - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x) \bigr]\, p_t(x) \Bigr)$$

Continuity equation to PF-ODE. This has the form of the continuity equation, $\partial_t p = -\nabla \cdot (v\, p)$: the density changes only because mass is moved around by a velocity field $v$, with nothing created or destroyed. So recognise the bracket as a velocity,

$$v(x, t) = f(x, t) - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)$$

and move every particle with it deterministically:

$$dx = \bigl[ f(x, t) - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \nabla \log p_t(x) \bigr] dt$$

This is the probability flow ODE. In it, $f$ and $g$ are modelling assumptions, the same ones chosen for the forward process (VP or VE), and the score is approximated by our trained model.

The factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ now has a clear origin: it is the $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in front of the Laplacian in Fokker-Planck. In the SDE, half of the work of moving density around was done by randomness. With the randomness removed, the velocity field has to do that work itself, and the bookkeeping balances at exactly one half of the reverse SDE's coefficient.

sections.heading: 28. What the PF-ODE means, and what it does not
sections.text:
Probability flow: the equation moves probability mass like a fluid. It satisfies the continuity equation with velocity $v(x, t)$, so the density it produces at every time is exactly $p_t$, the same as the SDE.

Ordinary differential equation: no random term, $+ \varnothing$ on the slide. Given a starting point, the path is fully determined.

The warning sign on the slide is the subtle part: same marginal densities is not the same as same trajectories. The cloud of points has the same shape at every time under both processes, but individual points travel completely different routes. Picture a crowd leaving a stadium: everyone could walk the shortest path calmly, or everyone could stagger randomly with a slight bias towards the exits. At every moment the crowd may occupy the same areas, while each person's walk looks entirely different.

sections.heading: 29. Reverse SDE or PF-ODE
rows: $\bigl[ f - g^2 \nabla_x \log p_t \bigr] dt + g\, d\bar{W}$

sections.heading: The reasons behind the rows
sections.text:
Diversity. The SDE draws fresh noise at every step, so even from the same starting noise each run ends at a different image. In the ODE all randomness is in the starting point; fix it and the output is fixed.

Quality. The injected noise acts as error correction. If a step throws you somewhat off, the randomness lets you explore and the score term pulls you back over the following steps. The ODE follows a single trajectory, and every discretization error it makes is carried along with no way back. With a generous step budget, the SDE usually gives better samples.

Speed. Determinism is what lets ODE solvers take large steps safely, finishing in tens of steps instead of hundreds.

The slide then lines this up with what came before: DDIM is to the PF-ODE what DDPM is to the reverse SDE. Each pair is a deterministic and a stochastic way of sampling, DDIM can reuse a model trained for DDPM exactly as the PF-ODE reuses the score network, and the trade-offs match: lower diversity, lower quality at equal steps, faster.

sections.heading: 30. Solving the ODE: counting network calls
sections.text:
Generation is now solving $dx = v(x, t)\, dt$ with a known starting point $x(t_0) = x_0$, here pure noise, backwards to the data. The cost that matters is the number of function evaluations (NFE): how many times the network has to be run, because each evaluation of $v$ requires the score, and so a full forward pass.

The simplest method is Euler: evaluate the velocity once and step in a straight line, $x_{t_{i+1}} = x_{t_i} + v(x_{t_i}, t_i)\, \Delta t$. One NFE per step, but a large error wherever the path bends, as the slide's picture shows with the straight red line missing the curve.

Runge-Kutta 4 evaluates the velocity at four cleverly chosen points along the step and averages them, $x_{t_{i+1}} = x_{t_i} + \frac{k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4}{6} \Delta t$. Four NFE per step and a much smaller error, so far fewer steps are needed for the same accuracy.

sections.heading: 31. A smarter solver: DPM-Solver
sections.text:
Both methods treat $v$ as an unknown black box. But we know its form: $v(x, t) = f(x, t) - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)$, and in diffusion the drift is linear in $x$, $f(x, t) = f(t)\, x$ (in VP, $f(t) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)$). So the right-hand side splits into two parts:

$$f(t)\, x - \tfrac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)$$

The first part is linear in $x$, and a linear equation can be solved exactly with pen and paper. Only the second part, non-linear in $x$ and containing the network, really needs numerical approximation. Traditional solvers discretize both parts and so make an error even in the part that could have been solved exactly. A smarter solver solves the linear part exactly and discretizes only the network's part.

That is DPM-Solver (Lu et al., 2022). Using variation of constants and a change of variables, the exact solution from $t_i$ to $t_{i-1}$ is

$$x_{t_{i-1}} = \frac{\alpha_{t_{i-1}}}{\alpha_{t_i}}\, x_{t_i} - \alpha_{t_{i-1}} \int_{\lambda_{t_i}}^{\lambda_{t_{i-1}}} e^{-\lambda}\, \hat{\epsilon}_\theta(\hat{x}_{t_\lambda}, t_\lambda)\, d\lambda$$

with $\lambda_t = \log(\alpha_t / \sigma_t)$, the logarithm of the signal-to-noise ratio, and $\hat{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t, t) = -\sigma_t\, \hat{s}_\theta(x_t, t)$, the score network rewritten as a noise predictor (the relation of section 16). The first term is the linear part, solved exactly: it simply rescales $x$. All the approximation is pushed into one integral over $\lambda$, and the open question the slide raises is what to do with that term.

sections.heading: 32. The variants, and the result
sections.text:
The answer is a Taylor expansion of the network's output in $\lambda$. DPM-Solver-1 treats $\hat{\epsilon}_\theta$ as constant over the step, its value at the start: one NFE per step, and it turns out to be exactly DDIM. DPM-Solver-2 adds the first derivative, the rate at which $\hat{\epsilon}_\theta$ changes with $\lambda$: two NFE per step and a more accurate integral. In general DPM-Solver-k uses a Taylor expansion of order $k - 1$ and costs $k$ NFE per step.

The conclusion slides summarise the whole second half of the lecture. The mindset: forward SDE, then Fokker-Planck, then the continuity equation, then the PF-ODE, and then exploiting the structure of the PF-ODE to build DPM-Solver. The performance: for a fixed budget of network calls it beats traditional solvers, most clearly when that budget is small. And in practice no retraining is needed, the same trained network is used, and reasonable images come out after only 10 to 20 NFE. The DPM++ options in Stable Diffusion interfaces are refined versions of this solver.

sections.heading: Beyond the slides: four disguises of the same network
sections.text:
Section 16 converted a noise predictor into a score, and DPM-Solver converted it back. These conversions are pure algebra, and there is a fourth common output, the velocity of v-prediction (Salimans and Ho, 2022):

$$\hat{x}_0 = \frac{x_t - \sigma_t\, \epsilon_\theta}{\alpha_t} \qquad s_\theta = -\frac{\epsilon_\theta}{\sigma_t} \qquad v_\theta = \alpha_t\, \epsilon_\theta - \sigma_t\, \hat{x}_0$$

A network may be trained to output any of the four, and the others follow. They differ in how well-behaved the training target is: predicting $\epsilon$ is hard at small noise, predicting $x_0$ is hard at large noise, and the velocity sits between them and behaves evenly at every level, which is why it is popular for distillation and few-step sampling. It is also the link to flow matching: the PF-ODE's right-hand side is a velocity field, and flow matching learns such a field directly, choosing the paths to be straight.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text:
We wanted arrows pointing towards the data. The gradient of the density gives them in principle but fails twice: it contains the unknown normalization $Z$ of $p_{	ext{data}} = f(x)/Z$, and it fades to zero far from the data. Taking the logarithm first fixes both: $Z$ drops out because it is a constant, and $
abla p / p$ keeps the direction while turning the length into a relative rate that stays informative far away. That arrow field is the score. Its true value is unknown, but the score of the noise you add yourself is known, $-(	ilde{x} - x)/\sigma^2$, and training on it learns the score of the blurred data. Small noise is accurate near the data, large noise covers empty space, so NCSN learns all levels and annealed Langevin walks down them. The score target is DDPM's noise target rescaled. In continuous time the two methods become one SDE, $dx = f\, dt + g\, dW$, with VP and VE as two settings. Reversing it adds a score correction; rewriting the crowd's evolution with $
abla p = p\, 
abla \log p$ gives the deterministic PF-ODE with the same marginals but different paths, the common ground of DDIM and flow matching, and DPM-Solver solves its linear part exactly to sample in 10 to 20 network calls.
