sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text:
Course: CME 296 (Stanford), Lecture 2 — Score matching, by Afshine and Shervine Amidi. This walkthrough follows the order and the notation of the slides: Motivation, Score estimation, Differential formulation, Training, Inference, Probability flows.

Papers: Hyvärinen — Estimation of Non-Normalized Statistical Models by Score Matching (2005) · Vincent — A Connection Between Score Matching and Denoising Autoencoders (2010) · Song et al. — Sliced Score Matching (2019) · Song and Ermon — Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution (NeurIPS 2019) · Song et al. — Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations (ICLR 2021) · Anderson — Reverse-Time Diffusion Equation Models (1982) · Karras et al. — Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models (2022) · Lu et al. — DPM-Solver (NeurIPS 2022).

On this site: the DDPM walkthrough for the likelihood road to the same loss; the Flow Matching walkthrough for the velocity-field view that continues from the PF-ODE.

flow.title: Flow Matching and Rectified Flow — A Complete Walkthrough
flow.context: CME 296 Lecture 3, following the slides (t = 0 noise, t = 1 data) · CS231n 13
flow.summary: Transporting noise to data with a learned velocity: the time convention, trajectory, flow, probability path and vector field, velocity as a highway against score as a compass, one sample as an ODE and the distribution through divergence, flux and the continuity equation; why maximum likelihood was slow; the derivation from a Dirac target, the conditional Gaussian path and velocity, the marginal path and velocity and the conditional flow matching loss; training and Euler inference; crossing paths, reflow and its two proofs; and the three paradigms side by side.

sections.heading: 1. Where the course stands
sections.text:
The lecture starts by recalling the two previous ones. Lecture 1 (diffusion with DDPM) noised an image step by step with $q(x_t \mid x_{t-1})$ and learned to undo it with $p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)$, by predicting the noise to remove. Lecture 2 (score matching) learned the arrow $\nabla_x \log p_{\text{data}}(x)$ that points towards the data, at several noise levels. The two met in one identity, the score from noisy to clean is the noise to remove, rescaled, and in a unified view as one stochastic differential equation, forward $dx = f(x,t)\, dt + g(t)\, dW$ and its reverse with a score correction.

Both roads are long: a likelihood bound and Gaussian algebra on one side, an SDE and its time reversal on the other. And both end with sampling as a long walk. Lecture 3 asks the question directly. The problem was always the same picture: a random point far away, and somewhere the data distribution $p_{\text{data}}$, the cloud of teddy bears. Can we learn the way from one to the other directly?

sections.heading: 2. The idea: transport probability mass
sections.text: Think of two distributions as two piles of sand of the same total amount, $\int p_{\text{initial}}(x)\, dx = 1$ and $\int p_{\text{target}}(x)\, dx = 1$. The initial pile is simple, a round Gaussian heap. The target pile has the shape of the data. The idea of flows is to move the sand from the first shape to the second, continuously over time, without creating or destroying any. If we know how every grain moves, we can drop a grain anywhere in the initial pile, let it travel, and it lands somewhere in the target pile: a sample.

sections.heading: 3. Notation, and a warning about time
sections.text:
The lecture fixes the two ends:

$$p_0 = \mathcal{N}(0, I), \qquad p_1 = p_{\text{data}}$$

The initial distribution is noise at $t = 0$, the target is the data at $t = 1$. Time runs from $0$ to $1$.

This is the opposite of lectures 1 and 2, where $t = 0$ was the clean image and $t = T$ was noise. In flow matching, $x_0$ is noise and $x_1$ is the clean image. The slides put this behind a warning sign, and it is the single most common source of confusion when reading papers: Lipman et al. and this lecture use $t = 0$ for noise, while the rectified flow paper, CS231n and the SD3 paper use $t = 0$ for data. When a formula seems to have the wrong sign, check the direction of time first. This walkthrough uses the lecture's convention throughout.

sections.heading: 4. Four words: trajectory, flow, probability path, vector field
sections.text:
Trajectory, $x_t$: the path one point takes for $t \in [0, 1]$. Pick a starting point in the noise and follow it; the curve it draws to the data is its trajectory.

Flow, $\psi_t(x_0)$: the collection of trajectories starting from every possible $x_0$. It is the rule "start at $x_0$; where are you at time $t$?" A trajectory is one boat; the flow is the map of all boats.

Probability path, $p_t(x)$: the distribution of $x_t$ at time $t$. At $t = 0$ it is $p_0$, at $t = 1$ it is $p_{\text{data}}$, and in between it is a family of intermediate shapes, the slide's grey two-lobed cloud.

Vector field, also known as velocity, $u_t(x)$: where to move, direction and speed, at time $t$ and location $x$. This is the object that will be learned. Trajectories follow it, and the probability path is what it produces.

sections.heading: 5. Velocity and score: a highway and a compass
sections.text:
Lecture 2's score and this lecture's velocity both put an arrow at every point, so they look alike. The slides separate them with two pictures.

The velocity is a highway. It tells you how to drive: in which direction and how fast, right now, so that the whole traffic gets where it is going on time. It describes a movement in time.

The score is a compass. Standing at a point of the landscape $p$, it shows the direction in which the landscape rises, the direction of higher density, at this frozen moment. It describes a shape, not a movement.

A small example makes the difference concrete. Take the simplest flow, used later in the lecture: noise $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ carried in a straight line to a single data point $x_1 = 3$. Halfway, at $t = 0.5$, the cloud of moving points is centred at 1.5 with width 0.5. Look at the point exactly in the middle, $x = 1.5$. The compass says: you are already on top of the cloud, every direction goes downhill, score $= 0$. The highway says: keep driving right at speed 3, because you must reach 3 by $t = 1$. Same point, same moment, opposite advice: the score describes where the crowd is dense, the velocity describes where the crowd is going.

sections.heading: Score and velocity at the same three points
sections.caption: The cloud at $t = 0.5$ of points travelling in straight lines from $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ to $x_1 = 3$. At each of three points, the score (amber) points to the middle of the current cloud and vanishes at its centre; the velocity (green) points to the data and is largest for the points that are furthest behind. In diffusion the two are connected by a formula (lecture 2's probability flow ODE), which is why they can feel like the same thing; they still answer different questions.

sections.heading: 6. One sample: an ordinary differential equation
sections.text:
Following the highway is an ordinary differential equation:

$$dx = u_t(x)\, dt$$

Read it with the slide's labels: $dx$ is the change in sample position, $u_t(x)$ the vector field at location $x$ and time $t$, $dt$ the change in time. In a small time step the point moves from $x$ to $x + u_t(x)\, dt$.

The trajectory starting from $x_0$, which is $\psi_t(x_0)$, is unique if the velocity $u_t(x)$ is Lipschitz continuous, that is, if it never changes infinitely fast from one place to the next. Uniqueness is the key property: two trajectories can never cross, because at the crossing point there would have to be two different velocities. Remember this; it comes back in sections 21 and 23.

sections.heading: 7. The whole distribution: mass conservation
sections.text:
Now step back from one grain of sand to the whole pile. Fix a small box at location $x$ and watch the density inside it change over time. The slide writes the balance in words:

temporal evolution of the density at time $t$ at a particular location $=$ "inflow" of density $-$ "outflow" of density at that location.

The left side is $\partial p_t(x) / \partial t$. The right side needs a way to measure net outflow, and that is what the divergence is.

sections.heading: 8. Divergence in one dimension
sections.text:
Picture a pipe of water in one dimension, with $f(x)$ the speed of the water at $x$, positive to the right. Look at a tiny piece between $x$ and $x + \Delta$. Water enters at the left end at rate $f(x)$ and leaves at the right end at rate $f(x + \Delta)$, so the net outflow is $f(x + \Delta) - f(x)$. Per unit length, in the limit, this is a derivative:

$$\operatorname{div} f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$$

The slides draw the four cases. Divergence $\geq 0$: leaving more than what is coming, or everything leaving in both directions; the box empties. Divergence $\leq 0$: coming more than what is leaving, or everything coming in from both sides; mass accumulates. With numbers: $f(x) = x$ on the piece $[1, 2]$ lets 1 unit per second in and 2 out, a net loss of 1, matching $\partial f / \partial x = 1$.

In $n$ dimensions the contributions of every direction add up:

$$\operatorname{div}(f) = \nabla \cdot f = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}$$

sections.heading: How to read the 1D picture
sections.svg: <svg width="560" height="200" viewBox="0 0 560 200" role="img" aria-label="1D divergence"><defs><marker id="ah" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><text x="15" y="20">divergence > 0</text><line class="axis" x1="15" y1="105" x2="260" y2="105" stroke-width="1"/><ellipse class="q-line" cx="145" cy="105" rx="6" ry="26" stroke-width="1.4"/><line class="p-curve" x1="105" y1="105" x2="131" y2="105" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line class="p-curve" x1="159" y1="105" x2="211" y2="105" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="118" y="69" text-anchor="middle">in, f=1</text><text x="185" y="69" text-anchor="middle">out, f=2</text><text x="15" y="161">out > in → the interval empties</text><text x="300" y="20">divergence < 0</text><line class="axis" x1="300" y1="105" x2="545" y2="105" stroke-width="1"/><ellipse class="q-line" cx="430" cy="105" rx="6" ry="26" stroke-width="1.4"/><line class="p-curve" x1="364" y1="105" x2="416" y2="105" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line class="p-curve" x1="444" y1="105" x2="470" y2="105" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><text x="390" y="69" text-anchor="middle">in, f=2</text><text x="457" y="69" text-anchor="middle">out, f=1</text><text x="300" y="161">in > out → mass accumulates</text></svg>
sections.caption: A tiny interval in one dimension and the flow speed at its two ends. On the left what leaves is larger than what enters and the interval empties; on the right the opposite, and mass accumulates in the interval.

sections.heading: 9. Divergence of what? The probability flux
sections.text:
Which $f$ should the divergence be taken of? The slide's first guess, the vector field $u_t(x)$, is wrong, and its example shows why. Suppose two points $x_1$ and $x_2$ have the same velocity, $u_t(x_1) = u_t(x_2)$, but $x_1$ sits in a thin region and $x_2$ in a dense one, $p_t(x_1) < p_t(x_2)$. The same speed carries much more mass away from $x_2$ than from $x_1$, so we want the quantity whose divergence we take to be larger at $x_2$: $\| f(x_1) \| < \| f(x_2) \|$. The velocity alone cannot see that.

The right choice is the probability flux, density times velocity:

$$(p_t u_t)(x)$$

It measures how much probability mass passes per unit time, not just how fast. Where the density is zero nothing is transported, however large the velocity.

sections.heading: 10. The continuity equation
sections.text:
With the flux in place, the balance of section 7 becomes an equation:

$$\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t}(x) = -\nabla \cdot (p_t u_t)(x)$$

The density at a location increases exactly by the net inflow of flux and decreases by its net outflow. Nothing is created or destroyed; for probability this is automatic, since the total mass is always 1. When a vector field $u_t$ and a probability path $p_t$ satisfy this equation, the slides say that the vector field generates the probability path.

sections.heading: 11. Two perspectives on the same velocity
rows: one point moves from $x$ to $x + u_t(x)\, dt$
density flows in and out of every small box

sections.heading: Why the two perspectives agree
sections.text: The slide joins them in one statement: if $x_0 \sim p_0$ and $\frac{dx_t}{dt} = u_t(x_t)$, then $x_t \sim p_t$. Draw many starting points from the noise, let each follow the velocity, and the cloud they form at time $t$ has exactly the distribution $p_t$ generated by $u_t$. This is what makes the whole method work: we can learn the field for single points and trust that the distribution follows.

sections.heading: 12. Flow models: the plan
sections.text:
Goal: map $x_0 \sim p_0$ to $x_1 \sim p_1$. The strategy has two steps.

Training: estimate $u_t(x)$ for all times $t$ and all locations $x$ with a network $u_t^\theta(x)$.

Inference: sample from the initial distribution and solve the ODE numerically with the learned field:

$$\hat{x}_1 = x_0 + \int_0^1 u_t^\theta(x)\, dt$$

The rest of the lecture is about the first step: how to train $u_t^\theta$.

sections.heading: 13. Earlier attempts: maximum likelihood, and why it is slow
sections.text:
Continuous normalizing flows (Chen et al., Neural ODEs, 2018) learned the vector field by maximum likelihood. The idea is to rewrite the continuity equation along a moving point, which turns it into an equation for the log-density:

$$\frac{d}{dt} \log p_t(x) = -\nabla \cdot u_t(x)$$

and then to integrate it along the trajectory to get the likelihood of a data point:

$$\log p_1^\theta(x_1) = \log p_0(x_0) + \int_0^1 -\nabla \cdot u_t^\theta(x)\, dt$$

The limitation: training is slow and expensive. Every training step has to simulate the whole ODE, calling the network many times, and compute a divergence at each step. Flow matching keeps the idea of learning $u_t$ but removes the simulation from training altogether; this is what simulation-free means.

sections.heading: 14. Flow matching: the goal, and the wall
sections.text:
The direct objective is a regression of the network onto the true velocity:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x} \Bigl[ \bigl\| u_t^\theta(x) - u_t(x) \bigr\|^2 \Bigr]$$

The red note on the slide: we don't have access to $u_t(x)$. The vector field that carries $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ onto the whole data distribution depends on the entire distribution at once, and nobody can write it down. The same wall as in score matching, where the true score was unknown.

sections.heading: 15. Fall back to an easier setup: one data point
sections.text: The way around the wall is the same move as in lectures 1 and 2: solve the problem for a single example first. Instead of the whole cloud of teddy bears, pick one image $x_1$ and pretend the target distribution is just that point, a Dirac distribution $\delta_{x_1}$, all the mass sitting on $x_1$. How do we go from the initial Gaussian to this Dirac?

sections.heading: 16. The conditional probability path
sections.text:
The lecture proposes a Gaussian that slides towards $x_1$ and shrinks as it goes:

$$p_t(x \mid x_1) = \mathcal{N}\bigl( t\, x_1,\ (1 - t)^2 I \bigr)$$

Read the two parameters. The mean $t\, x_1$ moves on a straight line from $0$ at $t = 0$ to $x_1$ at $t = 1$. The standard deviation $1 - t$ shrinks from $1$ to $0$. So at $t = 0$ this is exactly $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$, the noise, and at $t = 1$ it has collapsed onto $x_1$, the Dirac. In between it is a Gaussian blob gliding along the dashed lines of the slide.

sections.heading: The conditional path to one data point
sections.caption: The conditional probability path $p_t(x \mid x_1)$ for $x_1 = 3$ in one dimension, computed at four times. The Gaussian starts as $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, its centre moves as $t x_1$ (0, 0.75, 1.5, 2.25) and its width shrinks as $1 - t$ (1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25), until at $t = 1$ all the mass sits on $x_1$.

sections.heading: 17. The conditional vector field
sections.text:
Which velocity produces this path? Each point of the blob must move so that it arrives at $x_1$ exactly at $t = 1$. A point at $x$ at time $t$ has distance $x_1 - x$ left to cover and time $1 - t$ left to do it, so it moves at

$$u_t(x \mid x_1) = \frac{x_1 - x}{1 - t}$$

distance remaining over time remaining. The example of section 5 used exactly this: at $t = 0.5$ the point $x = 1.5$ moves at $(3 - 1.5) / 0.5 = 3$.

One more line, which the lecture uses later. A point that started at $x_0$ is at $x = (1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1$ at time $t$. Substituting, $x_1 - x = (1 - t)(x_1 - x_0)$, so

$$u_t(x \mid x_1) = x_1 - x_0$$

along the path the velocity is constant: every point drives in a straight line at constant speed from its starting noise to the data point.

sections.heading: 18. The conditional field generates the conditional path
sections.text: The slides state the link in the same form as section 11, now conditioned on $x_1$: the conditional vector field $u_t(\cdot \mid x_1)$ generates the conditional probability path $p_t(\cdot \mid x_1)$, which can be checked by plugging both into the continuity equation. The consequence: if $x_0 \sim p_0(\cdot \mid x_1)$ and $\frac{dx_t}{dt} = u_t(x_t \mid x_1)$, then $x_t \sim p_t(\cdot \mid x_1)$. For one data point, the problem is completely solved, in closed form.

sections.heading: 19. The marginal probability path: aggregate over the data
sections.text:
Real data has many points. Do the construction for each one, $x_1^{(1)}, x_1^{(2)}, \ldots$, giving one sliding Gaussian per data point, and mix them in proportion to how common each data point is:

$$p_t(x) = \int p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\text{data}}(x_1)\, dx_1$$

This is the marginal probability path. Its two ends are right by construction. At $t = 0$ every conditional path is $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$, so $p_{t=0} = p_0$, the initial distribution. At $t = 1$ every conditional path is a Dirac on its own data point, so the mixture is the data itself, $p_{t=1} = p_{\text{data}}$, the target. (The slides draw the mixture for two data points for readability.)

sections.heading: 20. The marginal vector field: given where you are, where should you go?
sections.text:
The velocity of the whole crowd is the average of the conditional velocities, but weighted:

$$u_t(x) = \int u_t(x \mid x_1)\, \frac{p_t(x \mid x_1)\, p_{\text{data}}(x_1)}{p_t(x)}\, dx_1$$

The weight is the posterior $p(x_1 \mid x)$, by Bayes' rule. The slide gives its interpretation in one sentence: given where you are, where should you go? A point at $x$ at time $t$ could be on its way to any of the data points. It is more likely to be heading to the data points whose sliding Gaussian is near $x$, and the posterior says how likely each is. The marginal velocity averages "go to $x_1^{(i)}$" over all $i$, weighted by that belief. The slide draws it with two data points: the point $x$ has two candidate arrows, one towards each, and $u_t(x)$ is their weighted average.

And the generation statement holds again at this level: the marginal vector field $u_t$ generates the marginal probability path $p_t$ (shown with the marginal definition and the continuity equation). So if $x_0 \sim p_0$ and $\frac{dx_t}{dt} = u_t(x_t)$, then $x_t \sim p_t$, and in particular $x_1 \sim p_{\text{data}}$. This $u_t$ is exactly the field we wanted in section 14.

sections.heading: 21. Conditional flow matching: a tractable loss
sections.text:
The marginal field is still an integral over the whole dataset. The final step of the derivation is that we never need to compute it. The loss with the conditional target,

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x} \Bigl[ \bigl\| u_t^\theta(x) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \bigr\|^2 \Bigr], \qquad u_t(x \mid x_1) = x_1 - x_0$$

has the same gradient with respect to $\theta$ as $\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}$ (Lipman et al., 2022; the derivation expands the squared norm and uses the definition of the marginal). Same gradient means same training, so minimising the tractable loss minimises the intractable one.

Why it works, intuitively: the squared loss makes a network output the average of the targets it is shown for the same input. At a point $x$, the conditional targets from all the pairs passing through $x$ are averaged, with exactly the weights of section 20. A tiny example with only two data points, $-1$ and $+1$: at $t = 0.5$ the point $x = 0$ is reached with equal probability by the pair ($x_0 = -1$, $x_1 = +1$, velocity $+2$) and by the pair ($x_0 = +1$, $x_1 = -1$, velocity $-2$). The network sees both targets and learns their average, $0$: from the exact middle, there is no reason to prefer either data point yet. This is the same trick DDPM used when it trained on the noise of single examples.

sections.heading: 22. The derivation in four steps
rows: derive the target vector field for a simple case
a Dirac at one data point
construct the target vector field for our case
the continuity equation, marginalising over the data
the gradients of FM and CFM are equal
an incredibly simple loss: regress onto $x_1 - x_0$

sections.heading: Why it is called flow matching
sections.text: The name has historical reasons, from normalizing flows and continuous normalizing flows. And it is accurate: because the vector field is Lipschitz continuous, there is a 1:1 mapping between a vector field and the flow it produces. Matching the vector field means matching the flow. The recommended read is the paper that introduced it, Lipman, Chen, Ben-Hamu, Nickel and Le, Flow Matching for Generative Modeling (2022).

sections.title: Training procedure
lines: $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, $x_1 \sim p_{\text{data}}$, $t \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$ >> noise, clean image, time step
$x_t = (1 - t)\, x_0 + t\, x_1$ >> noised image
$\mathcal{L} = \| u_t^\theta(x_t) - (x_1 - x_0) \|^2$ >> use $x_t$ and $t$ to predict $x_1 - x_0$

sections.heading: Reading the two procedures
sections.text:
Training never runs the ODE. It draws a noise, an image and a time, places the point on the straight line between them, and asks the network for the direction of that line. That is all.

A one-dimensional check of what the target means: noise $x_0 = -1$, data $x_1 = 2$. Then $x_t = -1 + 3t$, the target velocity is $3$ everywhere on the line, and one Euler step of size 1 from $x_0$ lands at $-1 + 3 \cdot 1 = 2$, exactly the data. For a single pair the path is straight and one step is enough. The next section is about why the learned field is not that simple.

sections.heading: 23. Recap of flow matching training, and what goes wrong
sections.text:
Picture the training in the plane. A pair $x_0, x_1$ gives a dashed straight line and a red target arrow $x_1 - x_0$ at the point $x$ on it. A second pair $x_0', x_1'$ gives another line, and nothing stops the two lines from crossing at the same $x$. There the network receives two different targets and, by the squared loss, learns their average $u_t^\theta(x)$, the blue arrow between the two red ones.

But section 6 said trajectories of an ODE can never cross. So the learned flow cannot follow the straight training lines. Integrating it from $x_0$ and $x_0'$ gives curved paths ending at $z_1 = \psi_1^\theta(x_0)$ and $z_1' = \psi_1^\theta(x_0')$, which bend around each other and may land on different data points than the training pairs did.

sections.heading: The pairs are straight, the learned paths are not
sections.caption: A one-dimensional toy, computed: noise on the left at $t = 0$, two data points $\pm 1$ on the right at $t = 1$. Left: training pairs matched at random, each a straight line, crossing everywhere. Right: the paths of the exact marginal vector field for the same data, solved numerically. They never cross, so they bend, and each start ends at the nearer data point: the learned flow rewires the matching.

sections.heading: 24. Are we happy? Not quite
sections.text:
Two problems remain.

Learning complexity. Crossing paths lead to a different learned rewiring: the model does not reproduce the random pairing it was trained on but its own non-crossing version. And the problem exists even when paths are not strictly crossing; near-crossings already force the averaged field to turn.

Inefficiency at inference. The learned paths are not straight, so the ODE needs more steps to approximate them, and there is no magic solver to save the day: the right-hand side $u_t^\theta(x)$ in $dx = u_t^\theta(x)\, dt$ is a non-linear network. Every Euler step assumes the velocity stays constant along the step, and the more the path bends, the larger that error.

sections.heading: 25. The reflow procedure
sections.text:
Rectified flow (Liu, Gong and Liu, 2022) fixes the matching rather than the solver.

Step 0. Train an initial model on random pairs $(X_0, X_1)$, $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $x_1 \sim p_{\text{data}}$: the "1-rectified flow". This is ordinary flow matching.

Step 1. Create paired data out of the 1-rectified flow model. Draw fresh noise $z_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, solve the learned ODE, and record where it lands, $z_1 = \psi_1^\theta(z_0)$. The training set becomes $\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} = \cup \{ z_0, z_1 \}$. These pairs come from the model's own paths, which do not cross.

Step 2. Train on these paired data with the same loss: the "2-rectified flow", on pairs $(Z_0, Z_1)$. Because the pairs no longer cross, the straight lines between them barely conflict, and the new learned paths are much straighter.

Further steps: repeat steps 1 and 2 as desired, giving $(Z_0^k, Z_1^k)$. To rectify means to straighten.

sections.heading: 26. Why reflow works: two properties
sections.text:
Property 1: the resulting mapping still follows the target distribution $p_{\text{data}}$. Define the velocity of the new process as the average actual velocity at each point, $v^X(x, t) = E[\dot{X}_t \mid X_t = x]$, and let $Z$ follow it, $Z_t = X_0 + \int_0^t v^X(Z_s, s)\, ds$. Using the chain rule and the law of total expectation, both the original interpolation and $Z$ satisfy the same continuity equation,

$$\frac{\partial p_t^X}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (v_t^X p_t^X) = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial p_t^Z}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (v_t^X p_t^Z) = 0$$

with the same initial condition, and the uniqueness theorem then gives $p_t^X = p_t^Z$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$. Rewiring the pairs never changes the distributions, only who goes where.

Property 2: paths are provably straighter at each reflow. Define the straightness of a flow as how far its actual velocity deviates from the straight line between its endpoints:

$$S(Z) = \int_0^1 E\Bigl[ \bigl\| (Z_1 - Z_0) - \dot{Z}_t \bigr\|^2 \Bigr] dt$$

$S = 0$ means perfectly straight. A variance decomposition gives, for each reflow,

$$S(Z^{k+1}) \leq E\bigl[ \| Z_1^k - Z_0^k \|^2 \bigr] - E\bigl[ \| Z_1^{k+1} - Z_0^{k+1} \|^2 \bigr]$$

The right side is the drop in average transport distance. Summing over $k$ telescopes, and since the distances are bounded the best of the first $K$ flows satisfies

$$\min_{k \leq K} S(Z^k) \leq O(1/K)$$

Straightness improves at a rate of one over the number of reflows.

sections.heading: 27. Discussion: reflow in practice
sections.text:
Reflow is done once or twice in practice; otherwise errors accumulate, because each round trains on the outputs of the previous imperfect model. In exchange, we can afford simpler techniques at inference time, such as plain Euler with few steps, since the paths are nearly straight. It is a quality and speed trade-off. Nearly straight paths are also what make distillation to a single step easy; InstaFlow (2024) built one-step text-to-image generation this way.

One naming detail: when large models such as SD3 and FLUX say they use rectified flow, they mean the first stage only, the straight interpolation and the velocity loss, without reflow.

sections.heading: 28. Paradigms seen so far: the forward process
rows: How a noisy sample is built
Which symbol is the clean sample
$x_0$ at $t = 0$; $\epsilon$ is the noise at $t = T$
$dx = f(t)\, x\, dt + g(t)\, dW$, solved in closed form below

sections.heading: The score-based forward process in closed form
sections.text:
When the drift is linear, $f(x, t) = f(t)\, x$, the forward SDE can be solved exactly:

$$x_t = x_0 \exp\Bigl( \int_0^t f(u)\, du \Bigr) + \sqrt{ \int_0^t g(s)^2 \exp\Bigl( 2 \int_s^t f(u)\, du \Bigr) ds } \cdot \epsilon$$

The first term is the clean sample shrunk by the drift; the second is the accumulated noise, each bit of noise added at time $s$ also shrunk by the drift between $s$ and $t$. So all three paradigms build the same kind of object, a clean sample times a coefficient plus noise times a coefficient. They differ only in the coefficients, and in which end they call $t = 0$.

sections.heading: The shape of the path: curved or straight
sections.caption: Every noisy sample is a clean sample times one coefficient plus noise times another; each paradigm traces a path in that coefficient plane as $t$ runs. In VP diffusion (DDPM) the squares of the coefficients add to one, a quarter circle: halfway, both are 0.71. In flow matching the coefficients add to one, a straight line: halfway, both are 0.5.

sections.heading: 29. What is learned, how it generates, and the deterministic counterpart
rows: score $s_\theta$: $\mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,\epsilon} \| s_\theta(\alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \epsilon, t) - \nabla \log p(\alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \epsilon \mid x_0) \|^2$
$dx = [f(t) x - g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)] dt + g(t) d\bar{W}$

sections.heading: Reading the comparison
sections.text:
The same skeleton in three outfits: a forward process that hides the data in noise, a network that predicts one property of that process (the noise, the score, or the velocity), and a generation process that walks back with it. Diffusion's two generation processes are stochastic (a fresh $\epsilon$ or $d\bar{W}$ at each step) and each has a deterministic counterpart, DDIM and the probability flow ODE, obtained by dropping that randomness. Flow matching starts out deterministic, $dx = u_t(x)\, dt$ with nothing added, and its path is chosen to be straight. The three targets convert into one another by fixed coefficients: with $x_t = (1 - t) x_0 + t x_1$ and a velocity estimate $\hat{v}$, the predicted image is $\hat{x}_1 = x_t + (1 - t)\, \hat{v}$ and the predicted noise is $\hat{x}_0 = x_t - t\, \hat{v}$.

Stochastic interpolants (Albergo, Boffi and Vanden-Eijnden, a unifying framework for flows and diffusions) write all of these as special cases of one definition. The practical lesson for reading papers: the question is rarely "is this a new generative model?" but "what changed: the path, the target, or the sampler?"

sections.heading: Beyond the slides: three papers, one idea
rows: straight paths, transfer between two distributions
training continuous normalizing flows without simulation
a general interpolation between two distributions
proof that the conditional target gives the same gradient

sections.heading: How time is sampled in practice
sections.text: The training loss draws $t$ uniformly, but not every $t$ is equally informative. Near $t = 0$ the input is almost pure noise and the best answer is roughly "head for the mean of the data"; near $t = 1$ the input is almost the clean image and the answer is nearly determined by it. The hard, informative part is in the middle. The SD3 paper (Esser et al., ICML 2024) compared alternatives and found that a logit-normal distribution works best, $t = \text{sigmoid}(n)$ with $n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, which concentrates training in the middle of the path.

sections.heading: Today's recipe: latent + DiT + rectified flow
sections.text: The title of SD3 is Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers, and today's large image models combine three parts: latent diffusion (the flow is learned on a VAE latent instead of pixels, and the loss is unchanged), a Diffusion Transformer computing the velocity, and the rectified flow objective with logit-normal time sampling and 30 to 50 Euler or higher-order steps. FLUX uses the same recipe. Many of the large models called diffusion models today are, technically, flow matching models. (The SD3 paper writes time the other way: $t = 0$ data, $t = 1$ noise.)

sections.heading: Noise is not compulsory: a flow between two distributions
sections.text:
Nothing in the loss requires $x_0$ to be Gaussian. The rectified flow paper's title says it: learning to generate and transfer data. Put a sample from another distribution in place of the noise and the same loss learns a flow from one distribution to the other.

In MRI contrast synthesis this is direct: $x_0$ is the source contrast (T1) and $x_1$ the target contrast (T2) of the same patient. With paired data the pairs are given by the data, so no random matching is needed; generation starts from the source image instead of noise and solves the same ODE. This is close to the diffusion bridges studied in the lab (I²SB, BBDM, SelfRDB), which also build a path between two images but add noise in the middle; a straight transfer flow is their noise-free, deterministic end, at the price of producing the same output for the same input. With unpaired data the matching has to be built, which is where reflow or optimal-transport couplings come in. In reconstruction, a learned flow can serve as a prior, with data consistency enforced on the measured k-space after every Euler step.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: Flow matching moves noise $p_0 = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ at $t = 0$ to the data $p_1 = p_{\text{data}}$ at $t = 1$, the reverse of the time direction in lectures 1 and 2. What is learned is a velocity $u_t(x)$, a highway that says how to drive, not a score, a compass that says where the landscape rises. One sample follows $dx = u_t(x)\, dt$; the whole distribution follows the continuity equation $\partial_t p_t = -\nabla \cdot (p_t u_t)$, with the divergence taken of the flux $p_t u_t$. The true field is unknown, so the lecture solves the problem for one data point: the Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(t x_1, (1 - t)^2 I)$ slides to $x_1$ with velocity $(x_1 - x)/(1 - t) = x_1 - x_0$. Averaging over the data gives the marginal path and velocity, weighted by "given where you are, where should you go", and the conditional loss has the same gradient as the marginal one, so training is a plain regression onto $x_1 - x_0$. Because random pairs cross and ODE paths cannot, the learned paths bend; reflow retrains on the model's own pairs, keeps the distributions and makes the paths provably straighter, at a rate of $O(1/K)$. All three paradigms are a clean sample plus noise with different coefficients and a different target; flow matching's path is straight and its sampler deterministic from the start.

clip.title: Conditioning Signal — From CLIP to Guidance
clip.context: CME 296 Lecture 4, Parts 2 and 3, following the slides · text and image representation · contrastive learning · guidance
clip.summary: How a sentence becomes a vector that steers a generative model, in the order of CME 296 Lecture 4: the transformer, sub-word tokens, attention and positional encoding; ViT end to end; contrastive learning with two towers, cosine similarity, row and column probabilities, the CLIP loss and why it needs a temperature, CLIP's results and SigLIP; then guidance: the conditional Bayes derivation with its two detours ending in a shifted mean, the weight w and what it does to the distribution, the implicit classifier, classifier-free training with condition dropout and sampling by extrapolation.

sections.heading: 1. Where this part sits: the condition box
sections.text:
Lecture 4 draws multimodal guided generation as three boxes: a condition (the sentence "A teddy bear reading a book"), a black-box architecture, and the representation of the image that comes out. Part 1 settled the last box, the latent space the image lives in. Part 2 is about the first box: how a sentence, or an image used as a condition, becomes numbers a network can use. Part 3 is about the arrow from the condition into the black box, guided generation: how to make the model actually obey the condition.

The lecture builds the condition in three steps, and this walkthrough follows them: text representation (tokens and the transformer), image representation (the same transformer applied to patches, the ViT), and contrastive learning, which puts the two into one space so that a sentence and an image can be compared at all.

sections.heading: 2. Which class of model reads the text
rows: read a sentence one token at a time, with a memory
a gated memory that survives longer sentences
a learned vector per word, where similar words sit close
every token looks at every other token at once, through attention
transformers trained at scale on next-token prediction

sections.heading: Why the lecture lands on the transformer
sections.text:
The slide frames the last two lines in red: today's text encoders are transformers, usually pretrained as language models. The transformer was introduced in 2017 for machine translation, relies on attention, with its query, key and value, and is trained on a proxy task, next-token prediction, that needs no labels: any text on the internet is its own supervision.

Its two benefits, as the slide lists them, are weaker inductive biases and more generalizability. An RNN builds in the assumption that a sentence is read left to right, one token after another; a convolution builds in that only nearby things matter. The transformer assumes almost nothing about the order of its inputs, which costs data but means the same architecture works on words, on image patches, or on both together, as the rest of this part shows.

sections.heading: 3. Turning text into numbers: tokenization
sections.text:
The model sees neither letters nor words but indices in a fixed vocabulary. The slide splits the sentence "A cute teddy bear is reading." four ways.

Arbitrary: any split a person might choose, here keeping "teddy bear" as one unit. There is no rule a machine could apply consistently.

Word-level: one token per word. Sequences are short, but every word not seen in training is unknown, and in agglutinative languages such as Turkish, where one root takes dozens of endings, the vocabulary explodes.

Character-level: one token per character. The vocabulary is tiny and nothing is ever unknown, but the sequence becomes very long, and since the cost of attention grows with the square of the sequence length, this is expensive.

Sub-word, the one framed on the slide and the one used in practice: frequent words stay in one piece ("cute", "bear", "is") and rarer ones are split into frequent parts ("ted" + "##dy", "read" + "##ing"; the ## marks a piece that continues the previous one). The vocabulary stays a reasonable size, sequences stay short, and no word is entirely unknown, because in the worst case it falls apart into characters. Every token is an index, and every index is a learned embedding vector.

sections.heading: 4. The attention mechanism: query, key, value
sections.text:
The slide shows the token "teddy bear" deciding what in the sentence matters to it. Every token carries three vectors: a query $q$ (what am I looking for), a key $k$ (what do I offer), and a value $v$ (what I hand over if chosen). The query of "teddy bear", $q_{\text{teddy bear}}$, is compared with the key of every token, $k_{\text{a}}^\top, k_{\text{cute}}^\top, \ldots$; the better the match, the more of that token's value $v$ flows into the new representation of "teddy bear". "cute" should match well: it says something about the bear.

Done for all tokens at once, with the queries, keys and values stacked as rows of matrices $Q$, $K$, $V$, this is one line of efficient matrix computation:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\Bigl( \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \Bigr) V$$

Read it from the inside out: $Q K^\top$ is the table of every query against every key; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$, the square root of the key dimension, keeps the scores from growing with the dimension and saturating the softmax; the softmax turns each row into weights that sum to one; multiplying by $V$ takes the weighted average of the values. Multi-head attention runs $h$ of these in parallel with different learned projections and concatenates the results, so that one head can track which noun an adjective belongs to while another tracks something else. The full mechanics are in the Attention and Transformer walkthrough.

sections.heading: Where attention sits in the transformer
rows: every input token looks at every input token
every output token looks at the earlier output tokens only
the output side queries the input side; also how a text condition enters an image model (section 19)

sections.heading: 5. Input and positional encoding
sections.text:
The input block of the transformer does two things: the text is tokenised, and each token gets a learned embedding. Its two parameters are $V$, the vocabulary size, and $d_{\text{model}}$, the embedding dimension; the embedding table is a $V \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix with one row per token.

Then the slide's trick. Attention as written above does not know the order of the tokens: shuffle the sentence and every token gets the same weights. So position information is added to the inputs, the positional encoding. It can be learned (one vector per position, trained) or hardcoded. The hardcoded version of the original transformer uses sines and cosines of different frequencies: dimension pairs oscillate quickly or slowly with the position, like the hands of a clock.

The goal, in the slide's words: let the model understand relative input position. The figure below makes that concrete. The dot product between the encodings of two positions depends only on how far apart they are, not on where they are: with the 32 dimensions drawn, a position with itself gives 16 (the maximum), positions 0 and 1 give 14.92, positions 10 and 11 also give 14.92; eight steps apart, at 0 and 8 or at 10 and 18, both drop to 6.42. Attention works with dot products, so it can read off "how far is this token from me" directly.

sections.heading: Sinusoidal positional encoding, computed
sections.caption: Left: the encoding itself, one row per position and one column per dimension (the first 32 of 64), blue positive and red negative. Low dimensions oscillate fast, high dimensions slowly. Right: the dot product between the encodings of every pair of positions. It is largest on the diagonal and falls off the same way along every diagonal, which is what "relative position" means: the similarity depends on the distance only.

sections.heading: 7. Which vector is taken as the text embedding
sections.text:
For conditioning, the transformer is not used to translate but to describe: we want a vector that summarises the sentence. The slide marks where it typically comes from: the last hidden state of the encoder, the vectors that leave the final encoder layer, one per token, each enriched with the context of the whole sentence.

There is a choice here and the consequences differ.

A single vector (pooled). One representation summarising the whole sequence; usually the last-layer output of a special token is taken ([CLS] at the start, or the last token, [EOS], in a decoder-only model, as in section 12). This is what CLIP uses, because one vector is needed to make a comparison.

The whole sequence. The vector of every token is kept separately. Generative models prefer this, because different regions of the image should be able to look at different words of the sentence.

Modern text to image models often use both: the pooled vector gives the overall tone and the token sequence the detail.

sections.heading: 8. Image representation: it is just numbers
sections.text: Now the condition may itself be an image, and in any case the image side will need its own vectors for contrastive learning. The slide's observation is short: attention does not care that its inputs were words. Keys, values and queries are just vectors of numbers, drawn on the slide as coloured bars over the words. Remove the words and keep the bars, and nothing in the mechanism changes. Put small pieces of an image under the bars instead, and the same machinery represents an image. That is the Vision Transformer, ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., An Image is Worth 16x16 Words, 2020).

sections.heading: 9. ViT, end to end
sections.text:
The slides walk through one image in nine steps; the figure below collects them.

Cut the image into a grid of patches, here $3 \times 3$. Each patch is a small image of size $P \times P$ with $C$ channels. Flatten it into $P \cdot P \cdot C$ numbers and pass it through one linear layer that outputs $D$ numbers: the patch is now a token embedding, exactly like a word's. With the standard ViT numbers, a $224 \times 224$ image cut into $P = 16$ patches gives $14 \times 14 = 196$ tokens, each flattened patch has $16 \cdot 16 \cdot 3 = 768$ numbers, and $D$ is 768 as well.

Prepend one extra learned token, [CLS], that belongs to no patch. Add a position embedding to every token, so that the model knows where each patch was: the result is a position-aware embedding. Run the sequence through the transformer encoder, the ViT architecture, where every patch attends to every other patch. Out come encoded embeddings, one per token.

Only the first one is read: the encoded [CLS] token, which has gathered information from all patches. A small feed-forward network on top of it predicts the class, "teddy bear".

sections.heading: 10. Discussion: the limits of a supervised ViT
sections.text:
The slide's two limitations. A supervised ViT is good but needs labels: the FFN at the top is trained with cross-entropy on labelled images. And it fits a narrow, category-level representation that has to be specified in advance: it learns exactly the thousand classes it was given, and the [CLS] vector encodes "which of these thousand" rather than everything that is in the picture.

The slide's other approaches: we did not have this problem for text, because the tasks that work for text, next-token prediction, are already self-supervised. For images, a popular label-free route is self-distillation with no labels, DINO (Caron et al., Emerging Properties in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers, 2021), where a student network learns to match a teacher on different crops of the same image.

The gain so far is that text and image are now objects of the same type, sequences of vectors processed by the same architecture. But being of the same type does not mean being in the same space: if the two encoders were trained separately, the vectors they produce cannot be compared. Hence the slide's question: how to make image and text embeddings comparable?

sections.heading: 11. Contrastive learning: the idea
sections.text:
Motivation: how to learn general image and text relationships, without fixing a list of categories in advance? Idea, contrastive learning: group similar items together, and push dissimilar items apart.

The slides build it with two images and two captions. The picture of the teddy bear and the text "teddy bear" should be close; the picture of the water polo ball and the text "water polo ball" should be close. Crosswise, bear with "water polo ball" and ball with "teddy bear", they should be far. Laid out as a table, images as rows and texts as columns, the diagonal should be close, high similarity, and the off-diagonal far, low similarity.

The unmatched pairs serve as negative examples and do not need to be labelled: given a batch of matched pairs, every other caption in the batch is a negative for every image, for free. Computing a cosine similarity between a text vector and an image vector is meaningless unless training required it; contrastive learning is the training that requires it.

The matched pairs on the diagonal are around 0.8 and the off-diagonal values around zero. The loss is trying to bring exactly this matrix into this state: the diagonal up, the off-diagonal down.

sections.heading: 12. How to find a same space
sections.text:
Two encoders, each followed by a small projection, so that both land in the same space with the same dimension.

The image goes through the ViT; its encoded [CLS] token goes through a projection and becomes $u$, the image embedding.

The text goes through a transformer; the slide's text tower is a vanilla decoder-only architecture reading [SOS] [teddy] [bear] [EOS]. In a decoder-only model each token sees only the tokens before it, so the last one, [EOS], is the only one that has seen the whole caption: its hidden state goes through a projection and becomes $v_{\text{teddy bear}}$, the text embedding.

The projections are what make the two comparable: they are trained, together with the encoders, so that matching pairs end up pointing in the same direction.

sections.heading: 13. Loss formulation: the similarity
sections.text:
Notation. The similarity of an image and a text is the cosine of their embeddings:

$$s_{\text{img}, \text{text}} = \frac{u_{\text{img}}^\top\, v_{\text{text}}}{\| u_{\text{img}} \| \cdot \| v_{\text{text}} \|}$$

The numerator is the dot product; dividing by both lengths keeps only the direction, so $s$ lies between $-1$ (opposite) and $1$ (same direction). A long vector does not count as "more similar"; only the angle matters.

sections.heading: 14. From similarities to probabilities, in both directions
sections.text:
The slide turns similarities into a choice. Probability that the bear image matches the text "teddy bear", against the other text in the batch:

$$p_{\text{bear} \to \text{teddy bear}} = \frac{\exp(s_{\text{bear}, \text{teddy bear}})}{\exp(s_{\text{bear}, \text{teddy bear}}) + \exp(s_{\text{bear}, \text{water polo ball}})}$$

That is a softmax along the bear's row: the image picks a caption. And the other direction, probability that the text "teddy bear" matches the bear image, against the other image:

$$p_{\text{teddy bear} \to \text{bear}} = \frac{\exp(s_{\text{bear}, \text{teddy bear}})}{\exp(s_{\text{bear}, \text{teddy bear}}) + \exp(s_{\text{ball}, \text{teddy bear}})}$$

That is a softmax down the column of "teddy bear": the caption picks an image. The two numerators are the same similarity; the denominators differ, which is why both directions are kept.

sections.heading: 15. The loss for the two-pair example
sections.text:
Each term averages the log-probabilities of the correct matches, with a minus sign so that it is minimised:

$$L_{\text{img} \to \text{text}} = -\frac{1}{2} \bigl( \log p_{\text{bear} \to \text{teddy bear}} + \log p_{\text{ball} \to \text{water polo ball}} \bigr)$$

$$L_{\text{text} \to \text{img}} = -\frac{1}{2} \bigl( \log p_{\text{teddy bear} \to \text{bear}} + \log p_{\text{water polo ball} \to \text{ball}} \bigr)$$

Total loss, the average of the two directions:

$$L = \frac{1}{2} \bigl( L_{\text{img} \to \text{text}} + L_{\text{text} \to \text{img}} \bigr)$$

With numbers: take cosine similarities of 0.8 and 0.7 on the diagonal and 0.1 and 0.2 off it. The figure computes every probability; the total loss is 0.438. Every term is small when the correct match wins its row and its column.

sections.caption: The slide's blue shading: on the left the bear image's row (image to text), on the right the column of the text "teddy bear" (text to image). Same four similarities, two different normalisations. Note how unconfident the probabilities are, 0.668 for a clearly correct match: the next section explains why, and what CLIP does about it.

sections.heading: 16. CLIP: the same loss over a batch of N pairs
sections.text:
CLIP, Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (Radford et al., 2021), is exactly this with $N$ pairs instead of two. The slide's diagram: $N$ captions ("Pepper the aussie pup", ...) go through the text encoder into $T_1, \ldots, T_N$; $N$ images go through the image encoder into $I_1, \ldots, I_N$; the $N \times N$ matrix of products $I_i \cdot T_j$ is formed, and the diagonal, the blue cells $I_1 \cdot T_1, I_2 \cdot T_2, \ldots$, holds the true pairs. Each term now averages over $N$:

$$L_{\text{img} \to \text{text}} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log \frac{\exp(u_i^\top v_i / \tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp(u_i^\top v_j / \tau)}$$

with the same along the columns for $L_{\text{text} \to \text{img}}$, and the total loss is again $L = \frac{1}{2} ( L_{\text{img} \to \text{text}} + L_{\text{text} \to \text{img}} )$. Here $u_i$ and $v_i$ are normalised to unit length, so $u_i^\top v_j$ is the cosine similarity $s$, and $\tau$ is a temperature that the slides leave out.

sections.heading: Why the temperature is not optional
sections.text:
Without $\tau$, the similarities live in $[-1, 1]$, and that caps how confident the softmax can ever be. In the best possible case, cosine 1 for the true pair and $-1$ for every other, the probability of the correct match is $e / (e + (N - 1)/e)$. With $N = 2$ that is 0.881; with CLIP's batch of $N = 32{,}768$ it is 0.00023. The loss could never get close to zero, and its gradient would never stop pushing.

Dividing by a small $\tau$ stretches the scale. In the two-pair example above, $\tau = 0.07$ turns the bear's row from 0.668 into 1.000, and the total loss from 0.438 to 0.000. CLIP does not fix $\tau$: it learns it, starting at 0.07 and capping the scale $1/\tau$ at 100.

The same formula also explains why the batch size matters: the larger the batch, the more negatives each example is compared against, the harder the task and the sharper the representation. This is why CLIP is trained with batches of around 32 thousand.

sections.heading: This loss is in fact cross-entropy
sections.text: Read the formula closely and something familiar appears: the similarities in a row go through a softmax and the log-probability of the correct column is taken. That is an $N$-class classification problem, and cross-entropy. The difference is that the classes are not a fixed set of labels but the batch itself; the question asked at every step is "which of the $N$ texts in this batch belongs to this image?" That is how contrastive learning escapes the supervised ViT's narrow, fixed categories of section 10: the categories are whatever the captions say.

sections.heading: 17. CLIP's characteristics and results
sections.text:
Training, as the slide lists it. Dataset: 400M (image, caption) pairs collected from the internet; no labelling, captions and alt texts were already there. Visual encoder: ViT or CNN. Text encoder: transformer-based. And the loss works because of one assumption, in-batch negatives: every other caption in the batch is assumed not to describe the image. With 400 million web pairs that is almost always true, but not always (two photos of dogs captioned "a dog" in one batch are treated as a mismatch).

Results. CLIP reaches about 76% on ImageNet with no supervised training on it, zero-shot: you turn the class names into sentences ("a photo of a dog"), compute the text vectors, and choose the one closest to the image vector. The slide adds a caveat: arguably some of this is leakage, since images close to the supervised benchmark sets may sit in the web data, but the result is still remarkable.

That the sentence template changes the result, the birth of prompt engineering, is a side effect of the same mechanism: the texts in the training data were sentences, not one-word labels. The limits are clear too. Counting, spatial relations and fine detail are weak, because the training signal is "does this text belong to this image", which can often be answered without counting. And since the data comes from the internet, its biases are carried over.

sections.heading: 18. Discussion of CLIP: SigLIP
sections.text:
The slide's computational challenges: a large similarity matrix is required for a batch; the normalisation is global (each softmax denominator runs over the whole row or column); and it is memory intensive. In distributed training every device needs every other device's embeddings to compute one denominator.

The slide's other approach: reframe the $1 \leftrightarrow N$ softmax problem into a $1 \leftrightarrow 1$ sigmoid one, SigLIP (Zhai et al., Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training, 2023). Every pair becomes an independent yes-or-no question, does this image match this text:

$$L_{\text{SigLIP}} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \log \sigma\bigl( z_{ij} \, ( t\, u_i^\top v_j + b ) \bigr), \qquad z_{ij} = +1 \text{ if } i = j, \ -1 \text{ otherwise}$$

$\sigma$ is the sigmoid, $t$ a learned scale (the role of $1/\tau$) and $b$ a learned bias. Each cell of the matrix is a separate binary cross-entropy: no denominator couples the cells, so the matrix can be computed block by block across devices. The bias matters because the batch is lopsided, one positive per row against $N - 1$ negatives; it starts strongly negative so that "no match" is the default. In practice SigLIP gives a better representation for the same data and has begun to replace CLIP in newer models.

sections.heading: 19. Beyond the slides: how the embedding enters the generative model
sections.text:
The conditioning signal is ready; what remains is inserting it into the image model (the full treatment is in Lecture 5 and the Backbone walkthrough). Three routes are used, and which is chosen depends on the form of the signal.

Addition. If the signal is a single vector it is treated like the timestep embedding and added into the intermediate layers. Simple but weak in effect.

adaLN. Again a single vector, but that vector sets the normalization parameters (scale and shift) of the layers. The route DiT prefers; far stronger than addition.

Cross-attention. The natural choice if the signal is a sequence of tokens: the query comes from the image and the key and value from the text, the encoder-decoder attention of section 4. Every region of the image can then look at different words of the sentence. This is the standard method in text conditioning.

Modern text to image models generally combine two of them: the pooled vector sets the overall tone through adaLN and the token sequence carries the detail through cross-attention. And several encoders are used instead of one: CLIP's text tower brings semantic alignment with images, while pure language models such as T5 work better on long and complex sentences.

sections.heading: 20. Part 3: the condition is in the model, and it is still not enough
sections.text:
The last box: guided generation, the arrow from the condition into the black box. The slide's motivation is one line: the reverse step of Lecture 1, $p(x_t \mid x_{t+1})$, should become $p(x_t \mid x_{t+1}, y)$, with the condition $y$ added. (The slides of this part write the reverse step from $x_{t+1}$ to $x_t$, with $x_0$ the clean image, the DDPM convention.)

Everything in Part 2 produced a vector and found it a door into the network. That is conditional generation, and it works, but weakly. Samples follow the prompt loosely: ask for a golden retriever and a dog arrives, sometimes an indistinct dog, sometimes a scene cluttered with things nobody asked for.

The reason is not a bug. The model has learned $p(x \mid y)$ and samples from it honestly. That distribution also contains regions that match the label only weakly, and honest sampling visits them in proportion to their mass. What you actually want are the regions most typical of the label, which is a different request from sampling the distribution. Guidance is the family of techniques that make that request. All of them change sampling, not the generative paradigm; one of them adds a single line to training.

sections.heading: 21. The first idea: guide the generation with a classifier
sections.text:
Idea: use a classifier's knowledge to feed image generation with information on the target class (Dhariwal and Nichol, Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis, 2021). A classifier already knows what makes an image belong to a class; its gradient with respect to the image says "change the pixels this way and the image looks more like that class." The guided step gets two sets of weights:

$$p_{\theta, \phi}(x_t \mid x_{t+1}, y)$$

$\theta$ are the generation weights, the unconditional diffusion model, already trained. $\phi$ are the classifier weights, a separate model. The generative model says where to go next; the classifier tilts that direction.

sections.heading: 22. Main derivation, step 1: conditional Bayes' rule
sections.text:
We want to compute $p_{\theta, \phi}(x_t \mid x_{t+1}, y)$. Justification on the slide: apply the conditional Bayes' rule on $P(A \mid B, C)$ with $A = x_t$, $B = y$, $C = x_{t+1}$:

$$p(x_t \mid y, x_{t+1}) = \frac{p(x_t \mid x_{t+1})\; p(y \mid x_t, x_{t+1})}{p(y \mid x_{t+1})}$$

Two simplifications. The denominator does not depend on $x_t$, so for a distribution over $x_t$ it is just a normalising constant. And the class of $x_t$ does not depend on where the chain came from, once $x_t$ itself is known: $p(y \mid x_t, x_{t+1}) = p(y \mid x_t)$. What remains is the slide's line:

$$p_{\theta, \phi}(x_t \mid x_{t+1}, y) \ \text{ is the same distribution as } \ p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{t+1})\; p_\phi(y \mid x_t)$$

up to normalisation. The first factor, framed in red on the next slide, is the unconditional diffusion step; the second, framed after it, is the classifier. Each gets a detour.

sections.heading: 23. Detour 1: the diffusion step is a Gaussian
sections.text:
Let's focus on $p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{t+1})$. Justification: Lecture 1's derivation of the DDPM generation process, where the reverse step is a Gaussian with a learned mean and a fixed variance:

$$p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{t+1}) = \mathcal{N}\bigl( \mu_\theta,\ \sigma_{t+1}^2 I \bigr)$$

($\mu_\theta$ is short for $\mu_\theta(x_{t+1}, t+1)$, and the slide writes the covariance as $\sigma_{t+1} I$, meaning the variance $\sigma_{t+1}^2$ per dimension.) Using the density $\mathcal{N}(x; \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\bigl( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \bigr)$ and taking logs:

$$\log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{t+1}) = -\frac{\| x_t - \mu_\theta \|^2}{2 \sigma_{t+1}^2} + \text{constant}$$

A downward parabola in $x_t$, peaked at $\mu_\theta$.

sections.heading: 24. Detour 2: the classifier, linearised
sections.text:
Let's focus on $p_\phi(y \mid x_t)$. Its log is a complicated function of $x_t$, a whole neural network. Justification: a first-order Taylor approximation around the centre of the step, $\mu = \mu_\theta$:

$$f\bigl( \mu + (x_t - \mu) \bigr) \approx f(\mu) + (x_t - \mu)^\top \nabla_{x_t} f(\mu)$$

Applied to $f = \log p_\phi(y \mid \cdot)$, and absorbing $f(\mu)$, which does not depend on $x_t$, into the constant:

$$\log p_\phi(y \mid x_t) \approx (x_t - \mu)^\top\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p_\phi(y \mid \mu) + \text{constant}$$

A tilted plane. Why the approximation is reasonable: the step distribution is narrow ($\sigma_{t+1}$ is small), so $x_t$ stays close to $\mu$, where the linear approximation is good. This is the one approximation in the derivation.

sections.heading: 25. Main derivation, step 2: the guided step is a shifted Gaussian
sections.text:
Justification on the slide: plug both expressions into $\log \bigl( p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{t+1})\, p_\phi(y \mid x_t) \bigr)$ and recognise the density of a normal distribution. Write $g = \nabla_{x_t} \log p_\phi(y \mid \mu_\theta)$ for the classifier's gradient. The sum of the two logs is

$$-\frac{\| x_t - \mu_\theta \|^2}{2 \sigma_{t+1}^2} + (x_t - \mu_\theta)^\top g + \text{constant} = -\frac{\| x_t - \mu_\theta - \sigma_{t+1}^2\, g \|^2}{2 \sigma_{t+1}^2} + \text{constant}$$

The middle step is completing the square: expanding the right-hand side gives back the parabola, the linear term $(x_t - \mu_\theta)^\top g$, and $\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{t+1}^2 \|g\|^2$, which does not depend on $x_t$ and goes into the constant. The right-hand side is the log of a Gaussian, so:

$$x_t \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl( \mu_\theta + \sigma_{t+1}^2\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p_\phi(y \mid \mu_\theta),\ \sigma_{t+1}^2 I \bigr)$$

The slide frames the added term in red: a shifted mean. The variance is unchanged; the classifier's whole effect is to move the centre of each step by $\sigma_{t+1}^2$ times its gradient, towards the class.

sections.heading: A Gaussian times a tilt is a shifted Gaussian, computed
sections.caption: The unconditional step $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ (blue) multiplied by the linearised classifier term $\exp(g(x - \mu))$ (purple, dashed) gives a curve of exactly the same width with its peak moved to $\mu + \sigma^2 g$ (green). With the guidance weight of section 28, $w = 2$, the peak moves twice as far (amber). The shift is proportional to $\sigma^2$: large in early, noisy steps, vanishing in the last ones.

sections.heading: The same result, read on the score
sections.text:
The derivation can also be done without the Gaussian detours, directly on scores. Write Bayes' rule between $x$ and $y$ and take logarithms:

$$\log p_t(x \mid y) = \log p_t(x) + \log p_t(y \mid x) - \log p_t(y)$$

The last term does not depend on $x$, so it dies under the gradient:

$$\nabla_x \log p_t(x \mid y) = \nabla_x \log p_t(x) + \nabla_x \log p_t(y \mid x)$$

In words: the conditional score is the unconditional score plus the classifier's gradient. The first term is the diffusion model you already trained, the second is the classifier. The shifted mean above is this same sum, seen through one DDPM step.

sections.heading: 26. And what about the training loss?
sections.text:
Look at what the per-step generation rule actually needs, framed on the slides one after the other: the unconditioned generation model's predictions and parameters ($\mu_\theta$ and $\sigma_{t+1}^2$), and the classifier's score ($\nabla_{x_t} \log p_\phi(y \mid \mu_\theta)$). Nothing else.

So for the generation model: no retraining is needed of an unconditioned generation model. An unconditional model that already exists can be made conditional without touching its weights; this is purely a sampling technique.

For the classifier: it needs to be trained with a cross-entropy loss on noisy images. Sample $x_t$ and train $p_\phi(y \mid x_t)$ to predict the correct label. It cannot be any classifier: guidance is applied at every noise level, so the classifier must read corrupted inputs, with the timestep as an input, drawing $t$ the same way the diffusion model does.

sections.title: Training the classifier for classifier guidance
lines: $x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \epsilon$ >> the same noising as the diffusion model
$\mathcal{L} = -\log p_\phi(y \mid x_t, t)$ >> cross-entropy on the noised image
backpropagate through $p_\phi$ only >> the diffusion model is untouched

sections.heading: 27. Giving more weight to the condition signal
sections.text:
The derivation gives the classifier term a coefficient of exactly one. Empirically that produces disappointing samples, and the slide adds a weight $w$, in red:

$$x_t \sim \mathcal{N}\bigl( \mu_\theta + w\, \sigma_{t+1}^2\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p_\phi(y \mid \mu_\theta),\ \sigma_{t+1}^2 I \bigr)$$

Empirically, we observe that we need $w > 1$ for good conditioned samples.

It is worth being honest about what this means: you are no longer sampling from $p(x \mid y)$. On the score, the target becomes $\nabla \log p(x) + w\, \nabla \log p(y \mid x)$, the score of a distribution proportional to $p(x)\, p(y \mid x)^w$, in which the class likelihood has been raised to a power and therefore sharpened. Samples become far more typical of the label and visibly cleaner, and the diversity drops. The trade-off always runs the same way, and it never disappears: classifier-free guidance inherits it unchanged.

sections.heading: What w does to the distribution, computed
sections.caption: A toy one-dimensional world: two classes, $p(x)$ a mix of two bumps (gray), and a classifier $p(y \mid x)$ that is a soft step favouring the right bump. Honest conditional sampling, $w = 1$ (blue), still keeps 13% of its mass on the wrong bump, the "weak match" regions of section 20. With $w = 4$ (amber) that drops to 0%, and the right bump itself narrows and moves outward (its mean goes from 1.59 to 1.76): more typical of the class, less varied.

sections.heading: 28. Limitations, in two groups
sections.text:
The lecture splits them, and the split is useful because the two groups bite at different times.

New prerequisites. The classifier has to be trained on labelled data. It needs to operate on noised input, so an out-of-the-box classifier cannot be used. And the distribution of data between the two models has to be aligned: a classifier trained on a different corpus quietly steers the generator somewhere else.

Computational considerations. An extra classifier pass is needed at each step (forward and backward, to get its gradient). The new gradient signal needs scaling tuning, the $w$ above. And the Taylor expansion introduces approximations.

There is also a silent restriction: the condition is a class label. Free text does not fit this frame naturally, and text is where the field was heading.

sections.heading: 29. Refined goal: generation weights only
sections.text:
The slide crosses out $\phi$:

$$p_{\theta, \not\phi}(x_t \mid x_{t+1}, y)$$

Generation weights only. Motivation, as the slide states it: a classifier on noisy data is not found in the wild, and we want to avoid extra model calls at inference time.

Observation (Ho and Salimans, Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance, 2022): the conditional and unconditional signals define an implicit classifier. By Bayes' rule,

$$p^i(y \mid x_t) \ \propto\ \frac{p(x_t \mid y)}{p(x_t)}$$

The superscript $i$ marks it as implicit: it is not a network, it is a ratio of two things a generative model already provides, its conditional and its unconditional density. Take the gradient of the log and the classifier term of section 25 appears:

$$\nabla_x \log p^i(y \mid x_t) = \nabla_x \log p(x_t \mid y) - \nabla_x \log p(x_t)$$

You never needed a separate model; you needed the difference between two predictions you can produce yourself.

sections.heading: 30. Change of mindset: from the classifier to two predictions
sections.text:
Idea: compute both the conditioned and the unconditioned situations, and infer the classifier signal. Diffusion networks predict noise, so write everything with $\epsilon$. The score and the predicted noise differ by a fixed factor, $\nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t) = -\epsilon_\theta(x_t) / \sigma_t$ (Lecture 2). Classifier guidance on the noise reads:

$$\text{classifier-based:} \qquad \epsilon_\theta(x_t) - w\, \sigma_t\, \nabla_{x_t} \log p_\phi(y \mid x_t)$$

Now replace the classifier gradient by the implicit one, written with the same conversion: $\nabla \log p^i(y \mid x_t) = -\bigl( \epsilon_\theta(x_t, y) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) \bigr) / \sigma_t$, where $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, y)$ is the conditional prediction and $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing)$ the unconditional one ($\varnothing$, the empty condition). The $\sigma_t$ cancels and the minus signs meet:

$$\text{classifier-free:} \qquad \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) + w \cdot \bigl( \epsilon_\theta(x_t, y) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) \bigr)$$

The slide frames the two $\theta$'s in red: both predictions come from the same network with the same weights. $\phi$ is gone.

sections.heading: 31. Training for classifier-free guidance: one added line
sections.text:
One network has to produce both $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, y)$ and $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing)$. The slides show the training loop twice, once for each branch, and the only difference is the condition.

With probability $p_{\text{uncond}}$: sample a clean image $x_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}$, a noise $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and a time step $t \sim \mathcal{U}(0, T)$; build the noised image $x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \epsilon$; use $x_t$ and $t$ to predict $\epsilon$ via $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing)$; compute the loss $\| \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) - \epsilon \|^2$ and backpropagate through $\epsilon_\theta$.

With probability $1 - p_{\text{uncond}}$: the same, but the clean image comes with its condition $y$ (in red on the slide), and the prediction is $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, y)$.

So the training loop stays the DDPM loop; the single addition is at the input, where the condition is dropped and replaced by a null token with probability $p_{\text{uncond}}$. That is enough: one network learns both jobs, and the two live in the same weights. (Here $\alpha_t$ and $\sigma_t$ are the generic signal and noise coefficients, $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$ and $\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}$ in DDPM's notation.)

sections.heading: 32. Sampling for classifier-free guidance: three predictions, one step
sections.text:
At each step the network is run twice, once with the condition and once with the null token, and the two are combined:

$$\epsilon_{\text{CFG}}(x_t, y) = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) + w \cdot \bigl( \epsilon_\theta(x_t, y) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) \bigr)$$

The bracket is the direction the condition adds; the weight $w$ says how far to travel along it. The slide draws the three points on one dashed line: the unconditioned sample, the conditioned sample, and the guided sample beyond them, with a red arrow along the line.

The geometry explains the failure mode: this is an extrapolation, not an interpolation. At $w = 1$ the result lands exactly on the conditional prediction. At $w > 1$ it shoots past it, further from the unconditional prediction than the model itself would ever go. The guided $\epsilon_{\text{CFG}}$ then replaces $\epsilon_\theta$ in the ordinary DDPM or DDIM update.

sections.heading: 33. Practical considerations
sections.text:
Modeling, as the slide lists it. Flexibility of conditioning: what the condition is does not matter to the mathematics. A class label, a CLIP embedding of a sentence, another image; guidance only needs the pair of predictions, conditional and unconditional. CLIP embeddings are handy to represent the conditioning signal, which is why they became the standard carrier and why Part 2 and Part 3 belong to one lecture. Best results with $w > 1$ and $p_{\text{uncond}} = 10$ to $20\%$.

The scale is tuned per model; the usual band is roughly 2 to 8, and the slider labelled CFG scale or guidance scale in image generation interfaces is exactly this number. Push it high and the images saturate and turn cliched; leave it at one and prompt adherence falls back to what the plain conditional model gives.

Guidance is also independent of the parametrization. The identical operation can be written on the noise prediction, on the score or on the velocity, because the three are related by fixed coefficients, so the same technique carries over to flow matching without modification.

Computational, the slide's last two lines: no more bespoke classifier needed, but still two calls per step. A large part of the distillation literature exists to remove that second call.
