sections.heading: 34. Why this closes the conditioning story
sections.text:
Three stages have now been covered, and they are in order.

Representation: the sentence becomes a vector, in a space shared with images, through tokens, a transformer, a ViT and a contrastive loss. Condition: that vector enters the network, through adaLN or cross-attention. Guidance: at sampling time, the effect of the condition is amplified beyond what honest sampling would give, by a classifier's gradient or by the difference between two predictions of the same network.

Each stage is useless without the previous one, and the last is the one that is invisible in the architecture diagram and decides what the output looks like.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: A transformer reads text as sub-word tokens, each a learned embedding plus a positional encoding whose dot products depend only on relative position; attention is $\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$. The same encoder reads an image cut into $P \times P \times C$ patches, linearly projected to $D$, with a [CLS] token whose output summarises the image; trained with labels, it learns only fixed categories. Contrastive learning removes the labels: two towers with projections produce $u$ and $v$, the cosine $s$ is turned into probabilities along rows (image picks text) and columns (text picks image), and the loss averages both directions. CLIP does this over $N$ pairs with in-batch negatives and a learned temperature, without which the softmax could never be confident; it is cross-entropy whose classes are the batch, and SigLIP turns it into independent sigmoids. Guidance starts from $p(x_t \mid x_{t+1}, y)$: conditional Bayes splits it into the diffusion step times $p_\phi(y \mid x_t)$; the step is a Gaussian, the classifier is linearised by Taylor, and completing the square gives the same Gaussian with its mean shifted by $\sigma_{t+1}^2 \nabla \log p_\phi(y \mid \mu_\theta)$. A weight $w > 1$ sharpens $p(x)p(y \mid x)^w$: more typical, less diverse. Classifier-free guidance notices that $p(x_t \mid y)/p(x_t)$ is an implicit classifier, so with condition dropout ($p_{\text{uncond}}$ 10 to 20%) one network gives both predictions, and $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) + w(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, y) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing))$ extrapolates past the conditional prediction, at two calls per step.

sections.heading: Where to look
sections.text:
Course: CME 296 (Stanford), Lecture 4, Part 2 (text representation, image representation, contrastive learning) and Part 3 (guidance), by Afshine and Shervine Amidi. This walkthrough follows the slides' order and notation; the temperature, the SigLIP formula, section 19 on how the embedding enters the model, the score-based reading of guidance and the practical CFG notes are added from the papers and the site's cards. Part 1 of the lecture is in the Autoencoder and VAE walkthrough.

Papers: Vaswani et al. — Attention Is All You Need (2017) · Dosovitskiy et al. — An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (ViT, 2020; ICLR 2021) · Radford et al. — Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP, 2021) · Caron et al. — Emerging Properties in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers (DINO, 2021) · Zhai et al. — Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training (SigLIP, 2023) · Dhariwal and Nichol — Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis (2021) · Ho and Salimans — Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance (2022).

On this site: the inner mechanics of the transformer are in the Attention and Transformer walkthrough; the continuation into VLMs (LLaVA, Flamingo, Qwen3-VL) is in the Vision-Language Models walkthrough; where the condition enters a DiT is in the Backbone walkthrough; the CS231n treatment of CFG with code is in cs13.

vlm.title: Vision-Language Models — From CLIP to LLaVA, Flamingo and Qwen3-VL
vlm.context: CS231n 2026 · Lecture 16 — Vision + Language (and Foundation Models)
vlm.summary: What a foundation model is and the families it comes in; how CLIP aligns images and text with a two-way contrastive loss, turns its text encoder into a zero-shot classifier, and why it generalises under distribution shift but fails on specialised domains; its batch-size and compositionality limits, hard negatives and hard positives; SigLIP and CoCa; how LLaVA and Flamingo let a language model read images, and what Qwen3-VL and Molmo changed; and chaining with CuPL and VisProg.

sections.heading: 1. Two ways to build a vision system
sections.text:
Until this point the course followed one recipe: collect a labelled dataset for a task, train a model for that task, repeat for the next task. Four tasks meant four datasets and four models, and nothing learned for one of them carried over to the others.

A foundation model inverts this. One model is pre-trained once on a large and diverse dataset, and then serves many tasks, either through a little fine-tuning or with no further training at all (zero-shot, few-shot). Language showed the way first: a GPT trained on a web crawl to predict the next word can afterwards do arithmetic, symbolic reasoning, trivia and translation, although it was never trained on any of these as a task.

What makes a model a foundation model is one property that is always present: it is general and robust across many different tasks. Three further properties are usually present but are not the definition: a large number of parameters, a large amount of data, and a self-supervised pre-training objective, meaning the training signal comes from the data itself rather than from human labels.

sections.heading: 2. The families of foundation models

puts images and text in one embedding space and compares them
takes images and text as input, writes text
combines existing models through a language model
Segment Anything, Whisper, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Imagen

sections.heading: 3. The starting point: contrastive learning on images
sections.text:
The classification family grows out of SimCLR. There, two random augmentations of the same photograph are passed through an image encoder, and the training objective pulls their embeddings together while pushing apart the embeddings of every other image in the batch. No label is used; the fact that two crops come from the same photograph is the only supervision. Afterwards a small classifier trained on top of these features works well, because images of the same kind of object have ended up near each other.

The question that leads to CLIP is a small extension of this picture. If cats cluster in one region and dogs in another, could a sentence such as "A cute fluffy cat" also be placed in that same space, right next to the cat photographs? Then the space would be shared by vision and language, and a sentence could be compared with an image directly.

sections.heading: 4. Step one: the data
sections.text:
CLIP's answer begins with data rather than with an architecture. Images on the web often come with alt-text, a short description written for accessibility, and that pairing is a free and enormous source of (image, text) examples. The authors collected 400 million such pairs.

To keep the collection from being dominated by a few popular subjects, they searched for pairs using a list of 500,000 queries and kept at most 20,000 pairs per query, which approximately balances the concepts. The recipe was later reproduced in the open (Xu et al., Demystifying CLIP Data, ICLR 2024), which matters because the original dataset was never released.

sections.heading: 5. Step two: which loss?
sections.text:
The obvious objective would be to train a model that reads an image and writes its caption word by word, as image captioning does. The CLIP authors argue against this. Predicting the exact words is a needlessly hard task: the same photograph can be described in countless ways, and a captioning loss penalises every one of them except the single caption that happens to be attached. Much of the model's capacity goes into guessing phrasing rather than understanding content.

The weaker requirement is enough: the model only has to recognise which description belongs to which image. That is a matching problem, and matching is exactly what a contrastive loss does. Prior work had already found contrastive objectives to learn better representations than their predictive equivalents, and in CLIP's own experiments the switch made training several times more efficient.

sections.heading: 6. From SimCLR to CLIP
sections.text:
The architectural change is small. In SimCLR both inputs are images, so one image encoder is used twice. In CLIP the two inputs come from different modalities, so there are two encoders: an image encoder (a ResNet or a ViT) and a text encoder (a transformer). Each maps its input to a vector of the same dimension.

A training batch holds $n$ pairs. The image encoder turns the images into $u_1, \ldots, u_n$, the text encoder turns the captions into $v_1, \ldots, v_n$. Of the $n^2$ possible (image, text) combinations in the batch, exactly $n$ are correct, the ones on the diagonal, and every other combination serves as a negative.

sections.heading: 7. The CLIP objective
sections.text:
With $\langle u_i, v_j \rangle$ the similarity of image $i$ and text $j$, the loss is the same InfoNCE loss as in SimCLR, applied in both directions:

$$L = \sum_{i=1}^{n} -\log \frac{e^{\langle u_i, v_i \rangle}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{\langle u_i, v_j \rangle}} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} -\log \frac{e^{\langle u_i, v_i \rangle}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{\langle u_j, v_i \rangle}}$$

The first sum reads each row of the similarity matrix: for image $i$, which of the $n$ texts is its own. The second reads each column: for text $i$, which of the $n$ images is its own. Minimising both drives the diagonal similarities up and everything else down.

Two details are left out of the formula as written here. The vectors are L2-normalised, so $\langle u_i, v_j \rangle$ is a cosine similarity between $-1$ and $1$. And the similarities are divided by a learned temperature $\tau$ before the exponential; the next figures show why that matters. The row-by-row reading of this loss as a cross-entropy whose classes are the batch itself is worked out in the conditioning-signal walkthrough.

sections.heading: 8. What training leaves behind
sections.text:
After training there is a model that embeds images and embeds text into one space, and therefore can give a similarity score between any image and any piece of text. Everything that follows uses only this ability.

The first way to use it is the familiar one from self-supervised learning: keep the image encoder, freeze it, and train a linear classifier on its features for the downstream task. Averaged over 27 datasets, linear probes on CLIP features beat those on every other pre-trained model the authors compared, including models pre-trained on ImageNet with labels and the strongest self-supervised image models of the time. But a linear probe still needs labelled training data for each task.

sections.heading: 9. The question language models raise
sections.text:
A language model needs no linear probe. Pre-trained only to fill in the next word, it can be used in a creative way: ask it to complete "I love ___" and it says "cake"; ask it to complete "The movie review 'I hated the movie' is ___" and it says "negative", which is sentiment classification done without a single training example for that task.

So the question becomes: how can a vision-language model be used out of the box, with no fine-tuning, for image classification?

sections.heading: 10. The trick: build the classifier with the text encoder
sections.text:
Pass the image through the image encoder and a word, say "dog", through the text encoder. The dot product of the two vectors is a matching score, for instance 0.27. That alone tells little, but nothing stops you from doing the same for every class name of the task.

Encode "plane", "dog" and "bird" once each; these three text vectors now play the role of a classifier's weight vectors. For a new image, compute its similarity to each of them and predict the class with the highest score:

$$\hat{y} = \arg\max_{c} \langle f(x), g(t_c) \rangle$$

Here $f$ is the image encoder, $g$ the text encoder and $t_c$ the text for class $c$. This is a 1-nearest-neighbour classifier in which the training data are the text vectors, one per class. The set of classes is decided at test time by whatever names you write, which is why the approach is called open-vocabulary.

With $\tau = 1$ the differences of a few hundredths barely move the probabilities; dividing by $\tau = 0.01$ (CLIP's learned value is close to this) turns the same scores into an almost certain prediction for dog. The ranking never changes, so the predicted class is the same, but training with a small temperature is what makes the loss care about small gaps in similarity.

sections.heading: 11. Prompts: from a word to a sentence
sections.text:
The text encoder was trained on captions, which are sentences, not isolated words. A bare class name is therefore slightly out of distribution, and it can also be ambiguous: "boxer" may be a dog breed or an athlete, "crane" a bird or a machine. Wrapping the name in a template, "A photo of a {class}", puts it back into the kind of text the encoder has seen and fixes its sense. On ImageNet this alone improves zero-shot accuracy by 1.3 points.

A single template is still a bias: "a photo of" suggests a photograph, and ImageNet also contains drawings, toys and close-ups. The remedy is prompt ensembling. Encode each class with many templates ("A photo of a dog", "A drawing of a dog", and so on), average the resulting vectors, and use the mean vector as that class's representation. On ImageNet this gives about 5 points over the bare class names. The cost is paid once per class, not once per image, because the class vectors are computed in advance.

sections.heading: 12. The headline result
sections.text:
Trained on 400 million image-text pairs and used zero-shot, CLIP ViT-L reaches 76.2% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, exactly the accuracy of a ResNet-101 trained on ImageNet's 1.28 million labelled images. CLIP saw no ImageNet label at all.

Matching a supervised model is impressive, but the more important result is what happens when the test images change while the categories stay the same.

sections.heading: 13. Why the ImageNet model breaks and CLIP does not
sections.text:
A model trained on ImageNet learns whatever separates ImageNet's classes in ImageNet's photographs, including the shortcuts: typical backgrounds, typical viewpoints, photographic texture. ObjectNet keeps the categories but deliberately places objects on unusual backgrounds and at unusual angles, and the ResNet drops from 76.2% to 32.6%. The model learned the dataset rather than the concept.

CLIP's concept of a banana was formed from hundreds of thousands of banana images with captions, drawn from the whole web: photographs, illustrations, cartoons, product shots. Because its training distribution is so broad, a sketch or a painting of a banana is not out of distribution for it. That is the reason it reaches 88.9% on renditions and 60.2% on sketches.

sections.heading: 14. Reading the comparison
sections.text:
The pattern in the figure is informative. Zero-shot wins most clearly on Stanford Cars, Country211 and Food101, domains in which web captions routinely name the exact thing (car models, places, dishes), so the language supervision carries precisely the knowledge the task needs.

It loses most on EuroSAT and RESISC45 (satellite images), KITTI Distance (how far away is the nearest car), CLEVRCounts (counting objects), GTSRB (traffic signs) and PatchCamelyon (tumour detection in lymph-node histopathology). These are specialised or abstract tasks for which alt-text almost never contains the answer: nobody captions a photograph with the distance to the nearest car, and histopathology slides are rare on the web and are not described in the words a pathologist would use. For such domains, and medical imaging is the prime example, CLIP's features still help, but zero-shot use is not enough and some adaptation with labelled data is needed.

sections.heading: 15. How can no labels beat labels?
sections.text:
Three answers are usually offered, and only two of them hold up.

First, "no labels" is a bit misleading. Alt-text is a label, just a noisy and free-form one, written by humans about the image. What CLIP avoided was the cost of a curated label set, not human supervision as such, and a free-form label carries far more information than one of a thousand class names.

Second, scale. CLIP's largest model has about 307 million parameters against 44.5 million for an ImageNet ResNet-101, and it was trained on 400 million images against ImageNet's 1.28 million, more than 300 times as many.

Third, test-set leakage: perhaps the web crawl simply contained the evaluation images. The overlap was measured at roughly 2% of the data, and a later study that asked directly whether CLIP's generalisation comes mainly from high train-test similarity concluded that it does not.

sections.heading: 16. SigLIP: a sigmoid instead of a softmax
sections.text:
The softmax in the CLIP loss normalises each row over the whole batch, so the loss of a single pair depends on every other pair, and computing it requires the full $n \times n$ similarity matrix to be materialised. With batches of tens of thousands spread across many devices, that is a burden.

SigLIP treats every cell of the matrix as an independent yes-or-no question: is this a matching pair?

$$L = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \log \sigma\big(z_{ij} \, (t \langle u_i, v_j \rangle + b)\big)$$

Here $z_{ij} = 1$ on the diagonal and $-1$ elsewhere, $t$ is a learned scale (the inverse temperature) and $b$ a learned bias. Because each term involves only one pair, the batch can be split into blocks: each device computes the loss for its own images against one block of texts at a time, passes the texts on to the next device, and accumulates. No device ever needs the whole matrix. It is a common variant, and the vision encoder of recent VLMs such as Qwen3-VL is a SigLIP model.

sections.heading: 17. CoCa: adding a captioning objective back
sections.text:
CLIP deliberately dropped captioning; CoCa (Contrastive Captioners, 2022) shows that the two objectives combine well if the architecture is arranged for it. The image encoder produces patch tokens. The text side is a decoder split in two halves. The lower half, the unimodal text decoder, processes the caption on its own, and its final [CLS] token is the text embedding used for a CLIP-style contrastive loss against a pooled image embedding. The upper half, the multimodal text decoder, adds cross-attention: its queries come from the text and its keys and values from the image tokens, and it is trained to predict the caption one token at a time.

The total loss is the contrastive loss plus a weighted captioning loss, and one forward pass serves both. The contrastive half keeps the global alignment that makes zero-shot classification and retrieval cheap; the captioning half forces the model to account for details a single matching score can ignore.

The gains are large. Averaged over ImageNet and five distribution-shifted variants, zero-shot accuracy goes from 74.3 for CLIP to 85.7 for CoCa (ImageNet itself: 76.2 to 86.3, ObjectNet 72.3 to 82.7). Fine-tuned on ImageNet, CoCa reaches 91.0% top-1, ahead of every model before it on that benchmark; classification foundation models now dominate the ImageNet leaderboard.

sections.heading: 18. What makes CLIP-style models attractive
sections.text:
The comparison between image and text is a single dot product. That makes training simple enough to scale to billions of pairs, and it makes inference fast: the text or image embeddings of a collection can be computed once and indexed, so a query can be matched against 5 billion images in a retrieval system.

The vocabulary is open: any concept that can be written can serve as a class, without retraining. And because the interface is text, CLIP can be chained with other models, such as a language model that writes better class descriptions (section 26).

sections.heading: 19. The first weakness: concepts are only as fine as the batch
sections.text:
In April 2022 Thrush et al. showed that CLIP cannot tell "there is a mug in some grass" from "there is some grass in a mug". The two captions contain exactly the same words; only their order and roles differ.

The reason lies in the loss. The model only ever has to pick the right caption among the other captions in the batch, so it learns the distinctions that the batch makes necessary. In a batch of 4, telling a corgi photograph apart from the others may only require knowing it shows an animal. In a batch of 100 it must know it is a dog. In a batch of 32,000 there are other dogs, and it must know it is a Welsh Corgi. Larger batches force finer concepts, and this is why CLIP is trained with batches of about 32 thousand.

But there is a limit. Even in a batch of 32,000 captions it is very unlikely that both "a mug in some grass" and "some grass in a mug" appear, so the model is never forced to read word order. It can succeed by checking which objects are mentioned, behaving like a bag of words. Benchmarks built specifically to test this property, called compositionality, such as Winoground, CREPE and ARO, show the failure systematically.

sections.heading: 20. Hard negatives, and the problem they bring
sections.text:
If the batch does not contain the hard comparisons, put them in on purpose. Hard negative fine-tuning generates, for each caption, a confusable variant by swapping words, and adds it as a negative: for an image of a horse eating grass, "grass eating horse" becomes an explicit wrong answer next to the right one. Now word order matters for the loss.

The catch is that automatic swapping does not know what the sentence means. For an image of a black cat and a brown dog, swapping the colours gives "a brown cat and a black dog", a genuine negative. But swapping the nouns gives "a brown dog and a black cat", which describes the same image perfectly well. Treated as a negative, it teaches the model that a correct description is wrong. These are hard positives: captions that look like negatives to the generator but are in fact correct.

sections.heading: 21. Two more weaknesses
sections.text:
Image-level captions are insufficient supervision. A caption describes the whole picture, so the model is never told where in the image each phrase applies. One remedy is to train on region captions with bounding-box coordinates as well ("a man wearing a backpack", "man crossing the street"), which ties phrases to locations.

And a model cannot know everything from a single dataset, even one of 5 billion images, nor is everything in such a dataset something it should learn. The 2023 report from the Stanford Internet Observatory that found child sexual abuse material in LAION-5B, a widely used open web-scale dataset, made the point concretely. It is extremely important to be intentional about data collection and filtering, rather than treating a larger crawl as automatically better.

sections.heading: 22. From matching to answering: the motivation behind LLaVA
sections.text:
A language model trained on next-token prediction can do math, sentiment analysis and symbolic reasoning at inference time simply because all of them can be phrased as continuing a piece of text. CLIP cannot do this: it can score an image against a sentence, but it cannot produce a sentence. The question is whether a model can accept images and text as input and then output text. Such models are called vision-language models (VLMs).

They did not begin with LLaVA. ViLBERT (2019) already processed image regions and words together. But each task needed its own fine-tuning and often non-trivial task-specific machinery, for instance re-ranking Mask R-CNN boxes to locate the object a phrase refers to in RefCOCO. That is exactly the one-model-per-task paradigm of section 1. LLaVA's contribution was to build on a general-purpose language model instead.

sections.heading: 23. The key idea: give the language model visual tokens
sections.text:
Recall how a transformer decodes language. The input tokens "Cats are so" pass through a stack of transformer blocks, and the output at the last position predicts the next token, "cute". Attention lets every position use everything before it.

LLaVA's idea is to place image tokens $V_1, \ldots, V_N$ in front of the text tokens and run the same decoder. The language model then predicts "cute" with the image in its context, attending to image tokens exactly as it attends to words. Nothing in the decoder has to change.

The open question is which image tokens work best. CLIP's image encoder is the natural candidate, because its features are already aligned with language.

sections.heading: 24. Which CLIP features: the penultimate layer
sections.text:
A ViT cuts the image into patches, flattens and linearly projects each one, adds 2D positional embeddings, and processes the sequence of patch tokens together with an extra [CLS] token. In CLIP only the final-layer [CLS] token is used for the contrastive loss.

That creates a subtle problem with the final layer's patch tokens: nothing in the loss looks at them. They are not supervised; in principle they could be anything, even random, and the loss would not change. Using them as visual tokens would be using an untrained output.

The layer before it, the penultimate layer, is different. Its patch tokens feed the final layer's [CLS] token through attention, so they are forced to carry useful information, and they still have one token per patch, so spatial layout is preserved. In practice these tokens preserve spatial and linguistic information best for a language model, and dropping the [CLS] token from the sequence gives slight additional gains.

sections.heading: 25. LLaVA: architecture and training recipe
sections.text:
The full recipe has three steps. First, initialise from two pretrained models: a language model for the decoder (LLaMA, for example) and a pretrained image encoder (CLIP). Second, train a new linear layer that maps CLIP's penultimate-layer patch features into the language model's input embedding space, so that each patch becomes a token the language model can read. Third, fine-tune the language model and the linear layer together on examples of the form (image, instruction, desired answer).

The striking finding is how little data this needs: reasonable performance comes from about 178,000 such samples. The heavy lifting was already done during pre-training; the vision encoder knows what is in images, the language model knows how to reason and talk, and the linear layer plus a short fine-tuning only teaches them to communicate.

sections.caption: Left: LLaVA projects image patch features with a linear layer and prepends them to the text tokens; the language model is fine-tuned. Right: Flamingo keeps both pretrained models frozen and trains only two new parts, a Perceiver resampler that turns any number of image features into a fixed set of tokens, and gated cross-attention layers inserted between the frozen language-model blocks.

sections.heading: 26. Flamingo: fusing through cross-attention
sections.text:
Flamingo (Alayrac et al., NeurIPS 2022) fuses the modalities differently. Its vision encoder and its language model are both pretrained and kept frozen. Only two parts are trained from scratch.

The Perceiver resampler solves a size problem. An image, and even more a video, produces a variable and possibly large number of patch features. The resampler has a fixed set of learned latent queries (64 of them) that cross-attend to all those features, so its output is always the same small number of visual tokens, no matter the input size.

The gated cross-attention dense layers solve the fusion problem. They are inserted between the frozen LM blocks; in each, the text tokens provide the queries and the visual tokens the keys and values. Their output is multiplied by $\tanh(\alpha)$ with a learned scalar $\alpha$ initialised at 0, so at the start of training the gate is closed and the model is exactly the original language model. Visual information is let in gradually as $\alpha$ grows, which protects the frozen model's language ability from being disrupted early in training.

sections.heading: 27. Flamingo's data and in-context learning
sections.text:
Flamingo arranges its training data like language modelling. Web pages with interleaved images and text become a single text sequence in which an <image> tag marks where an image appears and an end-of-chunk token marks where its associated text ends, for example "Cute pics of my pets! <image> My puppy sitting in the grass. <EOC> <image> My cat looking very dignified. <EOC>". Each text chunk attends only to the image immediately before it, while still seeing all previous text through the language model's own attention.

Because the model was trained on sequences of image-text examples, it learns in context at test time, the way GPT does. Show it two examples, "<image of a chinchilla> This is a chinchilla. They are mainly found in Chile." and "<image of a shiba> This is a shiba. They are very popular in Japan.", followed by a picture of a flamingo and "This is", and it completes "a flamingo. They are found in the Caribbean and South America." The same works for visual question answering, reading text in images, and even simple arithmetic shown in images.

With 32 examples in its prompt and no fine-tuning, the largest Flamingo beat the best fine-tuned models of the time on 6 of 16 benchmarks, including OKVQA (57.8 against 54.4) and Flickr30K captioning (75.4 against 67.4), although fine-tuned specialists still won on others, such as VQAv2 (67.6 against 80.2).

sections.heading: 29. The state of the art in 2026
sections.text:
Among proprietary models, Gemini is widely considered the best vision-language model. For open models a distinction is needed: open-weight models can be downloaded and run locally, while fully open-source models also release what is needed to reproduce the training.

Qwen3-VL (technical report, December 2025) is a leading open-weight model, and it is instructive to list what changed relative to LLaVA. First, images are processed at native resolution, so a larger image simply produces more tokens; in the report's example a tall 1248 by 9376 screenshot becomes 11,427 tokens, a 1440 by 800 picture 1,125 tokens and a tiny 256 by 32 one 8 tokens. A 2D rotary position embedding (2D-RoPE) lets the model handle these varying sizes. Second, the vision encoder is SigLIP-2 instead of CLIP. Third, for video the time of each frame is written into the text, as a token such as <0.0 seconds>, rather than encoded implicitly. Fourth, features are taken not from one layer but from layers 8, 16 and 24 of SigLIP-2 and injected into the first layers of the language model (the report calls this DeepStack), so the language model receives both low-level and high-level visual information. Fifth, training runs in four phases, the first of which only bridges the vision encoder to the language model and a later one of which increases the context length.

sections.heading: 30. Open weights are not open science
sections.text:
Many open-weight VLMs reach strong scores, but they are largely distilled: trained on data generated by proprietary models such as GPT-4V. Their weights are available, yet the knowledge was copied from a closed system, and the recipe cannot be reproduced without it. Fully open models in the strict sense, with open weights, open data, open code and open evaluations, lagged far behind.

Molmo (Deitke et al., CVPR 2025) set out to close that gap without distillation, and its central lesson concerns data. LLaMA 3.1V was trained on about 6 billion image-text pairs; Molmo's PixMo dataset has about 700 thousand. Quality replaced quantity.

The difference is in what the text says. Internet text is incidental: it was written for some other purpose, so alt-text reads "pink, japan, aesthetic image" or "love this winter picture by person", which says almost nothing about the image. Human annotation for training is intentional: it is written to describe the image. PixMo's captions run to several paragraphs, describing the desk, the two monitors, the lamp, the stack of books, the floor tiles and what can be seen through the window.

Collecting such dense captions is hard, because people do not like to type long descriptions. But they love to talk. Annotators were asked to speak about an image for 60 to 90 seconds, and the speech was converted to text automatically. That one change in the collection interface is what made detailed captions affordable at scale.

sections.heading: 31. Chaining: when the classifier has never seen the concept
sections.text:
Back to zero-shot classification with CLIP. Prompts like "A photo of a marimba", "A photo of a viaduct", "A photo of a papillon" and "A photo of a lorikeet" work only if the text encoder has a good representation of those words. Rare names are exactly where it does not.

The chaining solution is two steps. First, ask a large language model to describe the concept; second, classify using the description. CuPL (Customized Prompts via Language models, Pratt et al. 2023) asks GPT-3 questions such as "What does a lorikeet look like?" and gets back "A lorikeet is a small to medium-sized parrot with a brightly colored plumage"; a marimba becomes "a large wooden percussion instrument that looks like a xylophone", a papillon "a small, spaniel-type dog with a long, silky coat and fringed ears". These descriptions, rather than the bare names, are encoded as the class vectors.

It improves zero-shot accuracy on 13 of 15 benchmarks, by up to 3.8 points on FGVC Aircraft and 3.7 on DTD, with small drops on Stanford Cars and RESISC45. It also replaces dozens of hand-written prompt templates (80 for ImageNet) with three generic questions to the language model.

sections.heading: 32. VisProg: chaining as programming
sections.text:
Can chaining be generalised to all vision tasks? Consider the statement "The left and right image contains a total of six people and two boats", to be checked against a pair of images. Many visual question answering models exist, but they answer questions about one image. The traditional route is to train a new multi-image model, which then generalises to two images and no further.

VisProg (Gupta et al., 2023) instead writes a short program that uses the models you already have, and lets a language model write it. Given the statement, GPT-3 produces:

ANSWER0 = Vqa(image=LEFT, question='How many people are in the image?'), then the same for the right image, then two more Vqa calls counting boats, and finally ANSWER4 = Eval('{ANSWER0} + {ANSWER1} == 6 and {ANSWER2} + {ANSWER3} == 2').

Running the program returns False. The language model is taught the format with a handful of in-context examples of instruction and program; no model is trained.

The available modules span image understanding (Loc with OWL-ViT, FaceDet, Seg with MaskFormer, Select and Classify with CLIP, Vqa with ViLT), image manipulation (Replace with Stable Diffusion, ColorPop, BgBlur, Tag, Emoji, crops), knowledge retrieval (List, answered by GPT-3) and arithmetic and logic (Eval, Count, Result). "Tag the 7 main characters on the TV show Big Bang Theory" becomes face detection, a GPT-3 list of the characters, CLIP classification of each face and tagging. "Replace desert with lush green grass" becomes segmentation, selecting the desert region and inpainting it with Stable Diffusion. Every step of the reasoning is visible in the program, which also makes errors easy to locate.

sections.heading: 33. Beyond vision and language: omni models
sections.text: The last step removes the boundary between modalities altogether. Starting with GPT-4o in 2024, and more recently with models from Thinking Machines and Google's Gemini, a single transformer is trained to take in and produce text, audio and video as one token sequence. The idea is the one that runs through this whole walkthrough: convert every modality into tokens a single large model can attend over, and let pre-training at scale provide the generality.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: A foundation model is pre-trained once on large and diverse data and then serves many tasks, the opposite of training one model per task. CLIP builds the vision version by matching images to their alt-text with a two-way contrastive loss, which is easier and more efficient than generating captions. Its text encoder doubles as a classifier: encode the class names, pick the nearest one, improve it with sentence templates and prompt ensembles. Trained without curated labels it matches an ImageNet ResNet on ImageNet and far surpasses it under distribution shift, because its training distribution is the whole web; it fails where web text never contains the answer, such as satellite, counting and histopathology tasks. Its concepts are only as fine as its batch, so it reads captions as bags of words; hard negatives help but introduce hard positives. SigLIP removes the batch-wide softmax, CoCa adds captioning back and wins substantially. VLMs make the image readable by a language model: LLaVA prepends projected penultimate-layer CLIP tokens and fine-tunes the LM with only about 178K examples, Flamingo keeps the LM frozen and adds a resampler and gated cross-attention, gaining in-context learning. Modern models such as Qwen3-VL use native resolution, SigLIP-2 and multi-layer features, while Molmo shows that 700K intentional, spoken dense captions can replace billions of incidental ones. Chaining (CuPL, VisProg) gets new abilities without training by letting a language model write descriptions or programs over existing models.

backbone.title: Backbone Choice — From U-Net to DiT, an Axis Independent of the Paradigm
backbone.summary: Because epsilon, score and velocity are outputs of the same shape, the backbone and the generative paradigm can be chosen independently. Why the U-Net fitted this job, its two structural troubles, how DiT changes only the backbone, the three entry doors for the condition (in-context, cross-attention, adaLN-Zero), MM-DiT's two-way flow, and the cost dials, and the position encoding line that runs from absolute sinusoidal embeddings to RoPE, 2D mixed RoPE, canonical coordinates and MSRoPE.

sections.heading: 1. What is asked of the backbone does not depend on the target
sections.text:
What all three paradigms ask of the network has the same shape: take the corrupted input and the time information, and produce an output of the same shape as the input.

$$\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t) \qquad s_\theta(x_t, t) \qquad v_\theta(x_t, t)$$

All three have the same dimensions as $x_t$. All three convert into one another by fixed coefficients. So the backbone does not even need to know which one is being predicted: the same architecture can produce any of the three by changing the loss.

The practical consequence: the choice of architecture and the choice of paradigm can be made independently. SD3 uses rectified flow but its backbone is a DiT; DDPM predicts epsilon but its backbone is a U-Net. All four combinations are legitimate.

sections.heading: 2. Why this job is dense prediction
sections.text:
The output having the same shape as the input puts the problem into a familiar class: producing a value for every position.

In segmentation a label was produced for every pixel. Here a number is produced for every pixel (or every latent position). The two problems have the same shape.

But there is an extra difficulty: the value produced depends both on the local texture and on the overall structure of the image. While predicting the noise, knowing the texture of a region matters as much as knowing whether this image is a face or a landscape. The architecture must carry both local and global information.

This is why the U-Net was chosen: it was a problem already solved for segmentation and the answer was ready to hand.

sections.heading: 3. The U-Net: the parts and their jobs
sections.text:
The encoder goes down, the resolution falls and the receptive field grows. Deep down, every position summarises a wide region of the image — this is where the global information comes from.

The decoder goes up. Skip connections carry the fine detail from the early layers of the encoder straight across; without them the high frequencies lost on the way down would not return.

Attention blocks sit at the low-resolution layers. Because convolution is local it cannot make the two ends of the image consistent with each other; attention does that job. It is not placed at full resolution, because its cost grows with the square of the number of positions.

The timestep is turned into a sinusoidal embedding and added inside every ResBlock. The addition is broadcast to all positions in the same way, because the question "how much noise is there right now" does not vary with position.

sections.heading: 4. The two troubles of the U-Net
sections.text:
The first is that its vision is local. Convolution looks at a neighbourhood; it can only relate distant regions by going deeper. This is why attention blocks were already being placed inside the U-Net — that is, the transformer had already crept in, but as a patch.

The second, and the essential one: the U-Net has no recipe for scaling up. How many levels to descend, at which resolution to place attention, how the channel counts should grow, where the skips attach — all of these are hand-tuned design decisions. When you want to double the model there is no single dial to turn, and you do not know how much you will gain by enlarging it.

In the transformer the opposite holds: increase the depth and the width, increase the data and the compute, and performance improves predictably. As engineering, this is the most valuable property one can ask of an architecture.

sections.heading: 5. DiT: change the backbone, leave diffusion alone
sections.text:
The point most easily missed: DiT is not a new generative model. The forward process is the same, the loss is the same, the sampling is the same. The only thing that changes is the inside of the network computing the prediction.

To feed an image into a transformer, ViT's route is used as is. Let the latent be $32 \times 32 \times 4$; it is split into $2 \times 2$ patches, every patch turns into a token through a linear projection, and $16 \times 16 = 256$ tokens come out. A positional embedding is added on top. Then N standard transformer blocks, and at the end a linear layer and a reshape turn the tokens back into a grid.

Working on the latent is a precondition here. Because attention grows with the square of the number of tokens, working in pixels would mean tens of thousands of tokens for a $256 \times 256$ image. The compression of latent diffusion is what makes DiT possible.

The patch size is directly a quality-cost dial: making it smaller increases the token count and raises quality, and raises the cost in the same proportion.

sections.heading: 6. Where the condition enters — three options
rows: the condition is added as an extra token at the start of the sequence
weak; the condition competes with the other tokens
query from the image, key and value from the condition
an extra attention in every block
strong; the natural choice if the condition is a sequence
the condition determines the scale and shift of the LayerNorm
adaLN plus a gate at the block output initialised at zero
the best result; the block starts close to the identity

sections.heading: 7. The intuition of adaLN and why zero
sections.text:
LayerNorm normalises a vector and applies a learned scale and shift. The single idea of adaLN is this: stop letting that scale and shift be fixed parameters and produce them from the condition. The timestep embedding and the condition embedding are summed and passed through a small MLP, and the resulting vector is divided into the modulation coefficients inside the block.

The effect: the condition stops being a term added to the activations and turns into a dial that determines the scale of the activations. Addition diluted the signal; modulation steers the behaviour of every block directly.

adaLN-Zero adds a gate on top of this and initialises it at zero. So in the first steps of training every block behaves close to the identity function, that is, the deep stack is not disturbed at the start; the blocks open up their contributions slowly. This is the variant that gave the best result in the DiT ablation.

sections.heading: 8. MM-DiT: making text and image equal citizens
sections.text:
Conditioning with a single pooled vector loses nuance. In a sentence such as "the red cube is to the left of the blue sphere", which adjective belongs to which object does not fit into a single vector.

Cross-attention is a step further: the condition is kept as a sequence and the image tokens can look at it. But the flow is one-way — the text tokens learn nothing from the image and are not updated among themselves in the image's context.

MM-DiT (SD3) joins the two sequences: the text tokens and the image tokens enter the same attention operation, so both directions see each other. But the weights are not shared — the two modalities have their own projection and MLP weights. This is called double-stream; SD3 and Qwen-Image have this structure.

The gain is that the condition turns into a representation that is updated together with the image throughout generation. The cost is that the sequence length grows by the number of text tokens.

sections.heading: 9. The position problem, as it appears in an image model
sections.text:
Attention sees its input as a set: shuffle the tokens and the same scores come out. In text this destroys word order; here it destroys the layout of the image, which is worse, because a patch means nothing without knowing where in the picture it sits.

The U-Net never had this problem. Convolution is defined on a grid; neighbourhood is built into the operation. The moment you move to a transformer you give that up, and you have to put the position back by hand.

What exactly do we want from the injected information? Not an identity tag for each position, but this: when two tokens meet in the dot product, the result should carry how far apart they are. Everything that follows is a series of attempts at that one sentence.

sections.heading: 10. Absolute sinusoidal embeddings: the first answer
sections.text:
The original Transformer's answer is to produce a vector for each position and add it to the token's embedding before the first block.

That vector is built from sines and cosines of different frequencies. Each dimension pair gets its own frequency, running from very fast to very slow — the usual picture is a clock: one hand for seconds, one for minutes, one for hours. A fast hand distinguishes neighbouring positions, a slow one distinguishes distant regions. Reading them together identifies the position.

$$\mathrm{PE}(p, 2i) = \sin\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \qquad \mathrm{PE}(p, 2i+1) = \cos\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)$$

Nothing here is learned and the formula is defined for every $p$, so in principle you can produce an embedding for a position longer than anything seen in training.

Does it deliver what was asked? Take the dot product of two position embeddings and plot it against their distance.

sections.heading: What the sinusoidal embedding actually conveys
11. What the figure says, and what it costs
sections.text:
The curve falls as the distance grows, so the dot product does carry distance. But look at how it falls.

In the first stretch it drops steeply: the high frequency terms go out of phase almost immediately and cancel. After that only the slow terms survive, and they do not decay — they oscillate. Two positions two hundred apart can score higher than two positions a hundred and fifty apart.

So the information is there but it is noisy, and it never settles at zero. The network can learn to read it, yet it is being handed a blunt instrument.

Three further costs are structural. The encoding is absolute, so a patch learns the behaviour of the index 37 rather than the relation to its neighbour. It is injected once at the input and then has to survive every block. And it is tied to the grid it was built for: change the resolution and the same index now means a different place in the picture.

This is nonetheless what the original Transformer (2017), the original ViT (2020) and the original DiT (2022) all used. The move away from it is recent, and it is the single most visible difference between DiT as published and the DiT-style models of today.

sections.heading: 12. RoPE: put the position inside the attention, not before it
sections.text:
The refinement starts from a question: if what we want is the relative distance to show up in the dot product, why inject position at the input and hope it survives, instead of putting it where the dot product happens?

RoPE does exactly that. Before the scores are computed, the query and the key vectors are rotated by an angle proportional to their position — each pair of dimensions is rotated in its own plane, with its own frequency, exactly the clock of the sinusoidal scheme reused as rotation speeds.

The payoff is an identity rather than an approximation. Rotating two vectors by $m\theta$ and $n\theta$ and taking their dot product gives the same answer as rotating one of them by $(m-n)\theta$ and leaving the other alone: a rotation preserves lengths and angles, so only the difference survives.

$$\langle R_m q,\; R_n k \rangle = \langle R_{m-n} q,\; k \rangle$$

That is, the score depends on the relative position exactly, not approximately. No vector is added to the content, so nothing of the token's meaning is overwritten, and the same rule applies inside every block rather than fading as depth grows.

RoPE is the default in current language models and has carried over to image generation along with everything else from that side.

sections.heading: 13. From one dimension to two: axial and mixed RoPE
sections.text:
RoPE was designed for a sequence, where position is a single number. An image patch has two: a row and a column.

The obvious transfer is axial RoPE — split the dimensions into two halves, use the row index to rotate one half and the column index the other. It works, and it is wrong in a specific way: the two axes never meet. No pair of dimensions ever sees the row and the column together, so a relation that is genuinely diagonal has to be reconstructed from two independent pieces. The split itself is also arbitrary, since nothing says which dimensions should belong to which axis.

Mixed 2D RoPE repairs this by building a single rotation that involves both coordinates at once, so a rotation plane can be sensitive to a diagonal displacement rather than only to a horizontal or a vertical one. Visually the difference is immediate: axial encodings leave axis-aligned artefacts in generated images, the mixed form does not.

sections.heading: 14. Scaling: making the coordinates mean the same thing at every resolution
sections.text:
A problem specific to image generation now appears, and it matters because generation models are deliberately trained across resolutions and aspect ratios.

If you use raw indices, the centre of a $3 \times 3$ grid sits at index $(1,1)$ while the centre of a $6 \times 5$ grid sits somewhere else entirely. The same physical place in the picture receives different numbers depending on the size of the grid, and the model has to learn each case separately.

The remedy is to stop using indices and use canonical coordinates: map every grid onto a fixed range, say $[-1, 1]$ in both directions, before computing the rotations. Then the centre is $(0,0)$ at any resolution, the corner is always the corner, and a model trained at one size has a chance of behaving sensibly at another.

This is the kind of detail that never appears in the headline of a paper and decides whether the model survives a resolution change.

sections.heading: 15. Multimodal: text is one dimensional, the image is two
sections.text:
The last complication comes from MM-DiT. Text and image tokens sit in the same attention, but their positions are not the same kind of object: a caption has a single index, a patch has a pair. Writing both into the same rotation scheme without interference is not obvious.

The naive route is to treat the text as if it lay on a line through the image, which makes the text positions compete with real spatial positions and distorts both.

MSRoPE, from Qwen-Image, arranges the two so that they can coexist: the image keeps its two dimensional coordinates, and the text is placed so that it behaves as ordinary one dimensional RoPE from its own point of view while not colliding with the image grid.

The closing note of the lecture is worth keeping as it was given: position encoding is still an open problem. There are many variants, the dust has not settled, and every choice is a trade-off. This is one of the places where a contribution is still available.

sections.heading: 16. Where the cost is and which dials exist
sections.text:
The cost of attention grows with the square of the number of tokens, while the cost of the feed-forward grows linearly with it. At high resolution the dominant term is attention.

The dials you hold:

The latent compression ratio. If you compress 16-fold instead of 8-fold the token count is divided by four, but the detail the decoder cannot unfold is permanently lost.

The patch size. A $4 \times 4$ patch instead of $2 \times 2$ divides the token count by four; quality drops.

The attention implementation. Kernels that reduce memory traffic (of the flash attention kind) run the same mathematics far faster.

The positional encoding. Relative encodings of the RoPE kind generalise better to resolutions not seen during training than fixed sinusoidal ones.

Mixed precision and gradient checkpointing. The two standard tools on the memory side; the second raises compute and lowers memory.

sections.heading: 17. Which backbone when
rows: better; the locality bias comes for free
weak; it learns everything from data

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: The paradigm and the backbone are separate axes: because epsilon, score and velocity are outputs of the same shape, the same network can compute all of them. What is asked of the backbone is dense prediction; both local texture and global structure are needed. The U-Net was the ready answer to this job, but its vision is local and it has no recipe for scaling. DiT changes only the backbone without touching diffusion and brings scalability; working on the latent is the precondition for that. The condition can enter through three doors, and adaLN-Zero gives the best result. MM-DiT puts the text into the same attention as the image and makes the flow two-way. The dominant term in the cost is attention, and the dials are the compression ratio and the patch size. Position has to be injected by hand once you leave the convolution: the absolute sinusoidal embedding carries distance only noisily and is tied to one grid, which is what the original Transformer, ViT and DiT used; RoPE moves the position into the attention by rotating the query and the key, so the score depends on the relative distance exactly; in two dimensions the axial split loses the diagonal and mixed 2D RoPE repairs it; canonical coordinates keep the meaning of a position fixed across resolutions, and MSRoPE lets one dimensional text and two dimensional image positions coexist. The lecture's own closing line stands: this is still an open problem.
