lifecycle.title: Training Lifecycle — From Pre-training to Distillation
lifecycle.context: How a generation model is actually built · CME 296 Lecture 6
lifecycle.summary: The four stages that turn a diffusion model into a product: pre-training, post-training, tuning, distillation. Why the timestep should not be drawn uniformly, why the schedule shifts with resolution, REPA, the data mixture and the curriculum, continued training against supervised fine-tuning, the three preference tuning methods, DreamBooth and LoRA, and the distillation chain in which each method is born out of the limitation of the previous one.

sections.heading: 1. The four stages of the lifecycle
rows: how to generate images at all
the largest share, weeks of GPU time
how to generate images for one special case
a few images, minutes to hours
a separate training run over the teacher

sections.heading: 2. Why each stage exists
sections.text:
A pre-trained model produces an image that matches the prompt, but it is not necessarily the image a person would prefer: the lighting is flat, the composition is ordinary, a detail of the instruction has been skipped. Post-training is about that gap.

Tuning is a different need again: the model knows teddy bears in general, but not your teddy bear. A handful of photographs have to teach it one specific subject.

And distillation is about the clock. A model that needs fifty network calls for one image is unusable in an interactive interface, in a high-volume service or in animation, where a user typically has limited compute, limited money and limited time.

The four stages are separate trainings and the order is not negotiable: each one starts from the weights the previous one left.

sections.heading: 3. One loop, three targets
sections.text:
Before the lifecycle there is one thing to settle, because everything that follows sits on it: the training loop of DDPM, score matching and flow matching is the same loop. Draw a clean example, draw a noise, mix them according to $t$, ask the network for something, take an MSE. What changes is only what is asked.

In DDPM the target is the noise $\varepsilon$ that was added. In score matching it is the gradient of the log-density, $\nabla_x \log p_t(x)$. In flow matching it is the velocity, $z - x_0$, that carries the point from data towards noise.

The three are connected to each other by fixed coefficients, so none of them is a separate architecture. This is why everything in this walkthrough — the choice of timestep distribution, the alignment loss, preference tuning, distillation — applies to all three in the same way.

sections.heading: 4. What the network is asked changes with t
sections.text:
Lay the noise level out on an axis. At one end sits the clean image, at the other pure noise, and in between the mixture.

Near the clean end the task is easy. The input is almost the image itself; the correct answer to what was added to this is nearly readable from the input.

Near the noise end the task is easy for a different reason. There is no information left in the input, so the best answer is the average of the dataset; the network cannot do better and it is not expected to.

The difficulty is in the middle. There the input still holds a structure, but that structure is compatible with several different images at once. The question of which way should I go from here has a real answer, and the answer is neither trivial nor hopeless. Most of the generative work is done exactly in this band.

sections.heading: 5. Consequence: do not draw the timestep uniformly
sections.text:
The classical training loop draws $t$ from the uniform distribution. Seen through the previous section that is a waste: half the draws go to bands where the task is either trivial or hopeless.

The proposal of SD3 (Esser et al., 2024) is to draw the timestep from a logit-normal distribution instead. You draw a normal variable and squash it into the interval $(0,1)$ with the logistic function:

$$u \sim \mathcal{N}(m, s^2), \qquad t = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-u}}$$

The density is then concentrated in the middle of the interval and thins out towards the two ends. Two parameters remain in your hand: $m$ shifts the centre of the emphasis (positive values push it towards the noise side), and $s$ sets how sharp the emphasis is.

Nothing else in the training changes. The same loss, the same network, only the distribution the timestep comes from.

sections.heading: 6. The same noise level does not mean the same difficulty at every resolution
sections.text:
There is a second adjustment and its reason is not obvious.

Take an image and its version at twice the resolution, and add noise of exactly the same variance to both. In the high resolution image the noise is perceptually less destructive, because neighbouring pixels carry nearly the same information; the redundancy is higher, and averaging over the neighbourhood recovers the signal. The same noise level destroys less at high resolution.

The consequence is that a schedule tuned at low resolution places the hard band in the wrong place when the same model is trained at high resolution. The solution is to shift the timestep towards the noise side as the resolution grows, so that the perceived difficulty stays the same.

A note on the convention, because it is the easiest place to get the sign wrong: in the SD3 paper $t=0$ is the clean image and $t=1$ is noise. CS231n and the flow walkthrough on this site use the same convention, while Lipman's flow matching paper uses the opposite one.

sections.heading: 7. REPA: give the network a representation instead of making it find one
sections.text:
A diffusion transformer has to do two things at once: understand what is in the image, and produce the target from that understanding. The first of the two is a problem that large pre-trained encoders have already solved.

The idea of REPA (Representation Alignment, Yu et al., 2024) is to hand that solution over. While training the generation model, take the clean image and pass it through a frozen pre-trained encoder such as DINOv2. Separately take the output of one of the early transformer blocks of the generation model. Push the second through a small trainable projection head and ask that the two match, measuring the match with cosine similarity. This term is added to the ordinary diffusion loss.

Three results are worth remembering. The speedup is large: the same quality is reached in a fraction of the training steps. Aligning only the early layers works best, because the later layers have to do generation, not representation. And the larger the diffusion model, the more it benefits — which is the opposite of what one would expect from a training aid.

The projection head is thrown away at inference. REPA changes training, not the model you ship.

sections.heading: 8. Pre-training: the data mixture and the curriculum
sections.text:
Pre-training is the stage that teaches the model to generate images at all, and most of the total compute goes here.

Two things are decided and neither of them is about the architecture.

The data mixture. Which fraction of the dataset is natural photographs, which fraction is design and illustration, which fraction is text-bearing images, which fraction is synthetic data. This composition directly determines what the model will be good at.

The curriculum. Training does not start at the final difficulty. It starts easy — low resolution, a fixed square aspect ratio, short and simple prompts — and is made harder in stages: higher resolution, variable aspect ratios, long and detailed prompts. The reason is cost as much as pedagogy: a step at low resolution is cheap, and the model learns the coarse structure of the world there.

sections.heading: 9. Why variable resolution is not a problem for a DiT
sections.text:
The curriculum demands that the same model work at different resolutions and different aspect ratios, and it is here that the choice of backbone pays off.

A DiT cuts the image into patches and turns each patch into a token. When the resolution rises the patches do not change size; their number changes. The transformer has no fixed input length, so a longer sequence is not a structural problem — the position encoding and the compute are what has to carry it.

This is the practical reason why the field moved from the U-Net to the transformer, alongside scaling. A convolutional stack with fixed downsampling ratios negotiates much less comfortably with variable aspect ratios.

sections.heading: 10. Post-training: two separate moves
rows: facts and concepts missing from the pre-training data

sections.heading: 11. Preference tuning: putting the human judgement into the loss
sections.text:
SFT teaches the model what a good image looks like through examples. Preference tuning goes one step further and puts a judgement signal, which image would a person prefer, directly into the objective. Three methods are worth knowing and they differ in where the signal comes from.

ReFL (Reward Feedback Learning, Xu et al., 2023) trains a reward model on human comparisons first. Then, during generation, the sampling chain is run to a late step, the image is decoded there, the reward model scores it, and the gradient of that score is backpropagated into the generator. Running only to a late step is what makes it affordable.

Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) carries the group-relative policy optimisation of the LLM world over to flow models. For one prompt several images are generated, the reward of each is compared with the mean of the group, and the ones above the mean are reinforced. Because it is online reinforcement learning the sampling has to be stochastic — a deterministic ODE sampler gives no exploration.

Diffusion-DPO (Wallace et al., 2023) removes the reward model altogether. It works directly on pairs of preferred and rejected images: the objective raises the model's likelihood on the preferred one relative to the rejected one. The same trick as DPO in language models, written on the diffusion loss.

sections.heading: What preference tuning actually changes: the target is no longer p_data
sections.text:
It is worth stopping on what has just happened, because it is a larger break than it looks.

Pre-training maximised likelihood. The target was **p_data**: imitate the distribution the training images came from, as faithfully as possible. Every design decision up to this point served that one goal.

Preference tuning abandons it. The new target is the data distribution **tilted towards what people prefer** — roughly proportional to $p_{\text{data}}(x) \, e^{r(x)/\beta}$, where $r$ is the reward. Mass is deliberately moved away from where the data put it.

This is the same shape as guidance, which sharpened the distribution to $p(x)\,p(y \mid x)^{s}$. Both tilt a distribution. **The difference is where the tilt lives.** Guidance tilts at sampling time and leaves the weights untouched, so setting the scale back to one undoes it completely. Preference tuning tilts **the weights themselves**, permanently; there is no dial to turn back.

The source of the signal differs too. Guidance derives its direction from inside the model, or from a classifier trained on the same kind of data. Preference tuning takes it from **outside**: human judgement, which is not a property of the data at all.

Two consequences follow and both are visible in practice.

The model stops being an honest estimator of the data. Whatever guarantee maximum likelihood gave you — that this is the distribution best explaining the observations — no longer holds, by construction. That is the intended trade, but it should be named rather than assumed.

And diversity falls, for the third time in this walkthrough. The reward model finds a region it scores highly and the generator settles there. Pushed too far it becomes **reward hacking**: outputs that satisfy the reward model while being worse by any other measure. The recognisable sameness of aligned image models — the polished light, the safe composition — comes largely from here.

This is what the KL term in every one of these objectives is for. It is a leash to the original model: go towards the reward, but do not leave the distribution behind. Without it the optimiser would abandon $p_{\text{data}}$ entirely.

The three stages in one line: **maximum likelihood imitates the data · guidance leans towards the typical region at sampling time · preference tuning moves the weights towards human taste for good.** Each one buys adherence and pays with diversity.

sections.heading: 12. Prompt enhancement: fixing the input, not the model
sections.text:
There is a cheaper move next to these. The user writes a short prompt, and a language model expands it into a long, detailed description before it reaches the generator: the material of the fabric, the direction and warmth of the light, the depth of field, the mood.

Nothing in the model changes. The reason it works is that the generator was trained on long and detailed captions, so a long prompt lands closer to the region it knows well.

This is the fastest of the four stages to deploy and the easiest to undo, which is why it sits in almost every production text-to-image system.

sections.heading: 13. Tuning: DreamBooth and the rare token
sections.text:
Now the special case. You have four or five photographs of one particular teddy bear and you want the model to be able to place that bear in new scenes.

DreamBooth (Ruiz et al., 2022) ties the subject to a rare token. A rarely used string is chosen, for example [V], and the model is fine-tuned on captions of the form a photo of a [V] teddy bear. A rare token is chosen deliberately: a common word already carries a strong meaning and fine-tuning would overwrite that meaning.

But fine-tuning on five images has an obvious danger: the model forgets what a teddy bear in general looks like and turns every bear into this bear. This is called language drift, and DreamBooth's remedy is to train, alongside the new examples, on images the model itself generated for the plain caption a photo of a teddy bear. That second term is the prior preservation loss, and it holds the general class in place while the specific subject is learned.

At inference the rare token is used inside any prompt: [V] teddy bear attending a lecture.

sections.heading: 14. LoRA: changing few weights instead of all of them
sections.text:
DreamBooth as described updates the whole model, which is expensive and produces a full copy of the weights per subject.

LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) starts from an observation: the update a fine-tune makes to a weight matrix is of low rank in practice. So instead of learning the full update, learn it as the product of two thin matrices:

$$W' = W + BA, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}, \quad A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}, \quad r \ll \min(d,k)$$

The original $W$ stays frozen; only $A$ and $B$ are trained. With a rank of a few tens this is a tiny fraction of the parameters, and the quality is comparable to a full fine-tune.

At inference $BA$ can be added into $W$ once, so nothing is slower afterwards. What you hand around is a file of a few megabytes rather than a full model.

The costs are on the other side of the ledger: the training run itself still takes time and money, and the result is tied to one subject and one base model — it is not reusable elsewhere. The method pays off when many images of the same subject will be generated.

sections.heading: 15. Distillation: the problem and why the obvious attempt fails
sections.text:
The last stage is about speed. The teacher is a trained, good, slow model; the student is usually a network of the same size, and what is asked of it is to do in few steps — ideally one — what the teacher does in many.

Note that this is not the traditional distillation of the classification world. There the student is small and the teacher large; here the sizes are typically equal and what is being compressed is the number of steps, not the parameters.

The first attempt is the obvious one: take the teacher's fifty-step result and ask the student to produce it in a single step. It does not work. The map from noise to image is heavily curved, and asking a network to learn the whole of that curve in one jump is too hard a regression problem.

Everything that follows is a series of answers to that difficulty, and each one is born out of the limitation of the previous.

sections.heading: 16. Progressive distillation: halve the number of steps at each round
sections.text:
Salimans et al. (2022) made the problem tractable by shrinking it. Instead of asking for the whole way at once, ask the student to reproduce two teacher steps in one step. That is a small regression and it is learnable.

When the round is over the student has become a model that generates in half the number of steps. That student is then made the new teacher and the same procedure is repeated. From 1024 steps to 512, to 256, and onwards down to a handful.

Because each round halves, reaching a single step needs on the order of $\log_2 T$ rounds. The quality at a given number of function evaluations comes out better than DDIM with the same budget.

Its limitations are three and they are what motivate the next method. The paths being distilled are curved, and that curvature is a constraint fixed in advance. The result requires the same discrete, fixed sampling grid at inference time. And the procedure needs that many separate training rounds.

sections.heading: 17. InstaFlow: straighten the path first, then distil
sections.text:
Here the mindset changes. Rather than trying to learn a curved path better, make the path straight and then the distillation becomes easy.

The tool is reflow, which comes from rectified flow. You take the trained model, generate pairs of noise and image with it, and retrain the model on those pairs with straight lines between them. The previously crossing, curved trajectories are thereby straightened. Most of the gain comes from the first reflow; the following rounds add little.

Once the path is straight, a single Euler step is nearly enough, and the distillation of the remaining gap is a small job. InstaFlow (Liu et al., 2023) distils the N-step model into a one-step one in exactly this way, and the loss is measured between the teacher's output and the student's.

The distance function is chosen in two stages: MSE first as a warm-up, then LPIPS, a perceptual distance, to polish. The reason is that MSE pulls towards the average and blurs, while LPIPS compares in the feature space of a pre-trained network and therefore tolerates small pixel shifts.

Its limitation is the computational burden. Before any of this begins the teacher has to pave the entire way — generating the noise-image pairs is a full sampling run per pair. And the learned intermediate paths are then simply skipped over.

sections.heading: 18. Consistency models: one map to the clean image from every point on the path
sections.text:
The next change of mindset is about what is learned. Instead of learning a global map from one end of the path to the other, attach a local rule to every point of the path.

Consistency models (Song et al., 2023) ask this of the network: from wherever you are on the deterministic ODE trajectory, predict the clean image at the end of that trajectory. The property this demands is self-consistency — two different points on the same trajectory must produce the same output.

$$f_\theta(x_t, t) = f_\theta(x_{t'}, t') \quad \text{for every } t, t' \text{ on the same trajectory}$$

There are two ways of training it. In consistency distillation a teacher generates the neighbouring point on the trajectory and the student is asked to agree on the two. In consistency training there is no teacher; the neighbouring point is obtained from the forward noising process itself. In the results distillation comes out ahead.

A fair objection: could the network not satisfy this condition by outputting the same constant everywhere? It could, and two design choices prevent it. The boundary condition pins the function at the clean end to the identity, so the output is anchored to the real image there. And the target branch is kept under a stop-gradient with an EMA copy of the weights, so the two sides cannot collapse onto each other together.

The limitation is quality. Because the loss is a regression towards the target pixels, the solution regresses towards the mean and the outputs come out smoothed and blurred. An image that is perfectly valid and realistic is still penalised if its pixels do not coincide with the target.

sections.heading: 19. DMD: match the distribution instead of the sample
sections.text:
If penalising the exact pixels is the problem, then stop asking for the exact pixels. Distribution matching distillation (Yin et al., 2023) asks that the distribution of the student's outputs match the distribution of the teacher's outputs, and says nothing about individual images.

The objective is a KL divergence between the two distributions. Written directly it is intractable, because neither density is available. But its gradient can be expressed in a form that needs only the two scores — the score of the teacher's distribution and the score of the student's current output distribution.

The first is the trained teacher. The second does not exist, so it has to be manufactured: a second diffusion model is trained on the fly on the student's own outputs, purely to provide that score. The update then pushes the student in the direction of the difference between the two scores: more of what the teacher says, less of what the student already says.

The results are competitive at a single step. The costs are heavy. There is a small diffusion training loop running inside the distillation loop. Two models are computing nearly the same thing. And the signal that steers the student is soft — a difference of scores, not a definite verdict on any particular image.

sections.heading: 20. ADD and LADD: bring in a discriminator
sections.text:
The last change of mindset replaces the soft signal with a hard one. What gives a definite verdict on a single image is a discriminator, and that is the GAN's own instrument.

Adversarial diffusion distillation (ADD, Sauer et al., 2023) trains the student under two terms at once. One is the distillation term that keeps it close to the teacher's output. The other is an adversarial term: a discriminator tries to separate the student's images from real ones, and the student tries to fool it. The first keeps the student from drifting away from the teacher, and the second removes the blur, because a blurred image is easy for a discriminator to catch.

Its limitation is plumbing. The discriminator works in pixel space, so the student's latent output has to be decoded at every step, and the real images have to be moved into the same space. These conversions are the expensive part.

LADD (Sauer et al., 2024) removes them. The discriminator is moved into the latent space, and the feature extractor it works on is the teacher itself — a model that is already there and already knows what images look like. No decoding, no conversion, and the discriminator now sees features at several noise levels rather than raw pixels. This is the scheme behind the fast versions of the current large models.

sections.heading: 21. The distillation chain at a glance
rows: The limitation that gave rise to the next
halve the step count each round
curved paths, fixed sampling grid, many rounds
the teacher must pave the whole way first
from any point, map to the clean end
a diffusion loop inside the loop, soft signal
move the discriminator into the latent space

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text:
The lifecycle has four stages and they are separate trainings: pre-training teaches generation, post-training teaches quality, tuning teaches one special case, distillation teaches speed. All of it sits on a single training loop in which only the target changes between the epsilon, score and velocity parametrizations.

Two adjustments to that loop are worth carrying: draw the timestep from a logit-normal rather than the uniform, because the task is hardest in the middle of the noise axis; and shift the timesteps towards noise as the resolution grows, because the same noise level destroys less when neighbouring pixels are redundant. REPA is a third: align the early layers with a frozen pre-trained encoder and the training gets substantially faster.

In tuning, DreamBooth ties the subject to a rare token and holds the general class in place with a prior preservation loss; LoRA makes the same fine-tune cheap by learning the update as a low-rank product.

The distillation chain reads as a sequence of limitations. Progressive distillation halves the steps but stays on curved paths; reflow straightens the path but the teacher must pave it first; consistency models learn a local map but regress to the mean and blur; DMD matches distributions but needs a diffusion loop inside the loop and gives a soft signal; ADD brings the discriminator's hard verdict but pays for pixel-space conversions; LADD moves the discriminator into the latent space using the teacher as the feature extractor. The recurring ingredients across all of them: a regression loss (MSE or LPIPS), distributional or adversarial pressure, and training in the latent space. One framing is worth carrying out of the post-training section: pre-training targets p_data, while preference tuning deliberately targets a **tilted** distribution, p_data weighted by the reward. Guidance does the same tilting at sampling time and is reversible; preference tuning bakes it into the weights and is not. The KL term exists to keep that drift on a leash.

eval.title: Evaluation — From Human Ratings to a Multimodal Judge
eval.context: How a generation model is measured · CME 296 Lecture 7
eval.summary: The two measurable axes, aesthetics and prompt adherence; the human rating ladder from an absolute scale to pairwise comparison and Elo; why a reference image cannot be used and how FID compares distributions instead; CLIPScore and PickScore; the reference-based chain MSE, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS; and the multimodal judges TIFA, VQAScore and VIEScore with the benchmarks that separate the failure modes.

sections.heading: 1. What exactly is being measured
sections.text:
A generation model takes a prompt and returns an image. There are two separate ways that image can fail, and confusing them is the first mistake in evaluation.

It can fail to be a good picture: the lighting is implausible, the anatomy is broken, there are artefacts, it does not look real. This axis is called aesthetics, and it covers physical plausibility, perceptual quality, cleanliness and realism.

Or it can be a beautiful image that is not the image that was asked for: the teddy bear is there but it is not reading, there are three objects when two were asked for, the text on the sign is illegible, the style is wrong. This axis is prompt adherence, and it covers object recall, counting, text rendering and style adherence.

Both have to be measured separately, because a model can be strong on one and weak on the other, and a single number that mixes them tells you nothing about which.

These two are only the tractable part. There are at least four other dimensions that matter and are harder to measure: safety, diversity, memorisation of training images, and bias.

sections.heading: 2. Asking people: rating on a scale
sections.text:
The most direct method is to show the image to a person and ask for a score.

The first attempt is a graded scale: very bad to very good, one to five. The model's score is the average of the ratings. The nuance is welcome, but there are two problems. The ratings are noisy, and rating on an absolute scale is hard — what exactly is a four, and is my four your four?

The second attempt simplifies the task: a binary scale, good or bad. The score becomes the proportion of passes. The task is genuinely easier for the rater, but the core difficulty remains: an absolute judgement is still being asked for.

sections.heading: 3. Pairwise comparison and the win rate
sections.text:
The third attempt removes the absolute judgement altogether. Two models' images for the same prompt are placed side by side and the person is asked which is better, with a tie allowed.

$$\text{win rate} = \frac{\text{number of wins}}{\text{number of comparisons}}$$

This is a much easier task, because relative judgement is what people are actually good at.

But a new problem appears immediately: the win rate depends on whom you were compared against. A model that beat a weak opponent and a model that beat a strong one have the same win rate, and that is clearly wrong. Beating a bad model proves nothing; beating a good model proves a lot.

sections.heading: 4. Elo: weighting the win by the strength of the opponent
sections.text:
The Elo rating, which comes from chess, answers exactly this. Each model carries a number, and every comparison updates it in four steps.

First, compute the expected score from the current ratings. Against an opponent rated far higher, your expected score is near zero:

$$E_A = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{(R_B - R_A)/400}}$$

Second, take the actual result: 1 for a win, 0.5 for a tie, 0 for a loss.

Third, compare the actual result with the expected one. Fourth, update the rating in proportion to the difference:

$$R_A \leftarrow R_A + K\,(S_A - E_A)$$

The mechanism is in this last line. If you beat an opponent you were expected to beat, $S_A - E_A$ is small and your rating barely moves. If you beat one you were expected to lose to, the difference is large and the rating jumps. The strength of the opponent is thereby priced into the result automatically.

The public text-to-image leaderboards are built on exactly this.

sections.heading: 5. Why human ratings are not enough
sections.text:
Human judgement is the ground truth of this field, and yet it cannot be the everyday measurement instrument. Four reasons.

It is expensive, because every number is paid labour. It is slow, so it cannot sit inside a training loop and cannot answer a question the same afternoon. It is subjective, and the variance between raters is real. And it is not automatically correct either: fatigue, an order effect in which the first image seen anchors the rest, and cultural bias all enter the numbers.

Everything that follows exists to automate this signal. And the last section of this walkthrough returns to the same point: whatever the automatic metric is, it has to be checked against human ratings before it is trusted.

sections.heading: 6. Why a reference image cannot be used
sections.text:
The obvious idea for an automatic metric is to compare the generated image against a correct image. It does not work, and the reason is fundamental rather than technical.

For the prompt a teddy bear reading a book there are countless valid images. Different poses, different lighting, different backgrounds, different framings — all of them correct. Picking one of them and calling it the answer, then penalising every deviation from it, measures the wrong thing.

The way out is to change the level at which the comparison is made. Do not compare a single image against a single image; compare the distribution of the generated images against the distribution of the real images. An individual image does not have to match anything. What is asked is that the cloud the model produces sit in the same place as the cloud of real images.

sections.heading: 7. FID: the distance between two distributions
sections.text:
But images cannot be compared as pixels, so both sets are first passed through a pre-trained encoder — classically the Inception network, from which the metric takes its name. Every image becomes a feature vector, and each set becomes a cloud of points in feature space.

Then comes an assumption that makes the computation possible: each cloud is taken to be a Gaussian. A Gaussian is fully described by a mean and a covariance, so all that is left is the distance between two Gaussians. The Fréchet distance between two Gaussians has a closed form:

$$\text{FID} = \lVert \mu_r - \mu_g \rVert^2 + \operatorname{Tr}\!\left( \Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2 (\Sigma_r \Sigma_g)^{1/2} \right)$$

The expression has two terms and each one measures something different.

The first is the difference in location, the distance between the two means. This is about quality and style: if the generated images systematically sit somewhere else in feature space, they systematically look different.

The second is the difference in shape, the mismatch of the covariances. This is about diversity: a model that produces near-identical images has a tiny covariance, and the term catches that even when the mean is in exactly the right place.

Lower is better. Zero would mean the two Gaussians coincide.

sections.heading: 8. What to be careful about with FID
sections.text:
FID is the standard number of the field — the curves in the DiT paper and in the REPA results are all FID — but three things about it have to be kept in mind, because comparing two FID numbers from different papers is often meaningless.

It depends on the sample size. FID is biased downwards as the number of samples grows, so the count has to be reported; the common convention is 50,000 samples, written FID-50k.

It depends on the reference distribution. The FID of the same model against ImageNet and against COCO are different numbers. There is no absolute scale.

And it rests on the normality assumption. The feature clouds are not really Gaussian, and everything beyond the mean and the covariance is discarded by construction. Two distributions with identical first two moments and very different shapes get an FID of zero.

sections.heading: 9. Prompt adherence without a reference: CLIPScore and PickScore
sections.text:
FID says nothing about the prompt. It only asks whether the generated images look like real images; it does not check whether they show what was asked for.

The measurement of prompt adherence uses CLIP, which was trained to place text and images into a shared space. CLIPScore takes the cosine similarity between the embedding of the prompt and the embedding of the generated image, clips it at zero and rescales it:

$$\text{CLIPScore} = w \cdot \max\bigl(\cos(E_{\text{img}}, E_{\text{txt}}),\, 0\bigr), \qquad w = 2.5$$

No reference image is involved, which is why this is a reference-free metric. The model used is plain CLIP as it comes.

PickScore changes one thing: instead of plain CLIP it uses a CLIP fine-tuned on human preference data, from a dataset of pairwise choices between generated images. The formula is the same; what the number measures is not text-image agreement but predicted human preference.

sections.heading: 10. When a reference does exist: MSE, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS
sections.text:
There are cases where a correct image really does exist, and there the comparison against a reference is legitimate. Three of them come up constantly: the reconstruction of an autoencoder, where the input itself is the target; image editing, where the source image has to be preserved outside the edited region; and distillation, where the teacher's output is the target for the student.

The chain of metrics here is a chain of dissatisfactions.

MSE is the pixel-wise squared distance. It is not interpretable — a value of 0.003 means nothing on its own — and it is sensitive to position: shift the image by one pixel and the number explodes while the eye sees nothing.

PSNR normalises the same quantity and puts it on a decibel scale:

$$\text{PSNR} = 10 \log_{10} \frac{\text{MAX}^2}{\text{MSE}}$$

It is now interpretable, since numbers of around 30 to 40 dB have a known meaning, but the sensitivity to position is unchanged, because it is still MSE inside.

sections.heading: 11. SSIM: comparing statistics rather than pixels
sections.text:
SSIM takes a different route. Rather than comparing pixels one by one, it compares the statistics of corresponding patches, and it splits that comparison into three questions.

Luminance: is the brightness the same? This is a comparison of the means.

Contrast: is the spread the same? This is a comparison of the variances.

Structure: do the pixels move together? This is the correlation, that is the covariance normalised by the two standard deviations.

The three similarities are multiplied and, with the stabilising constants that keep the ratios from blowing up when a denominator is near zero, the familiar form appears:

$$\text{SSIM}(x,y) = \frac{(2\mu_x \mu_y + C_1)(2\sigma_{xy} + C_2)}{(\mu_x^2 + \mu_y^2 + C_1)(\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + C_2)}$$

It is computed on a sliding window and averaged over the image. The value is between minus one and one, and one means identical.

SSIM is much closer to perception than PSNR, but the same weakness survives: it is still vulnerable to a spatial shift. Displace the whole image slightly and the patch statistics no longer line up.

sections.heading: 12. LPIPS: comparing in the feature space of a trained network
sections.text:
The last step gives up on hand-designed statistics. LPIPS passes both images through a pre-trained network, normalises the activations of several layers, takes a weighted squared distance between them and sums over the layers. The weights are themselves fitted on human judgements of which of two distortions looks worse.

Since the comparison is now made over features rather than pixels, a small shift, a slight change of texture or a minor colour drift are tolerated, while a structural difference that the eye notices is punished. This is why LPIPS is used as the polishing loss in distillation while MSE serves only as the warm-up.

Its cost is interpretability. An LPIPS of 0.18 has no intrinsic meaning; the number is only usable as a comparison between two systems measured the same way. And it depends on the backbone network it was built on.

sections.heading: 13. The gap that the fixed metrics leave
sections.text:
Look at the list that has accumulated: FID, CLIPScore, PickScore, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS. There are many of them, they operate at different levels — some on distributions, some on single images, some on text-image agreement — and none of them can say why.

A CLIPScore of 0.922 does not tell you which part of the prompt was missed. The meaning is fragmented across several numbers, and a mismatch between what the metric rewards and what a person would prefer is inevitable.

The idea that fills this gap is to use a model that can speak. Language models can explain their judgement; the question is how to make them look at images. That is the multimodal LLM, and the rest of this walkthrough is about turning it into an evaluator.

sections.heading: 14. How a multimodal LLM is built: two ideas
sections.text:
The task is to get an image and a text into the same model. Two architectures answered it and both are still worth knowing.

The first idea keeps the original encoder-decoder transformer and feeds the image in as the keys and values of cross-attention. The text passes through the decoder as usual, and at every layer it attends to the image features. Flamingo (2022) is the reference point, and the image path is separate from the text path throughout.

The second idea is simpler and is what won. Treat the image as ordinary input to a decoder-only language model: pass it through a vision encoder, project the resulting patch features into the token embedding space, and place them in the sequence in front of the text tokens. From the model's point of view nothing unusual is happening, it is reading a sequence. LLaVA (2023) is the reference point.

The current trend is a decoder with joint attention, in which text and image tokens attend to each other in the same stack. This is structurally the same move as MM-DiT on the generation side: rather than one modality conditioning the other, both are carried as citizens of the same sequence.

What these models can do now goes beyond captioning: working across resolutions, spatial awareness, OCR, other modalities, and explicit reasoning before answering. Those capabilities are precisely what makes them usable as judges.

sections.heading: 15. TIFA: breaking the score into atomic questions
sections.text:
The first use is the most direct one. If the complaint is that a single number cannot be debugged, then produce several small, checkable numbers instead.

TIFA takes the prompt and generates a set of yes-or-no questions from it with a language model. For a cute teddy bear is reading a book: is there a teddy bear, is the teddy bear cute, is there a book, is the teddy bear reading the book. A visual question answering model then answers each question by looking at the generated image, and the score is the proportion of yes answers.

The gain is diagnosis. A score of 75 does not merely say it is not good enough; it names the question that failed, and that is the part of the prompt the model ignored.

The drawbacks are two. All questions weigh the same, so a question about the main subject counts exactly as much as one about a background detail — conveying per-claim importance is not easy. And the generation of the questions is itself error-prone; a badly formed question produces a wrong score in a way that is hard to notice.

sections.heading: 16. VQAScore: the failure of CLIPScore on composition
sections.text:
There is a second, sharper complaint. Take two prompts: a cute teddy bear is reading a book, and a cute book is reading a teddy bear. The words are the same, the meaning is reversed. CLIPScore gives an image roughly the same score for both, because the embedding is largely a bag of concepts and does not carry who is doing what to whom.

VQAScore uses a multimodal LLM as a judge instead. It asks a single question — does this figure show the prompt, answer yes or no — and takes the score not as the answer but as the probability the model assigns to the token yes:

$$\text{VQAScore} = P(\text{yes} \mid \text{image},\ \text{"Does this figure show [prompt]?"})$$

Because the judge is a language model, the grammatical structure of the sentence is genuinely processed, and the two prompts above now separate.

Its limitations. It assumes access to the token probabilities, which is not available behind every API. Running TIFA and VQAScore together means several calls to a multimodal model per image, which is not cheap. And the general feeling is that both are still engineered: a fixed question format is being imposed on the judge.

sections.heading: 17. VIEScore and MLLM-as-a-Judge: give a rubric, ask for evidence
sections.text:
The final step drops the fixed question format. Instead of engineering the outcome, let the judge infer it: hand the model the generated image, the prompt and a rubric, and ask for a graded judgement with its reasoning.

VIEScore works in exactly this shape. The rubric names the axes, typically two: semantic consistency, meaning how well the image matches the conditions, and perceptual quality, meaning how authentic and natural it looks. The judge is asked to return structured output — a rationale field and a score field, in JSON.

The order matters: the evidence is asked for before the score. A judge that first describes what it sees and then grades produces a more consistent number than one that grades first and justifies afterwards.

The workflow around it has three stages. Seed: collect human ratings on the task at hand. Calibrate: tune the judge's prompt and rubric until its scores agree with those human ratings. Automate: only then let the judge run on the general case. The human ratings do not disappear, they become the calibration set.

sections.heading: 18. The three ways of using a judge
rows: grade the quality of this one output
which of these two is better
comparing models, feeds a win rate or Elo
sensitive to the ordering, rarely used in practice

sections.heading: 19. Best practices for a judge
sections.text:
Five rules, and each one repairs a known failure.

Parse the score into atomic criteria rather than asking for one global number, for the same reason TIFA exists: a single number cannot be debugged.

Ask the judge to describe the evidence before it gives a score, so that the judgement is grounded in what is visible rather than in a first impression.

Use a low temperature and structured output, so that the same input does not produce a different number on a second run and the parsing does not break.

Randomise the A and B order in pairwise judging, because judges have a position bias and systematically favour one slot.

And validate the judge's scores against human ratings before trusting it. The judge is a model too, and an uncalibrated judge simply replaces one unknown bias with another.

sections.heading: 20. Benchmarks: which one tests what
rows: objects, counts, colours, position, colour attribution
object detection, geometry, colour classification; yes/no per task
following a long, dense prompt without dropping detail
a graph of entity/attribute/relation questions, answered by a VQA judge
rendering readable multi-line text inside the image
OCR extraction and match against the requested text
editing an image without destroying the rest of it

sections.heading: 21. Why these four and not one
sections.text:
The four benchmarks are not alternatives, they measure different failures.

GenEval is compositional: it catches the model that draws a beautiful cat when two cats were asked for, or that puts the red on the wrong object. Its value is fine-grained diagnosis, because the failure is attributable to a specific task type.

DPG-Bench is about semantic completeness. As the prompt lengthens, models drop details, and the question graph checks each entity, attribute and relation separately.

LongText-Bench isolates text rendering, which for a long time was the visible weak spot of generation models and which OCR can score objectively.

GEdit-Bench measures editing, where the criterion is double: the requested change has to happen, and everything else has to survive. There is no fixed metric for that pair, which is why the judge is a multimodal model.

sections.heading: 22. The last warning: sample images are not evidence
sections.text:
Every model release comes with a page of striking images. Those images are chosen, and they are chosen from among many generations by the people who want the model to look good.

A sample is a demonstration of capability, not a measurement of it. What a measurement requires is a fixed prompt set, a fixed number of samples, a declared metric and the same procedure applied to the compared model. Otherwise you are looking at the best case of one model against the average case of another.

The same warning applies in the other direction, to your own work: when you report your results, report the prompt set, the sample count and the settings, or the number cannot be compared with anything.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text:
Evaluation splits into two measurable axes, aesthetics and prompt adherence, and they must not be mixed into one number.

Human judgement is the ground truth but it does not scale. The move from an absolute scale to a binary one to pairwise comparison makes the task progressively easier for the rater; the win rate then depends on the opponent, and Elo fixes that by weighting each result with the opponent's strength.

A reference image cannot be used, because there are many valid images for one prompt. FID therefore compares distributions: the real and the generated sets are pushed through an encoder, each is taken to be a Gaussian, and the distance has two terms — the mean difference, which is quality and style, and the covariance difference, which is diversity. Its caveats are the sample size, the reference set and the normality assumption.

Prompt adherence is measured reference-free with CLIPScore, and with PickScore when human preference is wanted instead. Where a reference genuinely exists the chain runs MSE, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and each step exists because the previous one was too attached to exact pixel positions.

The fixed metrics cannot say why, which is where multimodal LLMs come in: TIFA breaks the prompt into atomic yes-or-no questions, VQAScore reads the probability of the token yes and thereby catches compositional reversals that CLIPScore misses, and VIEScore hands the judge a rubric and asks for evidence before a score. The judge itself must be calibrated against human ratings before it is trusted.

Benchmarks separate the failure modes: GenEval for composition, DPG-Bench for dense prompts, LongText-Bench for text rendering, GEdit-Bench for editing. And a page of sample images is a demonstration, not a measurement.

frontier.title: The Frontier — Recap, Current Models, Video, Editing and Diffusion for Text
frontier.context: CME 296 Lecture 8, the closing lecture, following the slides
frontier.summary: The whole course rewound lecture by lecture with its formulas and assembled into six labels; the May 2026 leaderboard and what its Elo gaps mean; FLUX.2, Qwen-Image and HiDream-O1 read off the labels and the return to pixel space; video with a worked token count, FVD and the Wan architecture; editing through a VLM and editing software; what images borrowed from text; diffusion language models with [MASK] as noise, commit and revise; use cases, prices, open challenges and how to stay current.

sections.heading: 1. The picture the whole course fills in
sections.text: The last lecture starts by rewinding the quarter, and it does so around one picture. A prompt, "A teddy bear reading a book", goes into a box called the generation model, and an image comes out. Each lecture of the course answered one question about that box, and the slides add the answers to the picture one label at a time: the generation paradigm (lectures 1 to 3), the condition and the image representation (lecture 4), the model architecture (lecture 5), model training (lecture 6) and evaluation (lecture 7). Sections 2 to 8 follow that rewind, with the formula each lecture ended on, and section 9 assembles the six labels into one table.

sections.heading: 2. Lecture 1 — Diffusion: add noise, learn to remove it
sections.text:
Two processes. The forward process $q(x_t \mid x_{t-1})$ adds a little Gaussian noise at each step, from the image $x_{\text{image}} = x_0$ to almost pure noise $\epsilon \approx x_T$. The reverse process $p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)$ is learned and walks back, from $\epsilon = x_T$ to an image.

The strategy for training it had four steps: derive a lower bound on the log-likelihood (the ELBO), expand its terms (KL divergences appear), show that every term is tractable (Bayes' rule and Gaussian properties), and deduce the final loss, an incredibly simple noise prediction:

$$\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon} \Bigl[ \bigl\| \epsilon_\theta\bigl( \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon,\ t \bigr) - \epsilon \bigr\|^2 \Bigr]$$

Read with the slide's labels: $\epsilon_\theta$ is the noise predictor, $\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\, \epsilon$ is the noised image, $t$ is the noise level, and the last $\epsilon$ is the actual noise.

sections.heading: 3. Lecture 2 — Score matching: arrows towards the data
sections.text:
The second view asks for the direction $\nabla_x \log p_{\text{data}}(x)$ that leads from a random point to the data, the score. It is learned by denoising score matching:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, x_t} \Bigl[ \lambda_t \bigl\| s_\theta(x_t, t) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t \mid x_0) \bigr\|^2 \Bigr]$$

and it meets lecture 1 through one identity, the score from noisy to clean equals the noise to remove from the noisy sample, rescaled:

$$\nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t \mid x_0) = -\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}$$

In continuous time the forward process is an SDE, $dx = f(x,t)\, dt + g(t)\, dW$, a deterministic drift plus a random diffusion; the slide draws one step from $x$ to $x + dx$ as a straight push $f(x,t)\, dt$ followed by a random kick $g(t)\, dW$. Its reverse adds the score as a correction to the drift:

$$dx = \bigl[ f(x,t) - g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x) \bigr] dt + g(t)\, d\bar{W}$$

sections.heading: 4. Lecture 3 — Flow matching: learn the velocity directly
sections.text:
The third view moves a simple initial distribution to the target one along a velocity field. For a single sample, the motion is an ordinary differential equation,

$$\frac{dx}{dt} = u_t(x)$$

so in a short time $x$ moves to $x + u_t(x)\, dt$. For the whole distribution $p_t$, the continuity equation says that density only changes because mass flows:

$$\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t}(x) = -\nabla \cdot \bigl( p_t\, u_t \bigr)(x)$$

Training estimates $u_t(x)$ with a network $u_t^\theta(x)$. Inference maps $x_0 \sim p_0$ to $x_1 \sim p_1$ by integrating it:

$$\hat{x}_1 = x_0 + \int_0^1 u_t^\theta(x)\, dt$$

The loss that makes this trainable is conditional flow matching, with the straight-line target velocity $x_1 - x_0$:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_1, x} \Bigl[ \bigl\| u_t^\theta(x) - u_t(x \mid x_1) \bigr\|^2 \Bigr], \qquad u_t(x \mid x_1) = x_1 - x_0$$

A notation trap: in lectures 1 and 2, $x_0$ is the clean image and large $t$ is noise. In lecture 3, $x_0 \sim p_0$ is the noise and $x_1 \sim p_1$ is the data, so time runs the other way. The pictures are the same; only the labels flip.

sections.heading: 5. Lecture 4 — Latent space and guidance
sections.text:
Two labels are added to the picture here: the image representation and the condition.

Image representation. Running diffusion on every pixel of an $H \times W \times C$ image is expensive. An autoencoder compresses it: the encoder maps pixel space to a small latent $h \times w \times c$ at the bottleneck, and the decoder maps it back. Diffusion then runs in the latent space. A plain autoencoder scatters the training images as isolated points in that space, with empty gaps between them; the variational autoencoder fixes this by regularizing the latent space so that it is filled continuously, with the loss

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}} = \underbrace{-\mathbb{E}_z \bigl[ \log p_\theta(x \mid z) \bigr]}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}} + \underbrace{\text{KL}\bigl( q_\varphi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z) \bigr)}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}}$$

the first term for reconstruction, the second for regularization of the latent space.

Condition. The prompt enters as embeddings from a text encoder (CLIP and its successors), and guidance strengthens its effect at sampling time.

sections.heading: 6. Lecture 5 — Image generation architectures
sections.text:
The fifth label is the model architecture. Whatever the paradigm, the network has the same interface: it takes the noisy latent $x_t$, the condition $c$ (the prompt) and the noise level $t$, and outputs a prediction of the same shape, here a velocity $u_\theta(x_t, t, c)$.

Two families fill that box. The U-Net and its variants, a convolutional encoder-decoder with skip connections, and the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) and its variants, which patchify the latent into tokens and process them with transformer blocks whose normalization is modulated by the timestep and the condition.

The slide's timeline shows the shift: the original U-Net (2015), a U-Net in pixel space for DDPM (2020), a U-Net in latent space for latent diffusion (2021), the Diffusion Transformer (2022 to 2023), a big U-Net in Stable Diffusion XL (2023), then transformer-based models from 2024 on, Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX.1, Qwen-Image (2025) and Z-Image (2026). Since 2024 the frontier has been almost entirely DiT and its variants.

sections.heading: 7. Lecture 6 — Model training, in four stages
rows: curated data, preference optimization, reinforcement learning
how to generate images for a special case
fewer sampling steps from a student model

sections.heading: 8. Lecture 7 — Evaluation
sections.text:
The last label is evaluation, and lecture 7 offered three kinds.

Human preference, aggregated with Elo ratings as on the Artificial Analysis leaderboard. After each comparison, model $A$'s rating is updated by

$$R_A \leftarrow R_A + K \times \Delta$$

where $\Delta$ is the surprise of the result, the actual outcome (1 for a win, 0 for a loss) minus the expected outcome, and $K$ sets how fast ratings move. Section 11 turns rating gaps into win probabilities.

A distribution distance, FID. Real and generated images are both passed through a pre-trained encoder, each set of features is summarised by a mean and a covariance, $(\mu_r, \Sigma_r)$ for real and $(\mu_g, \Sigma_g)$ for generated, and the distance between the two Gaussians is computed. Section 15 writes it out for video.

A model as judge. A multimodal LLM is shown the image and asked a question ("How cute is this teddy bear?"), and answers ("Very cute!"). In practice the three are combined in a loop: image generation is scored by an MLLM-as-a-judge, which is calibrated against human ratings.

sections.heading: Why the labels matter more than the model names
sections.text: Any current text-to-image system can be read off these six labels, and this is the most durable thing to carry out of the course: model names change every few months, the labels do not. The next sections do exactly this reading for the models leading in May 2026.

sections.heading: 11. How far behind is "not too far"?
sections.text:
The best-performing models come from the top AI labs and are closed-source; the open-weights models, the slides say, are not too far behind. Elo makes that statement measurable, because a rating gap translates into a win probability. If model $A$ is rated $d$ points above model $B$, the expected share of comparisons $A$ wins is

$$P(A \text{ wins}) = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{-d/400}}$$

So a gap of 0 means 50%, and every 400 points multiplies the odds by ten. The best closed model (1,339) against the best open one (1,187) is a gap of 152, which gives about 70%: in seven comparisons out of ten, people prefer the closed model's image. GPT Image 2 against its own predecessor GPT Image 1.5 is a gap of 73, about 60%. And the four open models from Qwen to FLUX.2 Turbo are tied at 1,159, statistically indistinguishable given the confidence interval of about 9 points. "Not too far behind" means: clearly worse on average, but losing three times out of ten to the best model in the world, at a small fraction of the price (USD 5 to USD 20 per thousand images against USD 211).

sections.heading: Elo gap to win probability
sections.caption: The logistic curve behind Elo. A gap of 152 points (GPT Image 2 against the best open model) means the higher-rated model is preferred about 70% of the time; 73 points (GPT Image 2 against GPT Image 1.5) about 60%.

sections.heading: 12. Reading the open models off the six labels
What the table shows
sections.text:
Two of the leading open models make the usual choices: a flow matching family loss, a VAE latent, an MM-DiT, and text embeddings from a large language model (FLUX.2 uses Mistral 3) or from a vision-language model (Qwen uses its own Qwen2.5-VL). Note that neither uses CLIP as its main text encoder any more; the condition now comes from much larger models that understand long, compositional prompts.

The one that stands out is the newest. HiDream-O1, released in May 2026 and already first among open models, keeps the flow matching loss and the transformer, but removes two components everyone else treats as fixed: the VAE, so the generation runs directly in pixel space, and the separate pre-trained text encoder, so text and image are processed by one unified transformer. The slide asks it as a question, back to pixel-space diffusion?, and the honest answer is: a trend to watch. Latent diffusion was what made generation affordable in 2021, and the VAE has been in every pipeline since. Two things changed: compute is cheaper, and the VAE has become a visible bottleneck, since detail it loses in encoding can never be recovered by the decoder. A component that everyone treats as fixed is exactly where a contribution may still be available.

sections.heading: 13. From image to video: one extra dimension
sections.text:
A video is a stack of images, frames, along a new axis: time. Everything else in the course carries over, but that one axis brings three new problems, and the slides go through them in order.

Temporal consistency from one frame to another. Two consecutive frames $t$ and $t+1$ must show the same scene. The slide's good pair is the same teddy bear slightly moved; the bad pair has the bear suddenly wearing a hat and sunglasses. Each frame on its own can be perfect while the sequence is unusable, so a loss that looks at frames one by one cannot see the problem.

Computation. The amount of data is height times width times time, and time can be large: a few seconds at 16 or 24 frames per second is already a hundred frames.

Metrics. Image metrics such as FID score frames independently and are blind to flicker and drift, so video needs its own (section 15).

sections.heading: 14. How large is "large"? A worked count
rows: Raw video: 5 s at 16 fps, 480 x 832
After the spatio-temporal VAE (time / 4, space / 8, 16 channels)
Tokens for the DiT (patches of 1 x 2 x 2)
One image of the same size, for comparison

sections.heading: Reading the count
sections.text: Even after compressing 8 times along each spatial axis and 4 times along time, the video gives 32,760 tokens against 1,560 for a single frame, 21 times as many. Attention compares every token with every other one, so its cost grows with the square of that factor: about 441 times the work of one image, in every layer, at every sampling step. That is why compression along time is not optional for video, and why the first thing the leading model does is a spatio-temporal VAE.

sections.heading: 15. Measuring video: Fréchet Video Distance
sections.text:
FVD is FID's construction carried over to video:

$$\text{FVD} = \| \mu_r - \mu_g \|^2 + \text{Tr}\Bigl( \Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2 \bigl( \Sigma_r \Sigma_g \bigr)^{1/2} \Bigr)$$

Read it term by term. $\mu_r$ and $\mu_g$ are the mean feature vectors of real and generated videos; the first term asks whether the two sets are centred in the same place, on average the same kind of content. $\Sigma_r$ and $\Sigma_g$ are their covariances, how the features vary from video to video; the trace term asks whether the spread matches, which is where a lack of diversity shows up. The term is zero when the two covariances are equal.

The essential difference from FID is the encoder: the features come from a network trained on video, so they encode motion as well as appearance. A sequence of individually perfect frames that flickers ends up far from real videos in that feature space, which a per-frame metric would never notice.

sections.heading: 16. The leading model: Wan
sections.text:
The architecture of Wan (2025), the leading open video model, is the course's image recipe with time added.

The spatio-temporal VAE comes first. Its encoder takes an input video of shape $[1+T, H, W, 3]$ and, through blocks that downsample space only and blocks that downsample space and time together, produces a latent of shape $[1 + T/4, H/8, W/8, C]$. The first frame is kept separately (the leading 1 in $[1+T, H, W, 3]$), so that a single image is also a valid one-frame video. The decoder mirrors it to produce the output video.

The diffusion process runs in that latent with a stack of $N$ DiT blocks. The noisy latent comes in, the timestep $t$ enters every block, and the text prompt ("A panda is holding up a cardboard that says Wan2.1") is encoded by umT5, a multilingual T5, and enters through cross-attention. The Wan decoder turns the final latent back into frames. Read off the six labels: flow matching, a spatio-temporal VAE latent, a T5 text encoder, a DiT with cross-attention.

sections.heading: 17. A limitation that scaling does not fix
sections.text: Give a text-and-image-to-image model a photograph of a teddy bear reading a book and the instruction "Make this image black and white". It returns a black and white image, but a new one: look closely and the bear's paw is in a different position, the book has changed, details have moved. The model did what it always does, generate, when the task required it to preserve. For such a request the result is simply wrong, however good it looks.

sections.heading: 18. Reformulate the problem to put guardrails
sections.text:
The idea is to avoid from-scratch generation, which is prone to such mistakes, by putting guardrails around it. A vision-language model (VLM) reads the image and the instruction, but instead of producing pixels it produces editing actions, chosen from a fixed set, here the set of colouring actions. Those actions are executed by ordinary editing software, which applies them to the original image, and the VLM can inspect the result and issue further actions.

The guardrail is structural: pixels that the instruction does not concern cannot change, because nothing regenerates them. The model contributes its understanding of the request; the software guarantees fidelity. It is the same pattern as tool use for language models, and the suggested readings (SmartEdit, MonetGPT, JarvisArt, RetouchIQ) build exactly such agents for photo retouching.

rows: the backbone: patches as tokens, with the timestep and label injected through adaptive layer norm
learning from preference pairs without a separate reward model
group-relative online reinforcement learning, applied to flow matching models

sections.heading: 20. Traditional generation for text, and its bottleneck
sections.text:
Text generation models rely on next-token prediction. An autoregressive model (ARM) LLM reads [BOS] and writes "A", reads "A" and writes "teddy", then "bear", "is", "reading", [EOS], one token per forward pass, each conditioned on everything before it.

The problem is structural: inference-time generation needs $\mathcal{O}(\#\text{output tokens})$ iterations. A thousand-token answer means a thousand sequential passes, and no amount of hardware parallelism removes that dependency.

sections.heading: 21. What about diffusion for text?
sections.text: The idea is to adapt the diffusion paradigm to text. A diffusion-based LLM starts from text with random noise and refines the whole sequence at once, producing text with less noise, then less, until the final sentence. The number of iterations moves from $\mathcal{O}(\#\text{output tokens})$ to $\mathcal{O}(\#\text{diffusion steps})$, and the number of steps is a choice, independent of the length of the answer. The slide draws it side by side with the image case: the same stack of denoising passes, with a sentence in place of the teddy bear.

sections.heading: 22. Finding the equivalent of noise for text
sections.text:
Carrying diffusion over requires one answer: what is noisy text?

A noisy image is continuous, and its noise is Gaussian: a pixel can be slightly brighter, and an image halfway between a photograph and static is a meaningful object.

Text is discrete: there is no token halfway between "bear" and "dog". And replacing tokens with random tokens does not produce meaningless noise, because random tokens have a semantic meaning. "A teddy cat is reading" is not noise; it is a different, misleading sentence.

The answer is a special token, [MASK]. Noise becomes erasure. A token is either known or masked, and the noise level is the fraction of masked tokens, from 0 (the clean text) to 100% (all masks, the equivalent of pure Gaussian noise).

sections.heading: 23. Training: learn to fill the blanks
sections.text:
The training loop mirrors the image one. Step 1: sample a noise level $t \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$ and use it as the mask ratio, corrupting the text with noise level $t$, so "A teddy bear is reading [EOS]" might become "A [MASK] bear is [MASK] [EOS]". Step 2: the diffusion-based LLM predicts the tokens that were masked, here "teddy" and "reading", and the loss is the cross-entropy at the masked positions.

This looks like BERT's masked language modelling, and the difference is what makes it a generator. BERT masks a small fixed fraction, about 15%, and learns to fill small gaps. Here $t$ ranges over the whole interval up to 100%, so the model must also learn to write a sentence from nothing.

sections.heading: 24. Inference: coarse to fine
sections.text:
Initialize with a fully masked input, $t = 100\%$ noise. Then iterate. The model predicts every masked token at once. It commits the tokens it is confident about, in the slides "A", "is" and [EOS], shown in blue. And it performs remasking on the rest: its tentative guesses "brown", "bear" and "sleeping", shown in pink, are revised, turned back into [MASK]. The sequence is now at $t = 50\%$ noise: "A [MASK] [MASK] is [MASK] [EOS]". The next pass, seeing the committed context, fills the rest, and the output at $t = 0\%$ is "A teddy bear is reading [EOS]".

The revise step is what an autoregressive model cannot do. Once an ARM has written a token it is final, and every later token is conditioned on it, mistakes included. Here a tentative token is reconsidered in the light of everything decided elsewhere in the sequence, in both directions.

sections.heading: 25. Advantages, challenges, and why everyone is talking about it
sections.text:
Advantages. About 10x speed compared to an ARM of similar quality, because sequential cost no longer grows with length. And a natural fit for coding: code editing is a fill in the middle task, inserting into a file with context on both sides, and speed is the bottleneck for coding agents that call the model hundreds of times.

Challenges and current work. Training is significantly more expensive, since the model learns every mask ratio rather than one next-token task. The techniques developed for ARMs over the past years, post-training approaches in particular, have to be adapted. And current work combines the benefits of autoregression and diffusion, for example block diffusion: autoregressive across blocks of text, diffusion within each block.

It is currently a very hot topic. Google presented a diffusion approach to LLM deployment in 2025; Inception raised USD 50 million to build diffusion models for code and text and launched Mercury 2, described as the fastest reasoning LLM, about 5x faster than leading speed-optimized models; and the number of papers on diffusion language models grows steeply each year, discrete diffusion models dominating. The suggested readings run from D3PM (Austin et al., 2021) through LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) and its 100-billion-parameter successor LLaDA2.0, to Block Diffusion, Seed Diffusion and dLLM (2026).

rows: image generation through APIs at cents per image (section 27)

robotics: custom environments · medicine: accelerated MRIs · visual design: faster cycles

sections.heading: 27. What "democratization" costs today
rows: USD 120 per million output tokens; a 1K or 2K image is 1,120 tokens
USD 0.07 for the first megapixel, USD 0.03 for each further one

sections.heading: Reading the prices
sections.text: A single high-quality image from the best model in the world costs about 21 cents, and a low-quality one less than one cent. That is what "tomorrow: democratization" means concretely: the capability already exists and is becoming a commodity priced per image, the way compute is priced per hour. The interesting work moves to what is built on top of it.

sections.heading: 28. Ongoing challenges
sections.text:
The areas of improvement that are top of mind.

Costs. Training and inference are both expensive, and part of the search has moved down into hardware: analog in-memory computing for the attention mechanism (Leroux et al., 2025) computes the dot products inside memory cells instead of moving data to a processor, for speed and energy efficiency.

Data quality. Generated images are now everywhere on the web, so the next models are increasingly trained on the outputs of the previous ones. The slide's figure follows such a self-consuming loop through generations 2, 5, 10 and 20: the share of synthesized data grows, the real data recedes, and the distribution of what the model produces drifts away from it. This is model collapse (Alemohammad et al., Self-Consuming Generative Models Go MAD, 2023): without enough fresh real data at each generation, quality or diversity degrades.

Trust. Can a viewer tell that an image is generated? The C2PA standard writes content credentials into the file's metadata, and platforms display them, "Made with AI" on Twitter, "AI info" on Instagram and Facebook. But the flaw is trivial: metadata is stripped by re-saving or simply screenshotting. Watermarking puts the signal into the pixels instead, and a good watermark (SynthID-Image, Gowal et al., 2025) survives the usual manipulations, impulse noise, rotation, changes of saturation, so that it is still detected after them.

Safety. Deepfakes are the immediate practical harm, and deepfake laws are not moving at the speed of AI.

sections.heading: 29. How to stay up to date with vision advances
sections.text:
Papers: arXiv under Computer Science, Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, for the daily flow; the general ML venues (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR) and the vision venues (CVPR, ECCV) for the filtered view.

Code: the authors' GitHub repositories linked in their papers, and paperswithcode.com to browse state-of-the-art datasets and methods for each task.

Miscellaneous: Stanford course websites such as CS231n; academics and industry leaders on Twitter; YouTube channels, theoretical (Two Minute Papers, Yannic Kilcher) and practical (Google Developers, HuggingFace); and the technical papers and blogs of companies and labs (Amazon Science, Apple ML, Google AI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft Research, OpenAI). And for after the class, the course's VIP cheatsheet on GitHub.

One addition the slides do not make. A general-ML venue such as NeurIPS or ICLR is where a method is first published; a domain venue, a conference or journal for one field of application, such as MICCAI or IEEE TMI in medical imaging, is where that method is later applied. Reading only the domain venues therefore means meeting ideas that are already two or three years old.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: The course built one picture: a generation model with six labels, the generation paradigm (noise, score or velocity), the image representation (pixels or a VAE latent), the condition, the architecture (U-Net or DiT), training (pre-, post-, tuning, distillation) and evaluation (Elo, FID, MLLM judges). Every current model reads off it. In May 2026 the closed leaders are about 150 Elo points ahead of the best open model, a 70% preference rate, while the open models make the usual choices (flow matching, VAE latent, MM-DiT, LLM or VLM text embeddings) and the newest one drops the VAE and the separate text encoder. Video adds time, which brings temporal consistency, a token count tens of times larger and an attention cost hundreds of times larger, a spatio-temporal VAE, and FVD. Where preservation matters, a VLM emitting editing actions into software beats regeneration. Diffusion now travels back to text: [MASK] plays the role of noise, training fills blanks at every ratio, inference commits and revises, with roughly 10x speed and a natural fit for coding, at the price of costlier training. The open problems are cost, model collapse, trust (strippable metadata against watermarks) and safety.

lst01.title: LST 01 — Mathematical Description of Systems
lst01.context: EEE 501 Lecture Notes 1 · Chen, Chapters 1-2 · models: causality, dimensionality, linearity
lst01.summary: What a model is and what the course does with it; the suspension example from a free-body balance to a transfer function and its responses; a system as an operator y = Hu; memoryless and causal systems; the state as the summary of the past, with the RLC circuit; lumped against distributed systems, with the unit delay; and the definition of linearity, initial states included.

sections.heading: 1. What the course is about
sections.text:
The course is an introduction to model-based analysis and design of a class of physical processes. The notes draw it as a chain of three boxes: a physical system, a model of it, and a mathematical representation of the model.

Two examples run through the slide. A piece of metal pipeline connected to a battery is modelled as a resistor excited by a voltage source, and the mathematical representation is $V = RI$. An automobile suspension is modelled as a spring-mass-damper, and the representation is a second order differential equation.

The model is a deliberate simplification: the pipeline also heats up, the tyre also deforms. What is kept is what matters for the question being asked. Everything in this course happens at the last box, on the mathematical representation.

sections.heading: Course information, textbook and scope
sections.text:
Instructor: A. Bülent Özgüler (ozguler@ee.bilkent.edu.tr, office EE-407). Assistant: Sinan Topçakar (sinan.topcakar@ee.bilkent.edu.tr). Grading: homeworks 15%, midterm 40%, final 45%. Lecture notes are placed on MOODLE before or following the weekly lectures.

The textbook is C.-T. Chen, Linear System Theory and Design, 3rd edition (Oxford University Press, 1999, or later editions), and its content is the main responsibility; the lecture notes follow it. The course focuses on continuous-time systems throughout the semester; the notes remark that the discrete-time versions are much simpler.

The topics, in order: mathematical description of systems; linear algebra (review); state-space representations; realization from transfer matrices; input-output stability; stability of state-space representations; controllability and observability of LTI systems, then of time-varying systems; state feedback, pole placement and stabilization; the Luenberger observer; and the separation principle, observer and feedback combined. Lecture Notes 1 and 2 cover the first topic, 3 and 4 the linear algebra review.

sections.heading: 2. Example: the suspension system
sections.text:
Focus on one tyre. The car body (mass $m$) sits on a spring ($k$) and a damper ($b$) whose lower ends ride on the road. $x_i(t)$ is the vertical position of the road under the tyre, the input; $x_o(t)$ is the position of the body, the output. The notes write $D := d/dt$ for the time derivative, so $D^2 x_o$ is the acceleration.

Newton's law for the mass: mass times acceleration plus the damper and spring forces is zero. The spring force depends on the relative displacement $x_o - x_i$, the damper force on the relative velocity $D x_o - D x_i$:

$$m\, D^2 x_o + b\,(D x_o - D x_i) + k\,(x_o - x_i) = 0$$

Collect the output on the left and the input on the right:

$$m\, D^2 x_o + b\, D x_o + k\, x_o = b\, D x_i + k\, x_i$$

Take Laplace transforms with zero initial conditions, where $D$ becomes multiplication by $s$:

$$(m s^2 + b s + k)\, X_o(s) = (b s + k)\, X_i(s) \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{X_o(s)}{X_i(s)} = \frac{b s + k}{m s^2 + b s + k}$$

This is the transfer function, of second order (the degree of the denominator). Read it at two extremes: at $s = 0$ (a very slow road change) it equals $k/k = 1$, the body simply follows the road; for large $s$ (a very fast bump) it behaves like $b/(m s)$, and the body barely moves.
