sections.heading: 3. Analysis, step 2: test inputs
sections.text:
The notes apply two test inputs $x_i(t)$: a sinusoid for a smooth road surface and a square wave for a bumpy road.

For a sinusoid the response $x_o(t)$ is a sinusoid of the same frequency, with the amplitude and the phase modified depending on $m$, $b$, $k$. The reason is that a linear time-invariant system maps $e^{j\omega t}$ to $\hat g(j\omega)\, e^{j\omega t}$: the transfer function evaluated at $s = j\omega$ is one complex number, its magnitude scales the amplitude and its angle shifts the phase.

For a square wave the notes draw two possible responses, underdamped and overdamped. Which one occurs is decided by the roots of the denominator $m s^2 + b s + k$: if $b^2 - 4mk < 0$ the roots are complex and the body oscillates around each new level (underdamped); if $b^2 - 4mk > 0$ they are real and negative and the body creeps towards it (overdamped). The figure computes both cases from the transfer function above.

sections.heading: Square-wave road, two suspensions, computed
sections.caption: The road (dashed) jumps between 0 and 1 every 3 seconds. Top: a soft damper, $b^2 - 4mk < 0$, so the body overshoots and rings, the underdamped response of the notes. Bottom: a stiff damper, $b^2 - 4mk > 0$, so the body approaches each level without overshoot, the overdamped response. Both settle at the road level, because the transfer function equals 1 at $s = 0$.

sections.heading: 4. Mathematical representations of systems
sections.text:
In general a system has $p$ inputs and $q$ outputs, collected into vectors:

$$\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \\ \vdots \\ u_p \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_q \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{y} = H \mathbf{u}$$

A system with several inputs and outputs is called multi-input multi-output, or multivariable. $H$ is an operator: it maps whole input functions $\mathbf{u}(\cdot)$ to whole output functions $\mathbf{y}(\cdot)$, not numbers to numbers. The suspension is the case $p = q = 1$.

Three properties of such an operator are defined in this lecture: memory, causality, and the number of numbers needed to summarise the past (the state).

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Treating the system as an operator on whole signals is what allows the course to ask questions about the system itself rather than about one particular response: linearity, causality, time invariance and stability are all properties of $H$. The size $q \times p$ fixed here becomes the size of the transfer matrix and of $D$.

sections.heading: 5. Memoryless and causal systems
sections.text:
A system is memoryless if $\mathbf{y}(t_1)$ depends only on $\mathbf{u}(t_1)$, for any $t_1 \geq t_0$ with $t_0$ the initial time. A resistor is memoryless: the voltage now is $R$ times the current now. The suspension is not: the position of the body now depends on the whole history of the road, through the energy stored in the spring and the velocity of the mass.

A system is causal, or non-anticipatory, if $\mathbf{y}(t_1)$ does not depend on $\mathbf{u}(t)$ for any $t > t_1$, i.e. it only depends on $\mathbf{u}(t)$ for $-\infty < t \leq t_1$. The output cannot react to an input that has not arrived yet. Every physical system running in real time is causal. A non-causal operator is still meaningful when the whole signal is recorded first, as in offline processing of an image or an audio file, where "future" samples are available.

Causality with memory raises a practical problem, which the notes point out: keeping track of $\mathbf{y}(t)$ would require the input for all $-\infty < t \leq t_0$, which is inconvenient. One wants to summarise what happened before $t_0$. This brings us to states.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Memory is what makes dynamics: a memoryless system is just a function, and needs no state. Causality is what makes the state possible: because the future does not matter, the past can be summarized in a finite (or infinite) set of numbers at $t_0$. Every system realized by integrators is causal.

sections.heading: 6. The state
sections.text:
Definition: the state $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ of a system at time $t_0$ is the information at $t_0$ that, together with $\mathbf{u}(t)$ for $t \geq t_0$, determines $\mathbf{y}(t)$ uniquely for all $t \geq t_0$.

Thus $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ summarizes the effect of $\mathbf{u}_{(-\infty, t_0)}$, the input before $t_0$. Two different input histories that lead to the same state are, from $t_0$ on, indistinguishable: the future does not care how you got there. A good everyday picture is a saved game: you do not replay the past hours, the save file holds exactly what is needed to continue.

In circuits and mechanics the state is the set of quantities that store energy and cannot jump: capacitor voltages and inductor currents, positions and velocities of masses.

sections.heading: Example: the parallel RLC circuit
sections.text:
A current source $i(t)$ drives a resistor $R$, an inductor $L$ and a capacitor $C$ in parallel; the output is the voltage $v(t)$ across them. The input is $i(t)$, so $p = 1$; the output is $v(t)$, so $q = 1$. The two states are the inductor current $i_L$ and the capacitor voltage $v_C = v$.

The capacitor current is what is left of the source current after the resistor and the inductor take their share, $i_C = i - v_C/R - i_L$, and $i_C = C\, D v_C$. The inductor voltage is $v_C = L\, D i_L$. So

$$D v_C = \frac{i_C}{C} = \frac{1}{C}\Bigl(i - \frac{v_C}{R} - i_L\Bigr), \qquad D i_L = \frac{v_C}{L}$$

Two equations in two unknowns need two initial values, $v_C(t_0)$ and $i_L(t_0)$; these are exactly the state of the circuit. Collected in matrix form, the two equations already have the shape of the state equation of Lecture Notes 2:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix} v_C \\ i_L \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\frac{1}{RC} & -\frac{1}{C} \\ \frac{1}{L} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_C \\ i_L \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{C} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} i, \qquad v = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_C \\ i_L \end{bmatrix}$$

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The state is the central object of the whole course. Everything after Lecture Notes 2 is written for $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x} + B\mathbf{u}$, and $\mathbf{x}$ is this state. Three things to take from the definition. The number of states is the order of the system: it is the size $n$ of the matrix $A$ and the number of initial conditions you must give. The choice of states is not unique: any invertible change of variables $\mathbf{x} = Q\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$ gives another valid state (this is similarity, LST 03). And later questions are all questions about the state: can the input steer it anywhere (controllability), can the output reveal it (observability), does it decay by itself (internal stability).

sections.heading: 7. Lumped and distributed systems
sections.text:
A system (a mathematical representation) is lumped, or finite dimensional, if the number of its states is finite. It is distributed, or infinite dimensional, otherwise. The RLC circuit is lumped with two states; the suspension is lumped with two states (position and velocity of the body).

Example: the unit time-delay system, $y(t) = u(t - 1)$. To determine $\{y(t),\ t \geq t_0\}$ one needs $\{u(t),\ t_0 - 1 \leq t \leq t_0\}$, the whole last second of the input: infinitely many initial conditions. The number of initial conditions needed to summarize the effect of the input before $t_0$ on the output is not finite, so the system is distributed.

Distributed systems are common: transmission lines, heat conduction in a rod, a vibrating string, a network with transport delays. Their transfer functions are not rational, which Lecture Notes 2 makes precise with $e^{-sT}$.

sections.heading: What the state of a unit delay has to remember
sections.caption: For $y(t) = u(t - 1)$, the output over the next second is exactly the input over the last second (shaded). Continuing from $t_0$ therefore needs the whole curve on $[t_0 - 1, t_0]$, a function and not a finite list of numbers, which is what distributed means.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The whole state-space theory of the course (matrices $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ of finite size) applies to lumped systems only. Distributed systems are recognized by irrational transfer functions; in practice they are approximated by lumped models of growing order.

sections.heading: 8. Linearity
sections.text:
A system is linear if for all $\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \mathbf{R}$:

$$\left\{ \begin{matrix} \alpha_1 \mathbf{x}_1(t_0) + \alpha_2 \mathbf{x}_2(t_0) \\ \alpha_1 \mathbf{u}_1(t) + \alpha_2 \mathbf{u}_2(t) \end{matrix} \right. \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \alpha_1 \mathbf{y}_1(t) + \alpha_2 \mathbf{y}_2(t), \ t \geq t_0, \qquad \mathbf{y}_i(t) := H \mathbf{u}_i(t), \ i = 1, 2$$

Read it as an experiment. Run the system twice: once from initial state $\mathbf{x}_1(t_0)$ with input $\mathbf{u}_1$, giving $\mathbf{y}_1$, and once from $\mathbf{x}_2(t_0)$ with $\mathbf{u}_2$, giving $\mathbf{y}_2$. Now start from the combined state with the combined input. The system is linear if the output is the same combination of the two outputs.

Two things to notice. The scaling and the adding are applied to the initial states too: linearity is a statement about the pair (state, input). And it must hold for all $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$: superposition (adding) and homogeneity (scaling) together.

sections.heading: Why a straight-line law can fail to be linear
sections.text:
Take the memoryless system $y = 2u + 1$. Its graph is a straight line, yet it is not linear in this sense: with $u_1 = 1$ and $u_2 = 2$ the outputs are 3 and 5, but the input $u_1 + u_2 = 3$ gives 7, not $3 + 5 = 8$. The offset 1 is added once to the sum but twice to the sum of outputs. Such a system is called affine.

The same thing happens with a nonzero initial state: its effect, the zero-input response, behaves like the offset above. Lecture Notes 2 starts exactly from this point, and shows why input-linearity requires the initial conditions to be zero.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Linearity is what makes the rest of the course possible. It is the property that turns a system into an impulse response and a transfer function (LST 02), so that the response to any input is a sum of responses to simple pieces. Almost no real system is exactly linear; the course works with linear models because they can be analysed completely, and LST 02 shows how a nonlinear model is linearized around an operating point. When you meet a new system, the first question is always: is it linear, and if not, around which point can it be linearized?

sections.heading: In a problem
sections.text:
The situation. A system $\mathbf{y} = H\mathbf{u}$ is given by an equation, and you are asked to classify it.

Step 1. Memoryless and causal (section 5): look at which values of $\mathbf{u}$ the right-hand side uses to form $\mathbf{y}(t_1)$.

$$\mathbf{y}(t_1) \text{ uses only } \mathbf{u}(t_1) \Rightarrow \text{memoryless}, \qquad \mathbf{y}(t_1) \text{ uses no } \mathbf{u}(t),\ t > t_1 \Rightarrow \text{causal}$$

Step 2. Linearity (section 8): run the defining experiment with two pairs (state, input).

$$\left\{ \begin{matrix} \alpha_1 \mathbf{x}_1(t_0) + \alpha_2 \mathbf{x}_2(t_0) \\ \alpha_1 \mathbf{u}_1(t) + \alpha_2 \mathbf{u}_2(t) \end{matrix} \right. \quad \overset{?}{\Longrightarrow} \quad \alpha_1 \mathbf{y}_1(t) + \alpha_2 \mathbf{y}_2(t)$$

Step 3. Time invariance: shift the input and the initial time by $T$ and compare with the shifted output.

$$\mathbf{u}(t - T),\ \mathbf{x}(t_0 + T) = \mathbf{x}(t_0) \quad \overset{?}{\Longrightarrow} \quad \mathbf{y}(t - T)$$

Step 4. Lumped or distributed (section 7): count the numbers needed in $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$.

What it means.
- An integral, derivative or delay in the equation: memory; then a state is needed.
- A $\mathbf{u}(t + T)$ with $T > 0$: not causal.
- A constant term, a product of signals, a square: not linear (only the input-linear part survives, LST 02).
- A coefficient depending explicitly on $t$: time-varying, so no transfer function.
- A delay: infinitely many numbers in $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$, distributed; an ODE of order $n$: $n$ numbers, lumped.

sections.heading: 9. The classification on the examples of this lecture
rows: Suspension, $m D^2 x_o + b D x_o + k x_o = b D x_i + k x_i$

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: A model keeps what matters for the question, and the course works on its mathematical representation, $\mathbf{y} = H \mathbf{u}$ with $p$ inputs and $q$ outputs. For the suspension, the force balance $m D^2 x_o + b(D x_o - D x_i) + k(x_o - x_i) = 0$ gives the second order transfer function $(bs + k)/(ms^2 + bs + k)$; sinusoids come out as sinusoids of the same frequency, and the sign of $b^2 - 4mk$ decides between an underdamped and an overdamped response to a square wave. A system is memoryless if the output now depends only on the input now, causal if it never depends on the future input. The state $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ is the information that, with the future input, fixes the future output: it summarises the past, like a save file. Lumped systems have finitely many states (the RLC circuit has two), distributed ones do not (the unit delay must remember a whole second of input). Linearity requires that combining initial states and inputs combines the outputs, for all $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$; an offset or a nonzero initial state breaks it.

lst02.title: LST 02 — Impulse Response, Transfer Matrix and State Space
lst02.context: EEE 501 Lecture Notes 2 · Chen, Chapter 2 · models: causality, dimensionality, linearity, time invariance (continued)
lst02.summary: Input-linearity and why initial states must be zero; an input written as a sum of pulses, which turns linearity into the impulse-response integral; relaxed, causal and multivariable versions; time invariance and convolution; the transfer function and transfer matrix, rational or not, proper or not, poles, zeros and blocking zeros; the state-space form and its solution by Laplace; and linearization of nonlinear models.

sections.heading: 1. Input-linearity
sections.text:
A system is input-linear if all initial conditions are zero and if for all $\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \mathbf{R}$ it holds that

$$H(\alpha_1 \mathbf{u}_1(t) + \alpha_2 \mathbf{u}_2(t)) = \alpha_1 \mathbf{y}_1(t) + \alpha_2 \mathbf{y}_2(t)$$

This is the linearity of Lecture Notes 1 restricted to experiments that start at rest. It is the only property used to derive the impulse response below, which is why the results hold for lumped and distributed systems alike.

sections.heading: Why equal initial states are not enough
sections.text:
The notes' example: suppose $\mathbf{x}_1(t_0) = \mathbf{x}_2(t_0) = \mathbf{x}_3(t_0)$, and even suppose that for all $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$, $\mathbf{u}_3 = \alpha_1 \mathbf{u}_1 + \alpha_2 \mathbf{u}_2$ gives $\mathbf{y}_3 = \alpha_1 \mathbf{y}_1 + \alpha_2 \mathbf{y}_2$. This still does not give a linear system; just check the case $\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = 1$.

Here is why, with a scalar example. Take $\dot{x} = -x + u$, $y = x$, all three runs starting from $x(t_0) = x_0$. The output is the zero-input response $x_0 e^{-(t - t_0)}$ plus the response to the input. So $y_1 + y_2$ contains the zero-input response twice, while $y_3$, run once with $u_1 + u_2$, contains it once. The two agree only if $x_0 = 0$. With equal but nonzero initial states the initial condition is counted a different number of times on the two sides, exactly like the offset in $y = 2u + 1$.

The system becomes input-linear if $\mathbf{x}_i(t_0) = 0$ for $i = 1, 2, 3$ and if superposition holds for all linear combinations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The distinction between linearity and input-linearity explains a split you will see in every formula of the course: the response is the zero-input part (from the initial state) plus the zero-state part (from the input), and only the second is a linear function of the input alone.

sections.heading: 2. An input as a sum of pulses
sections.text:
Consider a single-input, single-output system that is input-linear. Cut the time axis into slots of width $\Delta$ at the points $t_i$, and approximate the input waveform by a staircase:

$$u(t) \cong \sum_{i = -\infty}^{\infty} u(t_i)\, \delta_\Delta(t - t_i)\, \Delta$$

where $\delta_\Delta(t - t_i)$ is a pulse of width $\Delta$ and height $1/\Delta$ starting at $t_i$, so of area 1. Each term $u(t_i)\, \delta_\Delta(t - t_i)\, \Delta$ is a block of height $u(t_i)$ on the slot $[t_i, t_i + \Delta)$: the factor $\Delta$ cancels the height $1/\Delta$ of the pulse. Adding all blocks gives the staircase, and as $\Delta \to 0$ the staircase becomes $u(t)$.

sections.heading: The pulse decomposition, computed
sections.caption: Left: an input $u(t)$ and its staircase approximation with $\Delta = 0.5$; one block, $u(t_i)\,\delta_\Delta(t - t_i)\,\Delta$, is highlighted. Right: the pulse $\delta_\Delta$ for three widths. It always has area 1; as $\Delta$ shrinks it becomes taller and narrower, and its limit is the unit impulse $\delta$.

sections.heading: 3. The impulse response
sections.text:
Denote the response of the system to $\delta_\Delta(t - t_i)$ by $g_\Delta(t, t_i)$. Input-linearity lets the response to the sum of blocks be the sum of the responses, each scaled by its weight $u(t_i)\Delta$:

$$y(t) \cong \sum_{i = -\infty}^{\infty} g_\Delta(t, t_i)\, u(t_i)\, \Delta$$

which as $\Delta \to 0$ gives

$$y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(t, \tau)\, u(\tau)\, d\tau \qquad (1)$$

Here $g(t, \tau)$ is the output observed at time $t$ when the unit impulse $\delta(t - \tau) := \lim_{\Delta \to 0} \delta_\Delta(t - \tau)$ is applied at time $\tau$. This one function of two times is called the impulse response.

The sum becomes an integral exactly as in a Riemann sum: $t_i$ becomes the integration variable $\tau$ and $\Delta$ becomes $d\tau$. The whole system is now one function of two variables. Know $g$, and you know the response to every input.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: For a linear system the impulse response is the whole system: once $g(t, \tau)$ is known, the response to every input follows from one integral. This is why so much effort goes into finding it. In practice you rarely compute the integral by hand; you take Laplace transforms. But the picture behind it, the output as a weighted sum of the system's memory of past inputs, is what you use to reason about delays, echoes and responses without computing anything.

sections.heading: 4. Relaxed and causal systems
sections.text:
If the system is relaxed at $t_0$, meaning that all its initial conditions are zero there, the integral can start at $t_0$:

$$y(t) = \int_{t_0}^{\infty} g(t, \tau)\, u(\tau)\, d\tau \qquad (2)$$

because nothing that happened before $t_0$ is stored in the system. If the system is also causal, the integral is cut at the top as well:

$$y(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} g(t, \tau)\, u(\tau)\, d\tau \qquad (3)$$

because an input applied after time $t$ cannot affect the output at $t$, that is, $g(t, \tau) = 0$ for $\tau > t$. Only input-linearity was used to arrive at (1), (2) and (3), so they hold for lumped and distributed systems alike.

sections.heading: 5. Several inputs and outputs
sections.text:
With $p$ inputs and $q$ outputs the argument is the same, applied to every input-output pair: output $i$ is the sum of the contributions of all inputs $j$. For a relaxed causal system,

$$\mathbf{y}(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} G(t, \tau)\, \mathbf{u}(\tau)\, d\tau, \qquad G(t, \tau) := [g_{ij}(t, \tau)] \in \mathbf{R}^{q \times p}$$

The entry $g_{ij}(t, \tau)$ is a scalar impulse response between one input and one output, while all other inputs are zero. The size $q \times p$ fixes which index is which: the row index runs over the $q$ outputs and the column index over the $p$ inputs, so $g_{ij}$ is the response at output $i$ to a unit impulse at input $j$. Each output is the sum of the contributions of all inputs, which is exactly a matrix-vector product inside the integral.

sections.heading: 6. Time invariance
sections.text:
A time-invariant system does not care when an experiment is run: the same initial conditions and the same input waveform give the same output waveform, whatever the starting time. Formally: if $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ and $\mathbf{u}_{[t_0, t]}$ give $\mathbf{y}(t) = H\mathbf{u}(t)$, then for every $T > 0$ the initial state $\mathbf{x}(t_0 + T) = \mathbf{x}(t_0)$ with the shifted input $\mathbf{u}(t - T)$ gives the shifted output $\mathbf{y}(t - T)$ for $t > t_0 + T$. Running the same experiment an hour later gives the same result, an hour later.

Consequences. The initial time can be normalized: $t_0 = 0$. The response at $t$ to an impulse at $\tau$ is a shifted copy of the response to an impulse at 0, so it depends only on the elapsed time:

$$g(t, \tau) = g(t - \tau, 0) =: g(t - \tau)$$

For a time-invariant system causality reads $g(t - \tau) = 0$ for $\tau > t$, or equivalently $g(t) = 0$ for $t < 0$: there is no response before the impulse arrives. Formula (3) then becomes a convolution integral:

$$y(t) = \int_{0}^{t} g(t - \tau)\, u(\tau)\, d\tau$$

Each past input value $u(\tau)$ is weighted by how the system responds after $t - \tau$ seconds: the impulse response is the system's memory profile.

sections.heading: Time invariance, as on the slide
sections.caption: Left pair: input $u_1$ applied at $t_0$ from state $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ gives $y_1$. Right pair: the same input applied $T$ seconds later, from the same state, gives the same output waveform, shifted by $T$.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Time invariance turns the two-variable $g(t, \tau)$ into a one-variable $g(t - \tau)$, which is what makes the Laplace transform and the transfer function possible. For time-varying systems there is no transfer function, which is why LST 05 to 07 treat them with $\Phi(t, \tau)$ instead.

sections.heading: 7. Example: determining an impulse response
sections.text:
The system of this example is a loop. The error $r - y$ passes through a gain $a \in \mathbf{R}$ and then through a unit-delay element, which produces $y$; $y$ is fed back with a minus sign (negative unity feedback). To find the impulse response, apply $r(t) = \delta(t)$.

Follow the impulse around the loop. It passes the gain and arrives at the output one second later: $a\,\delta(t - 1)$. That output is fed back with a minus sign, passes the gain and the delay again: $-a^2\,\delta(t - 2)$. Then $+a^3\,\delta(t - 3)$, and so on:

$$g_f(t) = a\,\delta(t - 1) - a^2\,\delta(t - 2) + a^3\,\delta(t - 3) - \cdots = \sum_{i = 1}^{\infty} (-1)^{i - 1} a^i\, \delta(t - i)$$

It follows by (3) that the response $y(t)$ to an arbitrary input is

$$y(t) = \int_{0}^{t} g_f(t - \tau)\, r(\tau)\, d\tau = \sum_{i = 1}^{\infty} (-1)^{i - 1} a^i\, r(t - i)$$

since each impulse $\delta(t - i - \tau)$ picks out the value of $r$ at $t - i$. The system contains a delay, so it is distributed: its impulse response is not a finite combination of exponentials but an infinite train of impulses. If $|a| < 1$ the echoes die out; if $|a| > 1$ they grow.

sections.heading: In a problem
sections.text:
The situation. A system is described (a block diagram, a loop, an equation), and its impulse response is asked.

Step 1. Relax the system and apply an impulse at $\tau$:

$$u(t) = \delta(t - \tau) \quad \Longrightarrow \quad y(t) = g(t, \tau)$$

Step 2. Follow the impulse through the system (as around the loop of the example) and write $g(t, \tau)$.

Step 3. Use it in (2):

$$y(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} g(t, \tau)\, u(\tau)\, d\tau$$

What it means.
- $g(t, \tau) = 0$ for $t < \tau$: causal, and the upper limit of the integral is $t$.
- $g(t, \tau) = g(t - \tau)$: time invariant, and $\hat{g}(s) = \mathcal{L}\{g(t)\}$ exists.
- $g$ is an infinite train of impulses or not a finite sum of exponentials: distributed, $\hat{g}(s)$ irrational.

sections.heading: 8. The transfer function
sections.text:
Let $\hat{y}(s) := \mathcal{L}\{y(t)\}$ and $\hat{u}(s) := \mathcal{L}\{u(t)\}$ be the (unilateral) Laplace transforms. For a causal, relaxed, time-invariant system:

$$\hat{y}(s) = \int_{0}^{\infty} y(t)\, e^{-st} dt = \int_{t = 0}^{\infty} \Bigl[ \int_{\tau = 0}^{\infty} g(t - \tau)\, u(\tau)\, d\tau \Bigr] e^{-st} dt$$

The upper limit $t$ of the convolution could be replaced by $\infty$ because $g(t - \tau) = 0$ for $\tau > t$. Split $e^{-st} = e^{-s(t - \tau)}\, e^{-s\tau}$ and swap the integrals:

$$= \int_{\tau = 0}^{\infty} \Bigl[ \int_{t = 0}^{\infty} g(t - \tau)\, e^{-s(t - \tau)} dt \Bigr] e^{-s\tau} u(\tau)\, d\tau$$

Substitute $\mu = t - \tau$ in the inner integral; its lower limit becomes $-\tau$, but $g(\mu) = 0$ for $\mu < 0$, so it can start at 0:

$$= \int_{\tau = 0}^{\infty} \Bigl[ \int_{\mu = 0}^{\infty} g(\mu)\, e^{-s\mu} d\mu \Bigr] e^{-s\tau} u(\tau)\, d\tau = \hat{g}(s) \int_{0}^{\infty} u(\tau)\, e^{-s\tau} d\tau = \hat{g}(s)\, \hat{u}(s)$$

$$\hat{y}(s) = \hat{g}(s)\, \hat{u}(s), \qquad \hat{g}(s) := \int_{0}^{\infty} g(\mu)\, e^{-s\mu} d\mu$$

$\hat{g}(s)$ is the transfer function of the system of impulse response $g(t)$. Convolution in time is multiplication in $s$; this is the whole reason the Laplace transform is used.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The transfer function turns calculus into algebra: convolution becomes a product, and connecting systems in series, parallel or feedback becomes multiplying and adding rational functions. Its poles tell you the behaviour before any computation: each pole $p$ contributes a mode $e^{pt}$ to the response, so poles with negative real part give decaying modes, complex pairs give oscillations, and a pole with positive real part means the response blows up. The stability lectures later in the course are built on exactly this observation.

sections.heading: 9. The transfer matrix
sections.text:
For a $p$ input, $q$ output system,

$$\hat{G}(s) := \int_{0}^{\infty} G(t)\, e^{-st} dt = [\hat{g}_{ij}(s)]_{q \times p}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{y}}(s) = \hat{G}(s)\, \hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)$$

is the transfer matrix of the system whose impulse response matrix is $G(t)$. Entry $\hat{g}_{ij}(s)$ is the transfer function from input $j$ to output $i$.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: For several inputs and outputs, one transfer function per pair is the whole input-output description; questions about poles, zeros, stability and realization are asked of this matrix. Its size $q \times p$ (outputs by inputs) is worth checking in every computation.

sections.heading: 10. Rational versus irrational
sections.text:
Whether a system is lumped (finite dimensional) or distributed (infinite dimensional) can be seen directly in its transfer function.

Example (the $T$-delay system): let $y(t) = u(t - T)$ for $T > 0$. Its impulse response is $\delta(t - T)$, so with the substitution $\tau = t - T$:

$$\hat{g}(s) = \int_{0}^{\infty} \delta(t - T)\, e^{-st} dt = \int_{-T}^{\infty} \delta(\tau)\, e^{-s\tau} e^{-sT} d\tau = e^{-sT} \int_{-T}^{\infty} \delta(\tau)\, e^{-s\tau} d\tau = e^{-sT} \cdot 1 = e^{-sT}$$

using the property of the impulse function (it picks the value of $e^{-s\tau}$ at $\tau = 0$). The result $e^{-sT}$ is an irrational function of $s$: no ratio of polynomials equals it. The transfer function of a finite dimensional system is always rational, $\hat{g}(s) = N(s)/D(s)$ with $N$, $D$ polynomials in $s$.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Rationality is the bridge to state space: a transfer function is rational exactly when a finite set of integrators can realize it (LST 05). Delays, which appear in networks and transport processes, are the typical source of irrational transfer functions.

sections.heading: Poles and zeros
sections.text:
A complex number $\lambda \in \mathbf{C}$ is a pole of $\hat{g}(s)$ if $\lim_{s \to \lambda} \hat{g}(s) \to \infty$, and a zero if $\hat{g}(\lambda) = 0$. If the pair of polynomials $(N, D)$ is coprime, i.e. has no common zero, then $\lambda$ is a pole of $\hat{g}(s)$ if and only if $D(\lambda) = 0$, and a zero if and only if $N(\lambda) = 0$.

The coprimeness condition matters. In $\frac{s - 1}{(s - 1)(s + 2)}$ the root $s = 1$ of the denominator is not a pole: the factor cancels and $\hat{g}(s) = 1/(s + 2)$ stays finite at 1. Read off poles and zeros only after cancelling common factors.

If $\hat{g}(s)$ is strictly proper, then $\lim_{s \to \infty} \hat{g}(s) = 0$ and $\hat{g}(s)$ has $\deg D - \deg N$ zeros at infinity. If it is improper, then $\lim_{s \to \infty} \hat{g}(s) = \infty$ and there are $\deg N - \deg D$ poles at infinity.

The zero-pole-gain form of a rational $\hat{g}(s)$ is

$$\hat{g}(s) = k\, \frac{(s - z_1) \cdots (s - z_m)}{(s - p_1) \cdots (s - p_n)}$$

where $z_i$ are the zeros and $p_j$ the poles, assuming no factor is shared between numerator and denominator. Being roots of the real polynomials $N$ and $D$, they may be repeated, and the non-real ones come in complex conjugate pairs.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Properness is a physical condition, not a formality. An improper transfer function grows without bound at high frequencies, like a pure differentiator $s$, which amplifies noise without limit and cannot be built; every transfer matrix coming from a state-space model is proper. Strictly proper means there is no direct path from input to output ($D = 0$). Later, the question "which proper rational $\hat{G}(s)$ can be realised by some $(A, B, C, D)$?" is the realization problem. And the warning about coprime $N/D$ matters: a cancelled pole-zero pair hides a mode from the transfer function, which is exactly how an unstable internal mode can be invisible from outside (internal versus input-output stability).

sections.heading: 12. Transfer matrix terminology
sections.text:
A transfer matrix $\hat{G}(s)$ is strictly proper if $\lim_{s \to \infty} \hat{G}(s) = 0$, and proper if $\lim_{s \to \infty} \hat{G}(s) = K \in \mathbf{R}^{q \times p}$, a constant matrix. If $p = q$ (square) and both $\hat{G}(s)$ and its inverse are proper, it is biproper, which is the case if and only if $K$ is nonsingular.

A complex number $\lambda$ is a pole of $\hat{G}(s)$ if it is a pole of at least one of its entries. Equivalently, $\lambda$ is a pole if and only if it is a root of the least common multiple of the denominators of all its entries (the notes leave this as an exercise; with every entry in coprime form, the lcm contains each denominator factor at its highest power). Example: $\hat{G}(s) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{s + 1} & \frac{1}{(s + 1)(s + 2)} \end{bmatrix}$ has denominators $s + 1$ and $(s + 1)(s + 2)$, lcm $(s + 1)(s + 2)$, poles $-1$ and $-2$.

A complex number $\lambda$ is a blocking zero of $\hat{G}(s)$ if $\hat{G}(\lambda) = 0$, which is the case if and only if it is a zero of every entry. The notes add that many other kinds of zeros of a transfer matrix are defined in the literature; the blocking zero is the simplest.

sections.heading: The notes ask: why are the poles the roots of the lcm?
sections.text:
The notes write "[Try to prove this?]". Write every entry in coprime form, $\hat{g}_{ij} = n_{ij}/d_{ij}$, and let $d(s)$ be the least common multiple of all $d_{ij}$.

Step 1. Because $(n_{ij}, d_{ij})$ is coprime, $n_{ij}(\lambda) \neq 0$ wherever $d_{ij}(\lambda) = 0$, so

$$\lambda \text{ is a pole of } \hat{g}_{ij} \iff d_{ij}(\lambda) = 0$$

Step 2. Every $d_{ij}$ divides $d$, and every factor $(s - \lambda)$ of $d$ comes from some $d_{ij}$ (the lcm only collects the factors of the denominators, each at its highest power):

$$d(\lambda) = 0 \iff d_{ij}(\lambda) = 0 \text{ for some } i, j$$

Step 3. Combine: $d(\lambda) = 0$ iff $\lambda$ is a pole of some entry iff, by definition, $\lambda$ is a pole of $\hat{G}(s)$.

The coprime form is essential: without cancelling, a factor such as $(s - 1)$ in $\frac{s - 1}{(s - 1)(s + 2)}$ would enter the lcm although $1$ is not a pole.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Poles of a transfer matrix decide its BIBO stability (LST 06). The rule "poles are the roots of the lcm of the denominators" is the one to use in exams: a pole of any single entry counts.

sections.heading: In a problem
sections.text:
The situation. $\hat{G}(s) = [\hat{g}_{ij}(s)]_{q \times p}$ is given; properness, poles and zeros are asked.

Step 1. Write every entry as $\hat{g}_{ij} = N_{ij}/D_{ij}$ with $(N_{ij}, D_{ij})$ coprime (cancel common factors first).

Step 2. Properness, entry by entry:

$$\deg N_{ij} \leq \deg D_{ij}\ \forall i, j \Leftrightarrow \hat{G}(\infty) \text{ finite (proper)}, \qquad \deg N_{ij} < \deg D_{ij}\ \forall i, j \Leftrightarrow \hat{G}(\infty) = 0 \text{ (strictly proper)}$$

Step 3. Poles: the roots of the least common denominator of all $\hat{g}_{ij}$.

What it means.
- $q \times p$: $q$ outputs, $p$ inputs.
- $\hat{G}(\infty) = D$ in any realization (LST 05).
- A pole of one entry is a pole of $\hat{G}$; the eigenvalues of any realization contain all of them (LST 06), and exactly them if the realization is minimal (LST 07).

sections.heading: 13. What a blocking zero does
sections.text:
Consider $\hat{g}(s) = \frac{s - z_0}{s - p}$ with one zero $z_0 \in \mathbf{R}$ and one pole $p \in \mathbf{R}$. Apply an exponential input $u(t) = e^{zt}$, i.e. $\hat{u}(s) = \frac{1}{s - z}$. If $z \neq z_0$ the output has both modes:

$$\hat{y}(s) = \frac{s - z_0}{(s - p)(s - z)} = \frac{A}{s - p} + \frac{B}{s - z}, \qquad A = \frac{p - z_0}{p - z}, \quad B = \frac{z - z_0}{z - p}$$

so $y(t) = A e^{pt} + B e^{zt}$ with nonzero constants $A$, $B$. Now apply exactly $u(t) = e^{z_0 t}$: the factor $s - z_0$ cancels, $\hat{y}(s) = \frac{1}{s - p}$, and $y(t) = e^{pt}$. The effect of the input mode is not observed at the output at all: $B = 0$. The blocking zero of a transfer function blocks inputs of similar dynamics.

sections.heading: A blocking zero, computed
sections.caption: $\hat{g}(s) = (s + 0.5)/(s + 2)$. Blue: the input $e^{-0.5t}$ has exactly the dynamics of the zero, so its own mode vanishes from the output, which is the pure system mode $e^{-2t}$. Green: the input $e^{-t}$ is not blocked, and the output carries both $e^{-2t}$ and $e^{-t}$, with the coefficients $A$ and $B$ from the partial fractions.

sections.heading: Exam thinking
sections.text:
Questions on this section ask why a certain input leaves no trace in the output, or which input produces a given output. Think in the Laplace domain: $\hat{y}(s) = \hat{g}(s)\hat{u}(s)$, and after partial fractions every pole $p$ of $\hat{y}$ gives a term $e^{pt}$ (or $t^ke^{pt}$) in $y(t)$. An input $e^{at}$ has $\hat{u}(s) = \frac{1}{s - a}$, so it brings the pole $s = a$. If $\hat{g}(a) = 0$ ($a$ is a zero of $\hat{g}$), the factor $s - a$ in the numerator of $\hat{g}$ cancels that pole, and $e^{at}$ does not appear in $y(t)$.

To find an input for a desired output, divide: $\hat{u} = \hat{y}/\hat{g}$. Reduce $\hat{g}$ to lowest terms first, and do not be surprised by an impulse $\delta(t)$ in the answer when the quotient is not strictly proper.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Zeros are as important as poles for design: they cannot be moved by state feedback (LST 08 shows the closed loop keeps the open-loop zeros), and a zero in the right half-plane limits how fast a system can be made to respond.

sections.heading: 14. State-space representation of an LTI system
sections.text:
Any $q \times p$ multivariable system that is finite dimensional, linear and time invariant can be written as a state equation together with an output equation:

$$\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = A\mathbf{x}(t) + B\mathbf{u}(t) \qquad (4)$$

$$\mathbf{y}(t) = C\mathbf{x}(t) + D\mathbf{u}(t) \qquad (5)$$

with $A \in \mathbf{R}^{n \times n}$, $B \in \mathbf{R}^{n \times p}$, $C \in \mathbf{R}^{q \times n}$, $D \in \mathbf{R}^{q \times p}$ and $n$ the number of states. The first equation is a linear, first-order vector differential equation driven by the input (non-homogeneous); the second is an algebraic read-out, with no dynamics of its own.

Read the four matrices as wiring: $A$ says how the states drive each other (the internal dynamics), $B$ how the inputs push the states, $C$ which combination of states is measured, $D$ the direct path from input to output with no dynamics in between. A unique solution exists on $[t_0, t]$ whenever an initial state $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ and the input $\mathbf{u}_{[t_0, t]}$ are specified. One way to obtain it is the Laplace transform.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This is the form the rest of the course works in. Its advantages over the transfer function: it keeps the internal variables (the transfer function only sees input to output), it handles several inputs and outputs naturally, it covers time-varying systems, and it turns analysis into linear algebra on the matrices $A, B, C, D$. That is why Lecture Notes 3 and 4 review linear algebra next: eigenvalues of $A$ will decide stability, ranks of matrices built from $A, B, C$ will decide controllability and observability, and $e^{At}$ will be the solution.

sections.heading: 15. Solving the state equation with the Laplace transform
sections.text:
Let $\hat{\mathbf{y}} := \mathcal{L}\{\mathbf{y}\}$, $\hat{\mathbf{u}} := \mathcal{L}\{\mathbf{u}\}$, $\hat{\mathbf{x}} := \mathcal{L}\{\mathbf{x}\}$. The derivative transforms to $s\hat{\mathbf{x}}(s) - \mathbf{x}(0)$, so (4) and (5) become

$$s\hat{\mathbf{x}}(s) - \mathbf{x}(0) = A\hat{\mathbf{x}}(s) + B\hat{\mathbf{u}}(s), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{y}}(s) = C\hat{\mathbf{x}}(s) + D\hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)$$

Move $A\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ to the left, $(sI - A)\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}(0) + B\hat{\mathbf{u}}$, and multiply by the inverse:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}(s) = (sI - A)^{-1}\mathbf{x}(0) + (sI - A)^{-1}B\hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)$$

$$\hat{\mathbf{y}}(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}\mathbf{x}(0) + \bigl[ C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D \bigr] \hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)$$

$\mathcal{L}^{-1}\{C(sI - A)^{-1}\mathbf{x}(0)\}$ is called the zero-input response: what the initial state does by itself. $\mathcal{L}^{-1}\{[C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D]\hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)\}$ is called the zero-state response: what the input does starting from rest. The output is their sum, which is the decomposition behind the "equal initial states" example of section 1.

The transfer matrix of the system (4), (5) is

$$\hat{G}(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D$$

Since $(sI - A)^{-1} = \frac{\operatorname{adj}(sI - A)}{\det(sI - A)}$ (LST 03), every entry is a ratio of polynomials whose denominator divides $\det(sI - A)$: the transfer matrix of a state-space system is rational and proper, and its poles are among the eigenvalues of $A$.

sections.heading: Exam thinking
sections.text:
In response questions, keep the zero-input part $C(sI - A)^{-1}\mathbf{x}(0)$ and the zero-state part $\hat{g}(s)\hat{u}(s)$ separate, compute each with partial fractions, and add. When $A$ is block diagonal or in Jordan form, invert $sI - A$ block by block instead of as a whole.

If a realization with fewer states is asked next, look for a common factor of the numerator and the denominator of $\hat{g}(s)$: each eigenvalue of $A$ that cancels this way can be removed, and the controllable canonical form (LST 05) of the reduced $\hat{g}$ is the smaller realization. Check $y(0) = C\mathbf{x}(0)$ and, when all eigenvalues of $A$ have negative real parts, the final value $y(\infty) = \hat{g}(0)$ for a unit step.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This is the first appearance of $(sI - A)^{-1}$, the resolvent, whose inverse Laplace transform is $e^{At}$ (LST 04). The zero-input and zero-state split here is the same as in LST 05, where it is obtained in the time domain.

sections.heading: In a problem
sections.text:
The situation. $(A, B, C, D)$, $\mathbf{x}(0)$ and $\mathbf{u}(t)$ are given; $\hat{G}(s)$ or $\mathbf{y}(t)$ is asked.

Step 1. Form and invert $sI - A$ (the resolvent):

$$(sI - A)^{-1} = \frac{\operatorname{adj}(sI - A)}{\det(sI - A)}$$

Step 2. Read the two parts:

$$\hat{\mathbf{y}}(s) = \underbrace{C(sI - A)^{-1}\mathbf{x}(0)}_{\text{zero-input}} + \underbrace{\bigl[C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D\bigr]}_{\hat{G}(s)}\hat{\mathbf{u}}(s)$$

Step 3. For $\mathbf{y}(t)$: partial fractions of each entry, then $\mathcal{L}^{-1}$ term by term.

What it means.
- $\det(sI - A)$ is a common denominator, so the poles of $\hat{G}$ are among the eigenvalues of $A$.
- An eigenvalue that cancels in $C\operatorname{adj}(sI - A)B$ is not a pole: a mode hidden from the input-output map (uncontrollable or unobservable, LST 07).
- The zero-input part depends on $\mathbf{x}(0)$ only, the zero-state part on $\mathbf{u}$ only.

sections.heading: 16. Example: the mass-spring-damper
sections.text:
$y(t)$ is the displacement from an equilibrium position, $k$ the spring constant, $b$ the viscous friction constant, $m$ the mass and $u(t)$ the external force. From the free-body diagram, the equation of motion is

$$m\ddot{y} + b\dot{y} + ky = u(t)$$

Let $x_1 := y$ and $x_2 := \dot{y}$ be the state variables (position and velocity, the energy-storing quantities). Then $\dot{x}_1 = x_2$ and $\dot{x}_2 = (u - kx_1 - bx_2)/m$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_1 \\ \dot{x}_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -\frac{k}{m} & -\frac{b}{m} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \frac{1}{m} \end{bmatrix} u(t), \qquad y(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$$

Reading the matrices off by comparison with (4) and (5) gives $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D = 0$. With one input and one output the transfer function is

$$\hat{g}(s) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} s & -1 \\ \frac{k}{m} & s + \frac{b}{m} \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \frac{1}{m} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1/m}{s^2 + (b/m)s + k/m}$$

The 2 by 2 inverse swaps the diagonal, negates the off-diagonal and divides by the determinant $s^2 + (b/m)s + k/m$; only its top-right entry $1/\det$ survives the multiplication by $[1 \ 0]$ and $[0 \ 1/m]^T$. The impulse response is $g(t) = \mathcal{L}^{-1}\{\hat{g}(s)\}$. For $m = 1$, $b = 3$, $k = 2$:

$$g(t) = \mathcal{L}^{-1}\Bigl\{ \frac{1}{s^2 + 3s + 2} \Bigr\} = \mathcal{L}^{-1}\Bigl\{ \frac{1}{s + 1} - \frac{1}{s + 2} \Bigr\} = \begin{cases} e^{-t} - e^{-2t}, & t \geq 0 \\ 0, & t < 0 \end{cases}$$

sections.heading: 17. Linearization to obtain state-space models
sections.text:
Many $q \times p$ multivariable systems are described by nonlinear equations

$$\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{u}(t), t) \qquad (6)$$

$$\mathbf{y}(t) = \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{u}(t), t) \qquad (7)$$

where $\mathbf{f}$, $\mathbf{h}$ are nonlinear vector-valued functions of $n + p + 1$ variables. Suppose nominal functions $\mathbf{x}_o(t)$, $\mathbf{u}_o(t)$ can be found that satisfy (6), $\frac{d\mathbf{x}_o}{dt} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_o(t), \mathbf{u}_o(t), t)$: an operating trajectory. Assuming (6) continues to hold under small perturbations $\mathbf{x}_o + \tilde{\mathbf{x}}$, $\mathbf{u}_o + \tilde{\mathbf{u}}$, a first-order Taylor expansion gives

$$\dot{\mathbf{x}}_o + \dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_o + \tilde{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{u}_o + \tilde{\mathbf{u}}, t) = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o, t) + \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\Big|_{(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o)} \tilde{\mathbf{x}} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{u}}\Big|_{(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o)} \tilde{\mathbf{u}} + \cdots$$

The nominal terms cancel on both sides, leaving

$$\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} \cong A(t)\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(t) + B(t)\tilde{\mathbf{u}}(t), \qquad A(t) := \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\Big|_{(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o)} = \Bigl[ \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j} \Bigr]_{i,j}, \quad B(t) := \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{u}}\Big|_{(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o)} = \Bigl[ \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial u_j} \Bigr]_{i,j}$$

$A(t)$ is $n \times n$ and $B(t)$ is $n \times p$: the Jacobian matrices, whose entry $(i, j)$ says how much $\dot{x}_i$ changes per unit change of $x_j$ (or $u_j$). This is a linearization of (6), and in general a time-varying state equation, because the Jacobians are evaluated along a nominal trajectory that moves in time. In a completely similar way, for $\mathbf{y}_o(t) = \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o, t)$ and $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y}_o + \tilde{\mathbf{y}}$,

$$\tilde{\mathbf{y}}(t) \cong C(t)\tilde{\mathbf{x}}(t) + D(t)\tilde{\mathbf{u}}(t), \qquad C(t) := \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\Big|_{(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o)}, \quad D(t) := \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}}{\partial \mathbf{u}}\Big|_{(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o)}$$

sections.heading: What linearization keeps and what it drops, computed
sections.caption: $\sin x$ and its linearization at $x_0 = 0$, the tangent line $\tilde{x}$. The relative error is 0.7% at 0.2 rad, 4.3% at 0.5 rad and 19% at 1 rad: the linear model is trustworthy only near the operating point. This is the "small angle" assumption of the pendulum example below.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Controllers and observers in this course are designed on linear models; linearization is the bridge from the real nonlinear system. Keep in mind what it promises: the linear model is valid only near the operating point, and only as long as the perturbations stay small. A controller that keeps the system close to the operating point keeps its own model valid.

sections.heading: In a problem
sections.text:
The situation. A nonlinear model (6), (7) is given; a linear model around an operating point is asked.

Step 1. Find a nominal pair that satisfies (6):

$$\dot{\mathbf{x}}_o = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_o(t), \mathbf{u}_o(t), t) \qquad (\text{for an equilibrium: } \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_o, \mathbf{u}_o))$$

Step 2. Jacobians at the nominal point:

$$A(t) = \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\Big|_{o}, \quad B(t) = \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{u}}\Big|_{o}, \quad C(t) = \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\Big|_{o}, \quad D(t) = \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}}{\partial \mathbf{u}}\Big|_{o}$$

(row $i$ of $A$ holds $\partial f_i/\partial x_1, \ldots, \partial f_i/\partial x_n$).

Step 3. Write the model in the perturbations:

$$\dot{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} = A(t)\tilde{\mathbf{x}} + B(t)\tilde{\mathbf{u}}, \qquad \tilde{\mathbf{y}} = C(t)\tilde{\mathbf{x}} + D(t)\tilde{\mathbf{u}}$$

What it means.
- Valid only for small $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$, $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}$.
- An equilibrium gives constant $A, B, C, D$: an LTI model; a moving nominal trajectory gives an LTV model.

sections.heading: 18. Example of linearization
sections.text:
Consider

$$\dot{x} = f(x, \mathbf{u}, t) = \sin x + u_1^2 + u_2^2 - t \qquad (8)$$

for which $n = 1$, $p = 2$. The operating point functions are $x_o = 0$, $\mathbf{u}_o = [0 \ \ \sqrt{t}]^T$: check that they satisfy (8), $\dot{x}_o = 0$ and $\sin 0 + 0 + t - t = 0$. Then

$$A(t) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Big|_{(x_o, \mathbf{u}_o)} = \cos x \big|_{x = x_o = 0} = 1$$

$$B(t) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{u}}\Big|_{(x_o, \mathbf{u}_o)} = \Bigl[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial u_1} \ \ \frac{\partial f}{\partial u_2} \Bigr]_{u_{1o} = 0,\, u_{2o} = \sqrt{t}} = [2u_1 \ \ 2u_2]_{u_{1o} = 0,\, u_{2o} = \sqrt{t}} = [0 \ \ 2\sqrt{t}]$$

so that

$$\dot{\tilde{x}} = \tilde{x} + [0 \ \ 2\sqrt{t}]\, \tilde{\mathbf{u}} = \tilde{x} + 2\sqrt{t}\, \tilde{u}_2$$

is a linearization of the state equation. Two remarks: $\tilde{u}_1$ has dropped out, because along this trajectory $u_1 = 0$ and $u_1^2$ has zero slope there; and $B$ depends on $t$, so the linear model is time-varying even though $f$ only depends on $t$ through $-t$.

sections.heading: 19. Modeling example: the double pendulum
sections.text:
Two masses $m_1$, $m_2$ hang on rods of lengths $l_1$, $l_2$; $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ are the angles from the vertical, $u(t)$ a horizontal external force on $m_2$, and $g$ the gravitational acceleration. One set of equations of motion, obtained by equating the force components tangential to the trajectories of the masses:

$$m_1 g \sin\theta_1 + m_1 l_1 \ddot{\theta}_1 = m_2 g \cos\theta_2 \sin(\theta_2 - \theta_1) + u(t) \sin\theta_2 \sin(\theta_2 - \theta_1)$$

$$m_2 g \sin\theta_2 + m_2 l_2 \ddot{\theta}_2 = u(t) \cos\theta_2$$

Assuming $\sin\theta \cong \theta$ and $\cos\theta \cong 1$ for small $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ (which also kills the product $u \sin\theta_2 \sin(\theta_2 - \theta_1)$, being second order small), and choosing $x_1 := \theta_1$, $x_2 := \dot{\theta}_1$, $x_3 := \theta_2$, $x_4 := \dot{\theta}_2$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \\ x_4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{(m_1 + m_2)g}{m_1 l_1} & 0 & \frac{m_2 g}{m_1 l_1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{g}{l_2} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \\ x_4 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{m_2 l_2} \end{bmatrix} u(t)$$

Rows 1 and 3 just say that the derivative of an angle is its rate. Row 2: the first rod is pulled back by its own gravity and pulled along by the second mass. Row 4: the second rod swings like a simple pendulum, $\ddot{\theta}_2 = -(g/l_2)\theta_2$, plus the force. The notes remark that the same linear state equation results from the Jacobian technique of section 17 about the operating point $\mathbf{x}_o = [0 \ 0 \ 0 \ 0]^T$, the hanging rest position.

sections.heading: What should stay with you
sections.text: Input-linearity (zero initial states) is the only ingredient of the impulse response: write the input as a sum of area-one pulses, $u(t) \cong \sum u(t_i)\delta_\Delta(t - t_i)\Delta$, add up the responses, and let $\Delta \to 0$ to get $y(t) = \int g(t, \tau) u(\tau) d\tau$, with limits $[t_0, t]$ for a relaxed causal system and a $q \times p$ matrix $G(t, \tau)$ for several inputs and outputs. Time invariance makes $g$ depend only on $t - \tau$, so the output is a convolution, and causality means $g(t) = 0$ for $t < 0$. The Laplace transform turns the convolution into $\hat{y} = \hat{g}\hat{u}$. Lumped systems have rational transfer functions, a delay gives the irrational $e^{-sT}$; properness compares degrees, poles and zeros are read from coprime $N/D$, the poles of a transfer matrix are the roots of the lcm of its denominators, and a blocking zero $z_0$ removes the mode $e^{z_0 t}$ of the input from the output. Every finite-dimensional LTI system has the form $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x} + B\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{y} = C\mathbf{x} + D\mathbf{u}$; Laplace splits its output into zero-input and zero-state responses and gives $\hat{G}(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}B + D$. Nonlinear models are linearized with the Jacobians $\partial \mathbf{f}/\partial \mathbf{x}$, $\partial \mathbf{f}/\partial \mathbf{u}$ along an operating trajectory, generally giving a time-varying linear model valid only for small perturbations.

lst03.title: LST 03 — Linear Algebra I: Spaces, Rank, Eigenvalues and the Jordan Form
lst03.context: EEE 501 Lecture Notes 3 · Review of linear algebra: normed vector spaces, rank, nullity · helpful book: C. D. Meyer, Matrix Analysis and Applied Linear Algebra
lst03.summary: Vector spaces, subspaces, span and linear independence; basis, dimension and the representation of a vector, read as a matrix-vector product; norms and Gram-Schmidt; row echelon form, rank, nullity and the rank-nullity theorem; existence and the set of all solutions of Ax = y; determinants and inverses; a matrix as a linear map and similarity; eigenvalues, diagonalization, generalized eigenvectors and the Jordan normal form.

sections.heading: 1. Vector space and subspace
sections.text:
A vector space is a set $V$ (of vectors) and a field $\mathbf{F}$ (of scalars) over which vector addition and scalar multiplication are defined such that $V$ contains a zero vector $\mathbf{0}$, and $V$ is closed under multiplication with scalars and vector addition: for all $\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2 \in V$, we have $\alpha_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + \alpha_2 \mathbf{v}_2 \in V$.

The course deals with real or complex spaces $V = \mathbf{R}^n$ or $V = \mathbf{C}^n$, whose fields are $\mathbf{R}$ or $\mathbf{C}$:

$$\mathbf{R}^n = \Bigl\{ \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ \vdots \\ x_n \end{bmatrix} :\ x_i \in \mathbf{R} \Bigr\} = \{ \mathbf{x} = [x_1 \ \cdots \ x_n]^T :\ x_i \in \mathbf{R} \}$$

A subspace $S$ of $V$ is a subset that is itself closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication: $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2 \in S \Rightarrow \alpha_1 \mathbf{x}_1 + \alpha_2 \mathbf{x}_2 \in S$ for all $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$. Taking $\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = 0$ shows that every subspace contains $\mathbf{0}$.

Notation used throughout, as in the notes: boldface $\mathbf{x}_1$ is a vector, while plain $x_1$ is the first entry of a vector $\mathbf{x}$.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Subspaces are the shape of every answer in linear systems: the states reachable from zero form a subspace, the unobservable states form a subspace, the solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ form a subspace. Recognizing a subspace means you only need a basis to describe infinitely many vectors.

sections.heading: 2. Span and linear independence
sections.text:
Examples. $S_1 = \{ [x_1 \ 0]^T \} \subseteq \mathbf{R}^2$ is a subspace of $\mathbf{R}^2$, the horizontal line. $S_2 = \{ [x_1 \ \ m x_1]^T \} \subseteq \mathbf{R}^2$ is also a subspace: a line with slope $m$ passing through the origin of the $x_1 x_2$-plane. A line that does not pass through the origin is not a subspace: it misses $\mathbf{0}$, and the sum of two of its points leaves it.

Given $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k \in \mathbf{R}^n$, span$\{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k\}$ denotes the set of all possible linear combinations,

$$\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k\} = \{ \alpha_1 \mathbf{x}_1 + \cdots + \alpha_k \mathbf{x}_k :\ \alpha_i \in \mathbf{R} \} \subseteq \mathbf{R}^n$$

which is obviously a subspace of $\mathbf{R}^n$.

A set $\{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k\}$ is linearly independent if

$$\forall \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_k \in \mathbf{R}, \quad \alpha_1 \mathbf{x}_1 + \cdots + \alpha_k \mathbf{x}_k = \mathbf{0} \ \Longrightarrow \ \alpha_1 = 0, \ldots, \alpha_k = 0$$

In words: the only way to combine the vectors into $\mathbf{0}$ is with all coefficients zero. The set is linearly dependent if some combination $\alpha_1 \mathbf{x}_1 + \cdots + \alpha_k \mathbf{x}_k = \mathbf{0}$ has coefficients that are not all zero. Then any vector whose coefficient is nonzero can be solved for, so at least one vector is a combination of the others. Independence means that no vector is redundant.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Two subspaces carry the whole linear algebra part of the course: the range space $\mathcal{R}(A)$ (what $A$ can produce) and the null space $\mathcal{N}(A)$ (what $A$ destroys). Later the set of states reachable by the input will be a range space, and the set of states invisible at the output will be a null space. Linear independence is the test that a set of vectors carries no redundancy; most rank conditions in the course (controllability, observability) are linear independence questions in disguise.

sections.heading: 3. Basis and dimension
sections.text:
The dimension of a vector space, or of a subspace of it, is the number of vectors in a maximally linearly independent set contained in it.

Example 1: $\dim \mathbf{R}^n = n$, a maximally linearly independent set being $\{\mathbf{e}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n\}$ with $\mathbf{e}_i := [0 \cdots 0\, 1\, 0 \cdots 0]^T$, the 1 in the $i$-th place. Also $\dim S_1 = 1$, with maximally independent set $\{[1 \ 0]^T\}$.

A set $\{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k\} \subseteq V$ is a basis if (i) it is linearly independent and (ii) span$\{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k\} = V$. Condition (i) says there are no redundant vectors, condition (ii) that nothing is missing.

Example 2: the natural basis $\{\mathbf{e}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n\}$ of $\mathbf{R}^n$. It spans (ii), since any $\mathbf{x} = [x_1 \cdots x_n]^T$ equals $x_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + x_n \mathbf{e}_n$. It is independent (i), since $\alpha_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + \cdots + \alpha_n \mathbf{e}_n$ is just the vector $[\alpha_1 \cdots \alpha_n]^T$, which is $\mathbf{0}$ only if every $\alpha_i = 0$. In the same way $\{[1 \ 0]^T\}$ is a basis of $S_1$.

sections.heading: Exam thinking
sections.text: When an exam defines a new notion built like a basis (for instance a set whose combinations with nonnegative coefficients give every vector), reuse the structure of the basis proofs. Show the spanning half by constructing the coefficients for an arbitrary $\mathbf{x}$, and the independence half by assuming that one vector of the set is a combination of the others with coefficients of the permitted kind, and reaching a contradiction. Only the restriction on the coefficients is new, so watch where it is used: with nonnegative coefficients, the signs of the entries of $\mathbf{x}$ decide the construction.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The dimension counts the independent directions, and in this course it counts states: the order of a system is the dimension of its state space, and "rank $n$" tests ask whether some construction reaches all $n$ dimensions.

sections.heading: 4. Representation of a vector
sections.text:
Consider a basis $\{\mathbf{q}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_m\}$ of a subspace $S \subseteq \mathbf{R}^n$, so that every $\mathbf{x} \in S$ can be expressed as $\mathbf{x} = \alpha_1 \mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + \alpha_m \mathbf{q}_m$ for constants $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m$ that are unique by the linear independence of the $\mathbf{q}_i$'s (two different expressions would subtract to a nontrivial combination equal to $\mathbf{0}$). Collect the basis vectors as the columns of a matrix:

$$Q = [\mathbf{q}_1 \ \cdots \ \mathbf{q}_m] \in \mathbf{R}^{n \times m}, \qquad \mathbf{x} = Q\tilde{\mathbf{x}}, \qquad \tilde{\mathbf{x}} := [\alpha_1 \ \cdots \ \alpha_m]^T$$

This unique vector $\tilde{\mathbf{x}} \in \mathbf{R}^m$ is the representation of $\mathbf{x}$ with respect to the basis $\{\mathbf{q}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_m\}$: the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ when the $\mathbf{q}_i$ are used as measuring sticks.

Example 1: in the natural basis of $\mathbf{R}^n$ every vector is its own representation, because then $Q = [\mathbf{e}_1 \cdots \mathbf{e}_n] = I$.

Example 2: $\{\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2\} = \{[1 \ 3]^T, [2 \ 2]^T\}$ is a basis of $\mathbf{R}^2$ and

$$\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{11}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{3}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

so the representation of $[4 \ 1]^T$ with respect to that basis is $[-3/2 \ \ 11/4]^T$. Check: $-3/2 + 11/2 = 4$ and $-9/2 + 11/2 = 1$.

Most results below (range space, existence of solutions, similarity) are this sentence in disguise.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The same vector has different coordinates in different bases, and the change of coordinates is the matrix $Q$. In state space this is a change of state variables, $\mathbf{x} = Q\tilde{\mathbf{x}}$: the system is the same, only the description changes. Choosing a good basis (eigenvectors, a companion basis, a controllable/uncontrollable split) is how complicated systems are made simple in the later lectures.

sections.heading: 5. Normed spaces
sections.text:
Any nonnegative, real-valued function $\| \cdot \| : V \to \mathbf{R}_{0+}$ is a norm in a vector space $V$ if for all $\alpha$ and all $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2$:

$$\| \mathbf{x} \| \geq 0 \ \text{and} \ \| \mathbf{x} \| = 0 \iff \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}, \qquad |\alpha|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| = \| \alpha \mathbf{x} \|, \qquad \| \mathbf{x}_1 + \mathbf{x}_2 \| \leq \| \mathbf{x}_1 \| + \| \mathbf{x}_2 \|$$

Positivity, scaling, and the triangle inequality (a detour is never shorter). The following are norms in $\mathbf{R}^n$, with $\mathbf{x} = [x_1 \cdots x_n]^T$:

$$\| \mathbf{x} \|_1 := \sum_{i = 1}^{n} |x_i|, \qquad \| \mathbf{x} \|_2 := \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}} = \sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{i = 1}^{n} x_i^2}, \qquad \| \mathbf{x} \|_\infty := \max_i |x_i|$$

These are the one-, two- and infinity-norms. $\| \mathbf{x} \|_2$ is the familiar Euclidean norm, the distance of $\mathbf{x}$ to the origin $\mathbf{0}$. The one-norm is the taxicab distance on a grid of streets; the infinity-norm is the largest single coordinate.

sections.heading: The unit ball of each norm, computed
sections.caption: The set $\|\mathbf{x}\| = 1$ in $\mathbf{R}^2$ for the three norms: a diamond for $\|\cdot\|_1$, the circle for $\|\cdot\|_2$, a square for $\|\cdot\|_\infty$. The same vector has different lengths in different norms, but they are always ordered, and any one of them controls the others up to a constant.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: A norm is how the course measures size: the size of a state (is it going to zero?), of a signal (is the output bounded?) and, through the induced matrix norm $\|A\|_2$ of LST 04, of a matrix (how much can it amplify?). Stability statements later are norm statements: "bounded input gives bounded output" and "the state goes to zero" are both about norms. Which norm you use rarely changes the answer in finite dimensions, because all norms on $\mathbf{R}^n$ bound one another.

sections.heading: 6. Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization
sections.text:
A vector is normalized if $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$, and two vectors are orthogonal if $\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{x}_2 = 0$. A set $\{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_m\}$ is orthonormal if each one is normalized and they are pairwise orthogonal:

$$\mathbf{x}_i^T \mathbf{x}_j = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i \neq j \\ 1 & \text{if } i = j \end{cases} \qquad \forall i, j = 1, \ldots, m$$

Given linearly independent vectors $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_m\}$, Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization produces an orthonormal set $\{\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_m\}$ with span$\{\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_m\}$ = span$\{\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_m\}$:

$$\mathbf{q}_1 := \mathbf{v}_1, \quad \mathbf{u}_1 := \frac{\mathbf{q}_1}{\| \mathbf{q}_1 \|}; \qquad \mathbf{q}_2 := \mathbf{v}_2 - (\mathbf{u}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2)\mathbf{u}_1, \quad \mathbf{u}_2 := \frac{\mathbf{q}_2}{\| \mathbf{q}_2 \|}; \qquad \ldots; \qquad \mathbf{q}_m := \mathbf{v}_m - \sum_{k = 1}^{m - 1} (\mathbf{u}_k^T \mathbf{v}_m)\mathbf{u}_k, \quad \mathbf{u}_m := \frac{\mathbf{q}_m}{\| \mathbf{q}_m \|}$$

Why it works, in $\mathbf{R}^2$: $\mathbf{u}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2 = \| \mathbf{u}_1 \| \| \mathbf{v}_2 \| \cos\theta = \| \mathbf{v}_2 \| \cos\theta$, with $\theta$ the angle between the two vectors. So $(\mathbf{u}_1^T \mathbf{v}_2)\mathbf{u}_1$ is the projection of $\mathbf{v}_2$ along $\mathbf{u}_1$, and $\mathbf{q}_2$ is the component of $\mathbf{v}_2$ orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}_1$, equivalently to $\mathbf{v}_1$. Each step removes from the new vector its shadows on all the directions already built, and keeps the rest.
